*New Record of the Words and Phrases of the Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, Scroll One.

[Seal] ... [Seal] ... [Seal] ... [Seal] ... [Seal]. Compiled by Baoci Shoushi. Revised during his residence in Zhongxia at Miaoguo Temple to the west of the commandery, where he completed the draft. Because the phrasing differs from previous expositions, it is called the "New Record."
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Congyi of Yongjia. The first part of the preface, the "General Explanation of the Title," is divided into two sections.
First, regarding the recorded title: as for the term *wénjù* (textual phrases), the *Wénjù Jì* (Record of Textual Phrases) states: "Textual phrases..."

This refers to the entirety of the text from beginning to end (starting from the "Introduction Chapter" and ending with the "Praise of the Buddha"). Therefore, it is said that "text" (*vyañjana*) is identical to "syllables" (*akṣara*), serving as the basis for the two [names and phrases].

As the second volume of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "The *Baifa chao* says: 'Text' refers to the collection of texts (*vyañjanakāya*). Text has no intrinsic nature; it is provisionally established based on syllables. If there is no sense of modification or transition, it is merely called a 'syllable.

If there is modification beyond a single syllable, such that distinctions can be expressed, it is called a 'phrase' (*pada*). Precisely because this [text] serves as the basis for names and phrases when expressing intrinsic natures and distinctions, it is called 'text. Although the essence of text is thus..."

A *vyañjana* (phoneme/letter) is that which serves as the basis for the two [name and phrase] and possesses the sense of modification; only then is it designated as a *vyañjana*. If it does not serve as the basis for the two and lacks the sense of modification, it is merely called a *nāman* (name).

A *pada* (phrase) refers to the meaning of a syntactic pause (*viccheda*), encompassing both long and short [units] (i.e., long phrases and short phrases). Therefore, it is said: "Names express the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), while phrases express specific distinctions (*viśeṣa*).

Thus, the *Bai fa chao* (Commentary on the Hundred Dharmas) of the *Cheng weishi lun* (Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra) states: "Regarding 'names express the intrinsic nature,' this refers to the intrinsic nature of all phenomena. That is to say, all conditioned and unconditioned, contaminated and uncontaminated, material and mental, conventional and substantial entities—each restricted to its own essence—is termed 'intrinsic nature. This [name] expresses this..."

That which expresses intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is designated as a "name" (*nāman*); it is not restricted to a single or two syllables, but rather, anything that signifies intrinsic nature is collectively called a name. For example, a single syllable may form a name, such as *cakṣus* (eye), *śrotra* (ear), *ghrāṇa* (nose), *jihvā* (tongue), or *pṛthivī* (earth), *ap* (water), *tejas* (fire), and *vāyu* (wind). Two syllables may also form a name, such as *adhimukti* (resolute belief) or *vīrya* (diligence).

Three syllables may likewise form a name, such as *Vaiśālī*. A "phrase" (*pada*) signifies differentiation (*viśeṣa*). That is to say, upon the intrinsic nature of phenomena, there are meanings of distinction; these are called differentiations. This applies to all categories, including the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and so forth.

Any expression of two or more syllables that signifies only differentiation is termed a phrase. For instance, a phrase of two syllables signifying differentiation might be *buddhacakṣus* (the Buddha-eye). If one were to say simply *cakṣus*, it would signify only the intrinsic nature of the eye; however, since [the term *buddhacakṣus*]...

To add the character "Buddha" (*buddha*) above the word for "eye" is precisely the expression of the specific distinction of the eye. If one says "defiled eye" (*sāsrava-cakṣus*), then these three characters form a phrase that expresses a specific distinction.

[From the *Xianyang shengjiao lun* (Treatise on Manifesting the Holy Teachings): ... [omitted] ... because it makes various matters concerning the eyes known to the world. Furthermore, it enables the mind to perform various functions by means of oral transmission and narration. Question: What is the meaning of a "phrase" (*pada*)? Answer:

It refers to the complete manifestation of meanings not currently perceived by gathering together names (*nāman*). Question: What is the meaning of a "syllable" (*vyañjana*)? Answer: It refers to the manifestation of phrases and names as its meaning. This also does not discuss the substance of matter (*rūpa*) or formations (*saṃskāra*); the *Śata-dharma-śāstra* and other texts clarify that sound is the aggregate of matter (*rūpa-skandha*), while names...

Phrases and sentences (*gāthā-pada*) are subsumed under the aggregate of formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*); however, since the title here refers only to "phrases and sentences," the essential natures of matter (*rūpa*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) and so forth are not discussed.

Here, the text is divided by means of phrases, and thus it is called "phrases and sentences" (*gāthā-pada*). By means of long and short phrases, the entire text from beginning to end is divided; for this reason, the title is "Phrases and Sentences. In ancient commentaries (*śāstra*), some were titled simply "Commentary" (*śāstra*) and others simply "Chapter" (*pariccheda*).
"Chapter" (*zhang*) refers to literary elegance (*wen-zao*), and is also called a "section" (*zhang-duan*) or a "division" (*fen-duan*) for the purpose of analytical explanation.

The term "commentary" (*shu*) refers to words that penetrate the general meaning; it is also a record. Furthermore, the pronunciation of *shu* (as in *shū*) means to analyze, to categorize, or to carve out.

(Because one analyzes the purport of the sutra by extracting no fewer than five layers of major meanings, the reason why the *Jie shi liu guan jing* is called a "commentary" (*shu*) is precisely for this.

Now, [the title] does not say "Meaning" (*yi*), as explained above. (That is to say, because the text is divided merely by phrases, it is called "Phrases and Sentences" [*Wenju*]. Why? Because since the broad meaning of the title has already been explained in detail, regarding the main text of the sutra, one merely roughly divides it into sections and paragraphs.)

The title states: "The excellence of the *Wenju* (Textual Exegesis) is precisely due to this. This makes it known that the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) and the *Wenju* sections must be kept distinct and not confused; otherwise, how could one analyze the text while restating the Great Meaning, or discuss the profound and the contemplative while simultaneously explaining the literal words?

Therefore, it is said: "If they are explained in a manner that is mutually entangled, then neither will have a point of return. Furthermore, if they are explained as being mutually complementary, then the *Xuanyi* and the *Wenju* cannot be treated as entirely separate entities. When the texts themselves refer to the *Wenju* by the name "Commentary" (*Shu*), this is precisely what is meant.

Thus, although the *Vimalakīrti* and the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* have their own separate *Xuanyi*, they are also called "Commentaries" when analyzing the text; this is truly for this reason. Hence it is said: "Therefore, if one merely analyzes the text and sentences, the Great Principle will not be manifest."

If one speaks only of the profound mystery (*xuánzhǐ*), one becomes confused regarding arising and ceasing; this is because the explanation of the title cannot be undertaken hastily, for the interpretation beneath the title is not a matter of ease. Thus we know that those who are entirely ignorant of the grand purport of the *Xuánwén* yet wish to exhaust the Sūtra through mere textual phrases [are obstructed].

They obscure the subtle and profound contemplation of principle while interpreting the meaning solely through phenomenal characteristics (*shìxiàng*). Those who speak thus of such pedantry are far removed from the truth. For now, following the original classification of the sections, the explanation of the textual phrases must not be conflated with the *Xuányì*. Why?

Because when the textual phrases (*wénjù*) explain the Sūtra, whenever they reach a major point of meaning, they invariably refer back to the *Xuánwén*, whether discussing name, essence, purpose, and function; or the three and one; or the general and the specific; or by relying on practice or the provisional teaching. Guāngshān and Sìmiṅ did not understand this principle, and thus they said: [The text continues with their critique.]

To claim that the *Wenju* (Exegesis of Words and Phrases) does not contain the great meaning of the sutra, yet refers to it as "words and phrases," is merely the Master’s modesty. Now, since the fivefold explanation of the title has already provided a detailed account of the great meaning, how can there be any modesty in the three-part analysis of the text?

Thus we know that [the claim] that Siming definitively distinguished the three characters of the specific title as referring solely to a single dharma, and that the [other] characters were not modesty, is entirely erroneous. That the world collectively remains deluded, transmitting and practicing this based on hearsay—how lamentable!
Next, the teacher who was able to expound [the teachings] was named Tiantai, after the mountain where he resided;

"Zhizhe" (Wise One) was a title bestowed by the Emperor of the Sui dynasty—a designation used by later generations because he possessed great virtuous conduct and served as a teacher to the multitude, acting as a model for princes, dukes, and high officials.
"Shuo" (expounding) means to delight; it refers to delighting in what one cherishes. Because he personally received the Great Awakening at the Spirit Mountain (Ling Yue), [he is so called].
Having fully prepared the profound meaning of this sutra’s great principles through wondrous realization, the demarcation of phrases within the scriptural text is now contained herein;

thus, I have joyfully proclaimed what was in my heart. My disciple, the Chan Master Ding, recorded these virtuous words in writing and divided them into three fascicles, leaving them as a gift for future worthies so that we may together aspire toward the immeasurable.
It is merely the profound nature of phenomena, subtle and tranquil.
Next, the separate text is explained in two parts. First, there is a general indication of the number of sections in this fascicle;

"this" is a term used for specific designation, referring specifically to the one work in four fascicles consisting of eighteen sections translated by Master Kumārajīva (the ruler of the Juqu clan, whose name was Mengxun).

According to the records of the Northern Liang period at Guzang, the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema (also known as Dharmarakṣa; "Liáng" [the local dialect] translates this as Fǎfēng [Dharma-Abundance]) was a native of Central India. He left home at the age of six and could recite ten thousand words daily. Initially, he studied the various treatises on the five sciences (*pañcavidyā*) of the Hīnayāna. Later, he encountered a white-haired meditation master who instructed him in the Mahāyāna.

After ten days of debate, he finally realized its great principles and subsequently specialized in the Mahāyāna, becoming proficient in incantations (*mantra*) whose efficacy was verified in every instance. The people of the Western Regions called him the "Great Divine Incantation Master. He arrived in Northern Liang and translated the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* and other texts—this is what the biographer of the translator stated.

Furthermore, "translation" (*yì*) means to change or transform; it refers to translating Sanskrit terms into Chinese. According to the *Zhou Lǐ*, there were "Elephant-Translators" (*xiàngxū*) who transmitted the languages of the four quarters: those from the east were called *jì*, and those from the south were called *xiàng*.

The West is called *dikṣi* (狄鞮), and the North is called *yi* (譯). Commentators explain that because the North has many affairs and there was also fear that Buddhism might first arrive from Northern India, those who transmit speech and translate scriptures are called *yi* (translators).

Since this refers specifically to the number of chapters translated by Master Dharmakṣema, it is distinguished from the versions translated by other masters. This is because the translations of this sutra differ across its various parts:
first was the translation by Master Dharmakṣema, followed by those by Upaśūnya of the Cao Wei dynasty, and later by Guṇabhadra (which means "Excellence" [崛多]).
The *Zhēngzàng* (Correct Canon) translation consists of five fascicles and is more extensive; it contains twenty chapters on the Great Eloquence Dhāraṇī of Immense Lifespan.
Subsequently, during the Liang dynasty, Paramārtha—whose name translates as "True Meaning"—of the city of Ujjayinī in Western India, translated it in seven fascicles. Its title is:
*The Golden Light Sūtra: King, Chapter on the Distinction of the Three Bodies, Chapter on the Destruction of Karmic Obstacles, and the Supreme Dhāraṇī*.

The "Chapter on the Pure Ground" (*Śuddhabhūmi-parivarta*) and the "Chapter on Fulfilling Vows by Relying on Space" (*Ākāśapūrṇapraṇidhāna-parivarta*) complete the preceding eighteen chapters to form twenty-two chapters;

furthermore, there are thirteen volumes of commentary. Next, during the Sui dynasty, Jñānagupta—of the Gandhāra kingdom in North India, whose name translates as "Ultimate Virtue" (*Zhìdé*) or "Buddha-Virtue" (*Fódé*)—translated the "Chapter on Entrustment" (*Parindanā-parivarta*) and the "Chapter on the Silver-Lord Dhāraṇī" (*Rūpyaprabhāsa-dhāraṇī-parivarta*), completing the preceding seven volumes, making two [volumes].
The twelve chapters consist of eight fascicles; the twenty-four chapters were subsequently translated by Yijing of the Tang Dynasty in ten fascicles, titled *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra-rāja*.
It contains thirty-one chapters: first, the Introduction; second, the Life Span [of the Buddha]; third, the Analysis of the Three Bodies (*trikāya*);
fourth, the Confession; fifth, the Elimination of Karmic Obstructions; sixth, the Most Pure Ground Dharani; seventh, the Lotus Simile Praise.
1. The Aṣṭavajra-vijaya Dhāraṇī; 2. The Ninefold Manifestation of Emptiness; 3. Fulfilling Wishes by Relying on Emptiness; 4.
The Four Heavenly Kings Observing Humans and Devas; 5. The Four Heavenly Kings Protecting the Nation;
6. The Untainted Attachment Dhāraṇī; 7. The Wish-Fulfilling Jewel; 8. The Great Goddess of Eloquence and Wealth; 9. The Great Goddess of Auspiciousness.
17. The Seventeen Auspicious Goddesses who Increase Wealth; 18. The Firm-Earth Deity; 19. The Yakṣa General Saṃjñeya;
20. The Right Discourse; 21. King Sujāta; 22. The Various Celestial Yakṣas Who Provide Protection;
23. The Bestowal of Prophecy; 24. The Removal of Disease; 25. Longevity.
26. The Chapter on the Son of the River Flowing Water (Jalavāhana) Giving Up His Body; 27. The Chapter on the Bodhisattva of the Ten Directions Praising [the Buddha]; 28.
The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Wondrous Banner (Sudhvaja) Praising [the Buddha]; 29. The Chapter on the Tree Spirit of the Bodhi Tree Praising [the Buddha]; 30.
The Chapter on the Goddess of Great Eloquence (Mahāprajñā) Praising [the Buddha]; 31. The Chapter on the Entrustment and Commissioning. These were translated by the three former masters.
Thus, while the translations of the latter two masters do not contain it, Guishan remarked that later generations falsely attributed the "entrustment" (zhūlèi) [passage] to them.
Siming stated that the reason various masters' translations lack such an entrustment is likely due to an insufficient search; it is for this reason that they have made such conjectures.

Next, the section "From the Old Tradition Onward" (*jōrai*) describes the historical divisions of the text in two parts. First, the description of how ancient masters divided [the text] is further divided into two. First, the formal description is divided into two.
First, the description of how the old tradition divided the *Kenshon* (Prophecy Text) is further divided into two. First, regarding the general description of "the old tradition and so forth":

"old" (*kyū*) is named in contrast to "new" (*shin*), and furthermore, "old" (*kyū*) refers to the "ancient" (*ko*) in contrast to the "present" (*kon*). That is to say, it refers to that which has come from the old.

Since then, it has been divided and partitioned into three parts, resulting in differences regarding expansion and contraction, as well as advancement and retreat. Next, the text is separately arranged into two sections;

the first section describes the various masters of the north of the River. Regarding "the north of the River," the first fascicle of the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Zhiguan fmen*) explains that after the Sui dynasty extinguished the Chen, the name and title of Jianye were transferred to Yangzhou across the northern part of the capital’s river; this refers to the north of the River.

It is not that [the term] "Hebei" (North of the River) refers to this [specific location]. If one follows the tenth fascicle of the *Shiqian* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), which explains "three in the south and seven in the north":

"south" refers to the Southern Dynasties, specifically the area south of the Jiangjing River; "north" refers to the Northern Dynasties, which is indeed Hebei and not the area north of the Yangtze River.

Furthermore, the *Wenjuji* (Record of the Textual Phrases) explains "northerners" by stating that most instances mentioned in various texts refer to the Northern Route of Xiangzhou. "Qi" (迄) means to stop or conclude.

The concluding section describes how he made vows to provide secret assistance; thus it is said that "the Great Vows protect the sutra. Because he cures illnesses and saves fish, it is said that "Great Compassion receives all beings.

Next, regarding the various masters of Jiangnan: according to the intention of our own school, the introductory section (*nidāna*) is incorporated into the *Juryō-hon* (Chapter on the Duration of Life), while from the four Buddhas’ severing of doubts by those from below [the earth] constitutes the main exposition (*pravacana*). As for the section on the dissemination of the teaching (*pariṇāmana*), it is the same as [the other schools].
This is the Southern Master’s [view].
Next is the sequential arrangement of the *Zhendi fen* (Section on the True Meaning) according to the new text, which itself consists of three parts. First is the "Proper Sequential Section.

It should be understood that although the number of sections differs between the new and old versions regarding the divisions made by the Master of Zhendi and the various masters of the North, [the core meaning remains consistent].
The general meaning, however, does not differ. Yet, in the new version of the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, there are twenty-two chapters;

since the first chapter is taken as the introduction, and it is stated that from the "Life Span" chapter up to the "Relinquishing the Body" chapter—nineteen chapters in total—constitute the main body (*dharmatā*), while the final two chapters constitute the dissemination (*pariṇāmanā*), one should rather say that from the "Life Span" chapter up to the "Water Flowing" chapter—nineteen chapters—constitute the main body, thereby clearly showing that the final two chapters are the dissemination.
The "Circulation" (Prasāraṇa) refers to the two chapters from "Relinquishing the Body" (*Śarīraparityāga*) to the end.

If one takes the "Life Span" (*Āyuṣpramāṇa*) as the starting point for the main teaching up to "Relinquishing the Body," then it should be said that twenty chapters constitute the main body and the final chapter constitutes the circulation. Please examine this further in detail.

Next, under the section on Paramārtha, the reason for Paramārtha’s division of the text is explained; this, however, is merely an explanation of the reasons for the division of the "Main Exposition" (*Saddharma-paryāya*).
The former master [Jizang] takes the "fruit" (phala), "cause" (hetu), and "condition" (pratyaya) from the *Nītārtha-sūtra* to explain this, which can resolve the difficulty.
Regarding the three points following "former master fruit" (*qianshi guo*), he cites the various masters of Jiangnan as representing the True Meaning (*Satyasiddhi*) school.

He identifies the section beginning with "lifespan" (*shouliang*) as the portion concerning the "correct teaching" (*zhengshuo*). As for the latter master’s [Huiyuan’s] argument regarding how the "disciple," "cause," and "effect" could constitute the "circulation" (*liutong*) portion, this constitutes the objection.
The masters of the Jiangnan region regard the thirteen chapters from the "Four Heavenly Kings" downward as the *Pravartanā* (circulation) section.

Regarding the "causality of master and disciple," this means the master is the cause and the disciple is the effect; it is termed "causality of master and disciple" for the sake of literary style and linguistic convenience, not because there is a textual error or inversion.
Thus, the preceding and following sections on the causality of master and disciple are fundamentally the True Dharma (*tattva*) explaining the Correct [Teaching].

Because the text concerning the "Explanatory Section" (vibhaṅga) is such that it presents the meaning explained by [the author] himself, he raises this as an objection against the Southern Master for failing to distinguish my own text on the "Correct Exposition" (samyak-vyākhyāna) as being intended for its circulation.
Next, regarding the present master’s [critique] that "the present school refutes [this]," although the text below does not refute the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it says:

"The four kings... This refers to the main discussion of the power and function [of the ritual]. One should know, by analogy, that this is not meant to be exhaustive; there is no need for further elaboration. Why?

Because the power and function consist only of the two chapters on Repentance and Praise, which eliminate evil and generate good, while the Chapter on Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) guides their fulfillment. How could one take what follows from the section on the Four Kings and below and apply it [to those two]?
Is the "General Distribution" (Pṛthak-pravartana) considered a functional application? Within this, there are two parts. First, a general refutation of the various masters' subjective biases:

being ignorant of the true nature of the sutra, they all claim that the Introductory Section (Nidāna) has never distinguished the path of the Main Body (Saddharma). Consequently, they divide the "Introductory Chapter" (Nidāna-parivarta), separating it into a mere "Introductory Section.

Furthermore, they claim that the "General Distribution" is exhausted, scattered, and trivial, and thus cannot be discussed in terms of the cause and effect between teacher and disciple; they therefore take the [first] four...

From the account of the King down to the relinquishing of the body, all belong to the section on the "Correct Exposition," because bestowing predictions refers to the fruit of the disciple, while curing illness pertains to the cause of the teacher.
Now, to comprehensively refute these [assertions] as being incorrect, it is said: "This interpretation is not so."
Now, regarding the subsequent section on the analysis of the text, it is divided into three parts. First, concerning the mutual refutation based on the three divisions:
"Du" (杜) means to block or obstruct; "Duan" (斷) means to sever or terminate. As for the "Preface to the Preface" (*xuben xudu*), it serves as a preface to the main body (*zheng*).

There are three meanings to this, as clarified in the following text. The "Preface to the Preface" refers to the seventeen chapters that follow [the initial preface], which constitute the preface to the formal exposition (*zhengshuo*).
Because it pertains to the circulation [of the teachings], the introduction (*nidāna*) has three meanings. Guishan, not understanding this, arbitrarily dismissed it;

thus, the seventeen chapters explained below in the section on the "narrative" (*nirdeśa*) would be what Guishan refutes. Question: If the various sūtras lacked an introduction, would it not be the case that the introductory division (*nidāna-vibhāga*) could not introduce the main body (*samyaktva*) and the circulation (*pravartana*)?
Answer: If the various sūtras lacked an introduction... [text fragment] ...if the various sūtras lacked an introduction, [the structure would collapse].
The subsequent chapters serve as a manifestation that precedes the main body; since this scripture already contains a preface for these subsequent chapters, they cannot be excluded.
Regarding the "main body" (*zhengben*) and the "preface" (*xu*), there are three meanings for each: because the preceding preface precedes the main body, and now the main body precedes the preface.
Thus, the *Lifespan* chapter, the *Dispelling Doubts*, the *Repentance*, and the *Praise* constitute the main body within the context of the preface.
Furthermore, this current exposition is not only beneficial for those who are the primary audience (*ādhikārika*), but it also reaches those who seek worldly benefits;

thus, it is correctly categorized as a "general" discourse. Consequently, the section on the correct exposition also possesses three meanings. Regarding the general meaning, it extends through both the original sequence and the correct sequence, each of which also possesses three meanings.
As for the propagation (*pravāraṇa*), if it did not extend through the preceding correct sequence, by what means would it benefit those with the karmic affinity? Therefore, [it is necessary].

Regarding the statement that "the method of circulation is simply the circulation of the correct sequence, for the words of the beginning, middle, and end are all excellent," the subsequent passage also cites these words of the beginning, middle, and end;
this is a citation from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* says: "Excellent in the beginning, excellent in the middle, and excellent in the end.

The *Wenju* commentary explains: "Excellence in the beginning, middle, and end refers to excellence in terms of the stages [of the teaching]—namely, the introduction, the main body, and the circulation."

[The commentary] states: "The seven kinds of goodness [of that civilization], from the goodness of the seasons up to the seventh mark of the Brahma-conduct, constitute the goodness of unconditioned compassion. The *Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm) says: "Goodness takes 'conformity with principle' as its meaning;
because it quiets perversions and returns to the truth, it is called conformity with principle. Now, if these three parts do not interpenetrate one another, they would become obstructed and severed;
how then could they conform to the principle of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)?"

Furthermore, regarding the passage "Moreover, sentient beings... and below, which refutes the notion that the capacity for attaining the Way among sentient beings is not fixed by discussing the indeterminate nature of their attainment:
since the terms "superior," "middling," and "inferior" are all inherently wholesome, all three divisions possess benefit.

This is precisely the same principle as that shown in the *Fahua wenju* (Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra), where the characteristics of causes and conditions are demonstrated through these three stages. How could it be permissible to exclude this from the Preface?

The phrase "the flavor circulates and reaches the end" (Guishan changed the character *zi* [flavor] to *zheng* [correct]) means that since there is no contradiction in speaking of the cause and effect between teacher and disciple within the "Circulation" section, what inconsistency could there be in speaking of the "Correct" [Teaching] in the "Preface"?

Therefore, the fact that the "Circulation" section speaks of the cause and effect between teacher and disciple carries the intent of the "Correct Teaching," which further serves to urge (*du*, pronounced as in *dongdu*; the correct form is *du*) and exhort (*li*, pronounced as in *lizhi*; meaning to encourage and strive).
The practice of circulation does not contradict the intent of the sutra because its words—superior, middling, and inferior—are all excellent.
For example, in the *Lotus Sutra*, when Samantabhadra arrives from afar to exhort and request the teaching, the Tathāgata replies with the four [aspects] beginning with "protective mindfulness.

These four are precisely the opening, showing, awakening, and entering; is this not circulation within the formal exposition? Furthermore, are these not also the four lotuses within the introduction? Is it not so?

It is not that there is no introduction even in the *Circulation* [section]; for instance, at the beginning of the "Chapter on the Four Kings" in this sutra, the homage to the Buddha praising the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* as the king of all sutras, and the description of the profound and wondrous merits that adorn the bodhisattvas, constitute the name, essence, doctrine, and function.

Since these are precisely the name, essence, doctrine, and function, how could they not be considered the introduction within the *Circulation* section? This is because the introduction and the formal exposition are nothing other than the name, essence, doctrine, and function.

"Manifesting" refers to the qi; "qi" here means the categories of seasonal climatic influences, specifically the different types and distinctions among the six qi such as yin and yang, as well as the twenty-four qi.
Third, regarding "citing examples": "example" (lì) refers to a category or precedent, while "vinaya" (lǜ)—as Nanshan states—is the Sanskrit term *vinaya*, which is translated here as "law" (*lǜ*).
"Law" (*lǜ*) means "dharma"; it is named after the teaching, serving to adjudicate.

Because [the Vinaya] distinguishes between the heavy and the light, the permitted and the prohibited, the observed and the transgressed, the illegal and the indeterminate, it is the correct counterpart [to secular law].

Among the nine schools of secular thought, the "school of Dharma" (fǎliú) is but one; thus, while worldly legal systems generally rely on penal statutes and their application differs from the Way (Dharma), the actual adjudication must necessarily rely upon the constant Law (Dharmavinaya).

This is why the character for "Vinaya" (lǜ) combines the radical "zhí" (a hand) with the element "yù" (a pen), symbolizing the taking up of the writing brush to administer justice. *Chù* (處): To adjudicate; to apply.

Regarding the terms for the sections and clusters [of the Vinaya]: "sections" (*pian*) refers to the five sections. First is the *pārājika* (translated as "extreme evil," like a person whose head is severed who can no longer be a bhikṣu; also called "without remainder," named after the severance from the community according to the collective rules).

Second is the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (*saṃgha* means "community"; *avaśeṣa* means "remainder," referring to the initial granting of the *parivāsa* rite before the community; *śiṣa* means "remainder," referring to the final granting of the *āvarhaṇa* rite for the expiation of the offense).

If one commits this offense, it is named according to its objective basis (*ālambana*), just as when a person is being cut by another, even though the throat remains intact, it must be rescued immediately. Three *pāyattika* (the meaning is translated as "falling"; one falls into the hells of burning, boiling, and concealment).

The Saṃgha has one hundred and twenty types [of offenses]; thirty are derived from matters of property and arise from greed and arrogance toward others; because they involve forced forfeiture into the Saṃgha, they are called *naiḥsargika*. Since *naiḥsargika* is translated as "forfeiture," the remaining ninety are simple confessions made to an individual.

If one considers the nature of the offense, they belong to the same category for repentance. Four *prātideśanīya* (the meaning is translated as "confessing to that person"; the name is established based on the object of counteraction). Five...

*Duṣkṛta* (in which *duṣ* means "evil" and *kṛta* means "to do"): if divided into two aspects, it is called "evil action" (*duṣkṛta*) regarding the body and "evil speech" (*durbhāṣita*) regarding the mouth. The "aggregates" (*nikāya*) refer to the six aggregates, also called the seven aggregates.
Regarding the six aggregates: first, *pārājika*; second, *saṃghāvaśeṣa*; third, *sthūlātyaya* (translated as "great obstacle to the path of goodness," also called "great offense" or "gross evil");
fourth, *pāyattika*; fifth, *pratideśanīya*; sixth, *duṣkṛta*. Regarding the seven aggregates, the first six are as above, with the seventh being... [text ends].
"Evil speech" (*duṣkṛta*) is the opening [category] that divides *pāyattika* into two bodies: "evil action" (*duṣkṛti*) as the sixth group and "evil speech" (*durukta*) as the seventh group.
As for *Abhidharma*, this is translated as "Incomparable Dharma" (*anuttara-dharma*) and also as "Dharma Counterpart" (*pratisaṃyukta-dharma*).
A *khandhaka* (or *kaṇḍa*) is translated as "Dharma-aggregate" (*dharma-skandha*), because one division is made into eight aggregates: first, karma; second, the proclivities (*anuśaya*).

[The *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*] asks: Who composed the three knowledges (*trividyā*), the four concentrations (*catasraḥ samādhayaḥ*), the five faculties (*pañcendriyāṇi*), the six great [elements], the seven views (*sapta-dṛṣṭayaḥ*), and the eight miscellaneous sections (*aṣṭau vibhaṅgāḥ*)?
From where did the *Ṣaṭpādābhidharma* emerge? Answer: One hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, King Aśoka convened various masters of treatises (*śāstrakāra*).
Consequently, separate schools (*nikāya-bheda*) arose. Among them were those of keen faculties who had read the entire Tripiṭaka and desired to understand it thoroughly.
The Buddhist scriptures consist of eight *skandhas*; after these, the disciples, because later generations would not be able to understand them fully, composed an abridged *Abhidharma*.
Its original author was Kātyāyanīputra; this is the certainty of the terminology. Thus, the *Varga-saṃgraha* and so forth are likewise like the *Prakaraṇapāda*.
Next, from "In this manner" (*iti*) onwards, the explanation of the text of the introductory section (*nidāna*) is divided into two parts: first, the analysis of the text;

second, from "Next, the sequence of the introduction" (*atha krama-nidāna*) onwards, the interpretation, which is further divided into two: first, the explanation of the "sequence of the introduction," also called the "general introduction" (*sāmānya-nidāna*);

second, the explanation of the "narrative of the occasion," also called the "specific introduction" (*viśeṣa-nidāna*). This constitutes the condensation of three parts into two. Regarding the terms "general" and "specific": the general introduction applies universally.
The individual prefaces of various teachings may be called the specific prefaces for each individual sūtra, yet they may also be called the general prefaces common to all sections.

Furthermore, the individual preface of one section may be called the general preface common to all sūtras, while the individual preface of one teaching may be called the specific preface of that single teaching. Moreover, although the name "general preface" is common, its substance is distinct;

although the matter of the "specific preface" is distinct, its meaning is common. Because the meaning is common, it is "general," yet it possesses a specific preface; because the substance is distinct, the "specific" resides therein.

Now, from this scripture we know that the general and specific prefaces of this scripture are both distinct; the specific preface pertains to the immeasurable, profound *dharmatā*, the eternal fruit, and so forth.

Only when such elements are not shared with other scriptures can it be called the "Preface to the True Family" (*saddharmakula-nidāna*), and only by being the true preface can it be named the "Correctness of the Preface.
