Furthermore, because of subsequent dreams, one may also say that they were not among those who heard [the teaching] together (*saha-śruta*).

Following this precedent, even if one goes to the mountain with sentient beings as in the case of Śraddhālakṣaṇa, one may say they belong to the assembly of those who heard together, or one may say they do not belong to the assembly of those who heard together.

As for why the assembly of those who heard together is small and not in sequential order: it is because although devas, nāgas, and others gathered in the chamber of Śraddhālakṣaṇa, they attained the lifespan of those who heard together.
The result of the means of cognition (*pramāṇaphala*) is the same [in all schools], yet the various sūtras differ in their arrangement.

In these sūtras, the assembly of listeners is listed after the place where they reside; therefore, it is said that there is a slight lack of sequential order. (This is also like the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, which, following the general introduction (*nidāna*) concerning the Bhagavān, immediately clarifies the specific introduction (*pratyanubhava-nidāna*) regarding entering samādhi and manifesting signs;

only after the manifestation of signs does it list the assembly of bodhisattvas. Thus, in interpreting any sūtra, one must understand the intent behind the specific introduction. If this were not done, by what means could the purport of the main teaching (*saddharma*) be clarified? Therefore, the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā*, the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, and the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* require particularly careful examination.)

The commentary states "and so forth" to clarify the meaning of why those who heard it together are not listed in order: first, although those who heard it together were not in a fixed sequence, one cannot say that there were no such co-hearers;
second, this is because the time, place, and assembly of this sutra are explained in detail later in the text, showing they were not uniform, and thus they are not enumerated here;
third, although the version translated by Paramārtha (Chen) is brief and lacks sequential order, it was translated by various masters.

Fearing that such [omissions] might exist, the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) in its analysis of the teachings states: "The difficulty lies in the fact that those who heard the teaching together are not listed;
the Hu (Khotanese) version still contains many more [names], so why should it stop at four fascicles or seven scrolls? It may simply be that those texts have not yet been transmitted.
Thus, in the "Preface Chapter" (*Xǔpǐn*) of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* translated by Yìngjìng of the Táng dynasty, Śāriputra and the other bhikṣus are enumerated.
The assembly consists of the Bodhisattvas such as Vimalakīrti and others, and the assembly of the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings.
Fourthly, this sūtra was compiled by the Bodhisattva Nāga in the Hall of Faithful Signs; they heard the section on the Lifespan, but did not hear the preceding introduction nor the subsequent dream.

This distinction is made based on the exoteric perspective; however, if one were to discuss the esoteric perspective, how could it be that they did not hear it? Furthermore, regarding the exoteric aspect:
Although one has not heard it in the preceding preface, by inferring from the meaning of the subsequent dream, one recognizes that this [realization] is no different from hearing it;
were it otherwise, how could the constant fruit not merge with the *dharmatā* to give rise to the great function of repentance and praise?
Furthermore, since the preceding preface states: "If there are those who hear it, they will be able to contemplate the unsurpassed, subtle, wondrous, and profound meaning."

"How could there be such an intention to cause the two communities of Hecung and Chengshan to be forever separated?"—for this reason, the commentary states "and so forth. I shall now briefly analyze this;
the rest must await those of later virtue. As for the phrase "and so forth," it is like the dispersion of vapors:
like clouds in the sky, they cannot be measured all at once. This means that what has not yet been explained below is as vast as clouds.

Regarding these five or six [points], the following section describes their alternative names and variations in phrasing, which is divided into two parts. First, the formal description of the names and the definitive arrangement of the sequence:

it is said that all sutras of the Buddhas of the three periods of time begin with "Thus" (*evam*). One should say they all begin with "Thus and so forth" (*evam-ādi*). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
When the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, Ānanda’s mind was submerged in an ocean of grief; then Aniruddha spoke to Ānanda...
Regarding matters of the future, if there is any doubt, one should consult for a decision at once; why cause oneself distress?
Just as ordinary people do in the world, Ānanda immediately questioned the Buddha on four matters: first, how should one practice the Path after [the Buddha’s] parinirvāṇa;

second, who shall be our teacher after [the Buddha’s] parinirvāṇa; third, how shall we dwell together with the harsh-tongued Cāṇḍa after [the Buddha’s] parinirvāṇa; and fourth, [how shall we treat] the Buddha [after his passing].

At the beginning of the sutra, what words are established? The Buddha told Ānanda: "In the present and after my parinirvāṇa, you shall rely on the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) to cultivate the path and attain liberation according to this Vinaya-sūtra;
this is your Great Teacher. When Channa spoke evil words, he was punished by the Brahma-punishment (brahma-daṇḍa).

[At that time,] because the royal lineage held the bhikṣus in light esteem and did not reform them even after the Buddha had passed away, they were made to undergo the Brahma-punishment—meaning silent censure (tūṣṇīmbhāva-parivāsa). It is also said that the method of the Brahma-heaven for punishing offenses involves establishing a separate altar and requiring the offender to enter this altar, where all the Brahmās will no longer associate with him.

When conversing with others, if their minds are disciplined, one should preach the *Dāna-kātyāyana-sūtra* to lead them away from the extremes of existence and non-existence, whereby they immediately enter the first fruit (*srotāpanna*). This is the "Gate of the Double Negation" within the Tripitaka.
At the beginning of a sutra, one should place the formula: "Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was in such-and-such a country together with a great assembly.

It is not only my own teaching that begins with "Thus have I heard"; this is the case for all Buddhas of the three periods of time. For this reason, it is also called the "Entrusted Introduction" (*parinirvāṇa-nidāna*) of the Tathāgata.

Because it was left as an instruction to be placed [at the beginning], it is also called the "Preface to the Sūtra. This is because the sūtras of all Buddhas of the three periods of time likewise begin in this manner;
therefore, what follows is also called the "Preface to the Sūtra," as it was entrusted [to be placed there] for the same purpose. This is the identical meaning.
Regarding the term "seal of authentication" (*yin-ding*): "seal" refers to a seal or insignia, which is also a mark of trust.
Just as in worldly documents, only when they bear a seal do they become a permanent standard of authority; here it is the same. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* states:

"Phrases such as these also serve to authenticate that this was spoken by the Buddha and not by his disciples or non-Buddhists. It is also called the "General Preface" (*tong-xu*) because it is common to all sutras.
Because the beginning of all sutras uniformly establishes [the title] with "Thus have I heard" and so forth, this is explained here in terms of the commonality of their names.

However, if one discusses their distinct natures (*tattva*), they differ from various other sutras; therefore, it is said that while the "General Preface" (*sūtra-pūrva-nimitta*) is common in name, it is distinct in nature.

Furthermore, it serves as the basis for the common name. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of," *wei* (爲) means "to bestow upon. The *Vimalakīrti-sūtra-ṭīkā* states: "Based on the specific name, the name..."

The separate preface contains distinct verbal teachings; if one follows the general name, there is a general preface, and if one considers the practice and principle, there are both general and specific aspects.
It is because of this that there are both general and specific prefaces. Question:

If the two prefaces are established according to their two names, then when establishing the names, the specific should come first and the general second (the four characters "Expounded by Vimalakīrti" are specific, while the single character "Sūtra" is general; the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra* follows this same pattern, being specific first and general last). Why is this so?

Question: Why is it that the general introduction (*sāmānya-nirdeśa*) comes first and the specific exposition (*viśeṣa-nirdeśa*) follows? Answer: Regarding the convenience of establishing the title, the specific should come first and the general last;

regarding the convenience of the introduction itself, the general should come first and the specific last. Furthermore, according to one approach, the specific also comes first and the general last. Why is this?

It is because, for example, the manifestation of auspicious omens (*prātihārya*) is the means by which the preaching of the sūtra is enabled; these six matters are precisely what the Tathāgata employs just before entering parinirvāṇa.
Because these words are spoken, we know that [the title] comes later. The title of a sutra is the general [designation], while the sutra text itself is the specific.
In the *Vimalakīrti-vyākhyā*, the general is analyzed to discuss the specific; therefore, based on the two names—general and specific—there are both a general and a specific introduction (*nidāna*).

This is because the introduction originally introduces the main body (*samyag-deśanā*); thus, it does not conflict with the correct teaching of the circulation [of the Dharma]. In the present text, however, the specific is taken as the general.

Therefore, it is said that [the general introduction] also serves as the basis for the general name; since we are now clarifying the general introduction (*sūtra-pūrva-mīmāṃsā*), this statement is made.

One may understand this by applying the same principle to the specific introduction (*viśeṣa-pūrva-mīmāṃsā*) below. Regarding the specific introduction, the commentators Gusuan and Siming state that it serves as the basis for the specific name, saying:

"Because the specific introduction differs from other scriptures, a specific title is established, namely *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*. This interpretation applies to the current text’s general introduction as well.

To claim that the title *Āgama* (Thus) serves as the basis for the general designation [of "Sūtra"]—stating that all spoken by the Golden Mouth are established as *evam* (thus)—is it not an error to call them "Sūtras"?
Furthermore, the phrase "placed after the title 'Sūtra'" refers to what was added by the compilers;

it means that when the Buddha’s preaching of the Sūtras reached the period after his parinirvāṇa, Ānanda established them with the words *evam* and so forth during the compilation. As for the term "final testament," it refers to [the instructions] given at the time of his death.

This was because at the time of his passing, [the Buddha] bequeathed these virtuous words as an entrustment to Ānanda, so that they might remain secure. It is also called the "Preface to the Refutation of Heresies.

Regarding the phrase "refuting the heretical *āṭavika*" (the character *ā* is pronounced *wū hóu*; it is also written as *ōu* or *ōu*), the *Fahua Wenzhu* (Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra) provides a separate explanation, stating that this specifically refers to refuting the heretical *āṭavika*.
Although the present work provides a general explanation of these five terms beginning with "Thus" (*evam*), for the time being, we shall follow the specific interpretation starting from "Thus."
These two characters, "A" and "Oū," counteract the terms "A" and "Oū. "A" means non-existence; "Oū" means existence.

All external scriptures take these as their primary focus because their calculations are based on these two as their fundamental categories, and what is elucidated within them does not transcend these two.
Therefore, at the beginning of the Buddha’s sutras, the phrase "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) is established to counteract "A" and "Oū," meaning "not thus" and "not so."
Because one attains the Way only by relying on the Buddha-dharma and departing from the views of existence and non-existence, the *Śata-śāstra* states:

The Outsider asks: "What do you designate as wholesome dharmas? The Insider replies: "The cessation of evil and the practice of good. The Outsider says: "Your scripture has a fault, for it is inauspicious at the beginning. My scripture is not so;
it is auspicious both at the beginning and at the end. The Insider replies: "In general, all dharmas possess three aspects, namely: self..."

Because [the opponent] maintains that both existence and non-existence arise from self, other, or both—since these are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) according to your own auspicious doctrine—I have previously refuted arising from self, other, or both, as well as existence and non-existence.
Because such conceptualizations of existence and non-existence as being "self" or "other" are termed "evil," my sūtras first prohibit them. If you ask:

"The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* thoroughly refutes all four positions; why does it not refute 'arising from nature' (*svabhāvataḥ')? The answer is: those who maintain "nature" [assert] existence and non-existence.

Regarding the Middle [Way]—as cited in the *Zhiguan* (Cessation and Contemplation) from Zhou Hongzheng’s *Explanation of the Three Mysteries*: "The *I Ching* enumerates the eight trigrams, which clarifies the mystery by way of existence; Laozi’s 'empty fusion' clarifies the mystery by incorporating non-existence; Zhuangzi’s 'spontaneity' (*ziran*) clarifies the mystery by way of both existence and non-existence.
Furthermore, there is a spontaneity that is not subsumed under either existence or non-existence. For the time being, we follow one particular approach; thus, the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* says:

"If even that which arises from causes and conditions is itself untenable, how much more so that which is causeless and spontaneous? This is because that which is spontaneous is easily refuted; therefore, it is merely used as a point of comparison. These are simply the four types of conceptual reckonings (*catuskoṭi*).

To speak briefly now regarding the refutation of external views: the way the latter three teachings refute the four types of calculation is fully detailed in the *Zhi guan* (Mo-ho chih-kuan) and cannot be exhausted here.
This is also called the "Preface of Certification and Faith," intended to ensure that those who hear it do not harbor doubts.

The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* asks: Why are phrases such as "Thus have I heard" placed at the beginning of the sutra? It answers: Phrases such as "Thus have I heard" are established precisely for the purpose of severing doubt and encouraging faith. Therefore...

Such passages as these are primarily intended to encourage those who see and hear [the teachings] after the Buddha has passed into extinction, so that they may quell their doubts, increase their faith, benefit themselves and others, and achieve the perfection of the Way.
As the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-ṭīkā* states: "‘Thus’ refers to the principle being transmitted; ‘I heard’ refers to the person who upholds it;
‘at one time’ refers to the time of realizing the principle; ‘Buddha’ refers to the master from whom it was received; and ‘dwelling’ refers to..."
The places where [the teachings] were heard, the multitude who personally received them as companions, and their successive mutual verification serve to encourage faith that they are not false;
this is intended to ensure that future generations may follow them without confusion and verify them with confidence and without doubt—such is the meaning.

Next, regarding the Tiantai school, the present tradition judges these according to the four *siddhāntas*. The Master of Tiantai stated that all six of these explanations are entirely comprised within the four *siddhāntas*.
This is because the previous six meanings originally derive from ancient masters and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (*Dazhilun*). As the "Preface Established by Seal" states:

"The sūtras of the Buddhas of the three periods all begin with the phrase 'Thus have I heard' (*evam mayā śrutam*), etc. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and the *Dharma-pada-dhara-vyākaraṇa* (*Fufazangzhuan*) state: [text continues]
The Buddhadharma of the three periods of time all initially establish [the prefaces] in this manner; as for the names such as these, they originally derive from the ancient masters.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra* states: "The ancients called them the 'General Preface' (*tōng-xù*) and the 'Specific Preface' (*bié-xù*).

Furthermore, the text of the "Preface Refuting Heresy" (*pòxié-xù*) derives from the *Śata-śāstra*, while the "Preface of Verified Faith" (*zhèngxìn-xù*) also derives from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. Since these six types of prefaces originate from the ancient masters, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, and other such sources, [they are authentic].

Zhang’an cited the Master of Tiantai, saying: "It does not go beyond the four *siddhāntas*. *Siddhānta* is a Chinese term meaning 'pervasive' (*biàn*). *Dāna* is a Sanskrit term meaning 'giving' (*shī*).
The Buddha pervasively bestows these four dharmas upon sentient beings; thus, this is an instance where both the Chinese and Sanskrit terms are employed together.

That which is common to all Buddhas and all sutras refers to the fixed introduction and the general introduction. As for the three periods of time, they are distinct, and the various sutras are not one and the same."
All [beings] who hear this, numbering five or six, rejoice; therefore, this world is situated after the *Parinirvāṇa-sūtra* and before the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
This compilation was intended for the sake of producing roots of goodness in people of future generations; thus, it is "for the benefit of humans" (*pudgala-artha*).

(In the *Miaoxuan*, it is distinguished that "producing goodness for humans" is the primary [old], while "correctly severing evil" is the secondary [new]; likewise, "counteracting and destroying evil" is the old and primary, while "generating goodness" is the new and secondary, and so forth. Since this involves the refutation of heterodox outsiders, it is already a refutation.

Because it is free from evil, it belongs to the category of antidotes; because it is verified by faith, it is not false; because one accords with it without confusion, one immediately attains realization of the principle.
Therefore, it belongs to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).

Following the old commentary, the subsequent section provides a detailed explanation of the text in two parts. First, the formal explanation of the text, which is divided into five sections. First, the explanation of the phrase "Thus" (*evam*).

Regarding the first of the three [sections], the explanation of the text based on causes and conditions is divided into two parts. First, the presentation of the interpretations of various masters is divided into four sections.

First, the interpretation of the "Old Masters" regarding the simile of pouring water from one vessel into another: the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that Ānanda’s upholding and expounding the twelve divisions of the scriptures for others is like pouring water from one vessel into different containers;
the *Fahua Wenju* (Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra) states that he personally received them from the Buddha...

The essential meaning is as follows: one looks up to the transmission of the perfected vessel to transform others, like pouring from one vessel into another. Next, Master Zhaoshi explains the four disciples of Master Kumārajīva: Shi, Zhao, Rong, and Rui.
Dharma Master Sengzhao was a native of Jingzhao (Jingzhao Prefecture, belonging to Yongzhou). His family was poor, and he made his living by hiring himself out as a copyist;

it was through this work of transcribing that he came to study the classics and histories extensively. By nature, he delighted in the profound and subtle, and he devoted his mind to the *Zhuangzi* and *Laozi*. He once...
Upon reading the *Laozi*, he sighed and said, "How beautiful! Yet, it does not yet contain the means for dwelling the spirit in the realm beyond all burdens.

When he encountered the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, he sighed again, saying, "Only now do I know where I truly belong. He subsequently took Master Kumārajīva as his teacher and composed the *Wu-bian-wu-er-lun* (Treatise on the Non-transmigration of Things), the *Bu-zhen-kong-lun* (Treatise on the Non-reality of Emptiness), the *Bore-wu-zhi-lun* (Treatise on the Non-cognition of Prajñā), and the *Niepan-wu-ming-lun* (Treatise on the Namelessness of Nirvāṇa), as well as various other works.
Because Sengde annotated the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, what is cited here is precisely that commentary.

[The text includes: 3. The Explanation by Zhendi; 4. The Explanation by Nāgārjuna (the text is found in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*: at the time of his birth he was beneath a tree, later a dragon king brought him into the great ocean, and through this he attained enlightenment;

thus he was named Longshu. Furthermore, "Longshu" combines both the Chinese and Sanskrit names; in Sanskrit it is *Nāgārjuna*, which is translated here as "Dragon Fierce"). Following this, the present school judges the commentary according to the four *siddhāntas*.
Regarding the phrase "and so forth," this judgment holds that each of the preceding four interpretations relies on one of the *siddhāntas*, though this is merely a provisional assessment.

This is because, according to the *Fahua wenju* (Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra), Master Sengzhao’s interpretation is taken as the first-principle *siddhānta*; thus, we know that the current judgment is likewise merely provisional.

Furthermore, the present judgment establishes the four *siddhāntas*, whereas the *Wenju ji* (Notes on the Words and Phrases) states that the divergent explanations of various schools mostly [fall into these categories].
Since even the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is scarce when based on causes and conditions, how much more so for those [teachings] categorized by doctrine and so forth?

Next, the section beginning with "Now, making" provides an interpretation according to the meaning of the doctrinal categories (*yōkyōgi*), which is further divided into two parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation of the text beginning with "The Buddha, as below," which is itself divided into two.

First, the general explanation: regarding the note "etcetera" (*zunchū yunyun*), "general" (*tsū*) must necessarily pervade the "particular" (*betu*); how could the particular differ from the general? Therefore, looking at it from the perspective of the general...
Furthermore, when it says "the Buddha speaks according to the characteristics of phenomena" (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) and so forth, this must include the meaning of the four teachings (*catuḥśāsana*).

As will be fully cited below from the *Fahua Wenzhu* (Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra), there is a subsequent separate explanation divided into two parts. First, the direct explanation of the text, which is divided into four sections. First, refuting the heterodox and clarifying the correct teaching, which is divided into two parts.

First, the section on refuting the heterodox: where the text deviates from the principle, such as the passage concerning the heterodox views of existence and non-existence (*astitva-nāstitva-dṛṣṭi*), the text deviates [from the truth].

To see that the phrasing deviates from the correct principle (*nyāya*)—that it is neither existent nor non-existent—is because the correct principle itself does not admit of existence or non-existence.
Since the principle differs from its phrasing, the opposite can be understood accordingly. As for the subsequent passage, it clarifies the following:

when the phrasing accords with the principle, the phrasing is said to correspond to the principle; when the principle accords with the phrasing, the principle is said to correspond to the phrasing. This is because both the phrasing and the principle [are in harmony].

This is because it is free from the conceptualizations of existence and non-existence. The *Fahua wenju* states: "The Buddha clarifies that conventional truth possesses words and letters, while ultimate truth is devoid of words and letters.
Because Ānanda transmits the Buddha’s conventional truth of words and letters without differing from what the Buddha himself spoke, it is called 'Thus' (*tathā*).

Because these conventional words accord with the principle of ultimate truth, they are called 'So' (*iti*). This refers to the initial clarification of "Thus" (*evam*) at the beginning of the Tripiṭaka sūtras.

Next, the following section refutes difference to clarify sameness; this text is divided into two parts: first, the refutation of the two truths as being distinct; second, the clarification of their identity.
Regarding the former, if the conventional were real existence and the ultimate were the cessation of real existence, and since these two do not coincide, they would constitute distinct entities.

To say that "the principle is shallow" means that the provisional truth of partial reality is not the profound depth of the central, true reality. Following the passage on *mahāyāna*, the next section clarifies their sameness through the Mahāyāna.

This is called the Mahāyāna; the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) is the initial gateway to the Mahāyāna. Illusory existence is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and that illusory existence being empty is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Because these two truths are not separated, they are said to be mutually identical. One asks: Is the Shared Teaching called the "initial gateway to the Mahāyāna" in reference to its own specific teaching, or does it apply generally to the Distinct and Complete Teachings?
If there is such an analysis within the *Miaoxuan*, that passage refers to [the specific teaching].

To penetrate both the Separate (Pratyekabuddha) and Perfect (Bodhisattva) vehicles is called the "initial gate," precisely because the Mahāyāna gate directly penetrates the true reality (*tathatā*) while indirectly penetrating the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Now, when it is said that "the principle is profound," this refers to its remote penetration of the middle way within the Separate and Perfect vehicles.

Since the principle is profound and thus remotely penetrates the Middle Way, and since the two truths are mutually identical, how could it not be so? One should know that this meaning also possesses both indirect and direct aspects.
The secondary meaning is as follows: according to the primary principle mentioned above, it refers to the two truths of "containing the middle" and "entering the real.
The *Fahua Wenju* states: "The name of the Buddha is that form is emptiness, and emptiness is form; form and emptiness, emptiness and form, are non-dual and without distinction.

That emptiness and form are not different is 'as-it-is' (*tathatā*); that reality is present within phenomena is 'thusness' (*tathā*). Ānanda’s transmission of the Buddha’s words—being no different [from the truth]—is "as-it-is" (*tathatā*).
That the signifier is identical to the signified—this is how it is at the beginning of the *Tongjiao* (Shared Teaching) scriptures.
Third, regarding the section "Now I say" and below, which refutes the shallow to clarify the profound, the text is divided into two parts. First, the refutation of the shallow:

since it was previously stated that the principle (*li*) of the *Tongjiao* is profound, this section now clarifies the *Biejiao* (Distinct Teaching). As for the refutation of the shallow, it is because the *Tongjiao* involves manifesting the profound while still retaining the shallow; here, however, we simply...
It is called "refuting the shallow" because it refutes the superficiality of the previous lateral penetration; "hearing together" refers to hearing together the non-arising [of dharmas];

"each understanding" refers to the Śrāvakas entering emptiness by taking the general characteristics of phenomena as their essence, and the Pratyekabuddhas entering emptiness by taking the specific characteristics of phenomena as their essence;

the Bodhisattvas fully cultivate both general and specific characteristics. Thus, the *Daban Niepan Jing* (Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra) regarding the four teachings states: "The Buddha speaks of the true reality (*tattva*). (True Meaning) [This passage] is divided.
There are three types: if one attains the true mark (*dharmatā*) and extinguishes all afflictions, it is called the Śrāvaka Vehicle;

if one gives rise to great compassion and develops the unsurpassed resolve, it is called the Mahāyāna (that is, the Bodhisattva); and if, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when there is no Buddha in the world, one generates wisdom through seclusion, it is called the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle.
Thus, although they equally hear the Dharma of non-arising (*anutpāda*), there is a distinction between these three vehicles.

This refers to the fact that those who hear the same teaching each attain their own respective understanding. Regarding the superiority or inferiority of their realization, it is like the analogy of the three animals crossing a river found in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*:
the elephant represents the Bodhisattva, the horse the Pratyekabuddha, and the rabbit the Śrāvaka; the river water represents the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
When the three animals cross the river, the elephant’s strength is greatest, the horse’s strength is next, and the rabbit’s strength is most inferior. The river... [is the same for all].
Although water is one, the reflections of elephants, horses, and rabbits have varying lengths; thus, there are differences in the depth of the river they cross.

For this reason, although the three types of people enter emptiness equally, the Śrāvaka merely eliminates the active outflows (paryavasthāna), the Pratyekabuddha attenuates the habitual tendencies (vāsanā), and the Bodhisattva cuts off the active outflows while sustaining the habitual tendencies to nourish rebirth.
Thus, we know that entering emptiness is not without degrees of excellence. Fourth, Zhiyi distinguishes them according to their benefit.

The statement that "the dull bodhisattvas realize the existence of true-midpoint" (*bhūtakoṭi*) is intended to clarify their relative superiority and inferiority; it likely does not represent the primary intent of the text.

Regarding the phrase "only bodhisattvas," the following clarifies the profound meaning: "only" (*kevala*) means "exclusive. The Separate Teaching (*prātibhedika-yāna*) is exclusively the dharma for bodhisattvas; this is why it is said so. The *Fahua wenju* states:
"The Buddha clarifies that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) has limits and nirvāṇa is limitless; thus one exits from existence and enters into non-existence."

Emerging from the "Non-existence" and entering the "Middle," Ānanda transmitted this; it is no different from what the Buddha taught. Just as [the path] proceeds from the shallow to the deep, everything is affirmed as being thus;
such is the beginning of the Separate Teaching (Pratyekabuddhayāna) sutras.
Fourth, regarding the subsequent section on "Refuting the Distinctness of the Manifestation," the text is divided into two parts.

First, "Refuting the Distinctness of Words and the Distinction of Extremes" refers to the teaching as it is heard. Second, "The Middle Way Exists Outside the Two Truths" refers to the principle as it is realized.
If one were to say otherwise, the phrasing would become redundant; thus, following the passage "the nature of words is distinct," the next section clarifies the Middle Way.
Regarding the phrase "the nature of words is detached," the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* states that this means it does not reside within the four propositions of self or other.
That is, the character itself is the nature; since the nature is fundamentally non-existent, it is said to be "detached from nature.

Regarding the phrase "that which is precisely suchness (*tathatā*)," the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra* states that the detachment of the nature of words is liberation. Since we are now explaining "suchness," it is necessary to alter the phrasing; therefore, it is called "precisely" (*ji*).

Because this is the *tathatā* (suchness), it is called "suchness"; thus, it is the first statement in this sutra. That "all dharmas are the Buddha-dharma" means that the two truths are themselves the Middle Way.
The *Fahua wenju* states: "The Buddha clarifies that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is itself *nirvāṇa*, which is also the Middle Way;
how much more so, then, is *nirvāṇa* not the Middle Way? True suchness and the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) pervade all places."
All dharmas are none other than the Buddha-dharma; because Ānanda transmits this as being no different from what the Buddha taught, it is called "Thus" (tathatā).
Because it is thus and immovable, it is called "This. This is the opening phrase "Thus [have I heard]" of the Perfect Teaching (Vairocanayāna) sutras.

First, the refutation of heterodox views; next, the analysis of the text by means of the divisions of the schools (*nikāya*) and the teachings (*śāsana*). This section is divided into two parts: first, the analysis of the text by means of the teachings; second, from "In this sutra...

onwards, the analysis of the text by means of the schools and its inclusion within them. It is taught in various ways to universally accommodate the capacities of sentient beings—that is, it is taught for the four types of capacities through the four teachings.
Question: If the text is divided according to the four teachings, why does the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) provide a separate analysis of the teachings?

Therefore, while the teaching that "penetrates the general while carrying the particular" clarifies the Perfect [Teaching], it does not explicitly mention the Three Baskets (Tripitaka). When answering by correlating the teachings with the divisions, the Vaipulya division is, for the time being, correlated with the General;
since it subsequently carries the particular and clarifies the Perfect, how could it not also encompass the Three Baskets?

Furthermore, although the Baskets and the General Teaching are distinguished according to their doctrines, the principle realized is one and the same; therefore, in the classification of the teachings, they belong to the General and are not considered inferior to the Three Baskets.

Third, regarding the explanation by means of contemplating the mind (*guanxin*): the *Fahua wenju* (Textual Explanations of the Lotus Sūtra) contains only the "causes and conditions" (*yinyuan*) and the "explanation according to the teachings" (*yuejiao*), but lacks the sections on "contemplating the mind," "originality" (*ben*), and "traces" (*ji*).
This is because the *Fahua wenju* states that when explaining other sūtras, one uses only these three meanings, as they have not yet revealed the traces and manifested the original.
Within this [section], there are two parts; first, the direct explanation. Here, no distinction is made between the contemplative differences of the four teachings (*sijiao*).

The *Fahua wenju* states: "Contemplating such meanings as the previously mentioned *siddhānta* teachings and so forth as all being 'dharmas produced by causes and conditions' is the general contemplation (*tongguan*).
Contemplating that 'causes and conditions are themselves emptiness and themselves the provisional' is the specific contemplation (*bieguan*).
Using these two contemplations as skillful means to enter the Middle Way and simultaneously illumine the two truths is both general and specific contemplation; all of these are the Middle."
The Way is neither a state of penetration nor a state of separation. What is now called "contemplation" refers to being in accord with the object;

because it can conform to that which is to be conformed to, there is no difference. When it is said that the object is itself right contemplation, since the object is already identical to principle (*tattva*), there is nothing that is not so;
therefore, it is called "is. Next, the sutra provides scriptural evidence by citing the *Sūtra on the Contemplation of Samantabhadra* and the *Sixteen Contemplations Sūtra*.

They all said: "Regarding these four characters for contemplation (*guan*), one must call the first and third with a level tone (*ping sheng*) and the second and fourth with a departing tone (*qu sheng*).
As for the terms 'false' (*xie*) and 'correct' (*zheng*), their meanings have both general and specific applications when discussed across the four teachings.

Specifically, only the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*) is called 'correct,' because for those who rely on the text to perform contemplation, it occurs for the most part within the context of the Perfect Teaching."

Next, the explanation of "I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) is divided into three parts. First, the explanation based on causes and conditions, which is further divided into three: first, the explanation of the ancient masters; second, the explanation of Paramārtha;

and third, the interpretation from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "How is it that one hears? Is it heard by the faculty of the ear (*śrotra-indriya*), by the auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*), or by the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*)?
It answers: "When the faculty of the ear is unimpaired, the sound is within the range of audibility, there is the desire to hear, and there is mindfulness (*smṛti*)."
Because of the conjunction of various conditions, auditory consciousness arises; following auditory consciousness, one can differentiate various causes and conditions and thus hear sounds.
Question: One should say that "the ear hears"; why then do you say "I hear"? Answer: "I" is the master of the ear; by mentioning "I," all the contributing conditions are subsumed.

It should be understood that auditory consciousness hears only when four conditions are present: first, the sense organ (root); second, the object (sphere); third, space; and fourth, attention (manasikāra). The root is the ear.
The auditory faculty (*śrotrendriya*) is the purified great element (*mahābhūta*), the ultimate internal faculty, and not the superficial external faculty of the four subtle particles (*paramāṇu*).

The object (*viṣaya*) is the sound-constituent (*śabdadhātu*). "Space" refers to the location where hearing occurs. "Attention" (*manasikāra*) refers to the mental application of the desire to hear and the recollection of this matter.

As for the "conjunction of the sense-faculty, the object, and the mind," this collectively indicates that the auditory consciousness arises because the four conditions are fully present. [The text] mentions the self (*ātman*).
The gathering of all conditions is also the convergence of the four conditions. If it is visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), it arises from five conditions;

to the four conditions, one further adds the condition of light. Taking the eye as the faculty (*indriya*), visible form as the object (*viṣaya*), light as the illumination, space as non-obstruction, and mental attention (*manasikāra*) as the initiator—through these five conditions, visual consciousness arises. Now, regarding this auditory [consciousness]...

Since consciousness does not depend on the condition of light, it possesses only four conditions; thus we know that when hearing and retention are in harmony at one time, the four conditions are fully complete.

If even one condition is lacking, there is no harmony. If one reads the *Fahua Wenju* (Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra) and its commentaries (*Ji*), one should understand that this teaching is also found therein, though with omissions and errors;
the full details are as presented in the *Budazhu* (Supplementary Notes to the Great Commentary).
The middle section indicates (as detailed above). The reason why the four *siddhāntas* are not applied here as a criterion can be understood by reference to what preceded;

thus, there is no need for further elaboration. If one wishes to apply them, it should be done according to the traditional interpretation: "This world" corresponds to the *loka-siddhānta*; "the True Dharma" corresponds to the *prātipakṣika-siddhānta*;

the commentary on the causes and conditions of harmony and combination corresponds to the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta*; and Ānanda’s recounting of the Buddha’s final instructions to the assembly corresponds to the *paramārtha-siddhānta*. If...

The *Fahua Wenzhu* (Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra) judges and explains this treatise as belonging to the "Worldly" [teaching]; however, for the time being, we follow it provisionally and thus judge it as above.

Next, regarding the passage beginning with "I," the Master’s commentary explains the text according to the meaning of the teachings (*jiao-yi*) in two parts. First, the direct explanation, which is further divided into two; first, the opening...

"Explaining" (*shì*) means to analyze; it refers to analyzing the two characters "fen" (part) and "wen" (hear) individually within this context, which constitutes the first of two sections. First, regarding the explanation of "I" (*wo*) as "pairing" (*pèi*): "pairing" means to correspond.

The phrase "the four types of people according to their faculties" refers to the people of the four teachings according to their respective faculties. The intention is to cause them to be sequentially matched and correlated, thereby explaining the reasons for doing so;
hence the commentary states "and so forth. The "faculties of the Tripiṭaka" refers to that which possesses subject and object, as well as the self...
For this reason, it is said: "I" and "self" pervade the human body; when one thoroughly realizes that both self and other are empty, this is called "self" and "non-self.
For the person of the Separate Teaching, one enters emptiness and non-self during the Ten Abidings, and emerges into the provisional to establish a self during the Ten Practices.

The person of the Perfect Teaching realizes that both the extremes of having a self and being without a self are the Middle Way. Therefore, it is said that the Middle Way beyond duality is the reality, which is the meaning of the true self. Next, the explanation follows.

The *Wenjuji* (Record of Phrases) states that here, too, the four phrases from the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* are employed; however, while the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* reveals the Perfect [Teaching], here they are interpreted according to their meaning.

Vertically, they are applied to the four teachings for the sake of convenience regarding their names, and thus do not follow the original sequence. The full details of how the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* reveals the Perfect are shown in the supplementary notes (*buzhu*) to the *Dabubian*.

Here, following the intent of the teachings, the four "hearers" (*śrāvaka*) are explained: those who are called "hearers" by people of the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) school are said to possess the capacity [for realization].

Because one hears what is heard, it is called "hearing hearing. When the person who is the subject of this practice penetrates both the capacity (the hearer) and the object (what is heard) as being empty, this is called "hearing non-hearing.

When a person of distinct capacity enters emptiness and is further able to emerge into the provisional, this is called "non-hearing hearing. A person of perfect capacity realizes that the two extremes are themselves the Middle;
therefore, it is named "non-hearing non-hearing," which means not hearing existence and not hearing non-existence. These are the four methods of teaching.
In the preceding passage, when explaining "self" (*ātman*), the term "person" (*pudgala*) was used alone;
here, in explaining "hearing," it includes both the phenomenon and the person—that is, the person who hears and the dharma that is heard. With this intention, the commentary states [the following].

Furthermore, in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā*, the "Teaching of Commonality" (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*) is identified as "hearing what is not heard," because hearing is explained through the point that all things are like dreams and illusions, which are themselves empty.

The Separate Teaching (biejiao) is for those who have heard yet have not truly heard: because what they have heard is sovereign within the conventional truth (saddharma-saṃvṛti), at the moment of death they immediately hear;
hearing at the time of death, they are born [into a new state] possessing that hearing, and according to whatever they have heard, they are sovereignly able to maintain it.
Regarding the fourfold non-sequential synthesis, this refers to the collective explanation of the two characters "I heard" (evam mayā śrutam).
The *Ajaśeṣarāja-saṃvṛtti-sūtra* and the *Dharmaguptaka-dharmakośa-śāstra* clarify three types of Ānanda;

One regards the first dhyāna as suffering because it is oppressed by the agitation and disturbance of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*); it is regarded as coarse because the joy and bliss arising from applied and sustained thought are so;
and it is regarded as an obstacle because applied and sustained thought obscure the inner purity of the second dhyāna. The second dhyāna is different from this.

It is called "superior" (*viśeṣa*) because it is more excellent than the first dhyāna due to its internal purity and tranquility, which are free from the agitation of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).
It is called "sublime" (*praṇīta*) because the joy of the second dhyāna arises on account of that internal purity.

It is called "emergence" (*niḥsaraṇa*) because upon attaining the second dhyāna, one departs from applied and sustained thought. The same logic applies to the stages from the second dhyāna upward through the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).

The three types of delight (*abhirati*) and the three types of aversion (*vidveṣa*) each function according to their respective applications; they proceed sequentially, all taking their own level as the "lower.

"the provisional entering emptiness" is the illusory existence being emptiness in the *Sāmānya* (Common/Shared) teaching. Since both [approaches] proceed from the provisional to enter emptiness, they are all "I" and "non-I.

The two contemplations of the *Vibhinna* (Distinct) and *Pūrṇa* (Perfect/Round) teachings can be understood according to the text. It is stated that if there is an agent, it is not fixed according to the capacities of beings.

Therefore, [the text] provides three explanations for the passage as a whole, divided into three parts. First, regarding the explanation based on causes and conditions, it is further divided into three. First, Master Zhao’s explanation:
"Qi" (啟) means the first hearing; "yun" (運) means what is appropriate; "jia" (嘉) means good. The Great Movement of the Buddha's transformation must correspond to the nature of things.
Because it is a pivotal moment, it is called a "noble assembly" (*jiahui*). Next, the Tripitaka Master explains the text in two parts:
first, the formal exposition. "If one is superior" refers to a time of high attainment; "if one does not reach it" refers to a time of low attainment. [The author] privately comments:

the subsequent section where Zhanran (Zhang An) provides an explanation is likely because he feared others would not understand the terms "high" and "low," and thus he offers this clarification. He uses the term "privately comments" (*siwei*); the *Cangjie pian* states that this means "not public."

Since this was neither spoken by the Great Master in the midst of the assembly nor personally verified and recorded by him, but is merely words privately added by oneself at the time of the compilation, the Master’s commentary on the following three sections is as follows. Regarding the present school’s interpretation:

since it is said that when sentient beings elicit the Dharma and the Buddha’s compassion responds to their capacity through teaching, one knows that the current text must be understood in terms of causes and conditions.
Shi explains this as follows: "When time and the Way coincide" refers to the *paramārtha* (ultimate truth).
Zhaò says, "The time when the Dharma King initiates his auspicious enterprise" refers to the world (*loka*). It may also encompass the cultivation of goodness for the sake of living beings.
The Tripitaka Master’s usual state—neither high nor low—is the *pratipakṣa* (remedy).

Next, this section also explains the text according to the meaning of the teachings (yàojiào), divided into two parts. First, regarding the explanation of "time," the commentary notes "and so forth" (*yúnyún*).

This intends to explain the arising of the true vision of the truths (*chūfā zhēnjiàn dìyì*); furthermore, the Dharma-eye illuminating the world refers to the Distinct Teaching (*biéjiào*), while the Buddha-eye illuminating the Middle refers to the Perfect Teaching (*yuánjiào*).
Therefore, in the *Fahua wénjù*, when explaining "time" according to the teachings, it also says "vision of the truths" (*jiàndì*) and so on.
Furthermore, regarding the subsequent explanation: first, because it refutes what is incorrect, it says, "These two are not one.

Second, because it reveals what is correct, it says, "Delusional severance is suddenly awakened to. One should also provide a commentary here on the word "etc. (云云), though it is omitted from the text;
this is because the phrase "delusional severance is suddenly awakened to" contains the meaning of the four teachings.

Regarding the phrase "the three [aspects] explained by correlating them with the contemplation of the mind," the intent is to apply these three to the meaning of contemplating the mind within the four teachings;
this can be understood by following the previous explanation based on the four teachings.
