(53) Fifty-fourth, [the text] states: "Furthermore, the Buddha has long cultivated the three kinds of non-obstruction (*anāvara
Because those who rely on their own [attainment] can deliver themselves but cannot save others, the Buddha is distinguished from them by his compassion (*karuṇā*).

Because the mental application (*cittotpāda*) of other minor bodhisattvas is still partial, the Buddha is distinguished from them by his equanimity (*samatā*). The fact that others lack these qualities reveals that the Buddha alone possesses them.

As it is said in the *Guanjing* (Contemplation Sutra), "The most venerable and supreme is called Buddha"; thus, one knows that he is also distinguished from the great bodhisattvas, because [the state of] the great bodhisattvas...

This is because [the Buddha] is still at the stage of a cause (*hetu-avasthā*). Next, citing the *Śāstra* (the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*), it says: "The Buddha is the ninth title. The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states:

"The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* explains [the titles] as eleven phrases; the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* combines 'Unsurpassed Being' (*anuttara-puruṣa*) and 'Charioteer of Men' (*sārathi-puruṣadamyasārathi*) into one phrase, up to 'World-Honored One' (*bhagavat*) as the tenth phrase. The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-vyākhyā* states: "The *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* combines [these] with the *Āgama*."

The titles "Unsurpassed One" (*anuttara*) and "Tamer of Men" (*puruṣadamyasārathi*) constitute one single designation, continuing through to the tenth title, "World-Honored One" (*bhagavān*), which completes the full set of ten.
According to the *Śāstra* (Exegesis), "Unsurpassed One" and "Tamer of Men" are treated as two separate designations; thus, from "Unsurpassed One" to "Buddha," the ten names are already complete.
In summary, because he is fully endowed with these ten titles of supreme virtue and is honored by the world, he is called the "World-Honored One. This is consistent with...

The current text of the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) differs [from other versions], which suggests that Zhiyi (Zhang’an) may have made an error. The Buddha is named "Awakened" (*jue*); in the Western language, he is called *Buddha*.

The old translation is "the Awakened One. Furthermore, in the *Śāstra*, it is translated as "the Knower" (*zhe*). "Knower" is used in contrast to delusion, while "Awakened" is used in contrast to ignorance.

Although the names are the same, their specific applications both belong to self-awakening (*zijue*). It is precisely through this self-awakening that one awakens others; this is stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra*.

The *Yin-di-ren* (the followers of the *Yin-ch’i*) state: “To awaken oneself and awaken others. Chih-kan (Chang-an) rebukes this, saying: “To speak again of ‘awakening others’ is far too prolix” (*et cetera*).
To awaken to the mundane world is to understand suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*); to awaken to the supramundane is to understand the path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*).
The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* states: “The permanent is the fixed dharma; impermanence is merely the non-fixed dharma. Among the three trainings, it is like [the case of] the *Vibhāṣā*...”

In the *Vinayapiṭaka*, it is held that when one commits a grave offense with a conscious mind, it is definitively established as a karmic obstruction (*karmāvaraṇa*), which is termed "definite" (*niyata*); other precepts that do not constitute such an obstruction are termed "indefinite" (*aniyata*).

Now, since this is the case for the permanent and the impermanent, I suspect that the categories of "counted" (*saṃkhyāta*) and "uncounted" (*asaṃkhyāta*) are explained here in terms of the ultimate and the conventional truths.
Next, Tiantai’s subsequent explanation of the meaning of the classification of teachings (*jiao*) also consists of two parts. First, the formal explanation:

previously, it was clarified that because the "I who hear" differs according to the four teachings, the physical characteristics (*śarīra-lakṣaṇa*) of the Buddha bodies differ. Now, in contrast to the three types of wisdom (*trividya*), only the distinctions between the three Buddhas are explained.
If the three are expanded into four, then the *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge) possesses a sixteen-foot Buddha body, which belongs to the Tripitaka (*tri-piṭaka*).

Based on the knowledge of the modes of the path (*mārgajñatā*), there exists the sixteen-foot *zhèngtè* (special, exalted form). Although this properly belongs to the Shared [Vehicle], it also encompasses the Distinct [Vehicle];

thus, by using the two characters "exalted" (*zūn*) and "special" (*tè*) together, the knowledge of the modes of the path refers to the Bodhisattvas who emerge from the provisional to the ultimate (*chūjiǎ*).

Gushan says that although the two characters "sixteen feet" (*zhàngliù*) may have been included due to the interpretation of the meaning, they are ultimately unnecessary. I, however, say: [they are indeed necessary].

It is not that there is any redundant meaning here; rather, it is you who do not understand. That which possesses all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*) belongs to the Dharma-body Buddha (*dharmakāya-buddha*) and is associated with the Perfect [Teaching], by which one can perceive that all phenomena are empty, quiescent, and of a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*); this is called "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*).

To know all phenomena along with the distinctions between the various paths is called "knowledge of the aspects of the paths" (*mārgajñatā*). To know both the single characteristic and the various categories of all modes of practice is called "all-aspect knowledge" (*sarvākārajñatā*).
If wisdom is considered solely in terms of the threefold perfect clarity, then the Buddha-wisdom that illuminates emptiness as seen by the two vehicles is called *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge);

the Buddha-wisdom that illuminates the provisional as seen by the bodhisattvas is called *mārgajñatā* (knowledge of the paths); and the Buddha-wisdom that illuminates emptiness, the provisional, and the middle, seeing all as the true reality (*bhūtārtha*), is called *sarvākārajñatā* (knowledge of all aspects).
Therefore, it is said that the three knowledges are attained within a single moment of mind. Next...

Regarding the passage in the *Sanfo* (Three Buddhas) section on "Fusion" (*yōngtōng*) which states that "one cannot posit identity or difference": this is because if there were identity or difference, it would contradict the Dharma-body’s quiescence and purity.

As for "neither identical nor different, yet identical and different," this means that once the attachment to intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) has been shattered, there is no hindrance to provisionally speaking of identity or difference according to conditions.
This is truly because within that which is nameless and signless, one provisionally speaks of names and signs; it is precisely for this reason that this single phrase is so.
All other points should be understood by scholars according to their knowledge of the *Śāstra*.
Regarding the third point, "explaining the commentary by correlating the contemplation of the mind," the intention is to pair the three [wisdoms] with the four teachings.

It should also be evident that this follows the exposition of the three wisdoms; furthermore, it requires one to discern the essence of the Middle Way, which, because it doubly negates [extremes], is free from oneness or difference.
Because contemplation employs dual illumination, it is likewise both one and different.

The commentary on the passage concerning the "abiding place" is divided into two parts: first, a general explanation; second, a specific explanation beginning with the section on "Ultimate Truth. This latter part is further divided into two: first, the explanation of the text on "abiding," which is itself divided into three sections;
first, the explanation of the text by way of causes and conditions, which is divided into two: first, citing the explanation of Paramārtha; second, the [author's own] explanation.

In this section of the *Śāstra*, our school subsumes [the stages] according to the *Vyākhyāyukti*. First, I shall cite the *Wenju ji* (Commentary on the *Wenju*) to clarify the meaning of the "four abidings" (*catur-vihāra*) in the *Vyākhyāyukti*;
next, I shall clarify how they are subsumed within the "eight abidings" (*aṣṭa-vihāra*) of Paramārtha. Regarding the first point, the *Wenju ji* cites the *Śāstra*, which states:

"Abiding" refers to the four modes of deportment—walking, standing, sitting, and reclining. Furthermore, it says: "Because he terrifies the hosts of Māras, he causes his disciples to joyfully enter into various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*)."

Therefore, none of the various texts concerning the present school cite this [passage] while dwelling within it. Furthermore, there are three kinds: first, the Celestial Abode (*devasthāna*), which refers to the heavens of desire (the *Śāstra* says these are the six heavens of the desire realm);

second, the Brahma Abode (*brahmasthāna*), which refers to the heavens of form (the *Fahua wenju* also agrees with this explanation; perhaps it is due to abbreviation, for the *Śāstra* clarifies that everything from the First Dhyāna up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) constitutes the Brahma Abode);

third, the Pure Abode (*śuddhasthāna*), which refers to those from the third fruit of the path onward (in the *Śāstra*, it simply speaks of the "Noble Abode" [*āryasthāna*] rather than the "Pure Abode"; furthermore, in the *Śāstra*...).

It merely states that the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Arhats are called "Noble Ones" (*ārya*) because they abide in the "Noble Abodes" (*āryavihāra*) among the three abodes; it does not say they dwell in the city of Rājagṛha out of compassion for sentient beings. The reference in the *Ji* (Commentary) to those beyond the third fruit seems to be an error.

However, the texts of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-ṭīkā* and the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra-ṭīkā* regarding the four types of abodes are identical to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*; the difference is that the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-ṭīkā* specifically cites the causes of the four abodes, whereas the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra-ṭīkā* fully cites both the causes and effects of the four abodes.

Furthermore, since the *Śāstra* mentions "Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Arhats," while the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra-ṭīkā* speaks of the "Three Vehicles," this is because the Buddha represents the fruition and the Bodhisattva represents the cause; thus, the Bodhisattva Vehicle is used here to manifest the nature of the Buddhas. The *Ji* further explains the passage from the *Wenju* as follows:

The *Zhuzhansanmei yinlun* (Treatise on the Causes of Abiding in the Three Samādhis) states: "Entering the three samādhis, one immediately attains the first fruit. The commentary on this treatise explains that "abiding" (*zhù*) is not mentioned here; this is likely an error. The same treatise further states:

"Generosity, observance of precepts, and a virtuous mind constitute the Celestial Abodes (*devasthāna*); the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa-citta*) constitute the Brahma Abodes (*brahmasthāna*). [The *Jì* (Commentary) notes: "The former [section] proceeds from the fruit, while this proceeds from the cause. The treatise says:

"Loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are called the four immeasurable minds. The Noble Abodes (*āryasthāna*) consist of the three samādhis; the Noble Abodes are simply the Pure Abodes (*śuddhasthāna*). [The treatise says: "Emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and..."]

These three samādhis are called the "Noble Abodes" (*āryavihāra*). Because the Buddha dwells within them, they are known as the "Dharma of the Noble Abodes. In the *Śāstra*, there are two explanations of these three abodes; they do not go beyond [discussing] first the fruit and then the cause. In the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā* (Jì), what are termed the "Noble Abodes" are likely explained as being merely the "Pure Abodes" (*śuddhavihāra*), as this would harmonize with their names.

Furthermore, the *Śāstra* speaks of four abodes: those of the devas, the Brahmās, the noble ones, and the Buddhas. Adding the "Buddha-abode" to these results in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* mentioned at the beginning of the present text.

Therefore, the four abodes herein encompass the entirety of the *Śāstra*'s discourse. As the *Śāstra* states: "Furthermore, there are four kinds of abodes: those of the devas, the Brahmās, the noble ones, and the Buddhas. The latter three constitute the "abodes of the noble ones."

As previously stated, "the Buddha-abiding" refers to abiding in immeasurable samādhis such as Śūraṅgama, as well as the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the eighteen unique qualities, and so forth. One should know that the four abidings are merely added to this; they are mentioned alongside the Buddha-abiding for contrast, which is why it is said, "furthermore, there are four kinds of abiding.

If one were to categorize them according to the teachings, all four teachings possess the meaning of the aforementioned four *siddhāntas* (purposes), because the text correlates these four kinds of abiding with the four *siddhāntas*.
While all four Buddhas are equally the Heaven of the Ultimate Meaning (*paramārtha-deva*), one cannot say that the first two Buddhas employ the Śūraṅgama [Samādhi].

[The interlocutor] asks: "Regarding the present Śākyamuni Buddha’s dwelling, why do the three [types of] *siddhānta* (ultimate truth) all refer only to the realms of desire and form, as well as the three fruits?

[In the *Wenju* (Textual Commentary), the four modes of abiding in the world are designated as the 'worldly ultimate,' the celestial abodes and Brahma abodes as the 'human ultimate,' and the noble abodes as the 'remedial ultimate. The commentary states: 'To say they refer only to the realms of desire and form and the three fruits is to be understood by analogy with what preceded;

the mention of 'desire and form' is likewise an abbreviation. Are both the one who dwells and the place where he dwells not the Buddha? (However, in the treatise, among the three types of abiding, it is stated twice that the Buddha dwells within the 'noble abode of dharmas')."

[Question: It is simply that while the celestial abodes (*devasthāna*) and Brahma abodes (*brahmasthāna*) are mentioned, the Buddha-abode (*buddhasthāna*) is not explicitly stated. [Answer: There are two reasons: first, proceeding from the general toward the specific; second, using the superior to encompass the inferior.

Regarding "proceeding from the general," this refers to moving from the broad to the narrow. Regarding "using the superior to encompass the inferior," since the Buddha relies upon the royal city (*rājadhānī*), he necessarily encompasses the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the three fruits (*triphala*).
(The term "three fruits" should be understood according to what was previously considered. Someone objects, saying: "Now you explain his dwelling in the royal city; why then do you cite..."
Devas, Brahmās, and others dwell here; this person has never read the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. This is the commentary on that treatise explaining the actual text regarding "dwelling.

If one were to explain the term "dwelling" solely by means of the physical body (rūpakāya) dwelling in a land, then since the spiritual power of great Bodhisattvas is omnipresent and lacks a fixed location, they would have no place to dwell—how much more so for a Buddha?
Therefore, we know that others permit only the physical body to rely upon the royal city.

Since the attainment of Buddhahood has no mental factors (*caitta*) upon which it depends, the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-sūtra* clarifies that "constant quiescent light" is the Buddha’s dwelling place;

how could it be the royal city? (This refutes Master Ci'en Ji. Thus, the *Fahua xuanzan* by Ci'en states: "To 'dwell' means the place where one wanders and transforms others. To reside in the mountains while wandering and transforming in the city—the Buddha relies on this [quiescent light] to wander and dwell in peace.

Based on this, ancients have said: "The Holy Heaven, Brahma, and the Buddha dwell [there]. Although the name "dwelling" is the same, the meaning and intent are entirely different. In places where the language is profound and the meaning is obscure, one must never let the mind be attached to them; such texts where the names are identical but the principles differ are merely empty fabrications.)

[The bestowal: Based on this, it is not yet acceptable. Master Ming’s *Chao* states: "These four names have the meaning of 'the place where the mind abides. The present sutra speaks of them in the sense of 'where the body dwells. Since body and mind are different, they are entirely distinct.

By verifying this, we know that Ci'en (Kuiji) never read the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. If he had read it, why would he distinguish between body and mind as two separate things? How could it be that Nāgārjuna’s interpretation of the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* regarding his dwelling in Rājagṛha was inferior to that of Ci'en, a contemporary Mahāyāna master?

Nāgārjuna—who could surpass him—is someone how can one disparage him by claiming that the text "the name is the same but the principle is different" is a hollow fabrication used as a pretext? If one were to merely say that [the Buddha] dwelt in the mountains while traveling and teaching in the city, then when he attained Buddhahood and resided in the royal city, his body and mind would have no place of abode at all.

This teaching is such that where the language is profound and the meaning is obscure, one does not apply the mind at all, but instead turns it into self-reproach; how could this concern our present school?

Next, regarding the clarification of the inclusion within the eight abodes of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one should say that the celestial abodes (*deva-vihāra*) and the Brahma abodes (*brahma-vihāra*) encompass the celestial abodes, which abide in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and the Brahma abodes, which abide in the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*).
The term "abiding in concentration" (*dhyāna-vihāra*) is likely a textual corruption, as [the celestial realms] belong to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Since the middle [section] also discusses the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), it includes them;

however, Paramārtha states that those who dwell in meditative concentration must encompass all four *dhyānas* of the form realm and the four concentrations of the formless realm. Therefore, the "Brahma-abodes" (*brahmavihāra*) are specifically called the "four immeasurables. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Brahma-abodes are the four immeasurables... [text fragment].
The "abodes" (vihāra) refer to the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). They are subsumed under the "noble abodes" (*āryavihāra*), and their meaning is entirely identical;
they likewise subsume the fivefold qualities of the Dharma (*pañcadharmaguṇa*).
"Emancipation and the knowledge and vision of emancipation refer to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
Emancipating wisdom and the eye of wisdom refer to one’s own [realization].
Because of this, when the body is reduced to ashes, [the result] is attained; while remaining in the world, the fivefold [liberation] is established."
The Buddha... [omitted] ...this is merely abiding in the Śūraṅgama-samādhi. Furthermore, regarding those who abide in the royal city and gather [the assembly], the *Śāstra* says:
"Among the three types of abodes, he abides in the noble abode (*āryavihāra*), out of compassion for sentient beings...

Since his reliance and abiding are identical, and he already dwells in the royal city, how could his body not engage in walking, standing, sitting, and reclining? How much more so in the case of the King?
Since the city is within the trichiliocosm, we know that the *Śāstra* states: "Dwelling in the royal city, he encompasses the three abodes of the True Truth (*satyadharma*).

Next, regarding the explanation of the Tiantai stage according to the teachings, one may understand it by following the previous explanation of the Buddha’s intention through the lens of the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*).
However, while the three types of wisdom are categorized according to [the modes of cognition], the three truths pertain merely to the principle upon which they rely.
Furthermore, the preceding passage concerning the three Buddhas was explained by way of synthesis, whereas this current section on the four abodes of existence is explained by way of analysis.

Following the previous interpretation, among the four kinds of Ānanda who personally received the teachings from the four Buddhas, within the *dharmākhya-jñāna* (knowledge of the paths of practice), there exists both the sixteen-foot form and the *vairocana-kāya* (special majestic body). Now...

The treatise states: "Regarding the six-foot [body] and the sublime special body (zunte), if one discusses the six-foot body alone, it abides in the True Truth (zhendi); if one discusses the sublime special body alone, it abides in the Middle Way.
Since these two bodies—the six-foot and the sublime special—are united, they are..."

Therefore, it is called "dwelling in the true Middle Way," as this is stated in reference to the conjunction of the true and the middle. Consequently, one must also distinguish this from the previous passage concerning the "emergence into the provisional" via the *mārgajñatā* (knowledge of the paths).
Why? Because according to the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), those of sharp faculties who emerge into the provisional are able to perceive non-emptiness, which is precisely the Middle Way;
how much more so for the Distinct Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*), which may reside either in the provisional or in the middle. [The text here contains lacunae regarding the provisional...]
If the Way and the Principle are identical within the Perfect [Middle], it is merely the Path of Teaching (jiaodao). Therefore, it is said that...

[omitted] ...if one follows the conventional, then one subsumes the aforementioned reliance on the Knowledge of the Aspects of Phenomena (zhongzhizhi); if one relies on the Buddha of the Distinctive Marks (zuntefo), then...
[omitted] ...it can be understood that the Dharma-body Buddha (fashenfo) dwells in the Middle Way; however, regarding the Buddha of the Distinctive Marks... [omitted]
This is the application of the Middle Way, wherein the Dharma-body is the very substance of [the land].

However, in the *Fahua Wenju* (Textual Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), the explanation of the "Dharmodgata" chapter clarifies the basis of the marks and signs according to the Four Teachings; this is intended to show how the substance of the land corresponds to these teachings.

Furthermore, within the "Counteracting and Subsuming Dharmas" section of the *Zhi Guan*, the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings are used to realize True Suchness, while the Distinct and Complete Teachings are compared to copper and gold respectively.
Because the realization of the Middle Way is like a mirror, one knows that all texts follow the meaning and are not singular (and so forth).
Third, the explanation based on contemplating the mind follows the previous method; reflect upon it accordingly.

Next, the explanation of the passage concerning the location is divided into two parts. First, the explanation of the Royal City is further divided into two parts. First, the explanation based on causes and conditions: "Great" means...
"Extensive" means "abundant. The *Śāstra* (Commentary) is extremely extensive; I have now cited it only briefly. Regarding the "Five Mountains," the *Fahua Wenju* states:
first, Cave of the Lord of Heaven; second, Seven-Leaf Grotto; third, Snake Deity; fourth, Little Independent Strength; fifth, Vulture Peak.
Furthermore, the lower section of the text cites Paramārtha as saying: "The Five Mountains... [and so forth]. "To arrange" (*pai*) means "to push" or "to align," according to the *Wenju*.
The *Xiyuji* (Record of the Western Regions) states that this city is surrounded on all sides by lofty mountains serving as its outer wall;
it is one hundred and fifty *li* in circumference, being long from east to west and narrow from south to north. The inner city measures thirty *li*.

The northern gate of the city is the place where Devadatta released the intoxicated elephant, and to the northeast is the place where Śāriputra met Mañjuśrī [Maṅguśrī] and attained the first fruit of the path.
Next, regarding the interpretation based on contemplating the mind (*citta*), this text is somewhat brief. The *Fahua wenju* states: "The 'King' is the mind-king;

the 'palace' is the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). That the mind-king constructs this palace means that by analyzing the palace of the five aggregates until they are empty and void, one makes it into the city of Nirvāṇa.

Since this contemplation is shallow—like seeing earth and wood (as the *Xiangfa jueyi lun* says, "or seeing this place as soil, sand, grass, trees, and so forth")—if one instead realizes that the palace of the five aggregates is [itself]...

Taking emptiness and further emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*) as the city of Nirvāṇa is the Teaching of Penetration (*tongjiao*). If one contemplates the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) by abandoning causes and extinguishing them, one attains the eternal form (*rūpa*);
feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise so. These four virtues of eternity and so forth are the dwelling place where all Buddhas roam.

If one contemplates the five aggregates as the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), then within that Dharma-nature there is no feeling, perception, mental formation, or consciousness; this is the case for all sentient beings.
Birth itself is *nirvāṇa* and cannot be extinguished again; it is ultimately empty and quiescent. This *nirvāṇa* is precisely the true substance of *tathatā*.
The *Wenju ji* (Record of Explanations of Phrases) states: "In establishing the object of contemplation at the outset, it says that the 'king of mind' constructs the house.

Since the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is the king, all minds that construct karma must have mental concomitants (*caitta*). Now, wishing to explain the 'king,' we shall first take the wholesome and unwholesome kings of mind."

Because it is contrasted with the neutral "house," it is said to be "built by the King. If one examines the four [sections] below, this demonstrates that the method of contemplation differs from other sutras;
as in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Mo-ho chih-kuan), this applies to all subsequent sections of the ten vehicles and ten objects, as detailed therein.孤山 (Gushan) says:

"The house of the five aggregates is the object (*ālambana*); the mind-king dwelling within it is the contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). [Four] *Note: The original text contains a fragmentary reference to Gushan’s commentary on the relationship between the five aggregates and the mind-king, illustrating the distinction between the object of meditation and the subjective contemplation.*

The *Míngyún* states: "The indeterminate nature is the same as the other four aggregates (*skandha*) as the object of observation (*ālambana*), while the determinate nature of good and evil serves as the observing subject. Now, I say:

if we follow the *Jìyún*, when first establishing the object of observation, if one analyzes the lower four [aggregates] as the observation, then the object and the observation—the subjective and objective—are clearly manifested.

However, the text below explains the observation of Mount Qi, stating that [the body] is constantly observed by the mind-king (*citta-rāja*), causing all mental factors (*caitasika*) to be likewise [observed].

Regarding those who enter therein, the *Fahua Wenju* (Textual Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) states that this concerns the principle of the mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and its mental factors (*caitta*) taking objects as conditions;
thus, that which takes the object is contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), and that which is taken as the object is the realm. This is fully explained in that text (*et cetera*). Siming stated:

"The king and its factors—whether good or evil—are not separate from views and attachments. To directly use this mind to contemplate the principle of true reality (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*) is like attempting to suspend Mount Sumeru with a lotus fiber."

For those who follow the path of mountains (ascetics), conceptual discrimination only increases, making it impossible to sever thoughts. If one realizes that this mind is inherently evil (*prakṛti-pāpa*), then because inherent evil is all-pervasive and harmonious, there is no phenomenon that is not subsumed within it.
Thus, one understands that cultivated evil is itself the perfect and wondrous contemplation of inherent evil; therefore, even a beginner can practice it.
As the *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) says: "If one has not yet even heard the name of 'inherent evil,' how could one believe in the existence of 'inherent virtue'?"

Regarding the practice of the inherent virtues (*xingde*), one must hear of the inherent evil (*xing'e*); because one knows the inherent evil, the fundamental emptiness of cultivated evil (*xiu'e*) is realized.

Since there are no delusions to be shattered and no principles to be manifested through the Three Contemplations (*sanguan*) and the Ten Vehicles (*shicheng*), these practices are designated by the name "inherent virtue" (and so forth).
Now, I say this is not so; for the *Wenju ji* states: "Contemplating that each of the aggregates, bases, and elements (*yin-rulai-jie*) possesses the ten realms is precisely [the point]."
Although the "Wondrous Realm" (Miaojing) Shan City takes the provisional (yīn) as the object of contemplation, it has not yet established the inconceivable realm (bùsīyì jìng).

Furthermore, since the realm relies on the side of the provisional and its numerical categories are maintained, when even within emptiness (kōng) there are no such categories, how could they exist [in the provisional]? This must necessarily rely on the provisional to establish emptiness.
Once this single passage is understood, all others may be inferred accordingly; thus, the *Fǔxíng* says: "One is able to realize that deluded thoughts have no..."

Regarding the characteristics of identity and difference (the quiescence within emptiness): it is not merely that the phenomena of purity and defilement vanish, but rather that deluded affliction is transformed into purity. Upon realizing this signlessness (*animitta*), one possesses all minds;
when the three thousand realms are fully present, one is then able to illuminate the mutual identity of the one and the many (wherein the wondrous provisional is manifest).

Therefore, in the *Jinbi* (The Golden Scalpel), the three meanings of the essence, nature, magnitude, and virtue of the [Buddha-]nature are clarified; it is only in the third, the virtue of nature, that the mutual identity of the one and the many is fully realized.

The *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Practice) says: "In the great void of space, there is fundamentally neither light nor darkness; light and darkness exist only in relation to form (*rūpa*) and thus involve mutual exclusion.
The Dharma-nature of the great void is originally devoid of good and evil. It is the emotional conceptualization of ordinary beings that posits the mutual exclusion of good and evil;

therefore, one is led to cultivate *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* regarding evil so as to realize that evil is non-existent. By seeing the essence of evil, one knows that this essence is fundamentally devoid of both good and evil. (The meaning is to be inferred accordingly.)
The provisional [distinctions of] good and evil are fully present. The *Fahua Wenju* states: "Light and darkness merge together, just as with moonlight;
furthermore, when the sun rises, darkness does not flee to the ten directions, for darkness always remains without a place of resort. Light is likewise merged with darkness.
Thus, birth-and-death merges with the Way; the Way is itself birth-and-death. That which the Buddha has exhausted is already exhausted; that which he has delivered is already delivered.

Duzhou further stated: "The arising of light and the cessation of darkness cannot be definitively determined as preceding or following one another; yet, even though there is no sequence of before and after, darkness is certainly an obstruction.
The Record states: "That which is said to be 'ever-present' is merely the absence of darkness; it has no nature of darkness. To cite darkness is to point toward brightness.

The same applies to delusion and awakening: their fundamental principle is no different. The brightness of the causal stage is intermingled with ignorance; upon entering the stage of partial realization (*vibhūti-bhāga*), one portion of darkness is destroyed.
If the substance of the darkness being destroyed were transformed into light, how could it be said that the light of wisdom has arisen while the prior darkness still remains and persists?
Although it is said to persist, it must ultimately be destroyed; only when it is forever purified can it be called "persisting. (And so forth.

Furthermore, regarding the practice of inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*), one must hear of the inherent evil (*prakṛti-pāpa*); for within the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*), there is no ninefold inherent virtue, and thus the severance of self and other is exclusive.
By taking the principle of reality (*dharmatā*) as the condition, one refutes the nine realms to reveal the nature within the emptiness of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).

If this nature is clearly understood, it must necessarily possess the wondrous provisional [nature] of the evils of the nine realms (in actuality, the three thousand dharmas are perfectly present therein). Thus, the *Wenju* states: "If one knows that the earth possesses peach and plum trees, one recognizes the provisional within the real;

if one understands that there is no difference in the interpretation, then difference exists within non-difference. If one knows the solid characteristics of the peach and plum trees, one recognizes the real within the provisional."
Since there is a real distinction between the non-differentiated and the differentiated within the records, it is said here:

"If one has not yet even heard the name of 'inherently evil nature,' how can one believe in the existence of 'virtuous conduct of inherent nature'? Thus we know that the evil conduct of inherent nature is precisely the provisional [expedient] that accords with the real;

it is also called the phenomenon that accords with principle, the derivative that accords with the fundamental, and the function that accords with the essence. Therefore, it is only in this way that...
The *Bianpin Wenju Ji* (Notes on the Text of the "Chapter on Expedients") states: "Who would have known that this sutra allows even evil conduct to be called 'skillful means'?

Furthermore, the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) clarifies that the ten realms and the six paths of the wondrous realm are precisely for the purpose of knowing that the nature of evil pervades all things;
moreover, these are phenomena subsumed within the wondrous realm. Thus we know that that which is able to subsume them is precisely the quiescence of emptiness."

Although the nature of cessation is such that the initial mind employs contemplation where concealment and illumination occur simultaneously, this is because one's own practice (*svacaryā*) resides solely within emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

For the sake of transforming others, the wondrous provisional [aspect] manifests the three thousand realms to respond to sentient beings. Since the three contemplations are unified in a single mind, self and other are non-dual.

Thus, when one’s own practice dwells in emptiness, not even a single dharma can be apprehended within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); how then could there be the three thousand realms? Worldly... [text ends]

In truth, the teachings for transforming others are already immeasurable; how could they be limited to merely three thousand? People do not perceive this and speak exclusively of the practice of inherent evil (*prakṛti-pāpa*);

they take no pleasure in the emptiness, quiescence, extinction, and dissolution [of the Middle Way]. Is this not to abandon the root and grasp the branches, or to discard the essence while delighting in its function?
Furthermore, when one realizes that both defilement and purity are empty, they vanish of their own accord. To speak of "emptiness" in contrast to "flowers" is itself empty and nameless.
If even one does not exist, how could there be the nature of defilement? When characteristics are utterly severed and thought is extinguished, there is no basis for turning back to reproach oneself;
to increase conceptual discrimination in vain—how could that concern others?
Next, the explanation of the text concerning Gṛdhrakūṭa (Vulture Peak) is also twofold. First, regarding the etymological explanation:

it is translated as "Vulture Head" (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*), also translated as "The Peak," and also translated as "Spiritual Vulture" (*Śrī-gṛdhrakūṭa*), because various holy seers and sages dwell there, thus it is called the "Spiritual Vulture Peak.
Furthermore, its shape resembles a vulture, hence it is called "Vulture Head"; additionally, it is so named because vultures nest there. These vultures are black in color and prolific.

Next, the interpretation based on contemplating the mind follows the *Fahua wenju* (Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra). Herein, this refers precisely to the two contemplations of the Distinct and Perfect teachings.

That text first establishes the objects of contemplation, stating: "If one contemplates the aggregate of form as being insentient like a mountain, the aggregate of consciousness as being sentient like a spirit, and the other three aggregates as being like vultures";

it further states: "To contemplate this 'spirit-vulture' is the analytical contemplation (*khaṇḍa-śīla*) of impermanence; to contemplate this 'spirit-vulture' as emptiness is the contemplation of the essence (*tattva-darśana*)."
The *Yiji* (Record of Exegesis) also states: "To take the mountain as the object of contemplation (*guan-jing*), one first establishes the object;

this precisely corresponds to the contemplation of the aggregates (*skandhas*) as detailed in the fifth fascicle of the *Zhi guan* (Cessation and Contemplation). Since the *Dayi* (Great Meaning) points to the *Miaoxuan* (Profound Mystery) regarding the practice of contemplation, it also refers to the *Zhiguan*, and the title *Wenju* (Textual Commentary) is for this very reason.

Within the contemplations of the Separate and Perfect [Teachings], since it is stated that "the mountain is the Dharma-nature, the true cause, and the Dharma-body," the other two virtues are to be understood according to various texts; therefore, it is further established by way of this.

Mountains are the objects of contemplation; although the mountain city differs from the mountain, both are equally *niśraya-vipāka* (retributive support). Therefore, by taking them as a basis, one contemplates the *samyag-vipāka* (primary retribution).

Furthermore, the objects of all contemplations do not transcend the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Since it is convenient to categorize these mountains and so forth according to the aggregates, and because various texts simply refer to them as "object and wisdom" (*ālambana-jñāna*), one should likewise distinguish here the characteristics of the similarities and differences between these two types of contemplation for the sake of skillful means and correct cultivation.

[The text] briefly distinguishes the objects and the mind, as well as the provisional and the real in relation to the preceding two [categories], and so forth. Since it is thus with the "reliance on phenomena" (*toshi*), the same applies by analogy to the "attachment to phenomena" (*fuhō*).

Those of former times did not understand this and falsely claimed that reliance and attachment do not involve contemplating the five aggregates, nor do they discuss the distinction between objects and the mind, or the ten stages of practice (*jūjō*) and so on;
these views clearly contradict the *Wenju* and the *Ji*. Furthermore, the *Wenju* on the "Chapter on Emptiness" states that one should cite the *Zhiguan* [as an authority].
How can one not grant that the object and wisdom are determined by the broad [explanation] resolving the concise, so that the practitioner may practice immediately upon hearing?

Thus we know that Siming (Zhiyi) well grasped this essential point. How could it be that human sentiment now arbitrarily grants or denies this? It is hoped that future scholars will examine this with precision and produce elegant expositions (etc.).
Regarding the "mind-king" and all "mental factors" (*caitta*), if one follows the *Fahua wenju* (Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra), it says: "Mental factors..."

They are very numerous; however, approximately speaking, there are ten wholesome factors, namely: faith (*śraddhā*), energy (*vīrya*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), joy (*prīti*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), awakening (*bodhi*), and morality (*śīla*).
These ten factors assist the "King of the Mind" (*citta-rāja*) in transforming evil into good and reforming the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) into a sage (*ārya*). [As stated in the text...

these ten factors that pervade the universal ground (*mahābhūmika*) arise together with the King of the Mind, entering into both the wholesome and the unwholesome, and pervading all states—namely: perception (*saṃjñā*), desire (*chanda*), contact (*sparśa*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and mindfulness (*smṛti*).

Having contemplated liberation, recollected meditative concentration, and practiced the contemplation of reception until awakening, the cycles of the [six] kings are all exhausted; because the mind and mental factors no longer function, the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna* states:
"My own mind is inherently empty, and thus sin and merit have no master. Therefore, being without mind and without number is called the accomplishment of right contemplation.
When one practices within emptiness, the wondrous provisional three thousand realms appear in their full distinctness (and so forth).
Next, following this sutra, the reason why the assembly of co-hearers is not enumerated is explained in two parts.

First, the explicit explanation of why this sutra lacks an enumeration of the co-hearers refers to the fact that after the passage concerning the city and mountain in the present sutra, no assembly of co-hearers is listed.
Regarding the statement "there are five times and four places," this means that while there are five occasions for hearing the Dharma, there are only four locations upon which they depend.
Hearing the narrative at Mount Yaśas is the first occasion; hearing of the constant fruit within the chamber of Śraddhālakṣaṇa is the second occasion;
hearing the repentance in a dream is the third occasion; having awakened, going with the assembly to Mount Yaśas to hear the explanation of the dream is the fourth occasion;
and hearing the praise when the assembled multitude arrives at the land of the Buddha Golden Jewel Mountain King is [the fifth occasion]. This concludes the "Chapter on Praising the Buddha."

Regarding the five periods: because the accounts of hearing the description of the dream and hearing the narration itself both took place at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, there are only four locations for the setting.
Since the assemblies were not uniform, the text does not list the "concurrent audience" (saha-śruta-jana) following the descriptions of the city and the mountain.

Next, the section beginning with "If that were so" (*yadi cet*) explains the doubt; it is divided into two parts. First, regarding the one who raises the doubt: if it is said that the assembly was not seated in a single location...

Regarding those listed as co-hearers: if this were the case, Ānanda would not have been at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa when the teaching was given in the chamber of Śraddhālakṣaṇa, nor would he have heard what was spoken in the dream;

furthermore, it would be improper for the sūtra to begin with "Thus have I heard" (evam mayā śrutam). Although [this objection] has been raised below to resolve the difficulty, the Buddha spoke further to address it.
The *Bao'en jing* (Sūtra on Requiting Kindness) states: "The Buddha sought an attendant, and Ānanda gave his consent. Furthermore—
He made four vows: first, not to accept worn-out robes; second, not to accept special invitations;

third, that while the other bhikṣus were permitted to see the World-Honored One twice daily—at dawn and at dusk—he would not be so restricted, but could see him whenever he wished (one must consult the *Fahua Wenju Ji* for this passage);

fourth, that whatever Dharma the Buddha had preached over twenty years should be recounted to him again. The Buddha briefly indicated the general outlines of these points, and Ānanda [recounted them all].
Furthermore, regarding those who attain the Buddha-awakening samādhi and are able to achieve self-penetration, the *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states:
"Ānanda cultivated the dhyāna of non-forgetfulness and attained the Buddha-awakening samādhi; by the power of this samādhi, he was able to hear [the teachings] himself.

What is called "Buddha-awakening" refers simply to the power of the Buddha’s added awakening, like the "Buddha-ear" samādhi. Since one has already realized it, it is not something heard from the Buddha.
It is said that he was able to understand it on his own. Ānanda was born on the night the Buddha attained enlightenment; he became the attendant at the age of twenty-five.

Since he was already able to hear [the teachings] in accordance with the two aforementioned meanings in all the sūtras prior to this, how much more so would he not have heard what was spoken in the chamber of Śraddhālakṣaṇa and what was spoken within his dream?

Next, the explanation of the introductory section that sets forth the two sequences (the *nidāna* and the *upodghāta*) is divided into two parts. First, a general analysis of the text according to these two meanings is further divided into two sections.
First, the two meanings are collectively presented as also being called the "introductory section" (*pṛthag-nidāna*), which distinguishes it from other sūtras.

Regarding the term "introductory section," it encompasses both the *nidāna* (narrative setting) and the *upodghāta* (introduction); whereas the single term "narrative setting" (*nidāna*) refers only to that which constitutes the introductory section.

One should understand that the introductory section (nidāna) is distinguished as follows: the "General Introduction" (sāmānya-nidāna) is so named because its text is general while its meaning is general, as it encompasses all teachings;

thus there is a general meaning, yet its intent is specific, for it resides within the various flavors (rasa) of the teaching. The "Specific Introduction" (viśeṣa-nidāna), however, has both a specific text and a specific meaning, as it does not open up other sections;

this is like the incident of holding the bowl with the lid closed, which occurs in the sutra at hand and possesses a specific meaning. Furthermore, there is also a case where the meaning is specific...

The general introduction (samanta-nidāna) is universal because it applies to all teachings; furthermore, while it is universal in its introductory text, its meaning is distinct, as it varies in length according to each specific section and its corresponding teaching.
The specific introduction (pratiniyata-nidāna) is distinct in its text but universal in its meaning, as it universally describes the extent of the teachings within each specific section.

Because one wishes to encompass both the universal and the specific, these two introductions correspond to one another such that their names are self-evident, yet they also serve as the basis for their respective specific designations. As it is said: [text follows].
The previous section has already been shown.

Next, regarding the distinct meanings, there are seven; these are further divided into two pairs based on two meanings, which again form two sections. First, concerning the specific introduction (*nidāna*), there are two parts.
First, regarding the division of the text into seven distinct sections, there are two parts: first, the division of the text, and second, the "arising" (*utpatti*), which is merely—

Next, there are both general and specific [explanations]. Generally, all seven meanings are fully present; specifically, "arising" (*utpāda*) refers to what precedes, meaning that which is capable of producing what follows.
"Emergence" (*samudaya*) refers to what follows, arising from what precedes. That the Buddha is always in meditative concentration is as it is said:
"The *nāga* is always in concentration. (*Nāga* here means "dragon" or "elephant"; because its strength is greatest, it is used as a metaphor. It refers to the multitude and to striking.
Therefore, the demonstration of ritual protocols manifests the entry into meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

To state that the King of Sūtras is presented "upon emerging" means that from the beginning to the end of this sūtra, [the Buddha] remains entirely within concentration; it is only upon the tree deity’s earnest entreaty in the "Chapter on Praising the Buddha" that he rises from *samādhi*.
What is now called "presenting the King of Sūtras upon emerging" is merely a designation for the verbal narration occurring within concentration.
This is merely for the sake of clarification. If one follows Yi Jing’s translation of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, it says:

Regarding the five kinds of the three truths (*tri-satya*), there is no mention of a "Middle Truth" as established in the *Tongjiao* (Shared Teaching), and so forth. In the *Gushan Ji*, the three characters "Jin Guang Ming" (Golden Light) are taken to represent the three kinds of three truths, explained solely from the perspective of the perfectly interfused (*yuanrong*) doctrine and principle.
That is to say: if one clings to the expressive words (*neng-quan*) as being the sutra itself, then "Jin Guang Ming" would merely be conventional words;
thus, it is said to be the "three kinds of conventional truth" (*san zhong su-di*). If, however, one clings to that which is expressed (*suo-quan*)...
If the principle-body (*ri-tai*) is taken as the *sūtra*, then because the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* is free from verbal expression, it is said that there are "three kinds of true truths" (*tri-satya*).
If one does not cling exclusively to either of the two extremes and knows that letters are themselves liberation, then the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* is the Middle Way;

thus it is said that there are "three kinds of middle ways. (The Xichuan critique says: "If we were to interpret the meaning of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra-rāja* according to the feminine [principle], would this not be the sixfold three truths? And so forth. The Siming Record says: "Three..."

The conventional three truths are the three kinds of middle way of the aforementioned three teachings—namely, the Round teaching that connects with the Shared and Distinct, and the Round teaching in its own right.

(Xiachuan’s critique states: "The first seems like seven and two; the latter is like five and three," and so forth. Xiachuan’s *Zhangmen* says: "The three kinds of conventional and true [truths] correspond to the three teachings of the Shared, Distinct, and Round;

the three kinds of middle way correspond to the Round teaching that connects with the Shared and Distinct, and the Round teaching in its own right. Furthermore, he indicates the inclusion of all phenomena as follows:

Regarding the inclusion of the five kinds of threefold truths within the three kinds of threefold truths (I now briefly challenge this: the *Wenju* only clarifies the three conventional and three true aspects of the threefold truths;

why is it necessary to employ the principle of including the five kinds of threefold truths within the three kinds? Furthermore, the three kinds of threefold truths lack the truth and convention of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), while the five kinds of threefold truths lack those of the Distinct Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*) and the Distinct-Shared junction;

since these advances and retreats are not consistent, they cannot be used). I now say: The *Vimalakīrti-mahāyāna-sūtra-śāstra* states that there are two kinds of two truths: first, those outside the principle (*li-wai*); second, those within the principle (*li-nei*). First...
If one explains the two truths without relying on Buddha-nature, these are the two truths outside of principle (*li-wai*).

If one explains the two truths by relying on Buddha-nature, these are the two truths within principle (*li-nei*). There are two types of the "outside of principle": first, the two truths of non-identity and reduction;
second, the two truths of mutual identity and non-arising. The "within principle" also has two types: first, the non-identity of non-arising... [text fragment].
The measure [of truth] consists of the two truths. These two aspects are further the two truths of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Moreover, within the principle itself, there are again three kinds:
first, clarifying the two truths by conjoining the Middle Way with the True Truth; second, clarifying the two truths by conjoining the True Truth with the Conventional Truth;

and third, clarifying the two truths by means of the inconceivable (*acintya*). Regarding the first—clarifying the two truths by conjoining the Middle Way with the True Truth—it is still the Teaching of Commonality (*tongjiao*).
These two truths not only apply to the Two Vehicles, but also extend to the Separate and Perfect Teachings. Why is this? As the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Buddha-nature is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). The wise perceive both emptiness and non-emptiness;
non-emptiness is the Middle Way, and emptiness is the Real. Thus, we know that the Middle Way unifying with the Real constitutes the ultimate truth. Next...
First, regarding the synthesis of the ultimate truth with the conventional to form the two truths, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"I and Maitreya together spoke of the truths, yet the five hundred śrāvakas thought we were speaking of the ultimate truth. This refers to the two truths of the Separate Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*).

Third, clarifying the two truths through the inconceivable: the preceding explanation of the two kinds of two truths within the realm of principle—that they are non-dual yet dual—is the inconceivable.

Regarding the discussion of the two truths (*satya*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*): next, concerning what is to be accepted or rejected—if the two truths were outside of principle (*li*), then not only would the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) fail to be the essence of this sutra, but the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) would likewise fail to be so. If, however, the two truths are within principle, then the three kinds of conventional truths are also not the essence of the sutra;

rather, the three kinds of ultimate truths are precisely the true substance of the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) and the *bhūtatathatā* (suchness). Question: One should therefore accept only the Perfect Teaching.

Question: Since the inconceivable ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is the essence [of this teaching], how can it take the internal-ultimate truths (*tathatā-satya*)—both the Shared (*sādhāraṇa*) and the Distinct (*pratyekabuddha*)—as its essence? Answer:
If one were to directly abandon the provisional means (*upāya*) as in the *Lotus Sūtra*, one could simply take the single ultimate truth of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*) as the essence.
However, because this sūtra still retains the two types of provisional means—the Shared and the Distinct—the three kinds of internal ultimate truths may all serve as its essence. Nevertheless...
There is only the distinction between the lateral and the upright, and between the inconceivable and the true reality (paramārtha-satya) [as stated in that text].

Since the two truths within the principle have already been divided into three types—opening the two to make three—is this not indeed so? That text clarifies the two truths in their threefold aspect according to the internal principle, distinguishing the conventional from the real;
now, when clarifying the King of Sutras, how could it not likewise distinguish right from wrong by means of the threefold three truths?
Moreover, since the "Kings of Sutras" (the Mahāyāna sūtras) describe the very essence [of the Dharma], we know that while the names of these royal essences differ, their principle is identical.

Furthermore, since the present sutra and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* both belong to the Vaipulya (Vaipulya/ Fangdeng) category, we know that the three mundane and three true aspects within the present text—exemplified by the profound [teachings] of the *Vimalakīrti*—are simply the three kinds of the Three Truths within the realm of principle.
Thus, the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), in its analysis of the teachings, states: "The four teachings clarify..."

As for the meaning, within the "Shared Teaching" (Tongjiao) that subsumes the Shared, one immediately attains the "Distinct" (Bie) and the "Perfect" (Yuan). When principle and text coincide, this refers to the mutual identity of the True and the Conventional;
"coinciding" means being identical, just as, for example, the conditions (*pratyaya*) and causes (*hetu*) are unified with the nature (*dhātu*).

However, regarding the two types—the Shared and the Distinct—when they are called "the coincidence of principle and text," it is as stated in the *Shiqian* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning): "By means of the verses attached to the treatise, [they] temporarily..."
To name its reality immediately is not yet to reach it.
If one speaks of the other truths, the following section provides a further clarification: the "other truths" refer to the three conventional and three ultimate truths;
these are the scriptures but not the King, just as the three kinds of worldly truths cannot serve as the essence. The Middle Way is the scripture and is the King.
For example, the three kinds of *satya* (truths) constitute the essence of the true nature (*dharmatā*) and the real aspect (*lakṣaṇa*).

If one applies this analogy to the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, it should further be said that because this sutra still retains both the provisional and the distinct types of skillful means (*upāya*), all three kinds of Middle Way within the "inner principle" (*li-nei*) may serve as the sovereign.
Is the meaning of "collateral" (*bàng*) and "principal" (*zhèng*) not thus established? Siming [Zhiyuan] thereby connects the Perfect (*yuán*) with the Provisional (*jiē*) and the Distinct (*bié*).

Furthermore, regarding the "three kinds of Middle Way" within the *Zhengxuanyi* (Meaning of the Correct Explanation), it is said that the Great Master [Zhiyi] explained the essence (*ti*) from the perspective of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*),

yet judged the teaching (*jiaopan*) as belonging to the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*). To take the Middle Way of the Shared Teaching as the essence of the Dharma-nature King (*faxing wang*) of this sutra—
and even to say, "The name subsumes the three kings, while the judgment of the teachings distinguishes the four kings"— is this not an extreme case of erroneous exposition?

Regarding the resolution of doubts concerning the nine types [of teachings], specifically the lower three, some may harbor the suspicion: "If the three mundane and the three true [teachings] are merely *sūtras* and not *rājas*, why is it necessary to clarify them?
Therefore, this commentary explains: "As for the term 'king' (*rāja*), its meaning lies in 'ruling.

Among the three kinds of Middle Way, the King of the Threefold Middle Way possesses mastery over the texts of the three kinds of true and mundane teachings; thus, within the text, it is still designated by way of its capacity."

Because it is spoken in accordance with what is appropriate, it is merely said to be "ninefold. Question: Since the preceding and following texts all rely upon the four teachings (*catur-yāna*), why does this present text not mention the *Tripiṭaka* (Śrāvaka) teaching?

Answer: Since the term "beyond principle" (*li-wai*) already encompasses both the *Tripiṭaka* and the *Prativedha* (Skt. *pratyekabuddha*) teachings, how could it refer exclusively to the *Tripiṭaka* alone? Furthermore, the *Prativedha* teaching is the initial gateway to the Mahāyāna;

while it penetrates the Middle Way and the True Reality of the *Vaipulya* (Skt. *vaipulya*) and *Agrayāna* (Skt. *anuttara-yāna*), it nonetheless remains within the realm of principle (*li-nei*). If [the present text were to exclude it]...

Since the teachings of the Tripiṭaka are expedient means of the "clumsy" vehicle (*dauḥprajña*), the *Lotus Sūtra* and those preceding it—though manifest and revealed—do not yet discuss the Middle Way as the sovereign ruler of the Tripiṭaka;
thus, they simply do not speak of it. If there is a single sound with diverse understandings, then one distinguishes them by means of the four teachings (*caturvidha-dharma-paryāya*);
in explaining such matters, nothing of the Tripiṭaka is omitted.
However, following the King of Sūtras, it is now clarified that the establishment of teachings according to conditions differs.

Since the three types of Three Truths previously explained were based on the classification of teachings (*jiao*), the current explanation of the entire lifetime of the Buddha’s teaching must necessarily be based on the classification of sections (*bu*). If the essence of the King [of Sūtras] is elucidated, it manifests of itself;
therefore, its division from the Truth of Reality (*tattva-satya*) is distinct. This section is divided into three parts: first, the formal elucidation that the King of Sūtras alone is one.

Regarding these, although they are distinguished as three types of Middle Way according to their teachings—differing in being collateral or primary—when discussing the essential nature of the principle (*li-ti*), there is no distinction;

thus, it is but a single principle. Yet, although it is one, the names established according to its随缘 (following conditions) are likewise different. Therefore, the titles used in the *Avataṃsaka* and other sutras vary.
Because the *Prajñāpāramitā* can give birth to all Buddhas of the three periods of time, it is called the "Mother of Buddhas. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* explains...

The analogy of the topknot and the jewel illustrates that the revelation of the provisional to manifest the real (*kaiquan xianshi*)—what is called the *Nirvāṇa* and what is termed "the Dharma which is the Teacher of all Buddhas"—are all alternative names for the *dharmatā*.
This is because they take the manifestation of the real as being identical; therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the present [text] are no different.
Thus, the *Shiqian* states: "Among the bodhisattvas of the shared stage, there are those of sharp faculties who are able to perceive the non-empty," which refers precisely to this.
Amoghasiddhi constitutes the essence of this present sutra; however, if one speaks in terms of its *nikāya* (division), it still retains elements of expedient means (*upāya*).

Therefore, it must not be conflated with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-mahāyāna-sūtra-śāstra* states: "If the *Saddharmapuṇṇarīka* directly abandons expedient means, it may take as its essence only the single True Truth (*ekam satyam*) of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*);
this sutra, however, still retains the three types of principles within the internal [teaching] of both the Shared and Distinct [vehicles]."
Since all truths can serve as the essence of the Pure Name, and this being so, how could it not be the case here?
Therefore, the preceding text states that "among the three kinds of Middle Way, this sutra is the king"; this is precisely that meaning.

If, furthermore, the *Miaoxuan* takes five kinds of truths and five kinds of middle ways as the essence of the *Lotus Sutra*, this is because, within the context of the marvelous realm of revelation and manifestation, one further...

This is merely a simplification based on the contrast between the provisional and the real; therefore, it differs from the profound meaning expressed in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, which states that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* "directly abandons expedient means and employs only the single True Truth of the Perfect Teaching," thereby discarding the provisional.
Next, regarding the analogy [in the text] that mentions "the various surnames" and so forth: these are the surnames of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors.

"Responding to the destiny" (*yingyun*) means responding to the destiny of the Five Elements (*wuxing*) as they generate one another according to the mandate of Heaven. "Alternating" (*die*) means succeeding one another; "arising" (*xing*) means emerging.

Fuxi of the Great Clarity (*Taihao*) was of the Feng surname and ruled with the virtue of Wood. He was the first to establish the *jia* calendar and the five cycles (*wuyun*), taking the brilliance of the sun and moon as their model; this is called the "Great" (*Tai*).
Hao received the auspicious sign of the Dragon Chart and thus recorded his officials by dragon. Yan Di, the Lord Shen Nong, was of the Jiang clan;
he ruled with the virtue of Fire and recorded his officials by fire. Huang Di of Youxiong was of the Gong-sun clan; Zi Qingyang ascended the throne and became Shao Hao.
Shao Hao, the Lord Jintian, was named Zhi and styled Qingyang; he ruled with the virtue of Metal and received the auspicious sign of the phoenix.
The Bird Era was ruled by Guan Zhuanxu, Lord Gaoyang, whose virtue was Water; Emperor Kuo Gaosin, whose virtue was Water;
and Emperor Yao Taodang, named Fangxun, surnamed Yiqi, whose virtue was Fire. Emperor Shun Youyu, surnamed Yao and named Chonghua, whose virtue was Earth, ruled as King.
Those who established themselves as Hegemons according to the times were like names established according to conditions—though they differ, their unification under a single King is one.
This is an analogy for how [this sutra] serves as the essence for all scriptures, clarifying that this King of Sutras is one and the same.

The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is also like this. Regarding the following three points of correspondence: the names and essences of kings may arise or perish according to what is appropriate and pleasing to the conditions of sentient beings;
therefore, the *dharmatā* of this sutra acts as the king, just as in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, the Buddha [is the king].

While the rise of the Mother Jewel (Mātṛ-ratna) led to the cessation and disappearance of other names, this merely reflects that although the titles established by successive hegemonies differ according to the times,
it can be understood that the sovereign ruler remains one and the same.
Next, as for the concluding summary below: since the threefold Three Truths have already been established, this further clarifies how the entire dispensation of the One Vehicle is subsumed.
Therefore, above, it does not contradict the intent of the King of Sutras (the *Avataṃsaka*), and below, it does not increase the arrogance of sentient beings;

for in the various Mahāyāna sutras such as the *Avataṃsaka*, the Dharmakāya and so forth are explained with names different from the present "Dharmatā" (Dharma-nature), yet they are identical in essence—all being the sovereign body (*rājātman*).
This is not because it is a partial teaching intended to prevent those lacking wisdom from conceiving arrogance toward the various sūtras.

[The section] "Subtle and Wondrous" (Section Three) explains the text that sets forth the school's tenet; it is divided into two parts. First, the explanation of "subtle and wondrous," which is further divided into two:

first, recounting the interpretations of others, and second, clarifying the present author’s own intent. Regarding the phrase "the nature and virtuous qualities within the cause are profound": this means they penetrate the source of the three truths. If it were not...
Because even the Buddha-eye cannot behold it, it is said to be difficult to see. "Neither vertical nor horizontal" means that while it is one, it is three;
since these three are not separate entities, it is not horizontal. While it is three, it is one; since it is neither before nor after, it is not vertical.
This applies equally to both cause and effect.

Next, the explanation of the passage concerning the protection and sustenance by the four Buddhas of the four directions is divided into two parts. First, the explanation according to the doctrinal meaning, which is further divided into two.
First, the direct explanation: the term "protection and sustenance" (hùchí) also implies "protective mindfulness" (hùnian). Therefore, the subsequent text states:
"The Buddhas of the ten directions constantly mind this sutra. This is the first point. Next, the distinction between the peripheral and the primary is shown.

Next, the explanation of the text by way of contemplating the mind is divided into three parts. First, regarding the explanation by way of the Four Noble Truths: the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*) is "eye";
the knowledge regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*) is "wisdom"; the subsequent patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti*) is "clarity";

and the subsequent knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) is "awakening. The same applies to the remaining three truths. Therefore, one should know that contemplating these four truths gives rise to eye, wisdom, clarity, and awakening.
Because they are restricted by what is small, the contemplations of the four teachings all contemplate the Four Truths to give rise to the eye of wisdom and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding the subsequent contemplation of the [four] virtues, this *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* explains it within the section on "Harmonizing the Path Factors" (*Mārga-pakṣya-dharma*), stating: "The mind of the dharma-nature is fundamentally not permanent;

ordinary beings recklessly conceptualize it as such, which is called the 'inversion of permanence. The dharma-nature is in reality not impermanent; the followers of the Two Vehicles recklessly conceptualize it as impermanent. Now...
Contemplating that the mind is empty, all things are empty; within emptiness there is no permanence—how can one say that the mind continues in a succession of moments?

This is called the ordinary person’s perversion of permanence, which destroys the mindfulness of withered thoughts and establishes the contemplation of the mind as empty. Contemplating that the mind is provisional, all things are provisional;

if the mind were impermanent, how could it discern the infinite characteristics of the mind? This is called the Two Vehicles’ perversion of impermanence, which destroys the mindfulness of flourishing thoughts and establishes the contemplation of the mind as provisional.
When the foundations of mindfulness are established, one further contemplates that the mind is neither empty nor provisional, but the negation of both emptiness and provisionality;

it is neither permanent nor impermanent, neither withered nor flourishing, as the Middle Way principle is revealed. One should contemplate the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*) and so forth by analogy.
Regarding "from the east to the north," the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The pair in the east is a metaphor for permanence and impermanence; in the south..."
The pair in the eastern direction symbolizes pleasure and non-pleasure; the pair in the western direction symbolizes self and non-self;

the pair in the northern direction symbolizes purity and impurity (the current text states "northern non-self," etc.). Because each of the four directions has a pair, they are called the "Double Trees" (*yugandhara*).

In each direction, one tree withers while the other flourishes: flourishing symbolizes permanence and so forth, while withering symbolizes impermanence and so forth. Within this space, the Tathāgata lies with his head toward the north.
"Lying down signifies neither decay nor flourishing" (and so forth). To refute the notion of a "self," the character "equal" (等) is missing below [the phrase].

Regarding the three explanations and four names of the Buddhas under the "Truth of Accumulation" (*samudaya-satya*) of the Eastern Direction: the four Buddha names explained here are all spoken in reference to the contemplation of the mind and its adherence to principle;
therefore, they cannot be understood solely through conventional phenomena. For example, Amitābha is translated as "Immeasurable Life."
This is merely a reversal of the finite nature of the segmented birth-body (paricchinna-janma-kāya) by means of its immeasurability;
why is this so? Because the *sambhogakāya* of the *vairocana*-type is reversed by means of Vairocana.

Thus, Vairocana is translated as "Universal Radiance" (*prabhāsvara-vyāpin*), which refers to the immeasurable and boundless radiance and form of the *sambhogakāya*. Now, this [present discussion] concerns the [reversal] in terms of phenomena-as-such (*vastu*).
However, according to principle, one contemplates that the pure *dharmatā* of the Path Truth (*mārgasatya*) in the Western [Pure Land] is such that its lifespan is equal to empty space;

thus it is called "Immeasurable Life" (*Amitāyus*). This is also like Jingxi’s explanation regarding Śākyamuni possessing the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, which—similar to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*—state that each individual mark and characteristic is equal to empty space.
Therefore, in this context, we rely on the *dharmatā* which is the double negation of the two extremes.
It is called Akṣobhya because it is immovable; since *akṣobhya* is translated as "immovable" (*bù dòng*), this is the meaning.

"Eternally quiescent as the Self" refers to the quality of "Self" (*ātman*) among the four virtues. That which is named the "Secret Treasury" (*guhyagarbha*) is called the "Subtle and Wondrous Sound" because its three virtues are subtle and wondrous;
thus it is termed the "Secret Treasury. The phrase "note: etc. indicates that one should speak in such a manner. This is the *Buddhānusmṛtisamādhi*.
The Sūtra states: "In the north there is a land named Padmavyūha and a Buddha named Sūkṣmasvara; in the south there is a land named Nandā and a Buddha named Ratnākara.
Regarding these two Buddhas of the east and west, they are as clearly explained elsewhere [in the text] (etc.).

I shall now provide the fourth section of the commentary, which consists of two parts: first, the division of the text; second, the word-by-word explanation. This latter part is divided into four sections.

First is the explanation of the supreme dharma that performs the refutation. This section is further divided into two parts: first, the formal explanation of the division of the text, which is itself divided into three parts.

First is the general explanation of the "object-dharma" (*dharmadharma*) and "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*). These correspond to what is stated below regarding the "place of repentance. Therefore, the subsequent text explains the place of repentance as follows:
This is precisely the immeasurable and profoundly deep *dharmatā*; *dharmatā* is simply the principle of truth (*satya*), and the principle of truth is simply the wondrous realm (and so forth).

The "practicing dharma" and "guiding dharma" are merely the chapters on Repentance, Praise, and Emptiness. Thus, the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), in clarifying the function [of the repentance], states:
"The chapter on Emptiness guides both repentance and praise; without attaining emptiness, evil is not eradicated, and without attaining emptiness, good is not purified."

The text states that "all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*) serves as the root," which is precisely this meaning. Regarding the phrase "if they mutually assist," the following section distinguishes [the teachings] according to their doctrinal systems (*yāna*).
This section is divided into two parts: first, the Distinct Teaching (*pratyekabuddhayāna*). "Mutual assistance" (*zī*) means to aid; "manifestation" (*xiǎn*) means to clarify.

"Practice" (*xíng*) refers to the dharmas of practice, while "wisdom" (*zhì*) refers to the guiding dharmas. "Principle" (*lǐ*) refers to the objective dharmas. When the principle is fully manifested and suffering is exhausted, it corresponds to what the Sūtra says: "it is able to destroy."
The exhaustion of all suffering, the perfection of wisdom regarding unwholesome karma, and the omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*) that serves as its fundamental merit—these are unsurpassed.
This is what the Sūtra means when it says, "the merits produced are unsurpassed. As for the phrase "mutually supporting," it means they are mutually required;
thus, the *Miaoxuan* states: "Now, 'practice' (*xing*) signifies advancing forward; without wisdom, one does not advance. Although wisdom guides practice, [without practice]..."

When the object is not [correctly perceived], it is called "non-right wisdom" (*asamyag-jñāna*). When one reaches the Cool Lake by means of the "feet of practice," one understands that this practice is the fundamental practice capable of accomplishing wisdom.
Thus, as practice is fulfilled, wisdom becomes perfect; wisdom can manifest principle, and when principle is exhausted, wisdom ceases.

Regarding such mutual dependence of practice and wisdom, the *Miaozong Chao* (Explanatory Notes on the Profound Meaning) states: "The practice of mutual dependence exists specifically in the Separate Teaching (*bhedavyākaraṇa*), and it is also present in the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings."

This meaning is shallow and superficial in principle; therefore, it is set aside and not discussed (and so forth). Next, regarding the Perfect [Teaching], it is as stated in the *Myōgen* (*Miaoxuan*):

"This 'wonderful' [nature] and the preceding object and wisdom are one when considered as three, and three when considered as one; thus, object, wisdom, and practice each possess the three. The *Shiqian* (*Shizhiguan*) states:
"Now, in clarifying the person of the Perfect [Teaching], because object, wisdom, and practice—each being one and yet possessing the three—are complete, they are called 'wonderful.'"
