Regarding these three sets of three practices, they do not depend upon one another; furthermore, the three functions of object, wisdom, and practice correspond respectively to the three virtues (triguṇa), neither vertically nor horizontally (and so forth).
Although this is the case for the Perfect and Distinct [teachings], the concluding summary for the three lower [teachings] is as follows:

since this sutra is common to the Three Vehicles, its repentance should also encompass the two teachings of the Treasury (Hīnayāna) and the Shared (Shared Mahāyāna); thus, the *Shiqian* states: "The two teachings of the Treasury and the Shared also possess this meaning."
Furthermore,

in the section "Raising the New to Reveal the Old," it says that the old text is abbreviated in its phrasing because the *Chen* (Prophecy) version contains only the passage concerning the four Buddhas preaching the fruit of permanence for those of superior faculties to receive benefit;
the new version, however, fully possesses the three cycles of the Brahmā’s discourse on the Dharma-body.
Regarding the passage "There are no relics, etc.," the new edition states after the Chapter on Lifespan (*Āyuṣpramāṇa-parivarta*):
"At that time, there was in the great assembly a brahmin of the Kauṇḍinya clan who wished to seek and make offerings to the relics of the Tathāgata.

Then, within this assembly, there was also a prince from the kingdom of Licchavi who, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, spoke these verses: 'Even if [one were to cast them] into a swift-flowing current...'"
If the *jīvaka* flower were to grow upon the body of the World-Honored One, his bodily relics (*śarīra*) would ultimately be unobtainable;
even if one could fashion garments from tortoise hair, the Buddha’s body is not false and thus never possesses relics.
Even if one could build a city tower from the legs of mosquitoes, there is no matter of relics in the Tathāgata’s tranquil body; it would be as if one were to construct a ladder from rabbit horns.

It is impossible for one on earth to ascend to heaven, for evil thoughts to accrue the merit of the *śarīra*, for a rat to climb a ladder made of rabbit horns, or for one to eat the moon and destroy the asuras;
likewise, it is impossible to exhaust all delusions and attain liberation through the *śarīra*.
At that time, having heard this meaning, Kauṇḍinya immediately spoke a verse in response to the prince, saying: "You are a true son of the Buddha, a person of great auspiciousness; all..."
The true Dharma of Perfect Enlightenment is the body; the purity of the dharma-realm is what is called the Tathāgata.

Having heard and understood this meaning, I have sought the śarīra relics to open the gate of skillful means for the purpose of requesting the Tathāgata to extensively expound and analyze the meaning of reality.
At that time, thirty-two thousand devaputras in the assembly heard this teaching on the profound lifespan of the Tathāgata.

Having thus fully awakened the mind set upon unsurpassed bodhi (and so forth), in the "Chapter on the Differentiation of the Three Bodies," after the Tathāgata had differentiated the meaning of the three bodies, the Bodhisattvas and devas addressed the World-Honored One, saying: "There are four benefits:
first, all kings shall have no enemies; second, their ministers shall be harmonious and joyful, free from strife; third, the people shall be peaceful, happy, wealthy, and prosperous."

Fourth, during the three periods [of the day], the four great elements are harmoniously balanced; these humans and devas increase their protective guardianship, and with a mind of compassion and equanimity, they harbor no intent to harm (and so forth).
The current mention in the introduction of "dharmas such as repentance" refers to the dharmas of the three subsequent cycles [of teaching].
Since the introduction states "dharmas such as repentance," it is known that this is a summary of the three sections of the formal exposition (*samyag-vyākhyāna*) below.
According to the Zhou dynasty’s legal codes, the original text of the *Zhengshuo* (Correct Exposition) merely clarifies that the four Buddhas preach the eternal fruit;
it does not mention that the Brahmins preach the Dharma-body or that there are no śarīras, and so forth. Therefore, we know that this is simply an abbreviation of the wording.

Next, the explanation of the evil offenses to be refuted: the phrase "narrating the Chapter on Emptiness" refers back to the preceding section, as it describes the exposition of the seventeen chapters that follow.
From the passage beginning with "those with impaired faculties" onwards is the actual narration of the Chapter on Emptiness. This section is divided into four parts: first, the division of the text;
second, the comparison with other sutras starting from "in other sutras"; third, the determination of the cause at the time of being able to provide a remedy; and fourth, [the conclusion].
Afflictions and karma are termed "causes," which can be remedied, halted, and eliminated through repentance;
however, the "fruits" are beyond remedy, for the retributive fruits are obstructed by karmic barriers and thus difficult to transform. Therefore, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:

"Karma may be prevented at the time of its cause, but once the fruit has manifested, there is nothing that can be done. For this reason, the Buddhas constantly teach and preach the Dharma during the causal stage.
When one is together with King Yama at the time of retribution, he then rebukes and interrogates one regarding which of the three obstacles is the most serious.
Some say that the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*) is the most serious because it cannot be transformed. Others say that because they follow along with the person, all are equally serious.
Question: Which of these can be transformed? Answer: All can be extinguished. If something can be transformed, it is not called an "obstacle" (*āvaraṇa*). (And so forth.)
That all three obstacles in this sutra can be transformed will be explained in detail below.

First, regarding the threefold explanation of the causes for the three obstacles, it is stated that they arise from the violation of the five precepts. The term "firstly" (*yīwǎng*) is used because the Buddha’s intention contains many layers of meaning;
for now, we shall rely upon one specific sense. Furthermore, the five precepts are the rules of discipline for laypeople who have received them.

Those who are called lay followers (upāsaka and upāsikā) must, if they wish to leave the household life, first receive the five precepts before they may receive the ten precepts and the full ordination (upasampadā).
This is because the Buddha-dharma is like the ocean, entering it gradually and becoming increasingly deep; there is a sequential order to it.
Since it is said that afflictions (*kleśa*) are the root, we know that it is precisely due to the obstruction of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) that the obstruction of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*) arises.

Now, proceeding directly to the explanation of the text concerning the three obstacles to be eliminated in the latter four sections, it is divided into three parts. First, the explanation of the text concerning the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*) to be eliminated, which is further divided into two parts.

First, the explanation according to the doctrinal meaning (*śāstrārtha*), which is again divided into two parts. First, the brief explanation, which is further divided into two parts: first, the general heading; second, [the detailed exposition].

The section on the specific explanation of the various faculties being externally deficient is divided into five parts. The first part explains the first two lines by way of the violation of the precept against killing; this is further divided into two.
First, the direct explanation of "the various faculties being externally deficient" refers here to the five faculties. Regarding "premature death within one’s lifespan":

"lifespan" (*āyus*) refers to a single period of existence, while "life-force" (*jīvita*) refers to that which maintains continuity. At the initial moment of conception, one possesses three factors: first, warmth (*uṣman*).

The second life-force (*āyus*), the third consciousness (*vijñāna*), and warmth (*uṣman*) constitute the body; it is because of warmth that the semen and blood do not decay. "Life-force" (*āyus*) refers to the cessation of the wind [of breath].
At the initial moment of entering the womb, there is a trace of vital energy; because this breath exists, it maintains the continuity of this body.

Since consciousness is the mind, when life ends prematurely—that is, "夭" (*yao*, meaning "to break off")—it is because the wind of the breath has been severed. Next, to cite scriptural proof, the *Huayan*...
The "Ten Stages" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The sin of taking life causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms;

if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution (the following four lines are cited here as an example): first, a short lifespan; second, much illness. Regarding the two retributions for stealing: first, poverty;
second, being unable to exercise mastery over shared property. Regarding the two retributions for sexual misconduct..."
First, one’s wife will not be chaste; second, one will not be able to act according to one’s will, and one’s kinsmen will speak falsely.
Regarding these two retributions: first, one will frequently be subjected to slander; second, one will be deceived by others.

As for the six kinds of offenses—divisive speech, harsh speech, and so forth, up to wrong view—each has two types of retribution, as explained in detail in the sutra, which should be understood from below. Next...

Regarding the explanation of the second two phrases concerning the violation of the precept against stealing, there are two parts: first, the direct explanation; second, the citation of scripture as proof. This second part is further divided into two:
first, the direct citation of those who are co-arisen and share the same name; specifically, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on the Human Dharma Realm," states:

"As soon as a person is born, two devas are constantly in attendance, following them: the first is called the Co-arisen Deva (*Sahaja-deva*), and the second is called the Same-name Deva (*Samāna-nāman-deva*)."
The statement that "humans commonly see one another, yet do not see heaven" implies that while the two heavens accompany one another, the dragon also provides assistance.
As for the statement that "Gongde Tian (Goddess of Merit) makes a vow to benefit [beings]," this refers to a deity who is neither co-nascent (*sahaja*) nor shares the same name;
it is as described in the "Chapter on Gongde Tian" of the present sutra (etc.). Furthermore, regarding the sequence of "first wealthy, then poor," this follows the order of priority.

The character *yan* (驗) is written as *qi* (棄) in modern times, though it was originally an archaic form. Third, regarding the violation of the precept against sexual misconduct, the commentary on the third couplet of the text is divided into two parts:

first, the direct explanation; second, the citation of scriptural evidence. This latter part is further divided into two: first, the direct citation from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (also known as the *Dazhidu jing*), which states:

"If a person guards [the precept], that person incurs anger; if one guards the Dharma, one destroys the [defilements of] the Dharma. Furthermore, women [are protected by] their parents, brothers, sisters, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the husband’s son is the Dharma-king of the world; how does he protect the Dharma?":

protecting the Dharma means that all women, whether ordained or lay, who receive the one-day precepts (upavāsa) are called "protectors of the Dharma. The subsequent passage from "formerly" onwards explains this by way of refutation, as can be seen.
Fourth, explaining the fourth phrase by way of the offense against the precept on false speech. Fifth, explaining the fifth phrase by way of the offense against the precept on alcohol.
The text is divided into two parts: first, the direct explanation; this also includes the phrase "internally failing in ritual propriety" added for its meaning.

*Hào* (pronounced huò) is the correct form of *xiāo*, meaning "to diminish" or "to extinguish. *Fèi* (pronounced fāng wèi) also means "to diminish. *Zūn jié* (pronounced zī sǔn) refers to the *Lìjì* (Book of Rites).

It says: "The gentleman is reverent and exercises restraint. The commentary notes: "Zun (樽) is a homophone for *ts'ui* (趨, meaning to hasten); *ai* (騃) means foolishness. Next, it cites a scripture as proof;
the text is from the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*. It states that because of drinking alcohol, resentment increases further, and thus [the consequences] are realized.
Next, the extensive explanation of the text below is divided into two parts. First, regarding the intent of the question:
why is it that this *Mahāyāna Suvarṇaprabhāsottama Sūtra* instead discusses its meaning by contrasting it with the five precepts of the *Hīnayāna*?
Next, the response is divided into two parts: first, a general demonstration of the opening [of categories], which refers to the manifestation of the ten wholesome paths of action and so forth;

and second, the closing [of categories], which refers to their synthesis into the three types of karma and so forth. Since it is said that the opening and closing of the five precepts relate to matters of great significance, we know that the preceding text constitutes a brief explanation, while from this point onward is the detailed explanation.
Next, regarding the *Tiwai jing* cited below as a separate scriptural source for explanation: the *Nanshan lüchao* (Commentary on the Vinaya of the Southern Mountain) classifies it as apocryphal.
However, according to the *Kaifu sanbao lu* (Record of the Three Jewels of the Kaihuang Era), Tanjing compiled the two-fascicle *Tiwai boli jing* at the Northern Terrace during the Yuan Wei dynasty.
Its text states: "The great mountain of the east is called Daiyue in the language of Han; because yin and yang alternate there, it is so named."

Regarding the term "Daiyaku" (代岳), there are two errors here: first, when a scripture was produced during the Wei dynasty, it should have been labeled "Wei-language" (魏言), yet it is instead labeled "Han-language" (漢言);
this failure to distinguish between eras is the first error. Second, Mount Tai (太山) is a term from this [Chinese] region, yet it is translated as "Daiyaku";
thus, these two terms are used interchangeably without recognizing their origins in either Sanskrit or Wei; this is the second error. There are many such instances, which cannot be fully enumerated.
The *Shujùlù* (Record of Narrating the Old) separately records one fascicle of the *Tíwèi jīng* (Sūtra of Tíwèi), which shares the same phrasing as various other sūtras;

however, it adds the "five phases" (*wǔ xíng*) and the "five directions" (*wǔ fāng*), using stone mixed with gold, which gives rise to doubt. Now, we take the version consisting of one fascicle as definitive (and so forth).
Nevertheless, what Tiantai cites does not distinguish between the authentic and the spurious; rather, he simply employs whatever corresponds [to his purpose].

These are merely [examples]; likewise, the *Qingjing faxing jing* (Sutra on the Practice of Pure Dharma) and the *Miaoshengding jing* (Sutra on the Sublime Samādhi), which the old catalogs designated as spurious, were included in the *Dazhou kan ding zhengzong lu* (Great Zhou Catalogue for Determining and Incorporating the Authentic Scriptures).
Furthermore, the *Jingdu sanmei jing* (Sutra on the Samādhi of Purifying the Crossing) was compiled and entered into the canon within the Great Zhou records.

Additionally, there are the *Jiushi liudao jing* (Sutra on the Ninety-Six Paths), the *Chujiao jingxiang* (Scripture on the Images of the Initial Teaching), the *Faxiang jueyi jing* (Sutra on Resolving Doubts Regarding the Semblance Dharma), and the *Ruguang jing* (Sutra of the Milk-Light Buddha), among others from the old [catalogs].

Some records may describe certain texts as doubtful or spurious; however, even if our own school cites them because their textual meanings are correct, it may be that the translators’ names were lost.

For instance, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (Latter Part) was included among the "spurious" catalogs until the time of the Tang dynasty’s compilation and verification, when it was finally admitted into the authentic canon.

Furthermore, the *Sūtra of Examining One's Karma* (*Zancha jing*) was only admitted into the authentic canon after the Great Catalog (*Dazhou lu*) was finalized. How can one conclude that a text is spurious simply because people of that time had not yet reached a definitive judgment?

The Great Master personally realized the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, yet his stage of realization belongs to the "first reliance" (*prathamāśraya*); one should not mistakenly cite this as being among the two [stages] in the middle. First, there is an explanation in terms of the mundane and supramundane;
next, there is an explanation in terms of phenomena and principle (*dharma-tattva*). The first [section] is further divided into two, the first of which explains according to the mundane.
This text consists of four parts. First, regarding the "Three Powers" (*trivarga*): in the *Tiewei jing* (Upāli-sūtra), an elder asks the Buddha why there are only five [precepts].

The Buddha’s answer to the five questions—rather than the four or six—constitutes the root of heaven and earth, the primordial state of the Grand One (Taiyi), and the beginning of the vital spirit (*shenqi*).
It governs heaven and earth, controls the Yin and Yang, and brings to fruition the spiritual essence of the myriad things and sentient beings.
Heaven sustains it through harmony; Earth sustains it so that the myriad things arise; and humans sustain it so that the five viscera are at peace. This is the spirit of heaven and earth.
The progenitor of the myriad things; thus there are but five (and so forth). Regarding the five planets: the Eastern Planet is the essence of wood, Jupiter;

the Southern Planet is the essence of fire, Mars; the Central Planet is the supreme essence, Saturn; the Western Planet is the essence of metal, Venus; and the Northern Planet is the essence of water, Mercury.
Regarding the five sacred peaks (*wuyue*), the *Erya* states: Mount Tai is the Eastern Peak, Mount Hua is the... [Western Peak].
Mount Huo of the Western Peak is the Southern Peak; Mount Heng is the Northern Peak; and Mount Songgao is the Central Peak.
It is further stated that "Heng is in Jiangnan," and the commentary notes that Mount Heng is the Southern Peak. Regarding the five viscera, these are the liver, heart, lungs, spleen, and kidneys.

Gu Shan says that the stars, peaks, and viscera are all correlated with the five elements (*wuxing*); however, when the five elements are paired with the five precepts, there are three [points of correspondence].

The meanings manifest themselves naturally: abstaining from killing corresponds to wood; wood governs growth, so that if one kills, there is no growth. Abstaining from sexual misconduct corresponds to fire;

fire governs illumination, whereas illicit lust is private and hidden. Abstaining from drinking corresponds to earth; earth is stable and tranquil, while intoxication causes instability and swaying. Abstaining from stealing corresponds to metal;

metal is associated with punishment and execution, so that if one steals, one encounters punishment. Abstaining from false speech corresponds to water; water takes on any shape according to its vessel.
To manifest non-delusion is to act truthfully; to be deluded is the opposite. To oppose Heaven is to turn one's back on the five planets;

to offend the Earth is to go against the five sacred peaks; to harm the body is to violate the five viscera. Wood presides over the East, and the East governs the liver; Metal presides over the West, and the West governs the lungs;
Water presides over the North, and the North governs the kidneys; Earth presides over the Center, and the Center governs the spleen.

Fire presides over the south, and the south presides over the heart. Next, regarding the correspondence with the Five Constant Virtues (*wuchang*), the *Tiewei jing* states that the five precepts one upholds shall bring about the fulfillment of the laws of the Five Bodies and the Five Virtues in accordance with the world. Killing is contrary to benevolence (*ren*); stealing is contrary to righteousness (*yi*);
lust is contrary to propriety (*li*); intoxication is contrary to wisdom (*zhi*); and falsehood is contrary to trustworthiness (*xin*). Furthermore, it expresses compassion for those who do not...
To kill [the unrighteous] and call it benevolence; to be clear-sighted and not steal, calling it righteousness; to guard against harm and refrain from lust, calling it propriety;

to restrain the mind and abstain from wine, calling it wisdom; and to speak nothing that is contrary to the law, calling it trustworthiness—these five cannot be compromised even in a moment of haste, nor can they be abandoned for even an instant.
The gentleman upholds them to establish his person. These three pairs constitute the Five Classics.

Gushan said: "The 'Shangshu' (Book of Documents) concludes with the Tang and Yu dynasties because it honors the abdication of the throne and disparages the use of force; thus, it corresponds to [the virtue of] not killing.

The Master, seeing that the House of Zhou had become weak and its edicts were no longer effective, compiled the Spring and Autumn Annals based on the records of Lu to replace the systems of reward and punishment;
consequently, rebellious ministers and treacherous sons were struck with fear; thus, it corresponds to [the virtue of] not stealing. There are five types of ritual."

Regarding the Rites, the *Zhou Li* (Rites of Zhou), in the section on the Grand Minister of Sacrifices (*Dazongbo*), states: "By means of auspicious rites (*jili*), one serves the spirits and deities of the states; 'serving' refers to sacrificing to them, offering to them, and entertaining them.

By means of calamitous rites (*xiongli*), one expresses sorrow for the misfortunes of the states; 'expressing sorrow' refers to relieving their distress and sharing their disasters. By means of guest rites (*binli*), one brings the states into intimacy;

'intimacy' refers to causing them to be mutually attached and harmonious. By means of military rites (*junli*), one unifies the states; 'unification' refers to intimidating those who are discordant or deviant. By means of celebratory rites (*jiali*), one brings the myriad [people] into intimacy..."

The people (the character *min* signifies "to admire the good," for it is by means of what the human heart admires that regulations are established). Sexual licentiousness is a failure to interact according to ritual;
therefore, the rites of admiration (*jia li*) are employed to warn against sexual licentiousness. Poetry praises the good and satirizes the evil—it is no idle speech.

The *Yi* is a book for exhausting principle and perfecting nature, a teaching of purity, stillness, refinement, and subtlety. How could one who is intoxicated and disorderly from drinking wine be capable of exhausting principle or attaining purity?

In the *Zheng* (The Quiescent), it is further stated that the *Zhi guan* (Cessation and Contemplation) says: "Rituals clarify the regulation of propriety, thereby preventing the drinking of alcohol; music harmonizes the mind, thereby preventing lust; the *Shi* (Odes) employ satire, thereby preventing killing;

the *Shangshu* (Book of Documents) clarifies righteousness and yielding, thereby preventing theft; and the *Yi* (Changes) divines the Yin and Yang, thereby preventing false speech. The *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Meaning of the Practice of the Way) states:
"This differs slightly from the meaning of the 'Confrontation' (*dìng*) with Tiwei; thus we know that all meanings of 'confrontation' follow a general, one-sided approach."

[The commentary on] the *Śruti* [states]: "The four pairs correspond to the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*). This is divided into three parts: first, the direct correspondence with the ten wholesome paths.
Regarding 'the three of the body,' namely killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct: 'not killing, not stealing, and not engaging in sexual misconduct' are the three wholesome actions of the body.

'Not lying' subsumes the four wholesome actions of speech: (1) not lying, (2) not divisive speech, (3) not harsh speech, and (4) not frivolous speech. 'Not drinking intoxicants' subsumes the three wholesome actions of the mind: (1) non-covetousness, (2) non-malice, and (3) right view."

Since evil deviates from principle while goodness accords with truth, they are called the "ten wholesome actions. Regarding the phrase "the secular cannot [attain] the lower [stages]," this next section clarifies the reason for establishing the precepts;
because the five precepts are specifically intended for lay men and women, they are termed "secular. The *Śāstra* asks:
"For what reason are there no three types of restraint within the verbal discipline of an upāsaka? The answer is that among the four types of verbal karma, [the first is] false speech.

Speech is the most serious [of the vocal actions], and furthermore, false speech arises from a deliberate mental state; thus, the others are also subsumed. Moreover, by mentioning only "false speech," all three [vocal misdeeds] are already included.
Now, these ten wholesome paths of action are the ancient law of the Wheel-Turning King and are called *prakṛti-śīla* (natural precepts).

Regarding the five precepts, the first four are natural (*prakṛti*) and the last one is prohibitory (*pratikṣepaṇa*). Being natural means they were not established by the Buddha's decree; because they are inherently good or evil, they are called "natural."
The term *pratikṣepaṇa* (prohibition) refers to those precepts established by the Buddha as prohibitions; thus they are called "prohibitions" (*pratikṣepa*). Therefore, the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"Among the prohibitions, the abstention from alcohol alone is for the sake of protecting the other disciplinary rules. Now, it is said that if one can restrain oneself from alcohol, this prevents the three poisons of the mental ground and nurtures supramundane wisdom.
As for the [other] prohibitions, once they have been established as inherent offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), a further "prohibited offense" (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) is added to each.
Question: If not drinking alcohol is a precept established by the Buddha, how can it be correlated with "Wisdom" among the Five Constant Virtues (*wuchang*) and with the *Yi* among the Five Classics?
Answer: The *Book of Rites* states that alcohol is used because of sacrificial rituals; it does not mean that one may drink it habitually.

Therefore, it can be correlated with "Wisdom" among the Five Constant Virtues and the *Yi* among the Five Classics. To drink when it is not for a sacrifice already violates worldly propriety, let alone the precepts established by the Buddha. Furthermore, as for...

"Facing [the situation] is for the purpose of preventing disorder; therefore, Zhongni said, 'Only regarding wine, there is no limit to its consumption, provided one does not reach the point of disorder.

Disorder leads to the impairment of wisdom; thus, one faces it [with restraint]. Third, this is the concluding summary of the lower section. Regarding 'inherent transgressions' (prakṛti-sāvadya) and 'inherent virtues' (prakṛti-kuśala):

as for inherent precepts (*śīla*), they are transgressions when violated regardless of whether one has received them or not, and they are virtues when maintained. If one receives prohibitory precepts (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*) and maintains them, then merit arises."

If one commits an offense against merit, one incurs transgression; if there is no merit, there is likewise no transgression. Therefore, the natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*) serve as the foundation for the prohibitive precepts (*pratikṣepaṇa-śīla*).

Furthermore, following the Five Precepts, the next section explains the text from the perspective of the supramundane, divided into two parts: first, an explanation according to the teachings of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*). Regarding the term "solitary" (*gū*):

The Mountain Master said: "If one does not kill, the physical substance remains complete; if one does not steal, painful sensations do not arise; if one does not engage in sexual misconduct, perverse thoughts do not emerge;
if one does not speak falsely, the flow of existence becomes pure and substantial; if one does not drink intoxicants, discernment becomes clear.

Thus, the five aggregates are bound together as the four foundations of mindfulness (catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni). As for what is called 'opening,' 'opening' means to open up and facilitate; from these four foundations of mindfulness, right [view] arises once again."

From diligence up to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, one further opens and penetrates the three gates of liberation—emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
From these three gates, one proceeds through to the city of Nirvāṇa. As for the statement that "form can give rise to morality" (*śīla*) and so forth:

since morality is a dharma of form (*rūpa-dharma*), form can give rise to morality; since meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is correct reception (*samādhi*), it receives meditative absorption; and wisdom (*prajñā*) is contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

Regarding "because of perception" (*saṃjñā*), the wisdom of perception awakens to the void. Gu Shan says that below the character "void" (*xū*), the character "penetrate" (*tōng*) is omitted; because one advances without indolence, one finally reaches the fruit of sainthood.

Thus, practice gives rise to liberation, and through self-knowledge, one realizes realization for oneself. Therefore, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is synonymous with knowledge-vision (*jñānadarśana*). As for the phrase "as stated," I have not yet seen this in the text.
Since the five precepts correspond to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), one transforms the five aggregates into the fivefold body of the Dharma (*pañcadharmakāya*).
This is precisely what the five precepts can accomplish. Furthermore, following the explanation of the five precepts, the next section interprets them according to the Mahāyāna Dharma.

It speaks of the "seal and talisman of longevity and immortality," for which the *Miaoxuan* (The Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra) further states: "The talisman of longevity refers to the teachings of the Three Vehicles;
the seal of eternal bliss refers to the Way of Nirvāṇa. Thus, one knows that the application of these [terms] is whether they are used or not; nevertheless, within the *Miaoxuan*:

The *Jian tiwei yun changsheng zhi fu zhuzai jiejing* (The Judgment on the Tiwei Sutra’s Discourse on the Talisman for Long Life Residing in the Precepts) states that seeing the Mother of all Buddhas is an indeterminate teaching, as [the statement] "killing in milk" refers to the manifest [teachings].
The *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Zhiguan fuxing chuanhong jue*) states that the Tiwei [Sutra] still belongs to the manifest [teachings] and does not yet rely upon the secret [teachings];

therefore, it was only at the Deer Park that the manifest and secret were distinguished, and the five precepts were categorized into three types of action: the first three constitute bodily action, while the latter two constitute verbal action.
The "intention" (manas) refers to the three karmas, the three absences of error, the three absences of need for protection, and so forth;
that is, because the Buddha’s three karmas are free from fault and require no guarding, his manifestation of supernatural powers and preaching of the Dharma reflect all things without omission.

Furthermore, because these cannot be fathomed by those in lower stages, this is also called the "three tracks" (triyāna)—namely, the true nature, contemplation, and practice—and the "three virtues" (triguṇa), which are fully possessed both horizontally and vertically.
As explained in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), there is no need to elaborate further here [etc.].

Furthermore, regarding the section "next, harming life," which explains by way of both phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*li*): although the preceding explanation was based on the mundane and supramundane, it did not yet distinguish between the characteristics of phenomena and principle;
therefore, this explanation is provided so that their profound depth may be seen. Within this, there are five parts, the first of which is as follows:

The text on the precept against killing is divided into three parts. First, the general indication of actual killing and non-killing—their underlying intent is understandable and is explained in detail as found in the *Bodhisattva-śīla-vyākhyā* (Pusa jie shu).

Regarding "killing in principle" (*li-sha*), various texts generally take the Threefold Canon (*tri-piṭaka*) as its analytical basis (*vibhāga*) and the Shared Teaching (*pāryāya-yāna*) as its essence (*tattva*).
However, within the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, all three—Mahāyāna’s Shared, Distinct, and Perfect Teachings—are taken as the essence. As for what is presented in the current text...

One who understands the principle that non-killing is essential must take the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) as the basis for the "dharma-nature of killing. If one proceeds with deliberate intent, the subsequent detailed explanation of the text is divided into two parts.

First, the direct explanation, which is further divided into two: first, clarifying the principle that while there is killing in substance according to the partial and small vehicles, there is no killing in reality.

This section is divided into two: first, clarifying the human realm’s observance of non-killing in substance. This is further divided into two, the first of which clarifies the case of humans. Regarding the text: "It is said... [End of excerpt].

Regarding the "one hundred and twenty years": there are three grades of human lifespan in the world—the superior being one hundred and twenty years, the middling eighty years, and the inferior forty years.

Here, the calculation is based on the superior lifespan; therefore, it is simply stated as "one hundred and twenty. If one follows the natural progression to the next [category], it refers to the "Middle Heaven" (madhyama-deva).

As for the term "perfected by nature" (*xing-cheng*), it is as stated in the *Shangshu*, the "Tai Jia" chapter: "Habituation and nature become perfected," with the commentary noting that "habituation... [leads to this state].

If one practices unrighteousness, it will eventually become one's nature; now, borrowing that terminology while not adopting its underlying intent, the meaning of the current text is that by habitually maintaining the precept of non-killing, one has already established this as one's nature.
Thus, it is a matter of the nature being spontaneously accomplished, which distinguishes it from the human practice of intentional protection.
Regarding the statement "the retribution lies in the six heavens for an extremely long duration," the *Nanshan Lüchao* (Nanshan Vinaya Commentary) cites Maudgalyāyana.

The *Wen zui bao jing* (Sūtra on the Retribution of Questioned Sins) states: "The lifespan of the Four Heavenly Kings is five hundred years; by human reckoning, this is nine hundred thousand years. (*Abhidharma* states:

fifty human years constitute one day and night for the Heaven of the Four Great Kings; thirty such days make one month, and twelve such months make one year. By this calculation of days, months, and years, the lifespan of the Heaven of the Four Great Kings is five hundred years, which equates to nine million years by human reckoning.
This pattern continues through the sixth heaven, with the lifespan increasing accordingly. ... up to the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations, where the lifespan is sixteen [thousand] years.
One thousand years [in the celestial realm] corresponds to nine hundred twenty-one billion six hundred thousand years by human reckoning;
because this is spoken from the perspective of the sixth heaven, it is described as "extremely long" and so forth.

According to the *Abhidharma*, however, the lifespan in the sixth heaven is sixteen thousand years, which equals nine hundred twenty-one billion six hundred million years by human reckoning. Such are the figures for years given in the sūtras and śāstras.
"The differences in addition and subtraction compared to the current text should be recalculated" (and so forth).
Next, the application of principle by the two vehicles and the bodhisattvas is explained through the elimination of textual passages in two parts.

First, it is clarified that although the impermanence and non-self of the two vehicles are described as "wisdom equal to that of the Tripitaka," these terms can also be understood inclusively; thus, one knows that the two vehicles correspond to both the Tripitaka and Shared [Teachings] (Zàngtōng).

Regarding the statement that "the retribution consists of a lifespan of seven hundred *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas in the realm of change," this merely adopts the explanation of others and is not the primary intent here.
Therefore, in the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra-ṭīkā*, within the fifth of the eight difficulties concerning the long-lived heavens (*dīrghāyu-deva-vighna*), it clarifies the principle:

"The two vehicles are called 'pure heavens'; if they enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and return to the Heaven of Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-deva*), how could there be anyone capable of transforming them?"

Regarding the statement that "entering nirvana without remainder" refers to the Great Cessation Samādhi (*mahā-nirodha-samāpatti*), it is said that after seven hundred *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, when a Buddha emits light upon having a karmic connection with them, they emerge and are then taught the Dharma.

However, according to the intention of our own school, based on the *Mahā-śāstra* (the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*), it is stated that once the two vehicles have transcended the triple world and attained the *dharmatā-kāya*, their lifespan is not said to be seven hundred *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. 4.
The explanation that one must necessarily wait for seven hundred *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* before entering the stage of true recompense (*sabhāga-vipāka*) is incorrect.
Next, the Bodhisattva mentioned refers specifically to the Bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*).

Since the Bodhisattvas of the Tripitaka Teaching suppress their afflictions while remaining identical to ordinary beings, and the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching are dull-witted and identical to the Two Vehicles, they are not separately indicated; subsequent cases should be understood by analogy with this.

Within this, there are two parts. First, regarding the wisdom that correctly clarifies permanence, impermanence, and so forth—"and so forth" includes the wisdom of being neither permanent nor impermanent.
The Lotus Treasury Ocean refers to the *sambhogakāya* (recompense land); "receiving the Dharma-nature body" refers to the *dharmakāya*.

As for the assembly of great disciples, they constitute one [category]. Since it is said that they have "partially attained the five eyes and eternal life," this must be explained in terms of their realization of the Path, where all are equally perfected.

Compared to the Buddha’s subsequent re-establishment of the precepts, these [earlier instances] are termed "incomplete faculties" and "diminished lifespan" because they represent only partial realization relative to the ultimate state;
thus, only the Buddha is one who ultimately maintains the precepts, while all others are termed "those who have broken the precepts.
How much more so for those of the preceding Tripitaka and Shared vehicles, as well as humans and devas—how could their faculties and lifespans possibly be complete?

If one proceeds from the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) downward, the next section clarifies the killing and non-killing of both phenomena (shi) and principle (li) for those of the Perfect capacity. The text is divided into two parts: first, it clarifies the non-killing of phenomena and principle;

second, it explains how to maintain the precept of non-killing through phenomena. This should be considered as previously explained. Furthermore, regarding the maintenance of non-killing through principle:

by realizing that the essence is neither destroyed nor severed, this very state of being without injury constitutes the maintenance of the precept of non-killing. This passage is excerpted from [the source].
Regarding the passage from the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* in the chapter "Rebuking Subhūti,"孤山 (Gushan) states: "It is not permissible to cite extensively from that [sutra] to explain this text.
What kind of statement is this? The *Jingming shu* (Commentary on the Vimalakīrti) says: "The two vehicles contemplate the *saṃskṛta-duḥkha-satya* (the truth of suffering as conditioned);

by examining, analyzing, and investigating provisional names and substantial dharmas, they finally perceive the principle, which is called the 'Bodhisattva who destroys the body. The [Mahāyāna] Bodhisattva contemplates the *asaṃskṛta-duḥkha-satya* (the truth of suffering as unconditioned)."
The true mark of the body is like seeing a reflection in a mirror; it does not require analysis, for it is not destroyed by the body.

To follow a single characteristic while remaining partial is not called the "one characteristic. When it is perfectly realized as the Dharma-body, there is no distinction between seeing and the characteristic;

therefore, it is called the "one characteristic. Thus, the sutra below says: "Observing the true mark of the body, one observes the Buddha likewise. Seeing this one characteristic is not the same [as ordinary perception]."

Ordinary beings do not destroy the body and thus differ from those of the Two Vehicles; therefore, they contemplate non-conditioned suffering and perceive the single true reality of the pure Dharma-body.
Those of the Two Vehicles eliminate the eight heterodoxies, enter the eightfold right path, give rise to the three insights, and enter the eight liberations.

This is the path of conditioned truth (*saṃskṛta-mārgasatya*), which severs ignorance and craving to give rise to illumination and liberation. Bodhisattvas, however, cultivate the non-conditioned path (*asaṃskṛta-mārga*).
Truly observe that all sentient beings are the very mark of bodhi; the nature of the eight wrong paths is itself the eight liberations.
If one were to sever [delusion] and then arise [in enlightenment], it would not be "non-action" (anabhisamskāra). Observing with the Buddha-wisdom, it is neither light nor darkness;

moving simultaneously through both light and darkness without mutual obstruction, one manifests bodhi. This is precisely practicing the non-path to penetrate the Buddha-way; therefore, it is called "not."

By severing delusion and craving, one gives rise to clarity and liberation; for clarity is the antithesis of delusion, and liberation is the antithesis of craving. Thus, the *Sūtra of Increased Benefit* states:
"To contemplate the Middle Way through the aspect of non-duality is called the Truth of the Path. Furthermore, the Sūtra says:

"Neither severing lust, anger, and delusion, nor being accompanied by them—this is the unconditioned Truth of Origination. Even by means of the characteristics of the five heinous crimes, one attains liberation, neither bound nor liberated.

Regarding the truth of cessation as non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*): for ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*), the three poisons arise and perish simultaneously with the mind; thus, they are "together" with them.
For those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), having already severed the origin of suffering (*samudaya*), this is "severed" and not "together.

For Bodhisattvas, who contemplate the truth of the origin of suffering as non-action, the nature of lust, anger, and delusion is like empty space; therefore, they neither sever them nor are they "together" with them.

Therefore, this is not the same as that of ordinary beings or those of the Two Vehicles. For the Two Vehicles, the severance of the bonds of cause and fruit results in the attainment of the two types of *nirvāṇa*, which is precisely the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).

Furthermore, according to the teachings of the Two Vehicles, even those who have committed the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*) are not permitted to leave the household life or receive full ordination;

how then could it be said that they attain liberation or the Truth of Cessation? It is not so in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*); therein, one realizes that the true reality (*shixiang*) of the heinous crimes is itself the Truth of Cessation, *nirvāṇa*.
The *Pāṇḍarā-sūtra* states that there are two kinds of liberation: first, the severance of the seed (*bīja-ccheda*), and second, the severance of the fruit (*phala-ccheda*).

Regarding what is called "non-severance," it refers to the fact that although the various Arhats have already severed the afflictions (*kleśa*) and the fetters (*saṃyojana*)—such that they are withered and rotten, and the flavor of the fruit has been severed—they are nonetheless called "bound by the fruit" because, although the fruit itself has not yet been severed, it is certain to be severed [in the future].
Thus, the afflictions are the "seed" of the fruit-household, and the aggregates (*skandha*) are the fruit; the fruit is the seed.

Regarding the fruit of the household, this person of the Perfect [Teaching] differs from those of the Lesser Vehicle; therefore, it is said that the "fruit-seed" is neither born nor extinguished. Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"All sentient beings are themselves Great Nirvāṇa; they cannot be extinguished later. Furthermore, the *Saṃghāṭasūtra* (or *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*) states:
"The Dharma is fundamentally unborn, and thus now there is no extinction. This is precisely that meaning. The accomplishment of wisdom is itself the wisdom of self-recompense (*svapratyaya-jñāna*).

Because it is identical with the essence (*tattva*), it dwells in the tranquil light (*śānta-prabhā*) and is thus sovereign; therefore, "seeing with the ears" and "hearing with the eyes" constitute the sovereign mutual functioning of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).

"Cultivation" (*xiū*) should be understood as "cultivating extension," for by attaining the life-force of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*) which is neither long nor short, one is able to manifest lifespans that are long or short, large or small.
Thus, when wisdom is identical with the essence, there is the greatness of these six capacities.
"It is employed" (and so forth).
Furthermore, in the next section of the *Yuanjiao* (Perfect Teaching), the text clarifying the killing of phenomena and principle is divided into two parts. First, the general demonstration:

"Those who practice the killing of phenomena" refers to the previously explained fact that a person of the Perfect Teaching maintains the precept against killing as their own practice; therefore, they must uphold the retribution [of the ritual] and cannot be negligent.

The Bodhisattva of the Present and Future perceives the capacities of beings and benefits others; therefore, he may kill those of the Two Vehicles, though seeing them, he would not permit the killing of others.

One should know that the Bodhisattva possesses both the provisional and the real: the provisional is the inconceivable transformation of the Dharmakāya, such as in the cases of King Śaṃbara and Aṅgulimāla.
The more they were killed, the more they were shown compassion; for although their lives were severed, they were granted happiness.

Therefore, in reality, it is through actual practice that one forgets transgressions while saving sentient beings; if one attains the welfare of beings, one does not discriminate against the prohibitions based on their nature.
For this reason, a bodhisattva does not personally fear sin, but if it benefits others, they perform it immediately. Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states:

"If a bodhisattva abides in pure ethical discipline and employs skillful means to benefit others, they may occasionally engage in minor instances of what are by nature sinful acts (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). By this, [it is shown that]...
Regarding the causes and conditions for not transgressing the bodhisattva precepts and generating great merit:

it is as when a bodhisattva sees a robber or thief who, out of greed for wealth, intends to kill many beings, or intends to harm a noble śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, or bodhisattva, or intends to commit many acts of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*); having seen this situation, he reflects with the thought: "If I..."
"If I do not take the life of that evil person, he will fall into hell; yet if I do not, his karma of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) will be established and he shall undergo great suffering.
It would be better for me to kill him and fall into the *naraka* hells than to allow him to suffer the pains of immediate retribution.
Having thought thus, he felt deep shame and remorse, and with a heart of compassion, he took his life. By this cause and condition, regarding Bodhi—

If observing the precepts without transgression generates such great merit, then one should understand that killing—and by extension, sexual misconduct, theft, lying, and so forth—is likewise explained.

Those who practice these acts should examine themselves with careful reflection: how can one who cannot endure even the slightest suffering in this world commit a violation of the precepts and enter hell?
I have observed those who lack a sense of shame, who either claim their nature is inherently evil and unimpeded, or speak of [the necessity of] principle...

If one possesses the principle of pervasive integration through the inherent evil of nature, one can universally manifest the form-body (rūpakāya) to perform all manner of deeds, responding like the likes of Aṅgulimāla or the Rishi Yuyudhāna, thereby causing others to awaken to and perceive the Buddha’s eye of longevity.
If one cannot do so, yet claims unimpeded integration, its function is not realized; it is merely a great falsehood born of shamelessness, whereby one deludes both oneself and others.
All sentient beings are great evil friends, yet they also act as rational killers; "killing" here means severance, which is precisely the meaning of non-severance.
Thus, the *Four Foundations of Mindfulness* states: "The Separate Teaching speaks only of severance regarding the path of teaching.

This implies that while the Perfect Teaching possesses both meanings—the path of teaching is called "severance," and the path of realization is "non-severance"—the preceding passage clarified non-killing by way of identity (*samāropa*), whereas the present text clarifies it by way of separation (*viveka*).
This clarifies the principle that "identity" (ji) is manifested through "separation" (li). Although ice is not separate from water, the principle requires that the ice be melted to become water;
the meaning is the same as saying that only through separation is identity revealed. Thus, it is said that "separation" serves to establish "identity.
One who perfectly grasps this intent will find the meanings of "severance" versus "non-severance," and "killing" versus "non-killing," to be brilliantly clear.
Regarding the section on "The Former Life as King Śāntamati," the subsequent detailed explanation of the text is divided into two parts. First, it clarifies the act of killing:
in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*, in the "Chapter on the Noble Practices" (*Āryacaryā-parivarta*), the Buddha first told Mañjuśrī, "In the past, I was once a king of Jambudvīpa named Śāntamati.
I cherished the Mahāyāna; at that time there was no Buddha in the world, so for twelve years I served brahmins, and only thereafter did I exhort them to resolve upon Bodhi."
When the Brahmin slandered me while I was concentrating my mind, I immediately took his life; from that time onward, he has not fallen into hell.
Therefore, one should know that upholding the Mahāyāna possesses such power. [This concludes the section on] the Chapter on Brahma-like Conduct.

The Buddha said that after cultivating loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), and sympathetic joy (*muditā*), one attains the stage of regarding all beings as one’s only beloved child, and sees all...
"All sentient beings are like an only son. Kāśyapa Bodhisattva addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"If this is so, why did the Tathāgata in the past, when practicing the bodhisattva path as a king, take the lives of so many brahmins?
If he had obtained this land [of enlightenment], he should have protected and cared for them; if he did not obtain it, for what reason would he not have fallen into hell?"
He addressed Kāśyapa Bodhisattva, saying: "I do not intentionally kill even an ant, much less a Brahmin.
At that time, I had attained the stage of 'One-Son' (ekaputraka), and because of my affectionate love for him, I severed his life-root; it was not out of an evil mind.
When those Brahmins passed away, they were immediately reborn in the Avīci Hell, whereupon three thoughts arose: first, 'From where have I come?'"
Immediately upon this, he knows from where he has come—namely, from the human realm—and realizes in two moments of thought where he has been reborn:
namely, in the Avīci Hell. In three moments of thought, he knows by what cause he was born here:
he knows that he was killed by a king for slandering the Vaipulya sutras and lacking faith in the Mahāyāna. Having had these thoughts, he immediately [realizes] regarding the Great...

Having conceived a heart of faith and reverence through the study of the Vaipulya sūtras, he immediately passed away and was reborn in the world-system of the Tathāgata Amṛtadundubhi, where his lifespan was full ten kalpas. In the past, I granted this person a lifespan of ten kalpas.
How can it be called "killing"? Although the sūtra speaks only of "all brāhmaṇas," the meaning established by the present text refers to five hundred.
Once one has been born in the world of the Buddha Amṛtaghoṣa-dundubhi, is it not as if one is granted the eye that beholds the Buddha?

Furthermore, to clarify the principle of "killing through understanding" (*prajñā-vadha*), it is said: "It is like a tree spirit who, when its branch is broken, does not harbor resentment toward the bird.

Thus, the treatise states: "For example, in a vast wilderness there is a tree named Śamālī; its branches and twigs are broad and expansive, and many birds gather there to roost overnight. A single pigeon arrives last."
As it perched upon a branch, the branch immediately snapped. The deity of the waters asked, "The *śyena* and the vulture are both capable of supporting themselves;
why then could this small bird not endure it? The tree deity replied, "This bird has come from my enemy’s tree, having eaten the seeds of the *nyagrodha* tree, and now perches upon me.
Should it void its excrement and the seeds fall to the ground, they will be harmful."
If the tree were to grow again, the harm would surely be great; therefore, harboring anxiety, it is better to abandon a single branch, for that which is preserved is greater.
The Bodhisattva is also like this: he has no such fear toward external paths, celestial Māras, their various provocations, or evil karma;
rather, he fears the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), for those of the two vehicles [regarding] the Bodhisattva path are like that bird—[they] destroy that Mahāyāna.
The *Cittaviveka-śāstra* clarifies the common stage of the three vehicles by extensively refuting the Lesser Vehicle; therefore, while we now borrow its text, we do not employ its underlying intent.

For the meaning of our present text takes up the "breaking and sweeping away" of accumulated attachments to purify all afflictions, just as one breaks off a branch so that it no longer harbors a resentful bird.
What is called "breaking" here is not the breaking of the Lesser Vehicle, but rather that of the Perfect [Vehicle].

Regarding the phrase "a person breaks [it] apart for the sake of snapping off the ears," the *Zhi guan* (Concentration and Insight) states: "The four teachings and four gates give rise to views and attachments; one must properly snap them apart. This is the intended meaning.

As for the analogy of the kalpa-fire burning wood and so forth, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "Although the two vehicles have destroyed the three poisons, their residual traces are not yet exhausted.
It is like fire burning grass, trees, or firewood: smoke emerges, but the charcoal is not yet consumed because the power of the fire is weak."

Therefore, the Buddha’s three poisons are forever exhausted without remainder, like Mount Sumeru consumed by the fire at the end of an eon, where everything is utterly gone, leaving neither smoke nor ash.
To say "only killing" refers to the severing of afflictions (*kleśa*); to say "only compassion" refers to the accomplishment of the bliss of nirvana within the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Furthermore, according to what is appropriate for beings, he may manifest either a long or short lifespan; this too is solely out of compassion. As for those with deficient or complete faculties:
Those with intact faculties can understand; as for those with impaired faculties, as stated in the *Myōgen* (The Profound Meaning):
"Because of his practice of illness, he manifests various bodies—appearing as if deaf or mute while preaching various dharmas, appearing as if mad or deluded," and so forth.

Regarding the summary at the end of the preceding section on the various precepts: although the preceding text has fully explained both killing and non-killing, the intent of this current sutra is specifically to clarify the observance of the precepts;

therefore, it must conclude with "non-killing. Why is this? Is it not because the intent of the sutra is that by committing the offense of killing, one's sense faculties become incomplete and one's lifespan is diminished and destroyed? Thus, in accordance with the intent of the sutra, the inversion of the offense constitutes the observance of the precept through "non-".

The elimination of fetters (*saṃyojana*) below follows this principle; it should be understood by reflecting upon it accordingly. "Narrow" (*ai*) means constricted or inferior; "vast" (*hong*) means great; "pathway" (*jing*) refers to a footpath.

Because their function differs while their substance is one, it is said that the pathways differ. Because matters and principles each have what is eliminated and what is not eliminated, it is said that the pathways differ;
because their substance has no distinction, it is said that they meet in unity. The subsequent sections below should be understood according to this.
In the section on the precept against killing within the "Reproving the Lower Three Bonds" (下三結斥), it says: "Vertical and horizontal. "Vertical" refers to the upright;

since the upright must be contrasted with the horizontal, they are called "vertical and horizontal. The first explanation concerns the sequential progression of the mundane and supramundane, which is why it is termed "vertical.
The second explanation concerns the mutual relationship between phenomena (事) and principle (理), which is termed "horizontal. Why, then, is this called the Small Vehicle?

Regarding the enumeration [of precepts], some dismiss them by claiming they refer only to the five precepts of the Hīnayāna; however, these are mere enumerations of phenomena and cannot serve as an exegesis of this Mahāyāna sūtra.
Furthermore, the following section clarifies the precept against stealing, which is divided into two parts. First, it provides a general indication, stating: "Do not take the property of others."
As it is said in the Āgamas, the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "You should cultivate one practice: do not take what belongs to others. A bhikṣu addressed the Buddha:

"I have already understood this. The Buddha asked him: "How do you understand it? The bhikṣu replied: "What belongs to others refers to forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects (dharmas).
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent! If this is so for the Hīnayāna, the Mahāyāna may be known accordingly. Regarding Bodhi—
The Way of Bodhi is not something bestowed by Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, devas, or humans, but is attained through one's own spontaneous resolve and practice;
therefore, it is said that "Bodhi has no giver, yet one attains Bodhi. To reverse this notion of "no-giver" and call it Bodhi is precisely what is meant by "non-stealing.
Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Non-attachment is Bodhi, for it relinquishes all攀缘 (pān-yuan, cognitive clinging)."
Regarding the section on "Holding the Precepts" and below, the detailed explanation of the text is divided into two parts. First, the formal explanation, which is further divided into two.
First, concerning the partial and limited [teachings], the explanation clarifies the theft of the Dharma-gate; this section consists of three parts.
First, it clarifies the theft of gods and humans: "If one maintains" refers to maintaining through restraint; "if one performs" refers to maintaining through action.

Although one may maintain the practice regarding worldly matters and not steal, if one seeks the wealth and pleasure of a single period as a god or human, yet looks toward the world-transcending Ultimate Heaven (Paramārtha-deva), one instead becomes impoverished;
therefore, this is called theft, for it is not non-theft. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "Just as..."
A young Brahmin boy, driven by hunger, saw an amra fruit in human excrement and immediately took it.
A wise person rebuked him, saying, "How can you, of a lineage of pure conduct, take this defiled fruit to eat?
Upon hearing this, the boy was ashamed and felt remorseful, replying, "I truly do not eat what is impure."
The wise rebuke those who would discard it, saying: "You are profoundly ignorant; if you intended to discard it, you should not have taken it up in the first place.
Zhanran’s commentary explains: "The Brahmin represents one who has newly begun the path of pure Prajñā; 'infant' represents the shallowness and weakness of understanding and practice;
being oppressed by the suffering of the three miserable realms is likened to hunger; and within the midst of impermanence, the fruits of the human and celestial realms are like..."
Regarding those foul excrement-like things, there are mango fruits; because one practices deeply and censures the shallow, it is said that "the wise censure.
When the youth heard this, he abandoned his shallow practice and felt ashamed. Because he did not crave celestial pleasures and sought to cultivate the Path therein, he cast them away;
thus it is said, "The wise censure and discard. The Bodhisattva exhorts all to abandon them together, stating that they need not even be received; having observed them further, one abandons them.
Knowing the intent of the sutra, this correctly uses the three storehouses (tripiṭaka) as an analogy. When a bodhisattva observes birth and undergoes rebirth, it is called "washing and discarding";

how much more so for a bodhisattva of the three storehouses who, while subduing afflictions, remains identical to ordinary beings? Therefore, all these are now employed together to serve as an analogy for the theft of humans and devas.

Even if they were to obtain [the fruits], their hearts would not find them sweet or joyful; these and others are all passages from the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra. As for the "four castes of the poor," this is the chapter [title].

An (Dao'an) says: they are "poor" because they have no master, and "miserable" because they have no kin. *Kṣatriya* is translated as "field-lord," referring to those such as kings who love the people and govern the state;
*Brāhmaṇa* is translated as "pure conduct," referring to those who are widely learned and proficient in the classics;
*Vaiśya* has not yet been seen translated, but it should refer to commoners such as farmers and merchants; *Śūdra* also has not yet been seen translated, but it should refer to the lowest class.

The "outsiders" (guests), such as those carrying dung or corpses, were formerly compared to the four castes. In the chapter on the four modes of birth and the six realms, Zhāng'ān compared them to the nine dharma-realms;
however, in the present text, they are fully utilized and compared specifically to the four modes of birth—namely, humans and devas.

Thus, these four castes are all equally poor, serving as a metaphor for the unsurpassed Dharma of the Tathāgata (and so forth). "Huí" (huí, pronounced hù kuī) means to flow against the current; it should also be written as "fú" (fú, pronounced fáng liù), meaning to flow back. If... [text ends].
The character "fu" (洑) signifies a swirling current. Regarding the "outflows of existence" (*bhava-āsrava*), the *Fuxing* (輔行) commentary states:

"Existence" refers to the three realms of existence—namely, the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. Because cause and effect do not perish within these three locations, they are called the "outflows of existence.

As for the "four outflows," because sentient beings are drifted and submerged by these four phenomena and cannot remain stable, they are called "outflows. The "outflow of views" (*dṛṣṭi-āsrava*) refers to the views of the three realms.
The *kāma-āsrava* (outflow of desire) consists of all afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), excluding views (*dṛṣṭi*) and ignorance (*moha*).

The *bhava-āsrava* (outflow of existence) consists of all afflictions of the two higher realms (*rūpadhātu* and *ārūpyadhātu*), likewise excluding views and ignorance. The *avidyā-āsrava* (outflow of ignorance) consists of the ignorance of the three realms.

Both Gushan and Siming both rejected [this interpretation], stating that one must not interpret the meaning as the "four outflows. I do not know for what reason they composed their explanation in such a manner.

This critique (and so forth) states that the "three obstacles" refer, for the time being, to the three realms of existence (*tribhava*) as the three obstacles. However, although the obstructing factors are proximate, that which is obstructed is remote;
therefore, it is said that they obstruct the Buddha, the Heaven of Ultimate Meaning (*paramārthadeva*), and are abandoned by him.
Furthermore, the three obstacles of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) remain entirely present (and so forth).
Next, the explanation of the two vehicles’ theft of the wisdom of the Four Noble Truths begins with a general summary.

"Contemplating body, sensation, mind, and phenomena" specifically clarifies the contemplation of the five aggregates to establish the four foundations of mindfulness; this is the contemplation of the Truth of Suffering.

"The mind of nirvana arises for oneself and for others" etc., correctly refers to the Mahāyāna in order to refute [the views of] those vehicles and clarify the characteristics of such theft. As for the term "momentary" (*ji-er*):
The *Shijing* says, “Grant you great fortune” (*jie er jing fu*). Zheng Xuan’s commentary states: “*Jie* means assistance; *jing* means great.
It means to assist your great fortune. Now, we merely borrow these words without employing their original meaning;

thus, the sense of the current text takes subtle thoughts as the "assistance," such that the arising of the mind is itself the grasping of external objects. The *Zhiguan* says, “A mere thought (*jie er*) exists..."
That "the mind itself possesses the three thousand [realms]" is precisely this meaning. It is because the mind is ultimately ungraspable that the three thousand also vanish;
yet, because there exists even a subtle and minute moment of mind, the three thousand appear vividly as they are.

Regarding the phrase "attaining realization at an improper time without awaiting an explanation of the cause," this refers to Śāriputra’s realization under the Deer Park teachings of the past, wherein he attained the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) based on the provisional teachings.
The fruit does not depend upon the time when the *Lotus Sūtra* preaches the Mahāyāna. The *Fahua Wenju* states that there are two meanings of "that which is depended upon":
first, not being "received" in relation to what precedes; second, not "stopping" in relation to what follows.

The first refers to the illumination of the high mountain—the wisdom that clarifies the three truths—which is the cause for attaining Buddhahood. Because this is "depended upon" by me, yet I do not "receive" it, I have failed in this regard.
Previously, it was said that after the long duration of the Buddhas' teachings, one must ultimately speak the truth;
I did not wait for this interval between the two pillars, but hurriedly took the small [vehicle], and so forth.

That "burnt seeds do not sprout" refers to Kāśyapa’s self-deprecation regarding this Mahāyāna in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, where he says they are like ruined seeds that will never grow again. "Seeing suffering," and so forth, refers to Vimalakīrti.

He rebuked Śāriputra, saying: "One who seeks the Dharma does not seek by seeing suffering, does not seek by abandoning the origin, does not seek by realizing cessation, and does not seek by cultivating the path.

Why is this? Because the Dharma is free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). To say, 'I shall see suffering, abandon the origin, realize cessation, and cultivate the path,' is conceptual proliferation; it is not the seeking of the Dharma. [He spoke thus] because of the body.
Since the Venerable Śāriputra entered the Path by relying on the Three Piṭakas and the four truths of arising and ceasing, he now critiques him from the perspective of the Mahāyāna gate.
If one clings to arising and ceasing as having real contention, this is merely the conditioned conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) within the realm of the triple world.

Even if one truly uses this insight to sever the afflictions of craving and views within the realm, it remains the unconditioned conceptual proliferation beyond the realm. Now, although Śāriputra has severed [the afflictions of] existence...

If one still clings to the Four Truths as being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), this is merely frivolous conceptualization (*prapañca*) and not the pursuit of the Dharma of the Three Truths of the Mahāyāna;
how could such a person see the Buddha-nature? As for those who are attached to emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and so forth, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:

"The Buddhas taught the Dharma of emptiness primarily to transform those attached to existence. Those who are attached to emptiness are not saved even by the Buddhas. Now, I shall likewise borrow this [passage] to refute the two [extremes].
The passage beginning with "Riding upon the nirvana of partial emptiness, the body is three hundred yojanas long" is a citation from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

This refers to bodhisattvas who emerge from the provisional [teachings] and penetrate the middle and superior [stages]; yet, if they enter the seventh stage, they fall into the rank of the two vehicles and are therefore rebuked by all Buddhas and bodhisattvas.
It is like a great bird whose body is three hundred yojanas long but which lacks both wings.

Just as one who follows from heaven experiences either death or suffering equal to death, so it is for the Bodhisattva. From the beginning, he single-mindedly cultivates emptiness until reaching the sixth stage;
this constitutes the "three emptinesses. If his body is fat but his wings do not grow, and he falls into the path of expedient means of the two vehicles, it is called "suffering equal to death.
If he falls into the first fruit (srotāpanna), it is called "death. If he perceives [the cessation of] exhaustion, that is "death."

The equality of suffering and the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) constitute "death. If one is equal to death, it is termed "equal to death" (*mṛtyusama*); yet because one has not yet actually died, it is termed "equal.

Therefore, through skillful means, the stage of cutting off views (*darśana-bhūmi*) is termed "equal to death. For those who have attained the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), their contemplation remains entirely in the realm of meaning, which is equivalent to being as yet undead.
Regarding the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-ṭīkā* states: "First, the unconditioned of space (*ākāśāsaṃskṛta*)."

The two are the unconditioned state of cessation through deliberation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha; the new translation calls it *pratisaṃkhyā-nirvāṇa-dhātu*), and the third is the unconditioned state of cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*;

the new translation calls it *apratisaṃkhyā-nirvāṇa-dhātu*). Of these three unconditioned states, one is *nirvāṇa* and two are not *nirvāṇa*. Here, they are mentioned collectively; therefore, it says "three.
If discussed specifically, however, the *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles pertains only to the unconditioned state of cessation through deliberation. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:

The two vehicles fall into the deep pit of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Furthermore, as Vimalakīrti rebuked Subhūti, saying, "Those who make offerings to you will fall into the three evil realms," the Commentary explains that this refers to those in the stages of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) as being the three evil realms.

When the *Lotus Sūtra* mentions "starvation" and so forth, these are the words of the four great disciples expressing their realization. The *Wenju* (Textual Exegesis) states that they had not attained the Great Vehicle.
The Dharma-food serves as nourishment for those who are hungry; lacking great power and function, it is emaciated; lacking great merit, it is lean.

Whether there is or is not wholesome goodness, one gives rise to views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), which are like sores and scabs. (Regarding "whether there is or is not wholesome goodness": according to the *Lotus Sūtra*, "either there is something attained or nothing is attained"—cultivating tainted wholesome deeds is "having something attained," while cultivating the wholesome deeds of the Two Vehicles is "having nothing attained.

As for the statement in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* regarding "not seeing the Buddha" and so forth, this is a citation of the passage from the *Vimalakīrti* where Vimalakīrti rebukes Subhūti; it is not [the case that]... [text ends].
If one sees the Buddha of the Dharma-body but does not hear the Dharma of non-action, and thus does not enter the ranks of the sages and worthies of the Perfect Teaching— how could such a person,
who lacks even the mutual functioning of the six sense organs found in the ten stages of faith of the Perfect Teaching, which is absent in the Two Vehicles, possibly be included among their number?

Regarding the statement that the Bodhisattva of the Threefold Knowledge practices the sequence of conduct and the sequence of training, etc.: "conduct" refers to generosity (*dāna*) and diligence (*vīrya*);

"training" refers to ethical discipline (*śīla*) and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); and "the path" refers to patience (*kṣānti*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). This is as detailed in the *Mahā-śāstra* (Treatise).

Since these are all sequential, there are degrees of depth and shallowness; for instance, having abandoned one thing and taken up another, one returns again, and having gone away, one goes once more, and so forth.
The Pure Name (Vimalakīrti) praised Mañjuśrī, saying: "Welcome, Mañjuśrī! You have come without the characteristic of coming; you have been seen without the characteristic of being seen.
Mañjuśrī replied: "It is so, Householder. If one has already come, there is no further coming; if one has already gone, there is no further going. Why?
Because that which comes comes from nowhere, and that which goes goes nowhere. This is because ordinary people of the partial and small vehicles [view things in such a way].

Because there is a "coming" that involves coming, once one has already come, there could still be further coming. For example, ordinary people and non-Buddhists may practice dhyāna as far as the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception, only to fall back into the three miserable realms;

or even Bodhisattvas of the Separate Teaching who practice the three contemplations of separate characteristics and come seeking the wondrous enlightenment, yet upon hearing the Perfect and Sudden teaching, must again change their minds—all such cases involve coming after having already come. Only the Perfect [Teaching] is free from this.
When a person sets out, if they are not deviant and do not subsequently alter their mind or change their perspective midway, this means that having come, they will not come again;

and having departed, they will not depart again. This is merely a restatement to establish the meaning of "coming. Furthermore, it is based on the ordinary persons of the partial and limited vehicles (*hīnayāna*) who depart with the mark of departure;
this is not a true or skillful departure. Thus, even after departing, they would still have to depart again, and so on, until the stage of separation (*pratyekabuddha*).

If one contemplates this teaching, it can be understood that only the person of the Perfect Teaching (yuanren) proceeds from the initial arousal of the mind through the correct contemplation of the Middle Way;

once they have departed [from delusion], there is no principle of changing the mind or changing the contemplation to depart again. Therefore, it is said that having departed, they do not depart again.

These two phrases refer to a single reality with different meanings, and thus their names are merely shifted. Consequently, one should know that everything from the Distinct Teaching (biejiao) downwards is entirely [of this nature].
Regarding the marks of coming and going in reality: these marks of coming and going in reality are the equal *tathatā* (suchness) and *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm), which even Buddhas cannot traverse;
therefore, there is no mark of coming. To speak of "coming" in reference to this means that there is nowhere from which one comes—this is called "coming without coming.
Furthermore, because the equal *dharmadhātu* is a place where even Buddhas cannot arrive, that which goes has no destination; thus, it is "going without going."

"Not coming, yet coming; though coming, there is no place reached. This is not the case in the Separate Teaching (biejiao), and for this reason it is called "humiliation" (辱). The rest of the text is clear.
