The third section, explaining his own marrow, bones, and blood, is divided into two parts:

first, distinguishing that he was not a prince who fed a tiger (the character "飤" is also read as "飼," with the phonetic "祥" and "更" as alternatives; it means to feed), as described in detail below in the *Sheshen pin* (Chapter on Giving Up the Body);

second, regarding Śibi’s exchange for the pigeon—Sanskrit *Śibika*, translated here as "Giving"—the *Dacheng da piposha lun* (Mahāyāna-mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra) states that the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni originally acted as a king.
The king was named Śibi; he regarded all sentient beings as his only son. At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, together with the celestial master-craftsman Viśvakarman, wished to test him.
Śakra transformed himself into a hawk, and Viśvakarman changed into a dove.
The hawk pursued the dove until it reached the king’s armpit. The hawk said to the king, "Give me back my dove! The king asked, "What do you want?"
The hawk said, "I am eating flesh and blood. The king then weighed himself against the pigeon; the pigeon’s body grew heavier while the king’s flesh gradually lightened.
The king then used his hand to hold the scale until it was perfectly balanced with the pigeon. The devas sighed in admiration, saying, "For the sake of this small pigeon, he has thus saved it;
he is a true Bodhisattva. Thereupon, his body and flesh were restored to their original state. It was not by picking up his own body, but because [he acted] for his father.
This is because the mother’s physical body is a false and extraneous thing. Next, regarding the phrase "one's own body" (*jishin*), the following provides the correct explanation:
taking the *dharmatā* (the true nature of phenomena) as one's own body means that it is not a false or extraneous thing; therefore, it is named "one's own body.

Because sentient beings have been deluded regarding the *dharmatā* since beginningless time, they fail to realize their own body and instead merely identify with the objects of transformation; thus, the appearance of birth and death exists.

That it continues infinitely does not mean that those who have not transgressed forget the characteristics of what is to be observed and what is to be transgressed; it does not mean that failing to observe [the precepts] is called "non-observance.

As for the claim that *dāna*, patience (*kṣānti*), and so forth should be considered "flesh," since the *Śāstra* (the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*) mentions only skin, blood, bone, and marrow, the Great Master [Vasubandhu] added *dāna*, patience, and so forth as "flesh" according to his own interpretation.
Fourth, this section below explains that [the Buddha] satisfies hungry sentient beings.

The passage beginning with "The King’s remaining food and drink" explains the phrase "let alone other food and drink. This text is divided into three parts: first, the direct explanation; second, the citation of evidence from the *Lotus Sūtra*; and third, the textual analysis which states:
"The Buddha’s wisdom is profound, not the other six provisional means; these others are not profound. This refers to the Distinct Teaching (*bipartite teaching*).

The sequential [teaching] is both "other" and "profound"; however, in the initial formal explanation, only humans, devas, and those of the Two Vehicles are treated as "other," because the Distinct Teaching (biejiao) is both other and profound, and thus it is set aside for now. Regarding "showing, teaching, benefiting, and gladdening," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Showing" means showing people [the realms of] birth-and-death and nirvana; "teaching" means teaching people to abandon evil and practice [virtue].
For those who seek wholesome benefit, he preaches the Dharma to lead them out; for those who are joyful, he praises their conduct according to its nature to cause them further joy.
Thus, he employs these four adornments to preach the Dharma. Third, the passage from "The Tathāgata" downward explains the reason for the arising of doubt:

"following others" refers to following their dispositions (*citta*), while "following oneself" refers to following one's own wisdom (*jñāna*). However, the three types of intention and speech—such as following others—and the four teachings [are explained here].
All three types of "reception" (sambandha) are present here, as explained at length in the *Zhiguan*, the *Miaoxuan*, and other works.

Furthermore, although the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings each possess these three types, when condensed, they are collectively termed "speech according to others' sentiments" (*tāntrika-vākya*) for the purpose of entering the Shared Teaching. When further condensed, they are termed "speech according to both self and others' sentiments.
The Perfect Teaching is termed only "speech according to one's own sentiments. Since this applies across the four teachings, it constitutes the three types of reception.
Since these four gates and the four *siddhāntas* differ in various ways, they are all described as "immeasurable and boundless";
this is a general explanation for why one might give rise to doubts regarding other foods, as well as one's own body and so forth.

Next, the explanation of the fourth section, the Preface on the Manifestation of Auspicious Omens, is divided into two parts. First is the explanation of the phrase that concludes the preceding and opens the subsequent.

Regarding the term "Mahāsattva" (Great Being): "Great" serves to distinguish it from the "lesser being," which refers to mundane affairs; a Mahāsattva is one whose mental activity is vast and who is capable of establishing the Buddha-work.

It is also referred to as an "Uttamasattva" (Supreme Being), an "Ādikarmika" (Opening Being), and so forth. This single phrase—referring to the meaning of the syntactic pause—is applicable to both long and short [readings], and here it is used as follows:
The twelve characters constitute one sentence. "To reach" (*shi*) means to arrive; thus it is said, "to penetrate and arrive at the source of the mind," and so forth.

Since the contemplation of the mind is thus, the contemplation of the Buddha is likewise; therefore, it is called "recollection of the Buddha" (*nien-fo*). One should know that "recollection" (*nian*) is precisely "contemplation" (*guan*).
Furthermore, because mindfulness maintains wisdom, the contemplation of the Buddha is explained as the recollection of the Buddha. The dharma-nature and empty space are nothing other than the mind.
This originates from the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) alone.

Following the passage on the appearance of the auspicious signs (*prātihārya*), the correct explanation is divided into two parts. First, the explanation of the intent behind the auspicious signs is further divided into two:

first, the correct explanation of the signs themselves. Regarding the "secret report" of the signs, these manifest the *Wenju* (Textual Phrases) of the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-ṭīkā*.

The explanation of the manifested omens is intended to clarify their significance; yet human sentiment tends toward discrimination, taking secret communications as omens and extraordinary occurrences as signs.
What do these signs report? The profound mysteries of the ultimate fruit are exceedingly difficult to expound. Human sentiment is often indolent and unable to accord due respect;

therefore, one first uses extraordinary signs to startle and transform ordinary perception. Once ordinary perception is transformed, a yearning and reverence arise; thus, the extraordinary is employed.
The explanation of the "signs" (*lakṣaṇa*) serves as a report on the "omens" (*prātihārya*); furthermore, one should know that an omen is itself a sign. Thus, it is called an "omen-sign.
An omen is that which manifests; it is, in other words, a report. If it did not manifest a report, then the omen-sign would merely follow from the outward appearance of the performance.

How would this differ from the initial moment of illumination, when the multitude [mistook it for] a malevolent spirit or a non-Buddhist practitioner? Therefore, in our school’s interpretation, an omen must necessarily manifest a report. An omen that manifests a report is not of an inferior kind.

Since this is what can be measured by the [conventional] ground, it is called "mysterious. Thus we know that if one attains the principle of manifesting auspicious omens as a sign of response, one will never mistakenly conflate the *pariccheda-śarīra* (segmented birth-body) with the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body), nor the *dharmatā-kāya* (dharma-nature body) with the *vairocana-kāya* (universal manifestation body).

This is because, in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā*, the explanation of the "Manifestation of Auspicious Omens" preface clarifies that the supreme response bodies (*saṃbhoga-kāya*) and *vairocana-kāya* manifest in four locations. Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* has a separate preface.
The meaning of "the three pairs and six auspicious omens" refers to the Tathāgata’s emission of light (and so forth).

Next, regarding the analysis within the text, there are two sections; the first section consists of two parts: first the question, then the answer. The second section also consists of two parts: first the question, then the answer.

This is further divided into two: first, a general indication; second, a specific explanation beginning with "If [regarding] the omens," which is itself divided into two, the first of which is the explanation.
The distinction regarding the aspect of faith is further divided into two parts: first, the formal explanation; second, the presentation of analogies.

The analogy of the auspicious omens appearing in the Zhang family illustrates that which is evoked by the specific aspect of faith. The analogy of the Zhang family receiving blessings illustrates that these are not summoned by anyone else.

Next, the section beginning with "Although so" explains the universal [attainment] through various conditions, which is further divided into two parts: first, the formal explanation. Since it is said that there is no possibility of solitary excellence, how could [it be otherwise]?
It is not universally established by various conditions; the subsequent citation from the *Lotus Sūtra* can be understood through the text.
Next, regarding the passage on the auspicious signs (*prātihārya*), the commentary divides it into four sections: first, the division of the text; second, the specific characteristics;

third, "as for the ten [signs] below," which clarifies what is symbolized; and fourth, the questions concerning this sūtra, which consist of two rounds of critical analysis. The first round is further divided into two parts.
The first question is followed by the answer; the subsequent turn is again divided into two parts. First, regarding the inquiry: "to summon" (*zhào*) means to verify (*zhèng*).

"Non-" (*fēi*) refers to the formative signs (*xíngzhǎo*); "zhèn" (pronounced *zhìyǐn*) also means signs. As for the "subsequent characteristics," they represent the total characteristics (*zǒngxiàng*) that manifest when causes complete into a single fruit. As for the "prior characteristics," they represent the manifestation when the causes of the ten stages (*shídì*) are completed.
How could one allow those in the ten stages of faith (*shìxìn*) to suddenly realize the ultimate fruit? How could it be possible for one at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*děngjué*) to regress?
In response to the sequence of the ten stages, the text refers to the "compiler of the sutra," which is Ānanda. Regarding the term "from*ong" (上七恭切), it means to determine or settle;

regarding "duan" (丁貫切), it means to sever. Since it is stated that both the preceding and succeeding [stages] are moistened, there is no contradiction in the fact that the two causes—the true and the semblance—distinctly lead to the two ultimate fruits.
Below, under the section "The distinct characteristics are ten," the fourth part is a detailed explanation of the text, which is divided into two sections.

The initial explanation of what is signified by the individual characteristics is further divided into two parts. First, regarding the term *fēnyún* (上符分切, 下於云切), the *Yùpiān* states that it refers to auspicious vapors.

Second, the subsequent section provides an explanation of the text, which is divided into three parts. First, concerning the explanation based on each [character] signifying a single stage, there are two sub-sections.
Regarding the first point—that the meaning signified is *fěiwěi* (the standard form of this character is *měnwěi*)—this describes the appearance of literary brilliance.
This means that by means of literary elegance, one imitates and approximates the consciousness to seek its general outline; one must not demand exhaustive detail from it.

Next, following the text below, the primary purpose is to clarify what is symbolized in ten sections; these may be understood through a word-by-word commentary. As for the notes marked "and so forth" (*yún yún*):
first, they symbolize the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*), which can only be approached through poetic imitation and tentative deliberation, and cannot be expected to be fully exhaustive.
Regarding "all" (the second point): for now, let us explain them sequentially according to the order in the text, as each stage (*bhūmi*) clearly possesses the merits of all stages within it.

Thirdly, regarding the correspondence between the ten stages and the ten perfections (*pāramitā*): these various meanings exist according to the path of the teachings, which is why the commentary states "and so forth.
As for the "ten perfections," if they are condensed, there are only six; if they are expanded, they become ten. Why is this?

In dhyāna, there is the power of aspiration which gives rise to the perfection of aspiration (praṇidhāna-pāramitā); in supernormal powers (abhijñā), there is the power of spiritual penetration which gives rise to the perfection of power (bala-pāramitā).

Regarding the fundamental concentrations (mauladhyāna), they maintain the perfection of dhyāna; within the perfection of wisdom (prajñā-pāramitā), there is the knowledge of the modes of the path (mārgajñatā) which gives rise to the perfection of skillful means (upāya-pāramitā), and there is the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) which gives rise to the perfection of knowledge (jñāna-pāramitā). Because the perfection of knowledge maintains the fundamental perfection of wisdom, it is taught in various sūtras such as the Avataṃsaka.
In the treatise, the ten perfections (pāramitās) are all paired with the ten stages (bhūmis), and these are subsumed under the path of teaching (*śāsana-mārga*).
Furthermore, the subsequent section explains that each individual stage is fully endowed with all virtues.

Since it is known that each stage possesses all virtues, one understands that the previous sequential pairing of the ten perfections with the ten stages was strictly according to the path of teaching; whereas now, in this [section],...

This is the meaning of "square" and "round" being complete; herein there are two parts: first, a general heading, and second, a detailed explanation based on what follows. The text is divided into two sections:

first, a specific explanation regarding the first bhūmi, which is further divided into two parts. First, the actual explanation of the text, which consists of ten points: first, representing the wisdom of the first bhūmi;
second, "azure as the color of heaven," representing the objective realm of the first bhūmi; third, "possessing wondrous... representing the compassion of the first bhūmi; fourth... [and so forth].

1. "In its lower part" refers to the four virtues of the first bhūmi; "five and four" refers to the six perfections of the first bhūmi. 2. "Emitting great light" refers to the four types of knowledge (*jñāna*) of the first bhūmi;

"this" refers to the three thousandfold world-system, while "other lands" refers to the ten directions. 3. "Raining down all [jewels]" refers to the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of the first bhūmi.
4. "Acting for the world" refers to the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) of the first bhūmi; "like joy" refers to delighting others. (The latter is above.)

The first "lè" (樂) is pronounced with the *wǔjiǎo* (五角) initial; the second "lè" (樂) is pronounced with the *lúgè* (盧各) initial. 1. "Receiving the whole world" (*shòu tiānxià*) symbolizes the dharmas of the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmi*). 2.

"Deficiency of the faculties" (*gēn quē*) symbolizes that on the First Ground, the various faculties are mutually interchangeable. Following this, the "merits of the First Ground" (*chūdì gōngdé*) indicates the intended meaning of these symbols.
The Buddha explains that which cannot be fully proclaimed: the realization of the Way (*zhèngdào*) is identical to the Perfect Ground (*yuán dì*), for it is precisely the state of abiding (*zhù*).
The *Avataṃsaka* states that all the merits possessed by a Bodhisattva in the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) cannot be fully extolled even by all the Buddhas of the three periods of time;
if they were to explain them in full detail, ordinary beings would hear them and their minds would become disordered and driven to madness.

The *Miaoxuan* commentary explains this as meaning that even the Buddhas of the three periods of time do not know the wisdom of the first stage of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). Furthermore, if even the first stage of the Perfect [Teaching] is already like this, how much more so for the subsequent stages?
Regarding the phrase "The Buddha of the Grounds distinguishes and proclaims the general outline": "general" (梗/槩) refers to the broad overview.

Since the first ground is thus established, the remaining nine grounds are illustrated by this precedent. Furthermore, regarding the "ten aspects" below, the latter three concern the manifestation [of practice];

within each individual ground, there is an explanation of both self-cultivation and the transformation of others. This commentary is divided into two parts; the first is the specific explanation of the first ground, which is further divided into two sub-sections.

First, there is a general heading; next, from "its chamber" (*tasyāḥ kuṭyāḥ*) onwards, there is a detailed explanation, which is further divided into two parts: first, explaining what is manifested regarding one's own practice (*sva-caryā*), and second, explaining what is manifested regarding the transformation of others (*parārtha*).
Next, from "the first stage" (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*) onwards, the remaining nine stages are illustrated by analogy.

Next, regarding the explanation of the general characteristics expressed as "the cause being perfected and the principle being revealed": this refers to the ultimate clarity and manifestation of the principle of the Three Virtues (*triguṇa*).

As for the specific correspondence between the three worlds and the Three Virtues, Gushan states: because the *dharmakāya* is the object (*viṣaya*), it corresponds to the *rūpakāya* (the land) and sentient beings;
since the sixteen types of cognition (*ṣoḍaśākāra-jñāna*) overturn deluded cognition to become true wisdom, they correspond to *prajñā*.
The fetters of the five aggregates are themselves the liberation from bondage; thus, they are contrasted with liberation.
Now, it is said that within this text, for the sake of specific exposition, three [categories] are paired with three; indeed, this is so. However, if explained universally, one should say:

the three thousand worlds are themselves emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. When the three thousand are the middle, the true aspect (dharmatā) is fulfilled; when the three thousand are emptiness, prajñā is fulfilled.
The three thousand realms being provisional is itself liberation; when the true reality (*dharmatā*) is perfected, what dharma would not be fulfilled?
Since the true reality of the Middle Way is ultimate, how could there be any deficiency among the phenomena of the two extremes? It is like a mirror that is perfectly bright and stainless:
all myriad forms appear therein as reflections without exception. By using this analogy to contemplate the Dharma, the essential meaning can be fully understood.
As stated in the *Yuantong yuyan dengji* (and so forth).

The third section, which explains the fifth doubt regarding the introductory text, is divided into two parts: first, the division of the text; second, from "rejoiced" (*huānxǐ*) onwards, the explanation of the text, which is further divided into two:
first, explaining the joy arising from seeing the signs; second, from "with a sincere mind" (*zhìxīn*) onwards, explaining the silent contemplation and the presentation of doubts.
The fourth section explains the sixth introductory passage which resolves doubts; it is divided into two parts. First, the division of the text to indicate the meaning. From "Now you...

onwards, the second part explains the text itself, which is further divided into two. First, the explanation of the actual resolution of doubts. Regarding the phrase "the three should not [be so]," these are the three bodies (*trikāya*):
"great function should not" refers to the *saṃbhogakāya*; "dharma-nature should not" refers to the *dharmakāya*; and "wisdom-measure should not" refers to the *nirmāṇakāya*.
This is precisely the *saṃbhogakāya*. Therefore, you should not now speculate that the lifespan of the Tathāgata’s three bodies is short.
Because the realm of the *dharmakāya* and the wisdom-realm of the *saṃbhogakāya* are in profound union (*yuganaddha*), they can give rise to great activity;
when conditions are long, it is long, and when conditions are brief, it is brief, and so forth. Since this has no bearing upon me, why do you cite the "immeasurable" [lifespan] from the *Śāstra*?
If one wishes to measure the Dharma, it should be known that such a person is one who covers themselves over and sinks into delusion.
Why is this? [The following section] explains the cessation of doubt; it may be understood by analogy with what precedes. Regarding the "eight assemblies": first, the assembly of devas;

second, the assembly of worldlings; third, the assembly of Māras; fourth, the assembly of Brahmās; fifth, the assembly of śramaṇas; sixth, the assembly of brāhmaṇas; seventh, humans; eighth, non-humans. (From the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*)
It merely states: "Among the Brahmā, Māra, śramaṇa, brāhmaṇa, devas, humans, and asuras. Regarding the textual records:

"Brahmā" refers to the lord of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and also the lord of the three realms; "Māra" refers to the lord of desire; "śramaṇa" means "one who strives for tranquility," so called because he exerts effort to pacify evil;
"brāhmaṇa" means "one of pure conduct," referring to those among the non-Buddhist outsiders who have left the household life and are said to be of the lineage of pure conduct.

Ancient scholars have indiscriminately used this [explanation] for the fourfold assembly (*catur-parṣad*). If the four assemblies already encompass all categories, why then speak further of "gods and humans" (*deva-manuṣya*) and so forth?

Thus, the listings differ; they are merely cited as representative examples. When "desire-realm beings" (*kāmadhātu*) and "form-realm beings" (*rūpadhātu*) are mentioned, they refer to the primary subjects;

when the "four castes" (*cāturvarṇya*) are mentioned, they represent the most eminent; when the "six paths of existence" (*ṣad-gati*) are indicated, they denote the virtuous. Furthermore, these are all taken from the superior, speaking of those who are easiest to lead into the Buddha-dharma. Now, the present sutra says:
The "various devas" refers to all the devas of the three realms, excluding the two lords, Māra and Brahmā. The "people of the world" refers to the inhabitants of the four great continents;
this is what the *Lotus Sūtra* means when it says "devas and humans. Regarding "humans and non-humans," in various texts this term concludes the list of the eight classes of beings (*aṣṭa-nikāya*).
"Humans" refers to the people of the world, while "non-humans" refers to ghosts and spirits. Thus it is.
Because the Dharma-body Bodhisattvas dwell in the Pure Land of the Dharma-nature, they are not mentioned here;

this is because the Dharma-body Bodhisattvas and the Pure Land of the Dharma-nature both pertain to the realm beyond the boundaries (*dharmadhātu*), whereas these eight assemblies concern only that which is within the boundaries.

Thus, the fact that Dharma-body Bodhisattvas reside in the Pure Land of the Dharma-nature is no longer mentioned. As for "birth-body Bodhisattvas," these are the physical bodies subject to分段 (*fen-duan*, segmented) existence within the boundaries.

Prior to abiding [in the stages], it is called the "birth-body" (*janmakāya*). Upon ascending to the stages (*bhūmi*) and abidings (*vihāra*), it is called the "birth-body attaining patience" (*kṣānti*), meaning that within this birth-body one is able to shatter ignorance and attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), thereby ascending to the stages and abidings.

Once the birth-body has attained patience, one abandons this birth-body and dwells in the Land of True Reward (*sambhoga-kṣetra*); only then is it called the "Dharma-body" (*dharma-kāya*). Just as it is for the Bodhisattvas, so it is for the Tathāgata.
It is likewise so; since the Buddha and his disciples both possess the two bodies—the birth-body (*janma-kāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*)—this is extensively taught in various texts.

How could one dare to obscure this? If one grasps this meaning, one will never mistakenly conflate the internal, delimited birth-body with the external, transcendent, and sublime dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*).
If one were to say otherwise, how could one account for the current teachings on the dharma-nature body and its land, as well as the birth-bodies of the bodhisattvas?
Is it not the case that our Great Master did not understand the resonance of the Middle Way, and thus falsely distinguished between the Dharma-body and the birth-body?

Or is it perhaps the birth-body Bodhisattvas of the *Zang* (Tripitaka) and *Tong* (Shared) vehicles? (And so forth. If those who have left home are subsumed within the fourfold assembly, let us point specifically to the four beginning with the *bhikṣu*;
since these four all possess the four [stages] beginning with "initiation," how could there be any contradiction? Furthermore, regarding their emergence...
The household community should consist of only two groups; the mention of four here includes laymen and laywomen (*upāsaka* and *upāsikā*) as well.
If one includes śrāmaṇeras, śrāmaṇerīs, and śikṣamāṇās, they constitute the five groups of the ordained.
The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra-śāstra* adds the ordained monks (*bhikṣu*), the ordained nuns (*bhikṣuṇī*), along with the laymen and laywomen to these five, thereby forming [the eightfold assembly].

Regarding the "nine assemblies" (and so forth): if one considers the renunciants and renunciant nuns together with the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, then there is apprehension regarding the four assemblies of renunciants (and so forth).

If the Dharma-nature body (*dharmatā-kāya*) manifests expedient means (*upāya*), it follows that from the true body of the Dharma-nature outside the realms, it assumes an expedient form identical to the birth-body (*janman-kāya*) within the realms; appearing as a human being is precisely its intent (and so forth). Since the nature of wisdom...

Since the profound and great function can thus be understood, there is no need for further prolixity in the sutra; therefore, it merely explains the *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Since the great function is already implicitly contained therein, this constitutes the explanation of the "three should-nots."
The fifth [section] explains the introductory text of the seventh chapter, "Gathering the Assembly," in four parts: first, the heading;

second, a comparison with other sutras to distinguish the sequence of events—such as in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, where the assembly is gathered first and the auspicious signs appear later (and so forth);

third, the section beginning with "At that time" which constitutes the formal explanation of the text in two parts; and fourth, the section beginning with "As for the visible assembly" which constitutes the explanation of the assembly text in five parts. First:
The phrase "the intention of gathering the assembly is for the sake of the devas of the desire realm" is an abbreviated expression;

it should properly state, "the devas and nāgas of the desire and form realms, the eight classes of spirits, the bodhisattvas, and so forth. The statement that "the benefit for a single individual such as Śraddhālakṣaṇa is small" correctly demonstrates the purpose of gathering the assembly.
As for why the sūtra mentions only the devas of the desire and form realms and does not mention the devas of the formless realm: [it is because they do not participate in the physical assembly].
Because their discipline is lax while their vehicle is swift, and because they are formless, they do not come to listen to the Dharma;

even if they were to come, they could not be seen, and for these reasons they are not listed [among the protectors]. (And so forth. As for the *nāgas*, they are the primary retribution (*vipāka*) of the animal realm and resemble snakes;

their secondary environment (*upabhoga*) consists of palaces made of the seven treasures, which are similar to those of the devas. They are also able to transform their bodies into handsome human forms. Their discipline is lax while their vehicle is swift.
This is why I have come. The Gandharva—translated here as "Fragrance-Body"—does not consume wine or meat, but sustains its physical aggregates solely through fragrance.

It is also said that this deity is the banner of the Lord of Heaven; it is a god of inverted music who dwells upon the Ten Jewel Mountains. Because its discipline is lax, it falls into the state of a spirit;
yet because it practices giving, its karmic fruit resembles that of a deva. Asura is translated as "Wineless"; they gather flowers from the sea to brew wine, but it does not succeed.
Therefore, they are named as follows: *Garuḍa* (translated as "Golden-Winged Bird"), which is categorized among the realm of animals;
*Kiṃnara* (translated as "Doubtful Spirit"), who has a single horn on its head and is the deity of the strings and pipes of the various heavens;
*Mahoraga* (translated as "Mongoose-Spirit" or "Earth-Dragon"), a legless, belly-crawling deity who is the guardian spirit of worldly shrines and receives offerings of wine and meat from humans.
They all entered the belly of a python because they violated the precepts, were deceitful and sycophantic, harbored much anger, gave little in alms, and greedily craved wine and meat;

due to their laxity regarding the precepts, they fell among the ghosts and spirits. Because of their great anger, insects entered their bodies and devoured them. However, because they had previously given a little in alms and practiced humility and respect, they still receive offerings from humans.

Furthermore, it should be understood that this is merely explained in terms of the division between the birth-body and the honored special body within the realm beyond (*dhātu-bāhya*), and thus speaks of the teacher and disciples, or the assembly and the multitude. Regarding the seeing of the Buddha in his birth-body (such as hearing the Dharma and advancing on the Path from other Great Beings or from the birth-body of Śākyamuni):

it is not that bodhisattvas in their birth-bodies do not see the currently manifest, most honored body—as seen in the *Nidāna-parivarta* of the *Lotus Sūtra*, where light is emitted and signs are manifested.

Since this is the case for the birth-body bodhisattva’s visual observation and seeing of the Buddha, it follows by analogy that the same applies to hearing the Dharma. Thus, [this refers to] the Buddha in his birth-body within the realm of segmented existence (*paricchinna*).

It is not only for the sake of Bodhisattvas with birth-bodies (*janma-kāya*) within the realm that the Dharma is preached, but also for the sake of Bodhisattvas with dharma-bodies (*dharma-kāya*) outside the realm;
that people fail to see this and claim that the birth-body exists only in the *Zang* and *Tong* [teachings] is a most egregious error.
Following the eight verses, the subsequent divisions of the text mention "first" and "next," which may perhaps indicate that these are the Master’s citations of ancient authorities.

Now, because our school adopts both, it is said that "both paths may be used. Furthermore, one might fear this is the wording of Zhanran (Zhang’an), who, because the Great Master’s own division of the text contains two intentions, refers to them as "the first" and "the second";
yet these two paths should not be subject to selection or rejection, as both are equally usable.

Next, the "Explanation of Meaning According to the Text" (as previously titled), consists of four parts. First, the explanation of the four verses establishing the analogies, which is divided into two sections.

First, the presentation of the traditional interpretation (jù), which is further divided into two: first, the formal presentation; second, the refutation by the present school (jīnjiā) starting from the words "This meaning... The question is:

since the preceding text states that the "four Buddhas" specifically refer to the *nirmāṇakāya* (response-body) Buddhas who are immeasurable, while the subsequent text states that the "four Buddhas" are cited as metaphors for those response-bodies—how can this be?

"Finite measure and infinite measure are merely manifestations of transformative function (*nirmāṇa-prayoga*) and have no bearing upon the fundamental essence (*tattva-mūla*); how, then, does this differ from the old interpretation?

The old masters claimed that the four verses merely illustrate longevity and have no other meaning; why do you suddenly reject this and instead explain the text according to the Four Truths, the Four Mindfulnesses, and the Three Virtues?
The answer is that the old masters were ignorant of the principle of the Truths (*satya*) regarding cause and effect, and merely stated that the four verses simply illustrate [longevity]."
Since there is no other intention than [the fact that] his lifespan is long, he must reject [the previous view].

Now, since it is clarified through the principles of the Truths (*satya*) and cause-and-effect (*hetu-phala*), the four verses speak of his longevity; how could this be compared to the old [interpretation]? Question:

Since the four verses are here explained by way of the principles of the Truths and cause-and-effect, whereas the preceding section merely resolved doubts, how can one claim that [the former] cannot be correlated with the three [Truths]? If this were so—
If the eight assemblies do not know the limits [of the Buddha's lifespan], is this not an explanation of the *dharmatā*? It should not be answered thus.
Although the following section explains the four verses by means of the internal fruits of the principles of truth (*satya*), it points out in each instance that the four Buddhas employ metaphors;

their longevity is merely a function of transformation (*nirmāṇa*) and does not concern the fundamental essence (*svabhāva*). Therefore, the statement in the preceding text that "the eight assemblies do not know" is an explanation of the *dharmatā*.

The meaning of these responses is significantly different; how can they be treated as identical? When asked, "What is the distinction between the long life [of this sutra] and that of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*?
the answer is: the past and future differ, and there is a difference in their retributive births.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* refers to the immeasurable *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body) of past long life, whereas this present sutra refers to the immeasurable *nirmāṇakāya* (birth body) of successive long lives. [Question: If this present sutra...
This physical body is that which should be extended to the immeasurable; yet this immeasurability is in fact measurable—is this not impermanence?

Why, then, does the subsequent passage refute the old attachment regarding the impermanence of numerical dharmas? The meaning of permanence and impermanence differs according to whether one advances or rejects [the truth].
Those of the old school who cling to the impermanence of numerical dharmas interpret them merely as having a finite measure; thus, they have already deviated.
Now, these four verses cite finite measures as a metaphor for the infinite; therefore, they are rejected.

While this infinity, when compared to the "short" impermanence of the *nirmāṇakāya*, may be considered long and permanent, if it is compared to the permanence and infinity of the *dharmatā-kāya* and the *sambhogakāya*, it is merely subsumed under the category of the finite.
Thus, one should know that the meanings of "permanent" and "impermanent" across various texts cannot be treated as identical.

(As stated above). Furthermore, the text clarifying the present intent is divided into three parts: first, the heading and enumeration; second, the explanation of the reasons based on the Four Noble Truths;

third, the detailed interpretation from "Above" onwards, which is further divided into three sections. First, the explanation regarding the correspondence with the Four Noble Truths, which is again divided into three parts. First, the general clarification.

Furthermore, there are three parts: first, a comparative analysis with the preceding section; second, the text itself, which consists of two sub-sections. First, the refutation of the erroneous reading; second, the clarification of the correct interpretation based on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

The *Śāstra* states that the Buddha is the "Perfectly All-Knowing One" (*sarvajña*) because he knows suffering as it truly is, knows the origin as it truly is, knows cessation as it truly is, and knows the path as it truly is.
Regarding this, the masters of the old school read it thus: "He knows suffering as suffering... [and so forth]. This is the refutation of their error.

The characteristic of equality is its objective reality; therefore, it is now refuted. If this characteristic were indeed an objective reality, then the Buddha would merely know phenomena through their equality and fail to manifest the principle (*li*);
how would this differ from the various Māras? Now, following the clarification above, the next section manifests this text in two parts.

First, regarding phenomena and principle within emptiness: they are unified as the principle, while conventional designations are treated as phenomena. Furthermore, there is another interpretation. Next, [the text] proceeds by way of the three [natures].
The truths of the ultimate and the conventional are the Middle Way among all phenomena; this is the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:

"Only the Buddha has fully exhausted the true mark of all phenomena," for it does not transcend the categories of phenomena and principle, or the middle and the extremes. Therefore, when we now explain the Buddha’s knowledge of the Four Truths, we clarify them by means of phenomena and principle, as well as the middle and the extremes.
Thus, phenomena and principle, and the middle and the extremes, are both instances of separation and integration. This constitutes the third [section].
"To be fully present in a single phrase" means to be fully present in the single phrase "knowing suffering as it truly is.

The commentary states "and so forth" because the remaining three truths are to be explained by analogy with the Truth of Suffering, thereby clarifying the phenomena, principles, middle, and extremes. The phrase "clearly identifying below" indicates the reason:
since the text of the Four Noble Truths is explained in terms of phenomena, principles, the middle, and the extremes, this constitutes a clear identification of the Four Noble Truths.
Since this is the realm for cultivating longevity, the four verses are correlated with the Four Noble Truths;
does this not clearly reveal the essential tenet of this sutra’s constant principle—the severing of doubts? Next, regarding the detailed explanation starting from "All" (*sarva*) and below:

although the four verses of the sutra speak of mountains, seas, earth, and space as being "knowable," this refers only to what the Tathāgata is able to know. If one were to consider it from the perspective of ordinary beings...
Because one cannot fathom it, the preceding passage states that the mountain scales and ocean drops have actual limits, which ordinary beings do not know.
That which has actual limits yet can be known is used as a metaphor for the Buddha’s lifespan having a definite measure;
that which ordinary beings do not know is used as a metaphor for the Buddha’s lifespan being said to be immeasurable. The scriptural text is elliptical, providing only a partial illustration.
The Tathāgata is able to know the reality of one extreme, whereas ordinary beings do not;
if it were otherwise, how could a measurable quantity be used as an analogy for the immeasurable, and how could one interpret the texts of the sūtras and commentaries?

All four verses state that the lifespan of the Śākya-muni Buddha is incalculable, which refers only to what ordinary beings cannot fathom. Therefore, the preceding passage says "not... [implying it is not limited].
If gods, humans, Māras, Brahmās, and other assemblies were able to calculate the lifespan of the Tathāgata and know its limit, then considering the Buddha’s wisdom, how could he not know it?
Therefore, the preceding passage states: "Except for the Tathāgata. This is a concise and abbreviated expression from the sūtra verses;
it is spoken from the perspective of ordinary beings who cannot fathom it. Thus, it says that the lifespan of Śākyamuni Buddha cannot be calculated, and so forth. If...
If this were not so, how could one reconcile the fact that the assembly of devas and humans cannot conceive or calculate [the Buddha's lifespan], except for the Tathāgata?
How can it be compared to Amitābha’s, which has a definite limit such that devas and humans cannot count it—an "immeasurable" that is actually measurable?
Since this present sutra is used as an analogy for Amitābha, we know that the long life mentioned in this sutra is likewise a transformative manifestation (*nirmāṇa*).

It is simply that what is finite is immeasurable. To explain these four points: first, regarding the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), it says "the river of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) submerges sentient beings.

This refers to what was previously mentioned: the very whirlpools of these three realms are suffering caused by origination; how could they exceed the flow of existence (*bhava-nadi*)? The character *huàn* (浣) should be read as *hàn* (汗);
*hào-hàn* (浩汗) describes the vast expanse of great waters, and *jìng* (亘) means pervasive or universal. "Within the realms" refers to the Shared Residence (*sahā-loka*).

The "earth" refers to the realm where ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) are submerged and drowned; the "realm outside the boundaries" refers to the stage of skillful means (*upāya*) and the stage of true recompense (*vipāka*).

Within this [latter], those of the Three Vehicles are submerged and drowned. If practitioners of the Three Vehicles have completely severed the pervasive delusions (*sāmānyakleśa*), they are submerged and drowned in the stage of skillful means outside the boundaries.
If Bodhisattvas have partially severed ignorance (*avidyā*), they are submerged and drowned in the stage of true recompense outside the boundaries. Thus, in the Great Sūtra, there is a river.

The swirling currents must encompass both the *pariccheda* (segmented) and *pariṇāma* (transformative) realms for the state of the Buddha’s exhaustive mastery over the domain of longevity to be revealed.

Since this is the case for the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), the same principle applies to the remaining three truths. Next, regarding the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya* cites the metaphor of the body being like Mount Sumeru;
this is spoken figuratively, as the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "Suppose there were a person whose body..."
"Suppose there were Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains; what do you think, Subhūti—is this body great? Subhūti replied, "It is very great, World-Honored One. Why is this?

Because the Buddha has said that what is not a body is called a 'great body. [The characters *pan* (盤) and *zhì* (峙) are corrected here: *pan* means to revolve or spread out; *zhì* means to stand tall or steeply.

Regarding the three citations from the *Dharma-paryāya-samudaya-sūtra* (Lotus Sūtra) concerning the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), since it states that the "ground of wisdom" is the Truth of the Path.

Just as those who reach this shore and the other shore by means of both the common and specific paths must have both the delusions to be eliminated and the specific and common paths that serve as their antidotes, how could it be otherwise?
Water represents the specific path and land represents the common path; the common path merely reaches this shore, whereas the specific path alone reaches the other shore.
This is because the Truth of the Path (mārgasatya) does not transcend the six *pāramitās*; by practicing them, one turns back toward and arrives at that [other] shore.

The path of the shore merely leaves behind this shore of segmented birth-and-death (*bhavāṅga*) and crosses the middle current of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) to reach the other shore of partial truth (*ekāntika-satya*);

the distinct path, however, leaves behind this shore of transformation (*pariṇāma*) and crosses the middle current of ignorance (*avidyā*) to reach the other shore of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*).

Therefore, while the common path reaches the other shore of partial truth, it remains on this shore of transformation. Thus, it is stated in the *Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm).
It is said that by means of these six dharmas, one can travel from this shore of the two kinds of birth-and-death to the other shore of the two kinds of nirvana;

hence they are called "Reaching the Other Shore" (pāramitā). Furthermore, it is said they are "Infinite Crossings" (du wuji): by practicing these six dharmas, one can cross over the vast distance of the various phenomena of both principle and fact;
hence they are called "Infinite Crossings. Regarding the four pairs [of noble ones], in contrast to the Truth of Cessation, the fifth is called "Medicine" (yi), while the others are "Smoke" (yan).
"Clouds, dust, and mist"—the hands of the asuras are said to "obscure," meaning they block light; now, because the essence of space is entirely pure, it is said that they cannot defile it.
The "three lights" are the sun, moon, and stars. The "transformed city" (nirmāṇa-pura) is a metaphor; "Nirvana" is the Dharma.

"Transformation" refers to what is produced by supernatural power—something non-existent suddenly coming into being. A "city" is for preventing wrongdoing and resisting enemies. Internally, this corresponds to... [the internal realization].

The *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles is brought about by provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). By the power of provisional wisdom, that which is non-existent is taught as having utility for the purpose of transformation;
it is called "nirvāṇa" because it serves to prevent conceptualization and ward off [wrong] views. In the past, this was considered real, yet it was not known to be a transformation.

Only upon reaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* does one know it is not real, and thus it is merely termed a "transformation. Furthermore, the praise of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*) based on the principle of the Four Noble Truths is divided into two parts.

First, the three bodies (trikāya) are established. Next, regarding the passage beginning with "The marks of faith" (*xìnxiàng*) which praises the skillful means of severing doubt: *yǔjīn* (語巾) means a bank or shore; *yǔjiā* (五佳) means the edge of water;
furthermore, *yújī* (魚覊) also refers to the water's edge. Next, the explanation of the text concerning the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) is divided into three parts.

First, it generally clarifies that the essence of the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness originally resides in the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), because it is by contemplating the body [that this realization occurs].

This is because the feelings, mind, and dharmas are merely the fruit of the Truth of Suffering within the five aggregates. Next, the section beginning with "All" provides a specific explanation of the three [truths].
The section beginning with "If one contemplates" concludes by showing the reason for this; the text is divided into three parts: first, the formal conclusion and indication;

second, from "If one contemplates the four aridities" onwards, it clarifies the function of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), meaning that the foundations of mindfulness possess the function of destroying inversions and manifesting virtues. This is based on the *Miaoxuan*.

The middle section cites the *Ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra* (Renwang jing) regarding the five aggregates of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) to clarify that the five aggregates of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) are themselves the dharma-nature of those aggregates;
since they are the dharma-nature of the aggregates of the conventional truth, how could they not be the virtuous qualities subsequent to the dharma-body? One should reflect upon this deeply.
The third section, "The Characteristics of Faith," below clarifies the skillfulness in severing doubt.

The threefold explanation of the passage on the four virtues is divided into two parts: first, the formal explanation; second, the concluding demonstration of the reason for [the virtues], beginning with "The accomplishment of the four virtues.

This section is further divided into two: first, the formal conclusion and demonstration; second, the clarification of the skillful means for severing doubt, beginning with "The marks of faith," which refers to that which is profound and obscure (the character *yǎo* is pronounced *jiǎo*;
it means deep). Regarding the phrase "Note: ...," there are briefly two meanings: first, this is the present school’s explanation of the verse on severing doubt.
Such is the ingenuity [of this teaching]; these two [points] refute others who are entirely deluded regarding this principle, for they merely claim that the four similes only illustrate long life.

Next, the explanation of one verse that synthesizes the similes is divided into two parts: first, the presentation of the thesis; second, the refutation of previous [interpretations]. This latter part is further divided into two, the first of which is the general [refutation].

Listing the two errors: the former [commentary] states that the following section separately refutes deviant attachments, which is further divided into two parts. First, the refutation of deviant interpretations of the text, which is again divided into two:
first, the narration; second, the present explanation. Below is the present school’s critique. Since the current text states:

"Even if one knows the number and knows the numberless, knows the measure and knows the immeasurable, this is merely the function of transformation (*nirmāṇa*) and does not concern the fundamental essence," it is therefore known that [the analogies of] the weight of mountains and the depths of the ocean [refer to the function].

The actual limit of [the Buddha's] lifespan is something unknown to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and impossible to calculate; yet, by citing the life-span of Śākyamuni as a measure, it is illustrated as being immeasurable.
This, however, refers only to the immeasurability of the actual limit within the extended application of the physical body (*janmakāya*).

How could one use the fact that the essence of the realized *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya* is truly immeasurable to explain the actual reality of the extended application of the transformational function (*nirmāṇakāya*)?

[Regarding the question] "Is it finite? (and so forth), next, to refute the meaning of biased attachment: the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*) possesses both permanence and impermanence. That sutra states:
"Thus, these three bodies are described as permanent and impermanent based on their respective meanings.

The Transformation Body is said to be permanent because it constantly turns the wheel of Dharma in an uninterrupted succession; however, it is not [permanent] in its fundamental sense, and therefore all its activities are not [eternal]."

Because it is fully manifested, it is said that the *āśraya* (basis) is impermanent; yet because it is a continuous succession of all the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*) of the Buddhas, it is therefore said to be permanent.
It is not permanent in its fundamental nature, for because its full functioning is not manifest, it is said to be impermanent.
As for the *dharmakāya*, it is like empty space; therefore, it is said to be permanent. (The note "and so forth" is intended to refute [the opposing view]).
If the former masters had lost the *nirmāṇakāya*, how could they have attained the *dharmakāya* and *sambhogakāya*?

Third, from "For this reason" (*iti*) below, two verses are explained to sever doubts; the *Mahāsattva-sūtra* states that the Mahāsattva is none other than the Tathāgata, and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* says, "Therefore, the Honored Great Awakened One.
Fourth, from "For this reason" (*iti*) below, one verse is explained to provide the conclusion.

Next, the section beginning with "At that time" explains the joy of Śraddhālakṣaṇa. From the section beginning with "When this was said," there are three explanations regarding the attainment of the Way by those suited to the teaching.
The *Jingming shu* (Vimalakīrti Commentary) states: *Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is translated here as "Unsurpassed, Right, and Universal Knowledge.
Although there are three types of generating the mind [of enlightenment]: first, nominal; second, semblance; and third, partial realization—the present generation of the mind is...

Regarding these "similar" [stages] and "similar-to-similar" [stages], both the general and specific positions encompass the stages of the Inner Ordinary Persons (*antarapudgala*). Why is it that they are merely "similar" to the arousal of the mind?

The answer is that for both the Śrāvaka’s stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) and the Bodhisattva’s stage of Subduing Patience (*vinaya-kṣānti*), there is as yet no meaning of "arousing" [the mind].

It is only at the Śrāvaka’s stage of Nature (*gotra-bhūmi*) and the Bodhisattva’s stage of Gentle Compliance Patience (*anuloma-kṣānti*) that the meaning of "arousing" first applies; therefore, these are primarily cited to clarify the stage of arousing the mind. Furthermore, regarding the Dharma...

The *Huayan-jing-wenju-shi* (Exegesis of the Phrases of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra), in the "Chapter on the Differentiation of Merits," states that the "arousing of the mind in eight worlds" refers to the purification of the six sense faculties, as it encourages entry into the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).
As the *Renwang jing* says, "A Bodhisattva of the ten good deeds arouses the great mind and forever parts from the ocean of suffering of the three realms of existence"—this is precisely that meaning.
Fourth, the explanation of the four Buddhas returning to the original text is divided into two parts; the first concerns the cause (*hetu*).

Regarding the passage "Following the explanation by Śākyamuni, [the text] next provides an exegesis based on the contemplation of the mind (guanxin)," this should be analyzed as follows: the contemplative mind, its objects, and the knowledge thereof are all quiescent and do not manifest.
In the first two Teachings (the Tripitaka and Shared), although they are both quiescent and non-manifesting, their principle remains like the vast void.

In the latter two Teachings (the Distinct and Perfect), although they are both quiescent and non-manifesting, their substance is like a bright mirror. Furthermore, since this contemplative understanding properly belongs to the Perfect Teaching, one should further distinguish it from the preceding three.
The instruction to contemplate the mind so as to manifest the perfect contemplation wherein both [subject and object] are quiescent and do not appear (and so forth).
*New Commentary on the Textual Phrases of the Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, Fascicle Three;
*New Commentary on the Textual Phrases of the Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, Fascicle Four.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Congyi of Yongjia.

Following the explanation of the "Chapter on Repentance" (Chānhuǐpǐn), the next three chapters are explained to clarify their practical application. This section is divided into three parts; first, the explanation of the "Chapter on Repentance" clarifies the text for the eradication of evil.
Second, the initial explanation of the title of the chapter is divided into two parts. First, a comparative analysis with other sutras:

regarding the term "mostly" (*bāhulyena*), since the *Samantabhadra-darśana-sūtra* (*Pu-xian-guan jing*) also exclusively clarifies repentance, compared to that sutra, various Mahayana texts clarify it diffusely across many sections.

Now, following the sequence of the text, the second part is the formal explanation of the content, which is divided into two. First, the formal explanation according to the meaning, which is further divided into two.
The initial formal explanation of the text consists of four parts.
First, regarding the explanation of the term "confession" (*chànhuì*): to preserve the Sanskrit original, one should say *kṣamā*, which is translated as "repenting of transgressions.

Because both the Sanskrit and the Chinese terms are presented together, it is called "confession" (*chànhuì*). Since such a translation is the common usage among people, we shall set that aside for now and instead focus on the act of "confessing" (*shǒu*).

I have merely humbled myself to explain its name. This section is divided into two parts; first, the formal explanation of the text, which consists of five sub-sections. First, regarding the explanation of "shou" (舒救切, *shū*) as "submission":

"shou" refers to the confession of one's own transgressions, while "kuan" (苦管切, *kuǎn*) refers to sincerity. Next, regarding the explanation of "qi" (去智切, *qì*) and "shang" (庶幾, *shù jī*) in terms of adoption and rejection:
"qi" means to look toward with hope, and "shang" means to aspire to. Thus, wholesome dharmas (*śukla-dharma*) should be adopted, and unwholesome dharmas (*kṛṣṇa-dharma*) should be rejected.

Therefore, it is said that one "adopts and abandons. Third, regarding the abandonment of what has passed and the seeking of what is to come: "vile" (*bi*) refers to loathing; "evil" (*e*, pronounced *wù lù* in the *qieyun*) refers to hatred.
Fourth, regarding the combined abandonment of the agent and the object: the "agent" (*neng zuo*) is the continuity of the mind, and the "object" (*suo zuo*) is the transgression.
Having already confessed the transgression, one further severs the continuity of the mind; this is the combined abandonment of both agent and object. Fifth, regarding...
Regarding the explanation of *hrī* (shame) and *apatrāpya* (modesty), the masters of Guishan and Siming divide these into general and specific categories:

"shame" (*hrī*) is termed the general confession, while "modesty" (*apatrāpya*) is termed the specific confession. These two lines constitute the general; that which follows from "shame" constitutes the specific. Within the specific there are five parts, which together with the general make six.
Adding the previous four [categories], they form ten sections; therefore, the conclusion below states: "An explanation of the names in ten sections."

However, since the text at both the beginning and the end concludes by stating, "Therefore, it is called repentance," if one were to separate the general and specific [explanations], it would likely not accord with the intent of the text (and so forth).
Within this, there are five parts; first, the explanation concerning humans and devas: because the fleshly eye has obstructions, it sees only what is manifest;

because the divine eye has no obstructions, it sees that which is "míngmíng"—"yōu" meaning deep and hidden, and "àn" meaning dark. Furthermore, "è" (pronounced *wù lù* in the *qieyun*) refers to the lower human realm.

Next, the explanation of the text according to the Tripiṭaka is divided into two parts. First, the explanation by way of the "Worthy" (ārya) and the "Noble" (ārya). "Worthy" refers to the seven types of Worthy Ones:

(1) the five stabilizations, (2) the specific characteristics, (3) the general characteristics, (4) the stage of Heat (uṣmagata), (5) the stage of Summits (mūrdhan), (6) the stage of Patience (kṣānti), and (7) the Worldly Supreme Dharma (laukikāgradharma). "Noble" refers to the seven types of Noble Ones: (1) those who practice through faith (śraddhānusārin), (2) those who practice through the Dharma (dharmānusārin), (3) those liberated through faith (śraddhādhimukta), (4) those who have attained vision (dṛṣṭiprāpta), (5) those who have realized through the body (kāyasākṣin), (6) those liberated by time (samayavimukta), and (7) those liberated at all times (asamayavimukta).
Since Bodhisattvas who subdue their afflictions are included within the stage of the Worthy, and Pratyekabuddhas are likewise subsumed within the stage of the Noble, [the text] proceeds accordingly.

However, when speaking of the worthy and sages (*ārya*), there are the three vehicles (*triyāna*). "Reaching" (*dai*) means to arrive at. Furthermore, following the section on the worthy and sages, the next part explains the Heaven of the Ultimate Meaning (*paramārtha-deva*) in terms of both phenomena and principle.

This "principle" refers to the principle of partial truth (*ekadeśa-satya*). Furthermore, regarding the section beginning with "shameful of the three vehicles," the third part explains according to the Shared Teaching (*paryāya-śāsana*).
This is further divided into two: first, explaining the three vehicles by way of the worthy and sages; the "sages" here refers to those at the stage of the eight persons (*aṣṭamaka*).

Having seen the ground, those who have transcended the worthies of the three vehicles are at the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*). Furthermore, regarding the "three vehicles" below, this is explained in terms of phenomena and principle;

this principle is also the partial truth (*pratisaṃvid-satya*). However, in the Tripiṭaka [teaching], true extinction is taken as the truth, whereas in the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), illusory existence is itself emptiness—this is the truth.
Again, regarding the "three vehicles" below, there are four points explained according to the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*), which is further divided into two parts: first...

Regarding the statement that "the worthies and sages of the three vehicles are not even equal to the worthies of the Bodhisattvas," this is because the worthies and sages of the three vehicles of the Shared Teaching do not know the Middle Way;

furthermore, because Bodhisattvas do not sever the "dust and sand" afflictions beyond the realms and do not subdue fundamental ignorance, they are not yet the worthies of the thirty stages of mind of the Distinct Teaching Bodhisattvas. If they do not even reach the level of the worthy, how could they be equal?
"Sublime! Thus, since the thirty minds are merely inner-worldly ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), they are called 'worthy ones' (*bhadra*) because they only suppress ignorance;

since the ten stages (*bhūmi*) have severed it, they are called 'sages' (*ārya*). Summarizing these [sections] below, the next is explained in terms of phenomena and principle. The 'first meaning' refers to the Middle Way.

Furthermore, from 'the thirty minds' downward, five sections explain according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*). This text is divided into two parts: first, an explanation based on the distinction between worthy ones and sages."

The reason those in the thirty minds [of the ten abidings, ten practices, and ten transferences] are excluded from being judged as sages is that it is only upon reaching the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) of the Perfect Teaching that one breaks through ignorance (*avidyā*).

The ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) belong to the rank of the worthy (*bhadra*) and are also considered "inner ordinary persons" (*antar-pṛthagjana*), yet they merely suppress [afflictions]. Regarding these [stages], the following section explains them by way of both phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*tattva*).

The "ultimate principle" (*paramārtha-tattva*) is also the Middle Way; however, there are differences between the incomplete and the complete, which are distinguished across various texts. This is the point.

There is no need to trouble oneself by listing the ten sections in full, as this is merely a summary; although there are only nine textual units, it is called "ten" following the conventional major number.

Next, the section on Repentance is divided into two parts: first, the heading, and second, the explanation. The explanation consists of four parts, the first of which is the general clarification of the text.

Second, first, citing the sutra to indicate the locus: because the "First Principle" (*paramārtha*), "Ultimate Truth" (*paramārtha-satya*), "Dharma of the Lotus Sutra," "place of practice," and "treasure-store" mentioned in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* differ in wording but are identical in meaning to the "profound *dharmatā*" (dharma-nature) discussed here, they may be cited to clarify the locus upon which repentance relies and to which it returns.
This section is divided into three parts; first, regarding the citation from the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, [the passage on] "coarse words and gentle speech," Master Zhangan merely...
The following one and a half lines praise gentle speech. Gentle speech is the opposite of harsh speech;

if we speak of them in their most general contrast, all words of reprimand are called harsh speech, such as when rebuking Devadatta by saying, "You are a fool who eats the spittle and saliva of others.
All words of reception and encouragement are called gentle speech, such as saying, "O Bhikṣus who ride the good vehicle," and so forth.
The provisional teachings distinguish between the small and the great, the true and the middle, and the partial and the perfect, alternatingly classifying them as coarse or subtle.

That all such coarseness and subtlety ultimately return to the primary meaning (*paramārtha*) is because the language of the coarse and the subtle constitutes the function of the whole; thus, by subsuming these functions back into their source, one returns to the primary meaning.
The *Fahua Wenzhu* (Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra) concludes its explanation of Piṅgala based on the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*).

Cao [Zongyi] takes the delusions that have been destroyed as the objects of the three contemplations—coarse, subtle, and intermediate—and regards their general and specific aspects as the primary truth (paramārtha-satya). [The ellipsis indicates further elaboration.
Next, he cites the *Lotus Sūtra*: "The place of practice, the place of proximity, abiding on the ground of patience" refers to the single ultimate truth (*eka-tattva*).

Since this ultimate truth simultaneously negates both extremes, it is said that one "does not practice even a single characteristic," and because it is non-existent, it is said that one "does not discriminate the treasure-place."

The "place of jewels" is merely a metaphor for the Single Reality (ekayāna). As for saying it is "near," having already traveled three hundred *yojanas* out of five hundred—leaving only two hundred more—it is not far away and can be reached by proceeding forward;
thus, reaching the Lotus Sūtra involves the opening of the provisional (*upāya*) to reveal the real (*bhūtārtha*), which is the abolition of the illusory city.
Reaching the place of jewels is the establishment of the real. All these are said to be "identical" (*tathatā*).

It is not a matter of different times; rather, because transformation through cessation must necessarily reach the place of treasure, and upon reaching the place of treasure, the city of jewels transformed by illusion must necessarily cease.

Thus, the provisional is discarded as the real is established, and the real is established as the provisional is discarded. This statement is made in accordance with the characteristics of the teachings.

However, the meaning of the present text is that when the initial mind clearly realizes the principle of the momentary nature and the single reality of dependent origination, this is what is called [the ultimate].

"The place where the treasure is located is near" refers to the site of repentance (and so forth). Third, citing the text of the present sutra, it is divided into two parts: first, the citation of the text;
second, "As for the place of taking refuge," which explains the underlying meaning. Next, "If one attains... concludes by demonstrating the reason.

Originally, the metaphor was established such that "attaining the place of repentance" corresponds to the Way arising, and "repentance" corresponds to the Dharma being accomplished. Conversely, this metaphor illustrates failing to find such a place, which is like [the Way] remaining level and unarisen.

"Ground-toppling" (*di-diān*)—the term "top" (*diān*) refers to the crown of the head. It is like toppling from the level ground at the crown of the head because, having no place to rest, one loses one's footing.
Furthermore, it means overturning and falling downward. For this reason, it is further likened to a blind person entering a thorn forest (*kaṇṭaka-vana*);

as they move about, they are entangled and obstructed. This is why it is necessary to clarify the place for repentance. Thus, following the *Samantabhadra-darśana-sūtra*, the next section distinguishes [the methods].

The textual presentation consists of five parts: first, citing the scripture, which refers to the *Sūtra on the Method of Contemplating Samantabhadra Bodhisattva*; the preface notes that it is also titled the *Samantabhadra Contemplation Sūtra*.
Second, from "Next, regarding the mark of non-offense" onwards, there is the explanation. Third, from "If [there are] three kinds" onwards, there is the doctrinal classification (*jiao-pian*).

Fourth, from "The great [beings]" onwards, there is the illustration of persons who practice and study. Fifth, from "If one recognizes" onwards, there is the concluding demonstration. These constitute the three major scriptures.

The following section presenting the analogies is divided into two parts. First, regarding the citation of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* as an analogy: the principle that all phenomena are inherently complete is like the water of the great ocean;

the practitioner of contemplation is like one bathing therein. "Practice" encompasses all names, which signifies what has already been employed. For now, setting aside the cultivation of practice, we take the water of the ocean specifically to serve as an analogy for the locus.
Regarding the citation from the *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*: the person in debt serves as an analogy for the multitude of those with transgressions.
The metaphor of a newborn relying on its mother and throwing itself into the king’s arms illustrates taking refuge in the locus of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).

The citation from the *Shu* (Book) serves as an analogy for this locus; the meaning of the passage is clear.孤山 (Gushan) states that the *Shu* refers to the *Liu Zi*. Following the section on "the traveler," the text applies the analogy to the Dharma;
furthermore, the application to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* can be understood, and thus [Gushan] does not elaborate further.
This is an elaborate explanation. If the practitioner understands this meaning, the following fourth section provides a summary and demonstration.

The third part, the text on the method of repentance, is divided into three sections: first, the heading and enumeration; second, the formal explanation beginning with "Next, the correct dharma," which is further divided into two parts.

First, the explanation of the correct dharma, which is again divided into two parts. First, clarifying the profound and subtle nature of the correct dharma, which is further divided into two parts. First, the direct clarification.
Since the previous place of repentance was already "one mind and three truths," how could the present method of repentance not be "one mind and three contemplations"?
If it were not so, how could one reconcile such passages as "the wisdom of the nature of contemplation" and "the mutual merging of object and wisdom"?
Next, the text of the citation from the sutra below is divided into two parts: first, the actual citation, which is from the *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, stating:
Both are called *prajñā* as the realization of the subject that contemplates; both are called *dharmatā* (real mark) as the realization of the object contemplated.

If categorized by the wisdom that contemplates, whether it be the wisdom itself or its locus, it is called *prajñā*. If categorized by the object contemplated, whether it be the wisdom or its locus, it is called *dharmatā*.
This is because the subject and object are non-dual, and the realm and wisdom are of one suchness. Taking the mind as the object, the mind is also able to illumine it.

When the mind and its mental concomitants mutually illuminate one another, the principle is easily understood (and so forth). The subsequent explanation is as follows. Regarding "interfusion," as stated in the *Zhi guan*:
"The nature of words is detached; this is itself liberation. This means that speaking is non-speaking. The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"If one knows that the Tathāgata never speaks the Dharma, this is true 'much-hearing'; not speaking is itself speaking. The *Fuxing* commentary clarifies this.
To speak of essence and nature is identical to words; words are material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), and material phenomena are the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Since the true mark has no separate explanation, this very explanation is non-explanation. The Tathāgata originally has no speech, yet he adapts to things and names them "much-hearing" (*bahuśruta*). Much-hearing does not depart from principle; thus, non-explanation is itself explanation.
Having observed this with wisdom, the following section clarifies how to cultivate contemplation through successive phenomena, as illustrated in the *Yili* (Examples of Meaning).
It is said that by means of this pure mind, one traverses all phenomena with spontaneous and seamless integration; from the fifth stage onward, there is nothing that is not thus.
Therefore, at the beginning of the "Chapter on Rejoicing" in the *Zhiguan Mingyi Chao*, it is stated that the three truths within a single mind are suddenly and clearly revealed.

Like gazing into a clear mirror, one comprehensively perceives all forms; within a single thought-moment, perfect understanding is achieved, and without the exertion of effort, one proceeds spontaneously and effortlessly.

Since it was thus in the first chapter of the *Ming* (Illumination), from the subsequent chapters onward, each section is superior to the preceding one. This is divided into three parts: first, a general heading;
second, the specific explanation of the text below, which is further divided into two parts. First, the formal explanation:

since one employs the wisdom of contemplation to pass through all phenomena, such as form and mind, such that there is nothing that is not the *tathatā* (thusness) or the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), one knows that this is precisely the *Samantabhadra-contemplation*.
Vairocana pervades all places. If Vairocana did not pervade all places, then the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) would not encounter phenomena to perceive their true reality (*dharmatā*).
Since it encounters all things and perceives their true reality, Vairocana is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Furthermore, since the Reward-body (*sambhogakāya*) and the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) do not depart from the Dharma-body, and because these two bodies are ever-present wherever the Dharma-body resides, one knows that the three bodies (*trikāya*) pervade all phenomena.
Therefore, whether walking, standing, or in light or darkness, one sees the Buddha in all things;

since not a single color or fragrance is not the Middle Way, there is nothing encountered by the six sense organs that is not the Buddha-dharma. Next, regarding the example of Jīvaka, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"Jīvaka first went to the country of Takṣaśilā, where he studied under a master of the Ātreya clan named Bhēḍila."

The medical path required seven years; his teacher then provided him with a basket and tools for digging herbs, instructing him to seek out all manner of plants within a one-yojana radius of the kingdom and bring back anything that was not medicinal.
Following these instructions, Jīvaka searched everywhere throughout the one-yojana area of the kingdom, examining every tree and herb he encountered.
"All things are distinguished; there is no grass or wood that is not medicine. The Master then told him: "You may now depart; your path as a physician is already perfected.
After I have passed away, you shall be next in line" (and so forth). The *Sudarsana-vinaya* states: "Śākyaputra was the son of the Buddha’s paternal uncle.
One month after [the Buddha’s] great enlightenment, he attained the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*. As the *Mahāsūtra* says, 'Śākyamoha'..."
The man held various shards and rubble, all of which became precious jewels; this was brought about by the power of his mental force in the past (and so forth).
Naluo (Aniruddha) reflected to himself: "Ninety-one kalpas ago, during a time of famine in the world, I sold firewood and saw a Pratyekabuddha begging for food.
I then invited him to my home and offered him wild millet and rice gruel. Immediately in this present life, I obtained [the fruit]."
From that time onward, for ninety-one kalpas, I have lacked nothing among gods or humans;
even until my present life as a householder, I have always lived in leisure and did not take pleasure in worldly affairs.
My elder brother Mahānāma was always full of complaints, yet my mother would say, "My son possesses great merit. Mahānāma would reply, "I alone am burdened with the anxieties of the household."
