His family estate was vast, and he lived in leisure, reclining and eating at ease; how could one say he lacked merit?

His mother, wishing to test him, sent him to the fields to supervise the work, ordering that no food be sent to him. I grew suspicious that his meal was being delayed, so I sent someone to his mother to ask for food.
His mother then sent someone to tell me, "There is nothing. I returned and said to her, "I only pray that you will give it to me."

When the Mother of Nothingness heard this, she immediately took precious vessels and adorned her utensils, covering them with a cloth, and sent them to me, instructing Mahānāman to follow and look after them.
Upon arriving at my place, he pulled back the cloth, and found that the trays were filled with food and drink of a hundred flavors (and so forth).
Therefore, I now borrow this as a metaphor for how wondrous contemplation passes through all things.

All phenomena spontaneously perceive the true mark; the Middle Way is likewise so (and so forth). Regarding the passage "If it is thus," the following three knots demonstrate the *Samantabhadra-vyūha-sūtra* contemplation:

"Contemplate that the dharmas of the mind do not abide in dharmas, and my own mind is naturally empty, such that neither sin nor merit has a master. To reckon that there is one who can contemplate is called "my mind.
Because this "my mind" exists, subject and object are not extinguished. If "what belongs to me" (*mama*) were extinguished, then sin... [would cease].
Merit has no master; both subject and object are exhausted. Therefore, it is called "contemplating the mind as no-mind.

Since mental phenomena do not abide and cannot be apprehended, the true mark (*dharmatā*) is revealed. Therefore, it is called "that which is contemplated": that offenses and merit are neither offense nor merit, but are both the true mark.
This true mark is what is termed "Great Repentance. Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "Contemplate all phenomena as empty."

According to the true mark (*tathatā-lakṣaṇa*), there is no name and no mark; in reality, nothing exists at all. This does not mean that the ten realms—with their marks of good and evil, or sin and merit—appear vividly before us.
One must know that the essence of the Middle Way is quiescent and still, simultaneously negating both extremes;

it is not even "emptiness," let alone "existence. Only when one illuminates both sides of emptiness and existence simultaneously can it be called the "sinless mark repentance" (*anavadya-lakṣaṇa-pratikramaṇa*).

Furthermore, regarding the Adornment Repentance (*Zhuāngyán Chàn*): if one does not understand that the two contemplations of principle and phenomena elucidated by our school involve reaching the Dharma-nature—which is inherently empty of both subject and object—through the contemplation of principle alone;

or if one focuses exclusively on the contemplation of phenomena by investigating the arising of the mind to enter emptiness, how then can one clarify that the offenses and blessings being contemplated are all the true aspect (*shíxiàng*)?
For the emptiness of all dharmas is the very substance of the true aspect, just like clarity itself.

The mirror is also like a wish-fulfilling jewel (and so forth). Next, the explanation of the text on the auxiliary methods is divided into two parts. First, clarifying the purpose of using the auxiliaries, which is further divided into two.
First, the actual clarification of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*: "First, one must know the ten minds of opposition and conformity and then fix the object upon the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*);

this is the foremost repentance. One constantly repents such that there is no time when one is not repenting; however, because the principle of the mind is subtle and secret, it is through the function of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) [that this is realized]."

Light, superficial, black, and evil [karmas] are shrouded and obstructed, making them difficult to clarify suddenly; therefore, one must employ the heavy operation of body and speech to assist and stimulate the mental karma (*manas-karman*), so that it may quickly correspond [to awakening].

Furthermore, the five repentances (*pañca-deśanā*) are added for this reason. Thus, the previous passage says, "Repentance is the foremost submission," and the subsequent passage says, "The body revolves in prostration," etc.;
this is precisely their intended meaning. Next, as for the phrase "so-called," it raises an analogy using the *jia* (古恊切, gǔ xié) and *huàn* (胡慣切, hú guàn) seeds. Next...
To speak briefly, the following section correctly elucidates the auxiliary practices, which is further divided into two parts.

First, it correctly elucidates the bodily circumambulations, prostrations, and so forth, as detailed in the ritual protocols for repentance in this very sutra (and so on). Second, under the phrase "as when following," an analogy is raised: a *gāo* (pronounced *gǎo*) is a pole used to propel a boat;

it is also written as *gāozhào* (pronounced *chíxiào*) or *jié* (pronounced *jíè*). Following the current is a metaphor for the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) that is the object of contemplation; following the wind is a metaphor for...

To say that being able to contemplate the True Dharma is "conformity" (*shun*) refers to conformity in nature (*xing-shun*) and conformity in practice (*xiu-shun*). "Conformity" means to take the realization of one's nature as one's conduct—is it not so?
The oars and poles are metaphors for the auxiliary dharmas, such as circumambulation and prostration; these three are thus categorized.

Below, this concludes the characteristics of the primary and auxiliary practices, as detailed extensively in the *Mohe Zhiguan*; here, they are merely summarized briefly for the purpose of explaining the title of the "Chapter on Repentance."

The fourth section, the explanation of the passage on the stage of repentance (*pratikramana*), is divided into two parts: first, the heading; second, the explanation of the text beginning with "If one has committed...
This explanation is further divided into two parts: first, refuting the restrictive interpretation; second, clarifying the universal application.

Regarding the latter, it is stated that in the *Karmāvaraṇapratiprasrabdhi-parivarta* (Chapter on the Extinction of Karmic Obstructions) within that New Translation version, after the extensive explanation of the text on repenting karmic obstructions is concluded, it says: "If one has already committed an offense, one should immediately repent."

If one seeks purity, one must repent in this manner. If one wishes to be born into a wealthy and prosperous family, a Brahmin family, or a Kṣatriya family, or among the gods of the Four Great Kings, the Thirty-three Heavens, up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, one must all repent to eliminate karmic obstructions.
If one seeks the first fruit, the second, third, or fourth fruit, or the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, or the state of a Pratyekabuddha, one must likewise do so.
The Bodhisattva’s *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should likewise involve repentance to eliminate and eradicate karmic obstructions (and so forth).
The present text—stating that humans receive their bodies from their parents and so on—is merely the Great Master [Zhiyi] expanding upon the meaning of that sutra according to its principles.

This section consists of six parts; first, it clarifies the repentance for karmic obstructions of the four miserable realms. *Ju* means to nourish; *fu* means to comfort and settle; *cun* means to preserve.
Regarding the term *yěwéiwéi* (也惟惟), Gushan cites an ancient interpretation stating that it describes the appearance of pitying one's child. *Shēng* (升) means "to raise.
"Teaching directions" (*jiàofāng*) means teaching them to know the cardinal directions such as east and west; "teaching numbers" (*jiàoshù*) means teaching them numbers such as one and two.
The *Neizé* chapter of the *Lǐjì* states: "At six years of age, they are taught numbers and the names of directions. The commentary notes: "The names refer to east, west, and so forth."
I have also committed the great treason of regicide. That the Buddha is the Teacher of Gods and Humans (*devamanuṣyaśāstṛ*) is one of his ten titles.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* asks: "If the Buddha can deliver beings such as nāgas, spirits, and deities, why is he specifically called the Teacher of Gods and Humans?
The answer is: those delivered from among other realms of rebirth are few, while those delivered from among gods and humans are many; furthermore, the fetters of gods and humans...
It causes one’s meager wisdom and keen sense of weary detachment to be easily attained (and so forth). Regarding the gravity of the teacher and the reverence for the Way, the *Book of Rites* states:

"In the way of learning, the most difficult thing is to treat the teacher with gravity. Once the teacher is grave, then the Way is honored; once the Way is honored, then the people know to respect learning.
Therefore, there are two instances where a ruler does not treat his ministers as subjects: when they act as the presiding spirit (*shi*) at a sacrifice, he does not treat them as subjects.
When one serves as a teacher, they are not treated as a subordinate; even when receiving instructions from the Son of Heaven, they do not face north, for this is how a teacher is honored.
The commentary states that "respect" (yan) means reverence. The "first category" refers to the *pārājika* offenses at the beginning of the five categories;

the "subsequent group" refers to the *duṣkṛta* (or *śaikṣa*) offenses following the six groups. These five and six categories appear in alternating literary styles, and here the initial ones are cited.
Regarding the subsequent intermediate cases, one should know that "you" refers to the recipient; "deceiving" means to mislead, and "betraying" means to turn one's back on [the precepts].

These three masters and seven monks are explained according to the regulations of the Central Kingdom (Madhyadeśa). Furthermore, in frontier regions where monks are scarce, there is the method of receiving the precepts with five persons.

If, at a later time, there are sufficient monks, one must employ the original formal method (*mūla-vidhi*) to obtain the precepts; otherwise, one incurs an offense, and so forth. Regarding the "corpse in the ocean of the Buddha," Nanshan says:
The ocean of the Vinaya is profound and deep, its currents reaching all phenomena; though it encompasses everything without exception, it harbors no corpses.

This can be understood by analogy with a flower garden where rotting flesh does not remain. As for those who commit the four grave offenses (pārājika) and ought to perform repentance, this is spoken of from the perspective of their gravity;

it does not mean that the four sections and five groups of precepts need not be confessed. If it is said that in the Mahāyāna one need not maintain the precepts, why then does this text prescribe repentance?
Regarding the transgression of breaking the precepts: not only does one commit an offense oneself, but it further obstructs others from upholding them.

If someone asks you about the precepts established by the Buddha, and you reply that the Buddha intended them only for the Hīnayāna, is this not slandering the Dharma and misleading immeasurable people? I urge you to seek out the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Calm Abiding and Clear Observation);

through the purity of upholding the precepts, you will have sufficient means to reflect upon yourself. Regarding the term *huǐ* (pronounced with the *xǔ wěi* rhyme): the *Erya* states that the *fú-huǐ* (viper) measures three inches in width, with a large head.
As for the "Splitting" (bài), the commentary states: its body is three inches wide and its head is as large as a person's split finger. This is one species of snake called the *fǔhuǐ*.

Regarding the characters *sī* (pronounced *shì*) and *yǐ* (cut by *yú yǐ*), they should be written as *yǐ* (cut by *jū yǐ*). Those who mutually harm one another devour each other, suffering without end.
Those who are greatly fearful always delight in fighting; their terror is boundless. Next, the confession is explained.

Regarding the karmic obstacles of humans and devas, concerning the statement on the eight sufferings, the *Catuḥsatya-śāstra* asks: "Briefly stated, what is the meaning of these eight sufferings? It answers:
"That which serves as the basis for all suffering is called the suffering of birth; that which causes transformation and decay is called the suffering of old age;

that which oppresses the body is called the suffering of illness; that which extinguishes the sense faculties is called the suffering of death; and the forced association with what is unloved is called enmity."
The suffering of association with the loathed is the state of being far removed from what is desirable; the suffering of separation from the beloved is the failure to fulfill one's hopes;

and the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks is the characteristic of these various sufferings. These are called the "suffering of the five aggregates" (*pañca-skandha-duḥkha*). As stated in detail in the eleventh fascicle of the *Mahāvaipulya-sūtra* (and so forth).

Regarding the "five signs of decay" (*pañca-vyasanāni*), the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* distinguishes between the great and small five signs of decay. The small five signs of decay are: first, the emergence of [stains] on clothing and ornaments...
1. Unpleasant sounds; 2. One’s own bodily radiance suddenly becomes dim and inferior; 3. At the time of bathing, drops of water adhere to the body; 4.
One’s naturally restless mind now stagnates on a single object; 5. The eyes, originally steady and tranquil, now blink repeatedly.
Regarding the five great signs of decay: 1. The flowers upon the head wither; 2. Sweat breaks out from under the armpits; 3. The light between the shoulders vanishes; 4. The two... [text truncated]
Regarding "the eyes blink frequently and one finds no joy in one's original seat," this refers to the five signs of decay (*pañca-vyasanāni*);

because their suffering is equal to that of the hells, they are so described. "Equal" means identical. Regarding "the gods of the form realm cannot quickly enter meditative concentration," this refers to the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñi-sattva*), which is a heaven of long life where non-Buddhists reside; because mental activity does not function there, it is so named.

Regarding the four mental states of suffering among the formless gods (*ārūpyadhātu*): although they lack even a single form, they possess four minds and ten kinds of subtle afflictions, as already shown previously (etc.).

*Fan* (pronounced *fúyuán*) means a screen or a fence; it refers to a boundary wall. If one leaves the household life, the following three sections clarify the practice of repentance for karmic hindrances according to the Tripiṭaka Teaching.
This text is divided into two parts; the first clarifies the Śrāvaka path, which is further divided into two sections. First...
Regarding the five afflictions of the ordinary stage (*pṛthagjana-avasthā*): first, excessive greed; second, excessive anger; third, excessive delusion; fourth, excessive distraction;

and fifth, excessive hindrance. Regarding the four perversions (*viparyāsa*): they are the arbitrary reckoning of permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Since these are both afflictions and perversions, why are they called "karmic hindrances" (*karmāvaraṇa*)?
It is because afflictions are able to give rise to unwholesome karma. As for the application of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), it serves as their antidote.
Regarding those four perversions (*viparyāsa*), one counteracts them by means of impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity.

Following this principle, one should first state that the five objects of cessation (*pañca-vastūni*) counteract the five afflictions (*pañca-kleśāḥ*), and subsequently clarify how the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) counteract the perversions.

If one does not diligently abandon the two evils (evil already arisen and evil not yet arisen) nor diligently produce the two virtues (virtue not yet arisen and virtue already arisen), one will fail to enter the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) within the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).
Regarding "not producing": the intention is that by means of the four right efforts (*samyak-pradhāna*), one corresponds to the stage of "warmth" (*uṣmagata*).

Since one does not diligently abandon the two evils nor diligently produce the two goods, even the dharma of warmth is not yet produced; how then could one enter the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*)?

Thus, we know that only by diligently abandoning the two evils and diligently producing the two goods can one correspond to the stage of warmth. In the present text, the phrasing is inverted; it first states that one "cannot enter," as follows: [text continues].

Following the "satisfactions of mind" (*iddhipāda*), it is said that the "dharma of warmth" (*uṣmagata*) does not arise; furthermore, it is said that the "five faculties" (*pañcendriya*) do not produce joy because there is still the possibility of falling back.

From this, we know that the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) correspond to the stage of the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) correspond to the stage of warmth, and the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*) correspond to the stage of the summit (*mūrdhan*).

The five faculties and the five powers (*pañcabala*) correspond to the stage of patience (*kṣānti*). The stage of the "worldly-first" (*laukikāgradharma*) can be understood by analogy with this. As for the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*), it follows the same principle.

These [factors] belong to the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) as the Seven Factors of Enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), and to the stage of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*) as the fourfold sets of the Path-constituents (*mārga-pakṣa-dharma*); specifically, they correspond here to the factors of the Path.
In this present text, for the sake of brevity, these are merely summarized by stating that within these four roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*), one must perform repentance.

Next, regarding the clarification of the stages of the Noble Ones (*ārya*) starting from "Patience with Suffering" (*duḥkha-kṣānti*): once Patience with Suffering has arisen, one will immediately and without interval enter the First Fruit (*prathamaphala*). Now...

To explain further according to the general teaching: once the Sage’s true illumination has arisen, he severs the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and thus does not fall into the three miserable states or the four evil destinies.
As for the nine grades of the delusions of desire (*kāma-kleśa*), which have the power to moisten seven births, they are as follows: the "superior-superior" grade moistens two births;

the "superior-middle," "superior-inferior," and "middle-superior" grades each moisten one birth; the "middle-middle" and "middle-inferior" grades together moisten one birth; and the "inferior" grade [moistens the remaining birth].
Since these three grades [of practitioners] together moisten a single lifetime, there are three types of persons who sever the afflictions of the desire realm: first, those who sever them gradually;

second, those who sever them progressively; and third, those who sever them by leaping over. Since the present text states that one undergoes seven births in the desire realm in succession, it should be known that this refers to a person who severs them spontaneously.
Although such a person has severed five grades of the five lower fetters of the desire realm, three grades still remain.

This is the Sakṛdāgāmin (Once-returner). Regarding the five lower fetters (*pañca avara-bhāgīyāni*): first, the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*); second, attachment to precepts and rituals (*śīla-vrata-parāmarśa*); third, doubt (*vicikitsā*); fourth, sensual greed (*kāma-rāga*); and fifth, ill-will (*vyāpāda*). Regarding the five higher fetters (*pañca ūrdhva-bhāgīyāni*):

first, restlessness (*auddhatya*); second, pride (*māna*); third, ignorance (*avidyā*); fourth, attachment to the realm of form (*rūpa-rāga*); and fifth, attachment to the formless realm (*ārūpya-rāga*). As the *Abhidharmakośa* states: "Because they accord with and benefit the lower realms—meaning that only those belonging to the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) receive the name 'lower,' while those that accord with and benefit the upper realms receive the name 'higher'";

thus, only those in the Form and Formless Realms receive the name 'higher,' and so forth. Therefore, according to the *Abhidharmakośa*, one who abandons six [fetters] attains the fruit of the Once-returner. According to the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, abandoning six grades in succession is called a Sakṛdāgāmin; abandoning six grades by means of leaping over [the stages] is called a "One-who-goes-once" (*ekavīcika*).

It is said: although one has severed the five lower grades and eight [of the nine] higher grades, leaving only one grade remaining, this is what the *Zhiguan* calls "leaping over" to the eighth grade, termed a "One-Seed" (*ekabījika*).
Although one has severed all [defilements] of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), leaving the portion of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) remaining, this is the third type of *anāgāmin*.

Regarding the phrase "with remainder," it means that while one has already attained liberation from the bonds of the seeds of [defilements of] view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa-bīja*), there remains further...

Because the body remains as the remaining fruit of suffering, it is called "with remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*). To prove this state of having remainder, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* cites the cases of Śāriputra’s wind-fever and Pindola Bhāradvāja’s eye pain.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "These noble ones, by the power of their wisdom, possess no mental suffering such as anger;
however, because they experience the karmic conditions of their past lives, the body composed of the four great elements suffers from physical illness."
Only when this body has perished is there "nirvana without remainder. The two delusions of views and thought are not peripheral; they are called "primary" because they actively drive and enslave one.

Because the remaining traces are categorized as residual habit-energies (*vāsanā*), they are termed "habit-energies. Next, regarding the statement that it is the same for the Pratyekabuddha, this means that even the fourth fruit must repent of its habit-energies.
The only difference is that while the fruit of the [Śrāvaka] Arhat is entirely [free of them], the Pratyekabuddha has only slightly diminished them.

The text does not mention the Bodhisattvas of the Three Piṭakas because their meaning regarding the subduing of afflictions is the same as that of the Seven Sages (the *saptakula-putra*). Regarding the four stages from "Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) downward, these are explained according to the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*):

they are called "nature" (*prakṛti*) because they have not yet attained [the fruit] and have not yet seen [the truth]. Among them, the eighth person at the stage of seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*) still possesses craving; the third, the eighth person at the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-bhūmi*), has severed afflictions within the "unimpeded samādhi" (*anantarya-samādhi*). Fourth, [the text states: "In the text, the Bodhisattvas of the Three Piṭakas are not mentioned because the meaning of their subduing of delusions is the same as that of the Seven Worthies (*saptakula-putra*). As for the four [stages] from Dry Wisdom downward, these clarify the repentance of karmic obstructions according to those of the Shared Teaching. Because they have not yet been moistened and have not yet seen [the truth], they are termed 'nature. Among them, the eighth person at the stage of seeing still has craving; the third, the eighth person at the stage of cultivation, severs delusions within the unimpeded samādhi."

Upon seeing the stage [of the Path of Seeing], one has severed all afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), yet afflictions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) still remain; the rest is as explained in the *Miaoxuan* and *Zhi guan* (and so forth).
Those on the Stage of Thinness (*tanu-bhūmi*) who have not yet attained supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) still possess the three lower grades of afflictions.

Those on the Stage of Completion (*kṛtāvi-bhūmi*) who cannot eliminate residual habits (*vāsanā*) do so because Śrāvakas only sever the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*). Pratyekabuddhas who only exercise supernormal powers do so because their powers are fully developed.

The six supernormal powers (ṣaḍabhijñā) are common to both, but the eighteen transformations (aṣṭādaśa-vaikārika-vidhi) are unique to the latter; this is not a pratyekabuddha, but rather a *pratyekajina* (solitary buddha).
While those who are *pratyekabuddhas* take birth by aspiration, these solitary buddhas appear in worlds where no Buddha exists. Furthermore, there are two types:

first, the "group-dwelling" (*vargacārin*), who, in a world without a Buddha, instructs disciples and benefits others through teaching the Dharma; second, those distinct from this, known as "non-group-dwelling" (*khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa*).

Since they do not encounter a Buddha, they do not hear the Dharma; although they internally realize meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), they do not externally manifest the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*).

If they wish to repay the kindness of those who provide offerings of faith, they can only perform transformations through supernatural powers (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*); therefore, it is said that they are unable to penetrate the literal words.

From the "Ten Faiths" downward, the fifth section clarifies the practice of repentance for karmic obstructions according to the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*); it explains how one enters the truth of the limited reality (*pratyeka-satya*) but only emerges from it.

"Provisionally, according to the path of teaching, it is said that one merely cultivates the 'Middle' (but-mid). (As stated above... Furthermore, from the sixth stage of the Ten Faiths downward, this is explained in terms of a person of the Perfect Teaching who performs repentance for karmic obstructions.

Because the three wisdoms are cultivated perfectly, the path of subduement becomes increasingly powerful, thereby destroying the views and afflictions within the realms, as well as the 'dust-sands' of both internal and external phenomena.
Thus, the *svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī* resides in the seventh faith, while the hundred-thousand-million-billion *dhāraṇīs* [arise] therefrom."

The *dhāraṇī of the skillful means of the Dharma-sound* (法音方便陀羅尼), which is situated at the stage above the eighth level of faith (*aṣṭama-śraddhā*), is precisely the path of subduing (*vibhava-mārga*) but has not yet entered the middle stage;
because it resides within the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), it is said to be merely a "skillful means *dhāraṇī*.

Regarding the "fourteen days of the moon" and so forth, the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* clarifies that the fourteen types of patience (*kṣānti*) and the thirty minds (*triṃśac-citta*) constitute the three *prajñās*, while the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*) constitute the ten *prajñās*.

The state of Equal Enlightenment consists of fourteen types of prajñā; while these reside within the mind of a bodhisattva, they are termed "patience" (kṣānti), but upon transitioning into the Buddha-mind, they are termed "wisdom" (jñāna).
This corresponds to the stage of "clear wisdom" on the fifteenth day of the lunar month. As the Mahāyāna Sūtra states regarding the Moon-Love Samādhi (*candrakānta-samādhi*):
from the first day until the fifteenth day of the moon, the light and color gradually increase, serving as an analogy for the fifteen types of wisdom.
The "Vimalaprabhā" (Pure Light) of the Supreme Heavenly King of Perfected Virtue uses the fourteen days of the moon as a metaphor for the fourteen stages of Prajñā;
therefore, it is so stated. The character *zhǐ* (pronounced *zhǐ*) is a particle used for emphasis. Furthermore, the word *fū* (pronounced *kuāngguò*) refers to the outer perimeter or enclosure.

From "Equaling this" (*qí cǐ*) onwards, the text is divided into two parts: first, the formal conclusion and refutation; second, from "Therefore" (*shì gù*) onwards, the citation of evidence. This extends up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*Samyaksambodhi*).

He causes all to repent; I have examined that sutra and have not yet seen this passage. Regarding the "fifty reckonings," as cited in the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra-ṭīkā*), it says [as follows].
Next, the section beginning with "If a person...

concludes the exhortation. The "flower-retribution" existing within the cause is also called the "fruit of practice" (*abhyāsa-phala*), which means it has not yet emerged from the stage of limited transmigration (*pariccheda*).

"Restricted-domain retribution" means that the fruit itself is the retribution. Regarding the "notes" (云云), the methods for repaying kindness and worshipping the Buddha are fully detailed in the *Guoqing Bailu*.

Following the section on Repentance (*Chanhui pin*), the next part explains the text according to the definitions of the characters, divided into two sections. First, the formal explanation: *ni* (pronounced *nü* with the second tone) means shame.
"Constricted," "pressing," and "urgent" [refer to the urgency of the situation]. The commentary on the *Sūtra on the Dharma-Gate of the Sequential Summary* is divided into two parts.
First, a general demonstration of these various explanations: the *Mahāyāna Sūtra* states that the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, always say:

"There are two pure dharmas (*śukla-dharma*) capable of saving sentient beings: first, shame (*hrī*); second, remorse (*apatrāpya*). Shame means not committing offenses oneself; remorse means not teaching others to commit them."

*Hrī* (shame) is the sense of self-reproach and disgrace felt within oneself; *apatrāpya* (modesty) is the disclosure of one's faults before others. *Hrī* is shame before men; *apatrāpya* is shame before the heavens.
These are called shame and modesty. Those who lack shame and modesty are not called human beings; they are called beasts.
Because they possess shame and modesty, they are able to revere their parents, teachers, and elders (and so forth).

There are three types of repentance; next, the text is divided into two parts for a detailed explanation. First, the headings and enumeration; second, the explanation of the text beginning with "The Hīnayāna," which is further divided into two.

First, the distinction of the three types of Hīnayāna repentance, such as the *pratikarmika* (exposure) and the *śaikṣa-dharma* (training rules), which refer specifically to the ritual repentance (*pratideśanā*) for a *pārājika* offense.
Regarding this, both Gushan and Siming maintain that although there are methods for repenting a *pārājika* offense even in the Hīnayāna, the text...

Regarding the statement that "the text does not lead [to this conclusion]," [the opponent argues] that although one has performed the confession (*pratideśanā*) and is training in repentance (*śikṣāmanatā*), if it still obstructs the attainment of the noble fruit (*āryaphala*), then this does not accord with the meaning of "returning to original purity" (*mūlapariśuddhi*) within this context.
Now, I say this is not so. Why? Because the method for confessing a *pārājika* offense is precisely the disclosure (*vibhāvana*) and training found within the Vinaya;

how then can it be said that the textual passage does not descend to this point? The concluding section of the text states: "Provided that the ritual procedure (*karmavācanā*) is successfully accomplished..."

Not obstructing the affairs of the Saṃgha is itself purity. Therefore, one should know that confession (*āviṣkaraṇa*) and training (*śikṣā*)—which do not obstruct the affairs of the Saṃgha—are themselves purity.
How can it be claimed that this is not the meaning of "returning to original purity"? The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:

"If a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī has committed a pārājika offense, provided they have no intention to conceal it, they may perform the Dharma-accordant repentance. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "If one has committed a pārājika offense..."
To those who weep and do not wish to part from their *kāṣāya*, one should grant the *śikṣādattaka-karman* (the rite of probationary training).

One must receive and practice all the precepts established by the Buddha and sit below the full assembly of monks (*bhikṣu-saṃgha*). The *Vinayamātṛkā* states: "Once the rite of confession through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* has been granted, one is called a pure upholder of the precepts.

(Please observe this passage; how could it be said that such a person is not pure? However, while in this single body, they cannot transcend birth and death; nevertheless, [it serves as] an obstacle [to further transgression].

"One shall not enter hell. The *Sūtra on Healing the Ailments of Dhyāna* states: "One who has committed a grave offense and performs repentance should remove the saṃghāṭī robe and put on the antarvāsaka, giving rise to a sense of shame and remorse.

One should perform menial service for the Saṃgha, such as sweeping latrines and carrying away excrement. According to the Vinaya, one should be instructed to request [the formal act], saying: 'Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
I, bhikṣu So-and-so, have committed the pārājika offense of sexual misconduct without concealment. Now, I seek [relief] from the Saṃgha.'"

"I request the *pārājika* precepts; may the Saṃgha grant me the *pārājika* precepts. Having made this request three times, the Saṃgha should seek the consent (*chanda*) and inquire for harmony before performing the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) for granting the *pārājika* precepts (and so forth).
Once the *pārājika* precepts have been granted, one must practice the conforming rules and undergo the forfeiture of the thirty-five matters (and so forth).
When the Saṃgha recites the precepts or performs formal rituals, whether one comes or does not come is according to one's own discretion (since [the precepts] have not yet...).

When one comes during the time for confession (*poṣadha*), one must be expelled; now that the confession is complete, one’s presence does not count toward the required number, as there is no distinction made for those who do not come. This is why it is called "acting according to one's will" (*svairacārya*). If one commits the offense again, one must undergo *parivāsa* (probation) and subsequent *nigarhaṇīya* (expulsion).

Although the first offense was permitted to be confessed, a second offense logically requires expulsion, precisely because the person lacks any sense of dread or restraint. Furthermore, Nanshan established three types of rational confession (*yuktikṣānti*): First, the realization that all phenomena are empty of self-nature and devoid of self;
illuminating the mind with this principle is termed the "Lesser Vehicle" (*Hīnayāna*). Second, the realization that the fundamental characteristics of all phenomena are empty... [text fragment ends].
To perceive this principle through deluded sentiment and regard its illumination and function as belonging to the stage of the small Bodhisattva;

and to realize that all dharmas and external objects are originally without reality and consist only of consciousness—a principle so profound and subtle that it can only be known through mental contemplation—this belongs to the great Bodhisattva and the realized practice of the Buddha-fruit.
The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states: "Regarding this passage from the *Nanshan*, although it has its basis, the first level of judgment assigns it to the Small Vehicle."
Since there is no principle for those who have mounted the vehicle to repent for grave offenses, how much more so for this stage, which is already separated from the initial resolve?
Furthermore, the second and third stages belong to Bodhisattvas and the fruit of Buddhahood; there is no ground for an ordinary person to rely upon them with a mind of regret.

Therefore, the Nanshan school judges these stages to be too high for the beginner, as they have no share in them, and since there is no offense at such a high level, why list them here? What is established now is simply...

It is clarified that if those of inferior capacity wish to employ Mahāyāna methods to repent for grave offenses, they should rely on such texts as the Vaipulya *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra*.

Furthermore, it is stated that even within the gates of the Hīnayāna teachings, confession (*pratideśanā*) is not permitted; although it is said that one may be reborn [in the human realm], one is unfit for the functions of the Saṃgha.

Once a *śrāmaṇera* has committed an offense and completed the repentance, he may proceed to full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*). This is a matter permitted by the Mahāyāna and may be generally practiced. However, if one allows a fully ordained monk (*bhikṣu*) to harbor a paramour and bring her in...

Furthermore, since the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra* (Precious Mound Sūtra) clearly establishes that [the number of monks] must be complete, even though there is no explicit text regarding the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles, we accept the regulations for training and practice as distinct.

Since the principle of not confessing a grave offense still constitutes a grave sin, what purpose would there be in using the Mahāyāna teachings to confess a *pārājika* offense so as to fulfill the monastic quota of the Small Vehicle?
Having already entered the path through the Mahāyāna confession, why should one confuse these matters to delude the sentiments of the age? (And so forth.)

Now, let us examine this in detail: the three types of repentance established by Nanshan are based on sūtras and śāstras as "repentance of principle" (*lǐchàn*), not "repentance of ritual action" (*shìchàn*).
The *Miaoxuan* states: "The Vinaya-piṭaka of the Hīnayāna does not permit repentance for the re-cultivation [of precepts];

it causes those who have committed a grave offense to contemplate the Buddha-body. To contemplate the Buddha-body is to contemplate emptiness" (this is identical to the "Repentance of Contemplating Emptiness" mentioned below). If that is so, then regarding the Hīnayāna...

Although the Vinaya-piṭaka contains repentance through principle (*lǐ-chàn*) and repentance through contemplating emptiness (*kōng-chàn*), with the latter being more weighty, the Sūtra-piṭaka likewise contains both repentance through principle and repentance through contemplating emptiness, with the latter being more weighty.

When the *Fǔxíng* (Subcommentary on the *Mohe Zhiguan*) states that "the Small [Vehicle] has no weighty repentance through principle," it merely attaches this to the Vinaya-piṭaka and does not establish a separate repentance through principle there to refute it.
If one were to use the Sūtra-piṭaka to refute Nanshan, it would likely be inconvenient; if not...

How, then, can one reconcile this with the text of the *Miaoxuan*? Question: If the Sūtra-piṭaka of the Hīnayāna establishes the principle of repentance for grave offenses, how does it differ from the Mahāyāna?
Answer: The Sūtra-piṭaka of the Mahāyāna includes texts such as the *Samantabhadra-darśana-sūtra*.

Furthermore, regarding the Vinaya-piṭaka of the Mahāyāna, such as the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*, it permits the repentance of the four pārājika offenses and allows for the restoration of those who have received the precepts. Therefore, it differs from the Hīnayāna.
The ritual confession and disclosure (*pratideśanā*) found in the Mahāyāna Vinaya-piṭaka cannot be compared to that found in the Śrāvaka teachings;

furthermore, the Mahāyāna Sūtra-piṭaka, such as the Vaipulya sūtras, clarifies that through ritual confession even pārājika offenses are extinguished, restoring one to original purity and allowing one to return to the status of a bhikṣu.

In contrast, although the Śrāvaka Sūtra-piṭaka explains confession through the contemplation of principle (*tattva*), it differs from the Mahāyāna approach regarding grave offenses, because [the former] pertains to the Vinaya-piṭaka.

This is because it is for the monks to employ at their discretion. However, the subsequent passage cites the *Āgama*, which clarifies that one should perform repentance by apprehending signs (*nimitta*), instructing those who have committed sexual misconduct to form the mental image of a snake’s mouth;
when this contemplation is perfected, the sin of lust is immediately extinguished. Thus, even within the sūtras, ritual repentance (*vastu-pratikramaṇa*) is clarified;

if there were no repentance of non-arising (*anutpāda-pratikramaṇa*), it would merely be called "principle" (*li*). Furthermore, the *Dhyanapāramitā-śāstra* states: "In the Vinaya, repentance has not yet been clearly elucidated."
Regarding the four grave offenses (*catur- pārājika*), the *Ādiśāsana-sūtra* clarifies the method for repentance for these four grave offenses. That sūtra states:

"One should invite thirty pure bhikṣus into the great assembly; the bhikṣu who has committed the offense shall confess it himself, and the Sangha shall perform the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) for him.
Furthermore, by performing various practices before the Triple Gem and reciting the Prātimokṣa one thousand times, one immediately attains purification."

Jing, you should know that although the Vinaya-piṭaka of the Hīnayāna does not explicitly clarify the ritual for repentance (*karmavācanā*) to extinguish a *pārājika* offense, such a method also exists within the Sūtra-piṭaka.

(The current text states: "Since the Dharma of the Hīnayāna, as found in the Vinaya, involves disclosure and the performance of ritual procedures to achieve success, it does not obstruct monastic affairs, and one immediately attains purity. Furthermore, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* and other texts cited previously all clarify methods of repentance, and these are all ritual procedures (*karmavācanā*).

Since the sūtras of the Initial Teaching [Hīnayāna] also involve ritual procedures, why do you claim that the Hīnayāna Vinaya-piṭaka does not clarify ritual procedures? Nevertheless, one must understand that although the ritual procedures of the Vinaya-piṭaka restore birth [to the precepts], they do not permit the use of the person for the community. )

If one were to say that committing [a grave offense] constitutes a heavy transgression, yet the *Āgama* scriptures clearly explain the ritual procedures (*vidhi*) for its extinction, then how could it be said that the precept treasury (*śīlapiṭaka*) does not clarify the ritual procedures for repenting a *pārājika* offense? If this were not the case, why would the *Sūtra-piṭaka* also contain such teachings?

Therefore, we know that while the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) *Śīlapiṭaka* has not clarified both the factual and principled repentances for extinguishing a *pārājika* offense, they are all present within the *Sūtra-piṭaka*.
Thus, when the *Nanshan Lüchao* (The Vinaya Commentary of Nanshan) rejects the *Āgama* scriptures as spurious, [it contradicts the fact that] Tiantai...

If one cites [these texts], they are not spurious. Regarding the *Questioning the Sutra on Healing the Illnesses of Dhyāna* (*Wen zhichanbing jing*) and the *Four-Part Vinaya* (*Sifen lü*), since these clearly explain the repentance for a *pārājika* offense, why does the *Sub-commentary on the Fahua Wenju* (*Fahua wenju xingshi chao*) state that "in the Small Vehicle there is no repentance for a grave offense"?

The answer is: "There is no repentance for a grave offense in the Small Vehicle" means that in the Vinaya-piṭaka of the Small Vehicle, a person who has committed a grave offense is likened to one whose head has been severed;

thus, there is no principle by which the transgression of a *pārājika* could be extinguished through repentance so as to allow them to return to the status of a Great Bhikṣu. It does not mean that [repentance] is impossible.

This is permitted for those who perform ritual services, repent and confess, and request the precepts; thus, "repenting and requesting the precepts" is called "learning through repentance" (*xuehui*) and is also termed "confessing grave offenses.
As the *Fuxing* (Commentary on the *Mohe Zhiguan*) states: "The minor [offenses] have no repentance; grave [offenses] cannot be treated as identical. Question:

if committed intentionally, one confesses once before another person; if committed unintentionally, one performs a mental repentance (*pratikaroti*) within oneself.
Provided that the ritual procedure is duly completed, it does not obstruct monastic affairs, and one is thereby purified. This concludes the section on the confession of remaining [offenses].
Regarding the "purity through the four articles" (*catvāraḥ pariśuddhayaḥ*) and the confession for purity from a *pārājika* offense:

"Whether he comes or not, his head is severed at will. This refers to the state of not yet attaining the fruits of sainthood (*āryaphala*).

First, the explanation of the ritual repentance (zuo-fa chan), which may last for eight hundred days; as for the "empty space" (ākāśagarbha) and the "cleansing of latrines," [the text continues as follows].
"Latrine" (*ce*) refers to "intermingling," because people intermingle there and the place is filled with various impurities. The *Gaganagañja-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states:
"In future ages, those who are skilled in the Vinaya should teach sentient beings the methods for treating transgressions. There are thirty-five Buddhas who save the world through great compassion;
one must establish a site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*), prepare all manner of offerings, first pay homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions, and recite their names."
Regarding the distinct names of the fifteen Buddhas, what is the specific name of the Great Compassionate One, Ākāśagarbha? Above the crown of Ākāśagarbha’s head is a celestial tiara;
within the tiara is a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*), and within the tiara appear the thirty-five Buddhas.

This Bodhisattva sits with legs crossed in the full lotus posture, or at times manifests in all manner of forms. Whether in a dream or while practicing seated meditation, the practitioner [should visualize him].
When this sign is seen within [the visualization], one should seal the arm of the practitioner with a *maṇi* jewel-seal, forming the characters for "extinguishing transgressions" (*mièzuì*).
If this sign is obtained, one may return to the saṃgha and recite the precepts according to the Dharma. The *Nanshan xingyi* (Rituals of the Nanshan School) also employs this text;

following this intent, it is sufficient to count [the practitioner] toward the quorum. (By this one may verify that while the disclosure of offenses in the Hīnayāna and the training [of novices] do not obstruct monastic affairs, they are nonetheless not counted toward the quorum. Therefore, [this is] the entrustment of the Dharma.
Once the grave offenses have been extinguished within the *kṣānti* (confession), people call such a person a "Pure Vinaya Master.

Since a lay follower (*upāsaka*) who has received this title is not obstructed from receiving the full precepts, the author of the *Chao* (Commentary) relies upon this to distinguish the boundaries for laypeople; this is not without basis (as shown in the *Supplemental Notes* to the *Mahāvibhāṣā*).
If one does not receive the title, one may chant that the offense is extinguished while in mid-air; furthermore, there is no such sign as this, yet those who know the *Vinaya* have seen it in dreams.
Ākāśagarbha said: "Vinisa, vinisa" means that the bhikṣu and upāsaka must undergo further repentance for one to seven days;
by the power of bowing to the thirty-five Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, their offenses become slight.

(The subsequent method of repentance through observing signs should be understood according to this. One who knows the Dharma further instructs them to smear the latrine for eight hundred days, telling them each day:
If you have committed impure acts, with single-minded devotion you should smear and repair all latrines so that no one knows of it.

Having finished the repairs, bathe and prostrate before the Thirty-five Buddhas while reciting the name of Ākāśagarbha. Facing the twelve divisions of the sūtras, cast yourself prostrate on the ground and confess your transgressions.
Furthermore, after a period of twenty-one days, you should gather your relatives and friends before an image of the Buddha and recite the [Thirty-five Buddhas' Names Sūtra].

The passage concerning the five Buddhas naming Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva and others as witnesses for the fourfold *karmavācanā* of the *Prakāśaka-vidhi*, and how receiving it again [after a violation] constitutes a grave offense and the loss of the precepts;
furthermore, if one has not lost them, how one should repent and receive them again (as shown in the *Fǔzhù* commentary on the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*).
The Sūtra says: The Buddha told Upāli, "For the sake of those in the future who are shameless and frequently transgress, you should..."

Perform such repentance (as detailed above). Alternatively, those who practice the *pratyutpanna* for ninety days—that is, the *sadāpratipanna-samādhi*—derive this method from the *Pratyutpanna Sūtra*.
*Pratyutpanna* here translates as "Buddhas Standing. There are three meanings to "Buddhas Standing": first, the power of the Buddha’s majesty; second, the power of samādhi;
and third, the power of the practitioner’s own fundamental merit. By these means, one is able to see the Buddhas of the ten directions currently present within meditative concentration.
Standing before it like a person with clear vision observing the stars on a clear night, seeing the Buddhas of the ten directions is likewise numerous;

therefore, this is called the Buddha-Stationing Samādhi (*buddhasthita-samādhi*). The body remains open and constantly practices without rest for a period of ninety days, while the mouth chants "Amitābha Buddha" (and so forth).
Alternatively, for those performing the Great Compassion Repentance (*mahākāruṇika-pūjā*) for forty-nine days, one should then invite Avalokiteśvara.

Because it is the Samādhi [of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara], the *Bai lu* (Collection of One Hundred Records) cites a sūtra stating: "The twenty-one days and the forty-nine days should all correspond to the six fasting days at the commencement of the period," and so forth.

As for the "twenty-one days" in the *Fahua* [Sūtra], the *Puxian pin* (Universal Worthy Chapter) of the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "In three..."

"During the seven days, one should practice with single-minded diligence... (and so forth). Regarding "seven days or more," this means that taking seven days as a single period, one must resolutely not cease;

When one confesses the offenses of the forty-eight light precepts face-to-face (*pratimukha*), the transgressions are immediately extinguished (and so forth). Furthermore, "also obtaining ritual efficacy" means also obtaining the ritual efficacy of the formal procedure (*vidhi*).
Therefore, even the confession by observing signs (*nimitta*) also incorporates the formal procedure; it is simply that taking the observation of signs as the primary method.
Thus, both the *Vaipulya Bodhisattva Precepts* and the *Ākāśagarbha Sūtra* contain the formal procedures; hence, [this is] the *Bodhisattva Precepts Daily Practice*.

To prostrate before the Buddha and recite the precepts at night is itself the performance of the ritual; however, if one distinguishes between the peripheral and the primary, the distinction will be clear and free from confusion.
As stated in the *Cānabōluómì* (Dhyānapāramitā): "If one simply applies the mind to practicing the Way, when the merit is perfected, the signs will manifest.

Judging by this, one will know whether transgressions are extinguished or not; it does not mean that during the time of practicing the Way, one should dwell on signs and phenomena, giving rise to grasping and attachment.

If one applies the mind in this manner, demonic obstacles will surely arise frequently, making it difficult to distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox; thus, one must not take anything for granted.
When such signs appear, only a skilled master can recognize them, and the matter must be settled face-to-face rather than through written records.
Therefore, one must rely upon a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) to discern what is heterodox and what is orthodox, and so forth.
Regarding the third explanation, the *Wushengchan Chanmen* (The Gate of Repentance for Non-arising) states: "All dharmas are originally empty and quiescent;

since there is not even merit, how could there be sin? It is only because sentient beings engage in unwholesome reflection and falsely cling to conditioned phenomena that the three poisons arise and they commit manifold transgressions—all of which are produced by a single moment of inverted thought. If one wishes to eliminate them, one should reflect back upon this."

"From where does the mind arise? (and so forth). One should know that when viewed from the perspective of principle (*li*), one penetrates only the fact that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is inherently empty of both self and phenomena;
when viewed from the perspective of phenomena (*shi*), one focuses exclusively on examining the arising of the mind until it enters emptiness.

This is what is meant by "sitting upright and contemplating the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*"), for the true mark is itself markless. Therefore, the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "Contemplate all phenomena as empty."

The true aspect (*yathābhūtalakṣaṇa*) is precisely this meaning: thus, in practicing for oneself, one dwells solely within emptiness; in transforming others, one reaches the three thousand worlds to respond to sentient beings.

Therefore, the three contemplations within a single mind constitute the non-duality of self and others. By realizing that deluded thoughts possess neither the characteristic of unity nor difference, and by attaining this signlessness (*animitta*), one is endowed with all minds.
Only when the three thousand realms are fully perfected can one illuminate the mutual identity of the one and the many; this is what is meant by "the person."
To see this is profoundly lamentable. Although it is not the primary method for performing the practice, it is nonetheless categorized as "secondary" in contrast to the "primary.

"Practice" refers to the performance of the rite; "characteristics" refers to grasping at signs. This primarily clarifies non-arising, while secondarily including the performance of rites and the grasping of signs.
Therefore, performing the six periods of worship to the Buddhas of the ten directions, repenting of the six sense faculties, and reciting the Mahāyāna sutras constitute the "performance."

The Dharma is as follows: wishing to see Samantabhadra and having him manifest his physical body, as well as dreaming of Samantabhadra preaching the Dharma for one’s sake, constitutes grasping at signs (*nimitta*).

Next, following the ritual procedure, the text clarifies the passage on the completion of repentance and the extinction of transgressions; this is divided into two parts. First, the main text itself, which is further divided into two sections. First, the clarification [of the practice]. [End of segment]
The elimination of various offenses is further explained in two ways. Regarding the elimination of offenses such as violating the *avijñapti* (unmanifested) precepts, the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* states:

"Cutting grass or harming livestock are both confessed through the *pratideśanīya* (confession before another), and both offenses are extinguished. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains: "While the offense of violating the *avijñapti* is extinguished, the obligation to repay the life [of the victim] remains.

The *Fuxingji* (Supplementary Notes on Practice) states: "By repenting for a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, both types of prohibitions (*vighāta*) are extinguished; however, regarding the harming of livestock, [the debt remains]."

Question: Since there is the fault of the nature [of the offense], one cites the treatise to explain that it can be expiated; yet as long as life remains, why is it necessary to perform a formal confession (*pratideśanā*) if the natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) has not been extinguished?

Answer: Having already avoided violating the prohibitions (*prajñapti-śīla*), one maintains the continuity of the mind. Even if one must undergo extensive retribution during the stage of fruition (*phala-avasthā*) for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, how could this be the same as violating the precepts?
Furthermore, "retribution" (*sādhana*) here means returning or restoring. This explanation is given specifically regarding the confession through ritual action (*vidhi-pratideśanā*).

If the ritual of repentance through grasping at signs (*nimitta*) can extinguish transgressions against the nature (*dharmatā*), how much more so the repentance of non-arising (*anutpāda*), which can extinguish even the fundamental delusions of ignorance (*avidyā-mūla-kleśa*);

how could it fail to eliminate the secondary, derivative offenses that obstruct the nature? Regarding the extinction of unmanifest offenses (*avijñapti-pāpa*) through the completion of the ritual of repentance:

since unmanifest precepts are acquired through ritual action (*vijñapti*), if one has now committed a violation, one must perform the ritual of repentance; only when it is completed will the offense be extinguished. Thus, grasping at signs is extinguished.

Regarding how repentance can extinguish natural offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*): because natural precepts are not established by the Buddha but are inherently offenses by their very nature, they must be extinguished through personal realization.
This is like felling a tree; though the branches and leaves wither, if the root is not removed, it remains.
Thus, while the repentance of grasping at signs may extinguish both natural and proscribed (*pratikṣepaṇa*) offenses, ignorance has not yet been eliminated.
Because ignorance that has not been eliminated causes one to fall back into the various realms of existence (*bhava*), innate offenses (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) and the like continue to arise as before.
"As before" means remaining as it was originally. Therefore, this ignorance must encompass both the general and specific delusions—the afflictions of the five stages (*pañca-vāsa*).
If it were otherwise, how could innate offenses and the like continue to arise as before? By contemplating non-arising (*anutpāda*) and performing repentance, one can extinguish this ignorance.
The wise understand that because of delusion regarding principle, there is ignorance (*avidyā*); if one does not contemplate non-arising, how can one eliminate it? "Fu" (覆) means "to reverse.
To contemplate the mind as non-arising and realize the principle of the true mark (*dharmatā*) is like covering the great earth: both the nature of ignorance and its obscuration cannot be found.

It is as if roots, branches, and leaves are all exhausted without remainder. Furthermore, following the section on the method of practice, the next part clarifies the extinction of the three [poisons].
Regarding the ritual method for repentance (*karmavācanā*) to extinguish the grave offenses of violating the precepts, it follows what was explained above; thus, the *Chanmen* (Chan Gate) states:

"First, ritual repentance supports the Vinaya. Regarding the extinction of grave offenses against meditative concentration (*samādhi*) through repentance involving the grasping of signs (*nimitta*), the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-ṭīkā* states:

"This clarifies that focused attention does not constitute meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Since one has committed a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) within a distracted state of mind, one performs repentance by grasping signs."
Since natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) are thereby eliminated, the *Chanmen* (Chan Gate) states: "Repentance that grasps signs supports the methods of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This is because one performs repentance by observing signs within a focused mind; thus, it is said that repentance which grasps signs supports concentration.

As for "repentance of non-arising (*anutpāda*) which extinguishes the grave offenses of transgressing wisdom," this means that because of ignorance, one does not realize the emptiness of nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*). Therefore, by contemplating non-arising, the offenses of transgressing wisdom are extinguished—thus says the *Chanmen*.
It is said that the Threefold Repentance of Non-arising supports the Dharma of Wisdom.

Furthermore, following the performance of the ritual, the next section clarifies the text on the elimination of the three obstructions, which is divided into two parts. First is the clarification of the individual eliminations, which is further divided into three.

First, it clarifies the elimination of the three types of retributive obstructions; because these obstruct the unconditioned (anabhisaṃskṛta) retribution and lead one to the three miserable realms, the ritual repentance is performed.
Because this karmic obstacle of retribution is extinguished, the *Dà yì* states: "By maintaining pure precepts, one leaves the evil realms; this is an example of that principle.

Since natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*) are merely obstacles of retribution within the human realm, they can be extinguished through repentance performed according to formal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

Because one undergoes the outflowing retributions of the triple world due to delusion regarding the principle, one contemplates non-arising and non-extinction to eliminate this obstacle. Furthermore, regarding the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) below...

Next, the elimination of the three types of karmic obstructions is explained: the obstruction of past retribution is addressed in terms of its fruit, while the obstruction of present karma is addressed from the perspective of its cause;

the threefold confession for their respective elimination may be understood according to what precedes. Furthermore, following the ritual procedure, the third section clarifies the elimination of the three types of afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*);

because these obstruct the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) through fear and sorrow, the Preface to the Precepts states: "At the time of death, one harbors terror. Thus, the ritual procedure for confession is performed.

Since these afflictions and grasping at signs support the dharmas of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and because the power of concentration is predominant in the Śrāvakas, the repentance involving grasping at signs can extinguish the afflictions of the four abodes (*catur-vāsabhūmi*).
The extinction of the afflictions of ignorance (*avidyā*) through the repentance of non-arising (*anutpāda*) may be understood by analogy with the preceding.

Furthermore, following the three types [of repentance], the text next clarifies that the karmic obstacles of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*) are difficult to transform; therefore, all three must be practiced together.
The elimination of the grasping at signs (*nimitta*)—which is without arising or ceasing—and the karma and afflictions (*kleśa*) should also be understood by referring to the preceding text.

Furthermore, regarding the ritual repentance (*vidhi-pratikramaṇa*), it is like taking medicine; next, the illustrative passage is divided into two parts: first, the actual illustration. Thus, the *Chanmen* (The Gate of Meditation) says:
"It is like a person with a cold illness who takes ginger and cassia; the ailment is eliminated and cured" (and so forth). [Those] who are unable to produce wholesome states...

These are capable of producing the goodness of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Regarding the five minerals and five fungi—namely white crystal (*śveta-śilā*), purple essence (*pura-aṅga*), gypsum (*gairika*), stalactite (*ghaṇṭākarṇa*), and mineral pitch—the *Shennong Jing* states:
"Superior medicines nourish life. This refers to the five minerals refining the physical form and the six fungi extending the years.
As for what are called the six fungi, they are green, yellow, red, white, black, and purple. Those who ascend to transcendence and attain the Way achieve divine transformations through them.
The sequence of the Way is as follows; next, the "concluding example" section follows.
Next, from the current text onwards, the meaning is explained in accordance with the present sutra, which can be understood.

From this chapter onwards, the text of the chapter is explained in two parts: first, the intent is stated and the text is divided; then, the secondary and primary aspects are presented in mutual relation.

In this chapter, the secondary discussion (*pāratantrika-vāda*) concerns the production of goodness while the primary subject (*mukhya-artha*) clarifies the elimination of evil; in the subsequent section, the secondary discussion concerns the elimination of evil while the primary subject clarifies the production of goodness.
Therefore, it is said that the secondary and primary subjects are presented alternately.

Next, from the passage beginning with "The dreamer," the text is divided into two parts. First, the explanation of what is seen and heard within a dream, which is further divided into two sections, the first of which is the explanation [itself].

The dream of seeing a golden drum is further divided into two parts. First, the formal explanation of the text is divided into three sections. The first explains the drum as the Samādhi of Dream-like Vision:
it means contemplating all phenomena as being like dreams, devoid of reality. Only a Buddha is without dreams;
because they exist during the causal stage, the night dream experienced by Śraddhālakṣaṇa represents entering the "dream-like samādhi" within the great night of birth and death, and so forth. (孤山)
As for the statement that the dream was a metaphorical expression of the Dharma by Xinxiang and not a literal dream, this is likely not the case.
The body of the drum is round, and within that roundness there is emptiness; because it is round and empty, its sound resounds.

Therefore, this is used to correspond to the Three Virtues (triguṇa), and since these Three Virtues are each mutually inclusive, a detailed discussion should state "round, beautiful, great," and so forth. Nevertheless, although...
Taken together and summarized, these are merely the three aspects of the single Dharmakāya; this is because they constitute the very substance of the *Zhengjian Gu* (Drum of Right View).

The character *mei* (pronounced *chāng zhū*) means "beautiful. Next, the term *jiàn gǔ guāng pǔ dà* is explained: *guāng* means "light," *pǔ* (pronounced *pǔ*) means "vast" or "broad," and *dà* means "great.
*Kè* means "to be able. Regarding "same substance and same intent," the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) cites the new edition of the *Sanyin Pin* (Chapter on the Three Bodies).
It is said that [the clouds] share the same substance as all Buddhas, share the same intention as all Buddhas, and share the same activity as all Buddhas.

This "substance" is the radiance of the *dharmatā*; this "intention" is the light of the *dharmatā*; and this "activity" is the clarity of the *dharmatā*. Is it not thus that the Dharma itself serves as the metaphor?
Since we have already seen the light of the drum, these three meanings, when bound together, are simply the *saṃbhogakāya* (Enjoyment Body); to mention any one of them is to [encompass all].
The third ear, Gu-shan, says: "One should say 'light' and 'sound' are both exquisite. [Regarding the phrase] "also light," this is an inversion of the text.
The three interpretations seen within the light are all Buddhas arising from the essence; therefore, they are the three types of *nirmāṇakāya* (response-bodies).

Next, the section beginning with "Beholding this" summarizes the various threefold Dharma-gates, which are precisely those explained in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) as being vertically deep and horizontally vast.
This summarizes the intent of the ten kinds of threefold dharmas and so forth. From this point, the teaching established is named *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*.

To establish the teaching of *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* based on the principle of the three virtues (*triguṇa*) is precisely what is clarified in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) regarding the general and specific aspects of the teaching.
Therefore, it is said that because it is "specific," the three characters *Jin Guang Ming* (Golden Light) are used to mark how this current teaching differs from all other teachings.
Because it encompasses both the words and the meaning, the single character "sūtra" (經) serves as the general designation for all scriptures.
Next, the explanation of the passage concerning the sound of the drum struck in a dream is divided into two parts: first, the textual analysis;

second, the interpretation of the passage beginning with "The drum is the Dharma-body," which clarifies that what is seen now is the functional wisdom capable of striking [the drum], while the previous explanation of seeing the golden drum in a dream refers to the three bodies, each having three aspects.

It was previously claimed that the preceding passage concerns the nine dharmas of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), while the current passage concerns the nine dharmas of cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and that these constitute three sets of nine, totaling twenty-seven dharmas;
however, this is not correct. In the preceding passage, the perception of the drum represents the three aspects of the *dharmakāya*, which are the three aspects of the object (*ālambana*);

the three aspects of the drum’s light represent the three aspects of wisdom (*jñāna*); and the perception of the immortals represents the three aspects of function (*kriyā*). This is the case in the current passage as well.
This merely clarifies that the person who strikes uses wisdom to strike the drum; it has never discussed the twenty-seven dharmas of the cultivated nature (*xiuxing*).
Furthermore, others see the *Niepan xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of Nirvana) explaining "Great Extinction" (*dadmiedu*) as:
one must not interpret "Great" (*da*) alone, nor "Extinction" (*mie*) alone, nor "Crossing Over" (*du*) alone; they then claim that this [method] must be applied.

To claim that the "Explanation of the Nine Dharmas" and the "Explanation of the Extinction of the Great Nine Dharmas" consist of nine defilements and nine crossings—making three sets of nine, or twenty-seven dharmas—is also incorrect.
Why? Because Zhiyi’s intention was to clarify that the three dharmas are themselves the nine dharmas, and the nine dharmas are themselves the three dharmas;
thus, he merely rejected the interpretation of the "Great" and so forth as being merely "single threes. How could he have ever clarified a system of twenty-seven dharmas?
Furthermore, as for the combination and separation of cultivation and nature, how could they exceed the "Gate of the Non-duality of Cultivation and Nature"?

It merely clarifies that there are two aspects of cultivation and one aspect of nature, along with three aspects each for cultivation and nature, totaling six; how can you arbitrarily increase them to twenty-seven dharmas and falsely create such a redundant appendage?
Next, to explain "having awakened," the *Jianwen jing* (Sūtra on Seeing and Hearing) states: "Awakened" (*wù*; pronounced with the *wù* of *wǔgù*) means precisely awakening.

This section is divided into two parts: first, the analysis of the text; second, from "As for dreaming... onwards, the word-by-word commentary, which consists of four sections. First, the explanation of the passage concerning going to where the Buddha was, which is further divided into two parts.

First, the analysis of the text according to its numerical categories, which contains two meanings: the first meaning concerns entering the Dharma-gate by way of names derived from virtues; the second meaning concerns [the assembly].

The term "transgressions" refers to delusions that have not yet been eliminated; specifically, this refers to the thirty minds of the *śaikṣa* stage, while generally it refers to the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*). Next, regarding the contemplation of the mind:
since the "partial realization" (*bhūta-avabodha*) is contrasted with the "contemplative practice" (*vipaśyanā-caryā*), this contemplative practice must be discussed in terms of two meanings.

If one follows the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the contemplative practice precedes the stage of semblance (*sādṛśya-bhūmi*); if one follows the *Bhadrapāla-buddhālambana-samādhi-sūtra*, the contemplative practice is situated within the stage of semblance.

This is fully as shown in the Supplementary Notes to the Great Section (and so forth). Next, the commentary on the scriptural passage concerning "being together with the conditions" begins from "At that time" and concludes with "went to where the Buddha was.
Regarding the textual phrasing: the previous section explaining the passage on "going to where the Buddha was" only explained the transition from night until dawn;
it did not yet explain [the departure] from Rājagṛha. Now, in explaining the passage concerning "being together with the conditions," the text finally addresses the act of going out.
The three explanations are presented by contrasting the cause with the fruit. To "extend reverence" means that speaking of dreams is an expression of oral respect;
since the discourse on dreams constitutes the fourth [section] describing dreams, we know it is merely brought forward by the natural flow of the text. Regarding "faith is the head and is noble":
among all mental states, faith is the first, just as the six parts of the body take the head as their primary part; thus, being at the top, the head is considered noble.
Compassion is considered base because it is that which transforms those below, just as the feet are considered base. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"Among the human body, the head is the most noble, for it is where the five sensory faculties reside and is situated at the very top; the feet are the most base, for they tread upon impure places and are situated at the very bottom.
Therefore, one uses what is noble—the head—to pay homage to what is base—the feet—thereby honoring the precious through that which is held in high esteem.

This is because it concerns nourishment. The fourth section, the "Explanation of the Dream Text," is divided into two parts. First, the division of the text: from "Because of this" down to "seeing the drum" constitutes three [sections];
the subsequent divisions of the text should be understood according to this principle. Second, the word-by-word commentary is divided into two parts.
First, the narration by the sūtra compiler, which consists of the four phrases beginning with "In that dream. If these are taken as four-character verses, then...
If a verse consists of seven characters, four lines constitute one stanza; if it is in prose, seventeen characters serve as the standard unit.
Generally, these follow worldly convention and sentiment, so there are often no fixed rules. Next, the explanation of the main text concerning the dream is divided into two parts.
First, the explanation of the general description of the dream is further divided into two. First, the explanation of the passage regarding seeing the golden drum is divided into three sections.

First, regarding the interpretation of "seeing the shape of the drum," the *Jian gu xing zhuang jing* (Sūtra on Seeing the Shape of the Drum) states that it means "shining" (*huàng*), "radiance" (*huī*), or "light" (*guāng*).

Second, regarding the interpretation of "seeing the light of the drum," the *Jian gu guāngming jing* (Sūtra on Seeing the Light of the Drum) states that "yú" means "to surpass" or "to exceed. Third, regarding the interpretation of "seeing the light within," the Buddha concludes by summarizing the meaning of the three categories;

thus he says, "it is precisely the three bodies (*trikāya*) and so forth" mentioned in the prose section (*dīrghapada*). Hereafter, when encountering the text, one should apply this principle accordingly.

Next, regarding the explanation of the passage on "seeing the drum-beating," the phrase "one sees oneself" means that the one with faith and signs sees for himself what appears to be a *brāhmaṇa* beating this golden drum;
how could it be anyone else? Next, the separate explanation clarifying the text on dreams is divided into two parts.

First, from the words "This great golden drum" down to "extinguishing evil and giving rise to good," the text is divided into six sections. Second, from "There are three kinds... [the second part begins].
The explanatory text for the following section is divided into two parts. First, the explanation of the golden drum’s power to eliminate evil and generate goodness consists of six sections.
The first explains how it eliminates the suffering of worldly causes and effects: it can remove all the afflictions that oppress sentient beings; it can eliminate the causal suffering of the world;
and it can eliminate the resultant sufferings of the hells and so forth throughout the three periods of time. It also eliminates the [attachment to] worldly resultant pleasures.

Concentration (*samādhi*) and the factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣadharma*) are the causes for the happiness of transcendence (*lokottara*). The cessation of fear and the absence of dread, whereby one leaves death behind and reaches the further shore, are the fruits of transcendence.
"Cessation of all fears" means being free from the five types of dread; "attainment of fearlessness" means acquiring the four kinds of intrepidity (*vaiśāradya*).
These three explanations cause sentient beings to fully possess both their own and others' welfare, thereby realizing the fruit of *bodhi* through their own practice.

4. "Fulfillment" means turning the wheel of the Dharma to transform others; "preparation" refers to the four [stages]. Regarding the explanation of "extinguishing karmic obstacles to receive the supernormal power of recollecting past lives":
while in hell, his body was being burned by fire, yet upon hearing the sound of a drum, he immediately prostrated to the Buddha, thereby extinguishing his karmic obstacles.

Having attained knowledge of past lives, he immediately manifested this supernormal power. 5. Regarding the explanation of "causing sentient beings to attain various Dharma-gates, starting from the few and progressing to the many," the sub-commentary below states:
