As for the term "a little" (*yún*): taken at first glance, practicing pure and white karma is called "a little," while causing all that is sought and requested to be fully accomplished is called "much.
However, when investigated thoroughly, since the practice of pure and white karma is said to be immeasurable, how could there be anything "little"?
Furthermore, obtaining the pure and white karma of humans and devas is termed "a little," whereas all that is sought and requested encompasses [the entirety of]...
That which transcends the world is called "much. If it were not so, how could it be called "fully accomplishing and perfecting"?
Regarding the six explanations for destroying the eight difficulties of sentient beings: since it speaks of "all difficulties," is this not the "eight difficulties"?

As for what are called the eight difficulties: first, the hells; second, animals; third, hungry ghosts; fourth, the northern continent (Uttarakuru); fifth, the heaven of non-conception (asaṃjñisattva); sixth, being before or after a Buddha; seventh... [text fragment].
The worldly wisdom of eloquence and discernment is like one born blind from birth, mute, and speech-impaired; yet, as a summary indication of the intent of the six categories, it is said:

"The explanation of these six meanings shows that all proceed gradually from the three miserable realms to the human and celestial realms, and for the two vehicles and Bodhisattvas alike, each possesses the power to destroy evil and give rise to good.
One should cite the tenfold benefits from the *Miaoxuan* (The Profound Meaning) to clarify the "destruction" [of evil] herein.
"From evil arises good; one may know that by this it is not fully recorded" (and so forth).
Next, the explanation clarifies the method of instruction for repentance, which is divided into three parts: first, the division of the text; second, the introduction:

"Those who obstruct the principle through perverse delusions and do not recognize the *dharmatā* possess a solitary ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*) and a particularly severe inversion of delusion, such that they do not recognize [it]."

The Dharma-body is that which is obscured by ignorance; those who do not recognize cause and effect do not know the Reward Buddha, for it is said that the Reward Buddha is that which is evoked through the practice of cause and effect. Those whose conduct is obstructed by evil karma and who do not recognize wholesome dharmas do not know the Response Buddha.

"Xie" (pronounced with the initial *l* in the *qiè* rhyme category) means "to penetrate. Thus, if one offers worship directly [without understanding], their cognition will not penetrate it. Therefore—
To chant and praise is to fully express one’s resolve. "The sages are equal" refers to what is stated in the introduction:
"I shall now explain the methods of repentance and so forth.
From "Repentance for oneself" onwards, the third section explains the text in five parts; first is the explanation of the passage on the Teacher personally confessing his own transgressions.
Second, the first part of the text: Regarding the section on the Dharmakāya, the subsequent explanation of its meaning is divided into three parts.
First, the explanation of that upon which it relies: although ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles do not know it, they do not transcend the *dharmatā*.
"Self" (*zì*) here means "to follow from" (*cóng*). As the *Miaoxuan* states: "Good and evil, ordinary and sage, etc., do not transcend the *dharmatā*. Therefore, [it is one].

All sufferings encompass the three lands and nine realms; because the Dharma-body of the Peaceful Light (*śānta-prabhāsvara*) is that to which one returns and upon which one relies, the sovereignty of the Dharma-body is precisely the meaning of the "True Self" (*ātman*).
As stated in the Preface Chapter: "I shall now expound the dharmas of repentance and so forth"—this is truly for this reason.
"All Bodhisattvas" refers to those of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*); those of the partial teachings are considered dull by comparison.

Regarding "the two vehicles" (*dviyāna*): this term serves merely to exclude ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*), while it simultaneously includes the bodhisattvas of the partial teachings (*pradeśa-śāsana*).
Although the internal foundation is established [within oneself], the following section explains that if one lacks the external protection and empowerment of the Buddhas, one cannot achieve success.

As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* states: "In the world there are those with false views who study meditation; they believe in the existence of the Buddha through faith alone, yet they do not believe in the [protection of] the various [Buddhas]."
Regarding the empowerment of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power (*buddhānubhāva*), the *Miaoxuan* (Profound Mystery) states:

"If a person who practices the contemplation of universal non-arising (*anupapatti*) believes only in the benefit of the internal mind and does not believe in the external empowerment of the Buddha’s majesty, this is an obstruction of the delusion of self-nature (*svabhāva-moha*).

Furthermore, if one believes exclusively in the external Buddha and does not seek benefit within the internal mind, this falls into the delusion of other-nature (*parabhāva-moha*). These cases may be understood by analogy with the [extremes of] eternalism and nihilism. Self and no-cause are to be treated accordingly.

O foolish person by nature, do your eyes not see that in this world, when one is unable to proceed while pulling a heavy load, they gain passage immediately through the assistance of others' strength?
Why then do you not believe [in the power of the Buddha]? For those whose defilements and sins are heavy, the Buddha’s majestic power establishes them; yet you do not recognize his kindness.

You are like grass and trees, which do not deliberate upon the benefits conferred by the sun, moon, wind, and rain (and so forth). Thus, by analogy with these other things, you are refuted as being without cause.

(As stated above... "Sīxū" (斯須) means "at this very moment. Regarding "fúshū" (扶疏): the character "fú" (扶) should follow the radical for wood (木), and the character "shū" (疏) should follow the radical for grass (艹).
Therefore, the *Wénxuǎn* (文選), in its reading of the poem on the *Shānhǎi jīng* (山海經), states: "In the first month of summer, the plants and trees grow long;

they encircle the house, their branches and foliage spreading out (*póshū*). The commentary notes: "Póshū" refers to the appearance of branches and leaves spreading in all directions. "Fēng" (豐) means luxuriant growth; "yù" (鬱) refers to the dense growth of leaves.
"Also" (*ye*) means "furthermore" (*cháng*) and "profound" (*yōu*). Since the internal and external conditions are already complete, one must perform repentance;

this follows the natural flow of the text’s structure to clarify what occurs after birth. The Sūtra says "World Hero" (*shìxióng*): the most refined and excellent among grasses and trees is called a "flower" (*yīng*), and the most outstanding among the herds of beasts is called a "hero" (*xióng*).
Humans are likewise; thus, those who are intelligent and stand out are called "flowers," while those with courage and strength... [are called heroes].
One who surpasses others is called a "hero" (*vīra*); the Tathāgata is likewise so named because his power is able to subdue Māra, restrain externalists, and transcend all bodhisattvas and the like.
Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "The Great Hero, the Fierce World-Honored One. "Great Hero" and "Fierce" are names for a "great man" (*puruṣa*).
Regarding the "Venerable One among Two-Legged Beings," some say that the Buddha is the most honored among all those with two legs, four legs, or many legs; yet in the sutras...
Regarding the term "Honored One Among Those with Two Feet" (dvipada-agrya): among all classes of beings, those with two feet are considered noble, namely humans and devas.

Therefore, the Buddha is the most honored among humans and devas and is thus called the Honored One Among Those with Two Feet; hence, among the Ten Epithets, he is referred to as the Teacher of Gods and Humans (śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām).

Thus, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra explains the title "Teacher of Gods and Humans" by stating: "Among all sentient beings, only gods and humans are capable of generating the aspiration for Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

With this mind, one is able to cultivate wholesome karma and attain the four fruits, the stage of a Pratyekabuddha, and the path of Samyak-saṃbodhi; for this reason, the Buddha is titled the Teacher of Gods and Humans.

Third, the explanation of the text of the correct repentance is divided into two parts: first, the analysis of the text, and second, the interpretation of the meaning. The text itself is divided into two sections: first, the explanation of the general repentance.

Next, the explanation of the text for the specific repentance (*pṛthak-kṣamaṇa*) is divided into two parts: first, the analysis of the text; second, the interpretation of the meaning. The text itself is divided into three sections.

First, the explanation of the specific repentance for the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*). Regarding the term "independent" (*mukhya*): this distinguishes it from that which is "associated" (*saṃprayukta*).

That which combines with the various proclivities (*anuśaya*) of views and thoughts is called "associated"; that which directly obstructs the principle (*tattva*) is called "independent. If one is deluded regarding the provisional principle, there is the characteristic of being within the realms (*dhātu*).

It should be understood as an independent [affliction]. If one is deluded regarding the true principle, there is the "independent" (du-tou) [ignorance] outside the realms; furthermore, this "outside the realms" applies to both the Separate and Perfect Teachings.

Since the preceding passage states that the Dharma-body possesses the three virtues and is thus the "three jewels in essence," the present "independent ignorance" and deluded inversion refer precisely to the failure to recognize the three bodies in their essential unity. Since the sutra merely says "not recognizing," [it implies this very point].
Therefore, it belongs to the independent (mūla) ignorance (*avidyā*). If it were associated (*saṃprayukta*), as the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:

"From this point onward, all are termed wrong views," which refers to the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*); or as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* mentions "clouds of incense smoke" and so forth, which refers to the delusions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*).

In such cases, these views and thoughts must necessarily involve ignorance, which would constitute association. Since the present text does not mention this, it belongs to the independent type. [End of quotation]
(Qú jīng qiè). Regarding "images," Gu Shan said they are Buddha statues constructed from earth and wood. While humans know to revere them, birds and wild grasses do not.
If one asks how the *dharmakāya* can be described in terms of the ten powers (*daśabala*), the answer is: the *dharmakāya* is the essence (*tǐ*) and the *nirmāṇakāya* is the function (*yòng*).

If one understands this application of function, one will immediately know that the ten powers are the essence of the *dharma*. What are these ten powers? The *dharmakāya* is a perfect mirror that clearly reflects both good and evil.
Because the good and bad retributions received from karmic conditions cannot be subverted, it is called the power of the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-bala*).

Furthermore, because one can perfectly discern the causes and effects of all karma throughout the three periods of time with total clarity such that nothing can subvert it, it is called the power of knowing karma (*karma-jñāna-bala*).

Because one illuminates all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*) such that nothing can subvert it, it is called the power of concentration (*samādhi-bala*). Because one illuminates the faculties (*indriya*) of sentient beings such that nothing can subvert it, it is called [the power of knowing the faculties].

The powers of the faculties (*indriya*), followed by the power of desire, the power of nature, the power of reaching destinations, the power of the path, the power of recollecting past lives, the power of the divine eye, and the power of the exhaustion of outflows—these may be understood accordingly. Since the Dharma-body is already omnipresent, it is therefore called the "Ten Powers.

Thus, the Dharma corresponds to the ten powers as a single essence without differentiation; this is, for example, as explained in the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary on the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*) regarding the Dharma corresponding to the ten titles [of a Buddha] (etc.).
The kindness of the parents is the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-prajñāpāramitā*). This interpretation follows the intent of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*:

the father as skillful means is provisional wisdom (*prajñā*), and the mother as the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is ultimate wisdom (*bhūtārtha-jñāna*). The *Fahua wenju* states that these two—provisional and ultimate wisdom—are themselves *prajñā*.
Since *prajñā* reveals the principle, it is itself skillful means. Because the parents of the Dharma-body can give birth [to the Buddha], they are not to be disregarded.
If one’s parents do not know how to repay the Buddha, it is because they have not practiced the wholesome dharmas that assist the path.
One should verify that the *prajñā* of one’s parents is itself the practice of the true path.

Next, the explanation of the text on the separate confession for repaying karmic obstacles is divided into two parts; first, the explanation regarding present matters, which concerns relying upon and depending on [them]. (Note: "Shi" is pronounced as in *shì*; "yī" means to rely upon.)
*Ā* (pronounced *gào*, level tone) means arrogance, negligence, disdain, and contempt. The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states:

"Relying on one's own cleverness and wisdom, high status, advanced age, noble lineage, prestigious family, great understanding, and abundant wealth and seven treasures—through these, one becomes haughty.
The *Fahua Wenju* quotes the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā Sūtra* to clarify the eight types of pride (*mada*), correlating them with eight birds; the first is the pride of youth and vigor (*yauvana-mada*).

As the *chī* bird is proud of its lineage, the *xiāo* owl is proud of its wealth, the *diāo* eagle is proud of its sovereignty, the *jiù* vulture is proud of its longevity, the *niǎo* bird is proud of its intelligence, the *què* magpie is proud of its virtuous conduct, and the *jiū* pigeon is proud of its color;

to disparage others is arrogance (*màn*), while to reproach oneself is pride (*jiāo*) (and so forth). Now, to further explain the precepts according to the Dharma, "years" refers to the number of years since one received the full ordination (*śīla-lakṣa*).
Regarding the phrase "my years are advanced," it refers to the *Lotus Sūtra* passage, "My years have declined and I am decrepit," which means my age is great and my body is aged.

The third section, the explanation of the text for the specific repentance of karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*), is divided into two parts: first, the structural analysis of the text from the beginning up to the twelfth section;
second, the word-by-word commentary on the text in twelve sections. First, the explanation of the causes of repentance: regarding the statement that evil karma is created through mind and speech...
Furthermore, regarding those who incite others to commit evil: because one commits evil through mind and speech, one necessarily teaches others to do so;
therefore, this pertains to the body, speech, and mind. As for those who personally commit evil, the character "zuò" (作) should properly be "zòng" (縱).

Although the sutra speaks only of mind and speech here, it mentions the body because it is only by possessing a body that mind and speech exist; since mind and speech rely upon the body, the three karmas are complete. Next...

Explanation of Repentance for Those Who Commit Evil Deeds Due to Internal and External Causes and Conditions: "External" refers to associating with evil friends; "internal" refers to afflictions that disturb the mind.
The Sūtra says, "The foolish practitioner": "foolish" means deluded. The character *xing* (行) is pronounced in the departing tone (*qùshēng*).

Threefold Explanation of Repentance for Those Who Commit Deeds Due to the Causes and Conditions of the Five Desires: Form, sound, fragrance, flavor, and touch—these five flavors can give rise to human desire. One must desire them.

1. The fourth explanation of repentance for karma created through faith in and acceptance of a false teacher: A "false teacher" refers to one who, being close to what is not holy, is indeed a false teacher.
2. The fifth explanation of repentance for karma created by following an evil master: Because one strikes [the enemy] on behalf of another, one thereby belongs to that evil master. 3.
The sixth explanation of repentance for committing evil karma under the influence of a loving heart: It is a disturbance... (and so forth).

7. Explanation of Repentance for Karma Created for the Sake of Food, Clothing, and Female Beauty: This can be understood. 8. Explanation of Repentance for Those Who Commit Evil Deeds Toward the Field of Reverence during the Buddha’s Lifetime:
Since it mentions the "Buddha-Dharma and the Holy Assembly," one knows that this refers specifically to the period when the Buddha was in the world.
9. Explanation of Repentance for Those Who Commit Evil Deeds Toward the Field of Reverence in a World Without a Buddha: Since it mentions the "Pratyekabuddhas" (Solitary Realizers)...

The Bodhisattva therefore knows that this is spoken with reference to the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa. All refer to the "field of respect" (*gaurava-kṣetra*) because the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others possess virtues that transcend the triple world and must be revered;
within this field, even inferior or middling seeds of goodness can produce untainted fruits (*anāsrava-phala*), hence it is called the field of respect.
Tenth, regarding the explanation of repentance for those who commit evil deeds against the True Dharma: they are ignorant and slander the Dharma.
This refers to performing actions against the True Dharma. I address you, future students who aspire to the Dharma and rely upon teachers:
you must eliminate human sentiments that lead to slander. (11) Explanation of the Repentance for Committing Evil Deeds Against the Field of Gratitude:
This is because parents and elders possess the grace of giving birth and raising one; furthermore, the term "elders" may also encompass all such figures, which can be understood through reflection.
The twelve explanations for repenting of evil karma created in all places can likewise be understood;
furthermore, the summarized meaning of these twelve sections is indicated by the statement: "If one wishes to explain them in detail, one begins with the human realm," and so forth.
By analogy with the preceding examples, it should also be understood that humans, devas, and others alike possess the power to destroy evil and give rise to goodness.
Next, the explanation of the text for making offerings to all Buddhas and practicing repentance to cultivate oneself and transform others is divided into two parts.
First is the section explaining the intent; from the beginning until the thirty-fourth line, it clarifies the "Dharma Offering," which constitutes the division of the text.
Next, the explanation of the meaning according to the text is divided into two parts. First, regarding the explanation of material offerings:

since the sutra merely states, "I now make offerings," it is clear that this refers exclusively to material offerings. As for the phrase "three thousand great thousand-fold worlds" (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*), Zhiyi (Four Illuminations) stated that within a single great thousand-fold world-system there are naturally hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas; however, I maintain this is not so, as it accords with the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* [which speaks of] the Sahā...
The "eight hundred billion" are but a single flower petal; the Dharma-offering constitutes the second [part]. Next, the explanation of the Dharma-offering is further divided into two sections.
First, the section stating the intent and dividing the text, which extends from the beginning up to "its meaning has four aspects"—this is the section stating the intent and dividing the text.

Regarding "phenomena and principle, etc.": material offerings pertain to phenomena (*dharma*), while Dharma-offerings pertain to principle (*tattva*). Furthermore, transforming others belongs to phenomena, whereas self-cultivation belongs to principle.

This belongs to the section on principles. Next, the explanation of the meaning according to the text is divided into two parts. First, the explanation of the Dharma-offering for the sake of transforming others is further divided into two.

First, the explanation of transforming others to lead them toward practice [is as follows]. This section consists of four parts; first, the explanation of the beginning of transformation through great compassion.

Extracting from Suffering: Second, explaining the exhortation to the practice of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) as the true cause; Third, explaining the exhortation to the great awakening of *bodhi* as the true fruit;

Fourth, explaining the exhortation to diligence so as to ensure the completion of practice. The text is divided into two parts: first, an explanation based on causes and conditions, where "qu" (劬) also means "labor";
second, an explanation based on the contemplation of the mind, wherein the phrase "this very meaning" refers to the text of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
This explains the meaning of presently contemplating the mind to subdue the sovereign mind (citta-rāja) and its mental factors (caitta).
Next, regarding the passage on transforming others by inducing them to practice repentance, the text "to explain a thousand kalpas" is an inversion;
it should instead read "to explain away a thousand kalpas. Third, the explanation of having completed the repentance.
Next, the explanation of the passage on the practice of self-offering through the Dharma is divided into two parts. First, the introductory section and the division of the text.

Regarding the phrase "having already completed the self-confession" (*zìchàn jìng*), this refers to the first section, consisting of nineteen lines and one character, which teaches the confession and repentance for one's own transgressions.
The term *hàoshǒu* (皓首) means white-haired. As stated in the letter from Li Ling to Su Wu: "I served as an envoy in my prime years and returned with white hair... (and so forth).

The character "duàn" (斷) is pronounced with the *dīngguàn* (丁貫) rhyme. The preceding section concerns the gate of self-cultivation (*zixingmen*), which refers to what was previously called the completion of one's own repentance.

The present section concerns the gate of Dharma-offering (*fagongyangmen*), which refers to these current twenty-five lines and a half that constitute the method for practicing Dharma-offering oneself;
this extends from the beginning up to the attainment of Bodhi. This constitutes the "Analysis of the Text according to the Intent. Next follows the "Explanation of Meaning according to the Text."
The text is divided into two parts. First is the explanation of one’s own practice, which is further divided into three sections. First, the presentation of the chapter;

second, the explanation of the causes for cultivation—the Ten Perfections (daśapāramitā)—which are described as the "feet" of the Ten Stages (daśabhūmi). This means that the Ten Perfections serve as the cause, while the Ten Stages are the result; these are thus the partial results.

Third, the explanation of the attainment of the result, which provides a general clarification of the fulfillment of the result; this refers to the single practice of attaining the unsurpassed state of Buddhahood. The scriptural text, however, merely...

Because it is said that this refers to the light of the unsurpassed merit of attaining Buddhahood, we know that this merely provides a general explanation of the characteristics of the fulfillment of the fruit.
As for the specific explanation of the fulfillment of the fruit, it consists of the three subsequent lines concerning all the Buddhas’ [attainments].
Since the scriptural text states, "all the immeasurable merits of the Buddhas, up to hundreds of thousands of various *dhāraṇīs*," we know that this indeed constitutes the specific explanation.
This clarifies that the fruit is fulfilled. Regarding the two kinds of adornment: merit constitutes the adornment of fortune, while radiance constitutes the adornment of wisdom.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "The light of wisdom shines immeasurably," and so forth.

Next, the explanation of the text for self-cultivation and repentance is divided into two parts: first, the presentation of the outline; second, the word-by-word commentary on the text, which itself is divided into two sections.
First, the explanation of the invitation to the Buddhas (occupying nineteen and a half lines); second, the explanation of the text for repentance, which is divided into two parts:

first, the division of the text; second, the word-by-word commentary on the text, which consists of five sections. First, the explanation of the text for repenting karmic obstacles, which is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the characteristics of karmic obstacles and the various evils committed.

Regarding "the *saṃjñā-skandha* and *saṃskāra-skandha* are suffering": because of *saṃjñā*, there is *saṃskāra*; since *saṃskāra* is volitional activity (*abhisamskāra*), the evil that is produced is precisely *saṃjñā* and *saṃskāra*.
Next, the scriptural passage for requesting their removal and extinction is clear. Next, the explanation of the text on repenting the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is divided into two parts:

first, the division of the text; second, the word-by-word commentary. This [second part] is further divided into two: first, presenting the characteristics of the hindrance. The Sūtra says: "The defilements of afflictions and karma."

This clarifies that these afflictions are merely the afflictions belonging to karma. Next, regarding the request for purity, there are three parts to the explanation of the text on repenting karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*).

This is divided into two sections: first, the analysis of the text; second, the explanation of its meaning. The text itself is divided into three parts. First, the explanation of the vertical discourse on the creation of karma throughout the three periods of time.
This is further divided into two parts. First, the direct explanation of past karma. Since that which is currently being experienced is a retribution-obstruction (*vipākāvaraṇa*), it is...
Therefore, it is those [karmas] that have not yet been experienced in the present that are taken as "karmic obstructions" (*karmāvaraṇa*). Next, the analysis of the text is divided into two parts:

first, the posing of the question; second, the explanation of the answer. This latter part is further divided into two: first, the direct explanation of the answer; and [second, the identification of schools].

The "School of Numbers" (*Saṃkhya*) refers here to the masters of the Sarvāstivāda, while the "School of Treatises" (*Śāstra*) refers to those who propagate the *Tattvasiddhi*. Since the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states that [karma] obstructs the future, the School of Numbers likewise speaks of the future.
Since that which is to be and that which has not yet been already exist, how can one not repent?
As for what is called the "Great Sūtra" prohibiting the future, in that sūtra the Buddha told King Ajātaśatru: "Form is of three kinds—past, future, and present—and thus it cannot be harmed.
Why? Because the past is already past; because the present perishes moment by moment; and because the future is prohibited, it is so named."

Regarding the killing of such a single form, there are cases where it may be killed and cases where it may not; since there are forms that are either killable or not killable, the nature of the form is not fixed.
Because the form is not fixed, the act of killing is also not fixed. Since the act of killing is not fixed, the retribution is also not fixed. Why, then, do you say that one is certain to enter hell?
To provide an illustrative example: "zhì" (陟救切) should be read as "huà" (胡麥切). (Note: This indicates a correction of a character from "zhì" to "huà" in the context of a calculation.)

"Ce" (策) means to plan; "du" (度) [with the phonetic gloss *tu-lo*] means to measure; "geng" (更) [with the phonetic gloss *gu-xing*] means to pass through or experience; "bing" (併) [with the phonetic gloss *bi-zheng*] means all, together, or simultaneously.

That which is inevitable when the time arrives refers to the sequence of stages that must be undergone. Those who repent and become pure refer to those who are simultaneously [freed from] the discrepancies of conditions.

"Suo ran" (索然) is equivalent to being dispersed or dissolved. Next, the explanation of the transverse [classification] clarifies the ten evils of the present life; this is the third explanation for seeking repentance.

The fourth section, the commentary on the text of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), is divided into two parts. First is the direct explanation of dedication, which is specifically intended to repent for the fault of attachment to existence.

Second, from "others" (*tadanya*) onwards, is the refutation of errors and the revelation of what is correct. Since the sutra concludes by stating, "All are dedicated," how could one contradict this by providing an explanation of rejoicing (*anumodanā*)?
The reason it says "rejoicing" appears later in the text is that it belongs to the fourth category: the cultivation of the vow (*praṇidhāna*).

The text of the repentance consists of two sections; the second section is the text on sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*). Therefore, the sutra below states: "I now [dedicate] these merits of sympathetic joy.

Fifth, the explanation of the two difficult passages concerning the repentance of good and evil is divided into two parts: first, the introduction to the meaning and the division of the text; within the discussion of good and evil, there are eight points.

The "difficulties" consist of four types of favorable conditions and four types of unfavorable conditions, totaling eight. The four favorable conditions can be understood as they appear in the sutras.

As for the four unfavorable conditions: the perils of the six realms of existence constitute one difficulty; the fickleness of the mind constitutes a second difficulty; and the perils of the three realms of existence constitute a third difficulty.

These three difficulties combined constitute a single obstacle to karmic retribution (*vipāka-āvaraṇa*). This is the first difficulty. Furthermore, the proximity to evil friends constitutes an obstacle to karma (*karma-āvaraṇa*), which is the second difficulty.
Furthermore, adding the three poisons constitutes the afflictive hindrance as the third difficulty.

If the perilous difficulty of birth and death exists, there are two interpretations, which constitute the fourth difficulty. Thus, the four difficulties do not exceed these three combined and one single [difficulty].

The first four lines concern the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*); the following section explains the meaning according to the text. Some editions read "the first four [lines concern] the practitioner," which is an error. This section is divided into two parts.

First, the explanation of the statement that directing evil toward others constitutes an "obstacle": this cites the sūtra, noting that various forms of lustful desire are the obstacle of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
[The text] briefly mentions "foolishness" and "affliction"; "obstacle" refers to agitation and restlessness. When the initial mind dwells upon objects, it is termed "awareness" (*jñāna*).

The subtle mind’s analytical discernment is called "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*). When an Arhat emerges from contemplation, there may be moments of a distracted mind. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"When those of the Two Vehicles arise from meditative concentration, they may enter a neutral (*avyākṛta*) state of mind, or a wholesome state, or even regress into a defiled (*sāsrava*) mind;
the Buddha is not thus. Furthermore, because Śrāvakas possess the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of afflictions and are subject to regression, they experience distraction; the Buddha is not thus.

Therefore, the Buddha always enters meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and lacks coarse consciousness characterized by discursive thought; because he possesses inconceivable wisdom, he is also able to teach the Two Vehicles—something they do not possess.

Regarding those who do not incur karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*): both Gushan and Mingzhou changed the character "obstruction" (*zhàng*) to the character "person" (*zhě*), and moved [the phrase] "at the butcher's (*tu*)" to read "at the side of the one who entrusts the Dharma.

(Note: *Jiù* [pronounced *jū yòu*] means a stable for elephants and horses; it is a place of gathering, where elephants and horses are assembled. *Tu* means to kill. [The phrase] "at the butcher's" refers to the one who transmits the Dharma.
The Tibetan tradition says: "To associate with the virtuous and hear the sublime Dharma brings great benefit to future lives.

This is illustrated by an ancient account from the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra (also pronounced *Chi* or *Jing*). There was once a white elephant there, possessed of great strength and courage, capable of crushing all enemies.
Whenever a criminal was brought before it, the elephant would trample him to death. Later, the elephant stable was consumed by fire; the elephant was moved to another location near a monastery.
A certain bhikṣu was reciting a verse from the *Dharmapada*: "By doing good one is born in heaven; by doing evil one enters the abyss.

Thereupon, the elephant became gentle and gave rise to a mind of compassion. Later, when it encountered the condemned man, it merely looked at him without harming him, sniffing and licking him instead.
When the king witnessed this, his heart was filled with great terror. At that moment, a minister addressed the king, saying: "The place where this elephant is tethered is near a monastery."

"It is precisely because he will surely hear the sublime Dharma that this is so. We may now move his bonds closer to the slaughterhouse; when he beholds the killing, his evil thoughts will surely intensify.
The King then issued an order to bind the elephant at the place of execution. Upon seeing the slaughter, the elephant’s malevolence became fierce and intense.
Therefore, one should know that the natures of sentient beings are not fixed; even an animal can still hear the Dharma and rejoice upon seeing it.
If evil is harmful even to animals, how much more so for humans? Yet one may fail to cultivate oneself and associate with virtuous friends.

Mengzi’s mother lived near a place where people wailed over funeral goods—Mengzi’s mother being the mother of Meng Ke. When Ke was young, he and his mother lived alone in seclusion near a cemetery; Ke would often play at burying the dead.
His mother said, "This is not a place to dwell," and they moved to live beside a marketplace. Ke again played at being a merchant.

The mother said again, "This place cannot be lived in. They moved to live beside an academy; Mencius then became refined in his gestures of bowing and yielding, and in his advancing and retreating with propriety.

His mother said, "This is truly a place where one may dwell. Mencius subsequently became a great Confucian scholar. As for the saying that "one cries over goods," "crying" refers to being near a cemetery, while "goods" refers to being near a market.
Regarding "red from cinnabar and black from ink," this refers to the principle that "by staying near vermilion one becomes red, and by staying near ink one becomes black."
[The previous section] was "Black.

Next, the explanation of the passage concerning the objection that [the Buddha’s teaching] obstructs the path toward goodness is divided into two parts. First, the formal explanation of the objection regarding the cultivation of merit:

the second objection in the current edition of the sutra is the objection regarding the difficulty of encountering a favorable time. Regarding the phrase "as in the case of a certain bhikṣu," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
During the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there were two brothers who left the household life to seek the Way. One observed the precepts, recited the sūtras, and practiced seated meditation;

the other extensively sought out donors to cultivate various meritorious deeds. When Kāśyapa Buddha appeared in the world, one brother was born into the family of an elder, while the other became a great white elephant whose strength could destroy wealth. Later, the son of the elder left the household life to study the Way.

There was an Arhat who had attained the six supernatural powers (ṣaḍabhijñā), yet because of his meager merit, alms-food was difficult for him to obtain. One day, carrying his bowl, he entered the city to beg for food;
though he searched everywhere, he found nothing. Upon reaching the stable of the white elephant, he saw that the King’s elephants were provided with every abundance.

At that time, the Arhat spoke to the white elephant, saying, "Both you and I have committed transgressions. The elephant was then moved by this and remained in distress for three days, refusing to eat.

At mealtime, the elephant-keepers were terrified; they searched for the aforementioned bhikṣu and questioned him, saying, "By what spell have you caused the King’s white elephant to fall ill and be unable to eat?
The bhikṣu replied, "He was my younger brother in a previous life, who left the household life to study the Path under Kāśyapa Buddha.
I merely observed the precepts, recited the sūtras, and practiced dhyāna, but I did not practice giving."
Although he has now attained the Way, because he was unable to obtain alms from his younger brother, he broke the precepts by extensively seeking out donors to perform various acts of giving;

consequently, he fell into the realm of animals where food and drink are abundant. In the *Nanshan Linggan Zhuan* (Biographies of the Miraculous Responses of the Southern Mountains), Vinaya Master Shenxuan says that in the age of the Dharma’s decline, wicked bhikṣus merely establish monasteries but do not cultivate dhyāna or wisdom, nor do they read the sūtras.

As for the phrase "those who recognize the written word," even if there are those who do so, please consider this: would you rather be an Arhat with the six supernormal powers, or a white elephant adorned with the seven treasures?
Furthermore, regarding the passage from the *Sutra of the Past Deeds of King Wondrous Adornment*, the text states:
"In the past, at the end of the Buddha-dharma, four bhikṣus made a pact to dwell in the mountain forests, their aspirations delighting in the Buddha's wisdom as they lived in seclusion."
Day after day his provisions for clothing and food were exhausted, leaving him in constant need; at times he lacked nothing, yet at other times he was destitute.

One man said, "We four are so impoverished that we cannot even sustain our own bodies; where, then, can the Dharma find its refuge? You three should simply devote your lives to the Way and have no anxiety regarding the court.
I shall sacrifice this body of mine and vow to provide whatever you require. Thereupon, he shook his mendicant’s staff and went from door to door to seek alms.
While three people were able to fulfill their sincerity and complete their task, that one person had frequently encountered sensory pleasures and appearances during his travels among humans;
as an unbaked vessel, he was difficult to preserve. By chance, he met a king who admired his splendor, and following his own thoughts, he received his retribution by becoming a king himself.
Yet, he possessed perverse views. The other three deliberated together: "I have escaped the cage and enclosure; this is my merit."
Because of this, after the king’s death from this point forward, he will lose his royal throne forever and sink into a pit of fire, making him difficult to save.

Fortunately, before he has fallen, it is still possible to transform and enlighten him. However, as the king is attached to desire and possesses wrong views, if not for the hook of love, by what means could he be rescued?
One person shall be transformed into a beautiful woman, and two others shall appear as intelligent children—the son and... [the daughter].

The wife’s words were to be followed with obedience and propriety; through this transformation, she attained the Way as the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara, her two sons became the Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata, and King Śrīghoṣa became the Bodhisattva Puṣpadhvaja.

As for the time at the beginning of the kalpa, when the lifespan was eighty-four thousand years, life was long and pleasure was extreme; because people did not feel the need for a Buddha to appear, they did not practice.

The northern continent of Uttarakuru is one of the eight difficult conditions (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*); how, then, could one cultivate the Path there? Regarding the case of Ciñcā and others, the *Bodhisattva-tsa-t'ai-king* (Bodhisattvagatyutpatti-sūtra) states:
"In the past, when the Buddha was in the city of Vaiśālī, there was a woman named Ciñcā who followed the instructions of a false teacher.
She went about everywhere, desiring to be seen by people, and thus made a belly out of grass, gradually making it larger until she later used a wooden bowl."
Her belly was bound like that of a woman about to give birth. At that time, the heterodox teacher asked the woman, "For what reason do you have this body?
The woman replied, "I go daily to the place of the śramaṇa Gautama, and it is because of him that I have come to have this body.
The heterodox teacher, filled with resentment, led his disciples and brought this woman to where the Buddha was. At that moment, the Buddha—
While he was extensively proclaiming the sublime Dharma to an immeasurable multitude, the false teachers and others raised their voices and cried out:
"The śramaṇa Gautama has committed sexual misconduct! He has truly not attained the Way, yet he claims to have attained it. He covets this woman, even to the point of desiring her body!
Having spoken these words, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, transformed himself into a yellow mouse and gnawed the cord of the bowl from within the woman’s skirt.
The alms bowl immediately fell to the ground, which everyone witnessed; they then rebuked the faction of the heterodox, who slandered the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*.

The sutra states that Shanxing was the son of a Buddha or Bodhisattva; after leaving the household life, he upheld and expounded the twelve divisions of the scriptures, destroyed the fetters of the desire realm, and attained the four dhyānas.
However, by associating with evil friends, he fell away from the four dhyānas and gave rise to evil and heterodox views.
Seeing that there was no Buddha-dharma and no nirvana, he saw the Buddha approaching from afar and gave rise to an evil and heterodox mind;
he entered the Avīci Hell. Devadatta’s practice of evil is as previously described (*et cetera*). Master Yuan said: "Śunakṣatra was the Buddha’s nephew, the son of his younger brother;
therefore, he is called 'son' [in the scriptures]. Master Zhan’an said: "Rāhula was his elder half-brother. The old [tradition] says: "Śunakṣatra has no [other name]."

The places where [the Buddhas] manifested their origins were indeed those of evil persons; yet now it is said that this is not so. The Buddha had two younger brothers and two sons who each practiced either good or evil:

Ānanda practiced good while Devadatta practiced evil, and both were entirely expedient means (*upāya*). Rāhula practiced good while Sunakṣatra practiced evil; by this analogy, one should know these were also expedient means.
Next, if one reads the character "biàn" (辨) in the phrase "biànnán" (辨難) with the side-stroke [as a radical], [it refers to the following].
The third section, the commentary on the text of praising and extolling the practice of repentance, is divided into two parts. First, the introductory section analyzing the text:

regarding the *nien-fo samādhi* (Buddha-remembrance samādhi), if it were not the remembrance of the Buddha, how could there be praise? Therefore, this praise is itself the dharma-gate of the *nien-fo samādhi*.

Second, the exegesis of the text according to its phrasing, which is divided into three parts. First, the explanation of the heading: because one praises by looking toward the ten directions in relation to one another, it is called [the "Praise"].

The sequential names for the three temporal dimensions are termed "vertical," while the retributive response is termed "horizontal"; because it is a function, it is called the "phenomenal Dharmakāya" (事法身), and because it is the essence, it is called the "principle" (理).
Thus, by simply designating "all Buddhas," both the horizontal and vertical, as well as the phenomenal and the principial, are subsumed therein. Why?

Because the horizontal and vertical phenomenal functions throughout the three times and ten directions must rely upon the essence of principle; therefore, when the entire essence gives rise to function, it is necessarily identical [to that essence].
Because there is nothing that surpasses the skill of using the essence to mark the chapter, the text immediately below states: "The three Buddhas are of one substance, relying upon the dharma-nature;
it is truly because of this. Regarding the term "ocean of Buddhas," it is used as a metaphor for its profound vastness and lack of bottom or limit;
it refers to the principle-essence of the dharma-nature pervading all places, which is thus named an "ocean. Therefore, Jingxi said: "My own body and..."

This refers to the meaning that the ultimate reality-body (*dharmatā-kāya*) of the Buddhas of the ten directions is fundamentally devoid of subject and object, which is termed the "Ocean of the Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu-samudra*).

Regarding the ten knowledges (*jñāna*): first, dharma-knowledge; second, inferential knowledge; third, knowledge of others' minds; fourth, conventional knowledge; fifth, knowledge of suffering; sixth, knowledge of origination; seventh, knowledge of cessation;
eighth, knowledge of the path; ninth, knowledge of exhaustion; tenth, knowledge of non-arising; and eleventh, knowledge of suchness. These are explained in accordance with the Dharma-realm.
[The sequence continues... Furthermore, one must understand that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and the *dharmakāya* are profound and vast, and are thus called an "ocean.
This is because in the present text, the vastness and boundlessness of the marks and minor characteristics (*lakṣaṇānuvyañjana*) of the *saṃbhogakāya* are designated as an "ocean.

Therefore, the *Wenju ji* states: "In the 'Chapter on the Ocean of the Tathāgata’s Marks' and the 'Chapter on the Radiance of Minor Characteristics' of the *Avataṃsaka*, Vairocana [should actually be called Rocana, yet it says Vairocana]..."

That is to say, the translators of the scriptures did not distinguish between the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*, nor could they discern the three or two [bodies]. He is fully endowed with marks as numerous as the atoms in ten *padma-garbha-loka-dhātu-samudra*s (lotus-treasury world-ocean).
Furthermore, according to the textual commentary, because he manifests excellence, the marks of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*) are called the "Ocean of Great Marks" (*mahālakṣaṇa-samudra*).

Moreover, the marks and secondary characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-anuvyañjana*) of the physical body (*rūpakāya*) of the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and transformation-body (*pariṇāmikakāya*), which are themselves the principle (*li*), are called the "Ocean. As the *Fuxingzhuan* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) explains regarding the "Ocean of Marks": "It is simply..."
The boundless marks and embellishments (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) of the form-body (*rūpa-kāya*) are called the "ocean"; this does not refer to the retribution body (*vipāka-kāya*).
Regarding the term "form-body," it refers to the segmented form-body (*prādeśika-rūpa-kāya*), which corresponds to the transformation body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*).

Regarding the term "ocean of marks," it means that one deeply understands that the marks and embellishments of the segmented and transformational form-bodies are identical in principle (*li*) and measure (*liang*) to empty space—vast and without limit—and thus they are called an "ocean. This does not mean...
The fact that the characteristics and functions of the segmented [body] pervade all things is what is called the "ocean.
If this were not the case, by what means could one clarify the infinite marks and signs of the *dharmatā*-body of the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*)?

For fear of confusing the segmented birth-body with the principle itself—thereby conflating it with the inconceivable ocean of the *dharmatā*-body of the Reward Body, whether in terms of its essence or its function—one must distinguish them.

"All" means to be universally pervasive. Although the principle is the same, one must distinguish them according to their function; thus it is said that while the essence is identical to the true reality (*dharmatā*) and is without differentiation, its function establishes dharmas with varying degrees of distinction.
How can one indiscriminately take the body born of分段生身 (segmented birth) and claim it to be the majestic and special marks of the *dharmatā*?
How can one explain that these marks are universally pervasive? And how can one, upon finally hearing the words "ocean of marks," immediately conclude [that this refers to such a body]?
All these are bodies of the *vairocana* (exalted) form. Regarding the *Lotus Sūtra*’s *Wenju* (Textual Exegesis), the three meanings are used to explain the admonition to Gadgadasvara.
First, regarding the Tathāgata’s seat, the admonition states: "The Buddha-body corresponds to the principle; one must not perceive it as lowly and forget its majesty. The *Ji* (Commentary) states:
"Relying on emptiness, the body devoid of marks is the principle of wondrous emptiness with marks; even a single speck of dust..."

If even the physical body is equal to the principle, how much more so should one not give rise to thoughts of inferiority regarding the form of the sixteen-foot body? Now, let me attempt to clarify this:
since the Dharma-emptiness is taken as the seat, the inferior response-body of sixteen feet relies upon the principle of ultimate, wondrous emptiness.

Thus, the lowliness of the sixteen-foot body with its conditioned marks is transcended, and one realizes that the dimension of the Dharma-body is all-pervasive; therefore, it is not... [the inferior].
To see the humble stature of the sixteen-foot [Buddha] and thereby forget the majesty of the wondrous emptiness is to mistake the finger for the moon;

it is merely the physical dimensions that are pervasive which are called "majestic," not the exalted response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) or the other recompense-body (*vipākakāya*), the sublime and distinctive marks, which constitute true majesty.

This is because although the exalted response-body and the other recompense-body are termed "majestic" and "extraordinary," they are still matters of conditioned form and do not rely upon [the ultimate reality].

This is because, within the principle of emptiness, the physical marks and signs (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) are extinguished and vanish. If people do not perceive this and instead claim that this [teaching] takes the inferior as superior, would they not be mistaken?

Let us stop here for a moment: the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra) clarifies that each of the thirty-two marks and signs in the *Lotus Sūtra* is itself the true reality (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*).

The *Fahua xuanzan* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra) further classifies these as being identical to those in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, wherein each mark and sign is like empty space.

Since it is stated that the marks and signs are equal to empty space, is this not the realization that phenomena are themselves the principle, such that by relying on emptiness, all characteristics vanish?
Thus we know that the principle of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is precisely wondrous emptiness. To have emptiness as the principle within emptiness—this is what is meant.

If even a body of a single speck of dust is equal to the principle and its measure is identical to empty space, how much more so for a physical form of sixteen feet (*ṣoḍaśahasta*), which could not fail to rely upon it?

If one were to think that emptiness, which is utterly extinguished and signless, still gives rise to the inferior perception of the *nirmāṇakāya* (the Response Body) as having signs, this would be profoundly erroneous.

Furthermore, in the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary on the *Mohe Zhiguan*), it is clarified that the thirty-two marks of the previous *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha* vehicles lack the essence of the Middle Way;

for example, obtaining copper cannot reflect one's face. Therefore, these marks are not called "extraordinary. Since the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha* vehicles have already been rejected, they are not so designated.

The "extraordinary" (qite) reveals the distinct and perfect [teachings]—the thirty-two marks and eighty-four thousand [minor characteristics], as well as the superior and inferior functions of the ten lotus-treasury worlds.
Since both possess the Middle Way as the fundamental principle of the Dharma-body, they are termed the "ocean of extraordinary marks.
This refers to the magnitude of the Dharma-body as the fundamental essence of both the superior and inferior; it does not refer to the physical dimensions of the mundane body.
The thirty-two marks of the birth-body (*janma-kāya*) are precisely the wondrously distinguished marks of the Dharma-nature Śākyamuni.

This is because the magnitude of the Dharma-body and the principle of its wondrous emptiness are as boundless as the ocean—profound, extraordinary, subtle, and majestic—and thus cannot be equated with the excellent functions of the marks of the supreme response-body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*).
Therefore, one should know that the fundamental principle of the birth-body is what is called "marks" (*lakṣaṇa*).

If the *samudra-vicitra* (ocean-like marvelousness) is not even the marvelousness of the *vipāka-rūpa* (retributive form), how can one falsely rely on this text to establish that the inferior response-body (*hīna-nirmāṇa-kāya*) is itself the superior response-body, or that the *vicitra-rūpa* (extraordinary marvelousness) is the *vipāka-śarīra* (retributive body)? Alas!

To be deluded by the name without reflecting upon the meaning, and to mistake principle for phenomenon—how could those who are thus obscured fail to realize that the ocean of marks (*lakṣaṇa-samudra*) is distinct from the majestic and marvelous [physical form]? How could it be otherwise?
For this reason, the physical body born of分段 (pén-duàn, *bhājana-loka* / *vipāka-kāya*) is, when viewed through the principle (*li*), called "dignified and extraordinary";
yet it must not be conflated with the dignity of the *dharmatā*-body or the *paranirmita-vipāka*-body.

Thus, since the *paranirmita-vipāka*-body is named the "body beyond the realms" (*jie-wai*, *dharmatā-kāya*), one knows that the dignified and extraordinary marks and signs of Śākyamuni are boundless, like the ocean; this is indeed what is meant by [the term].
Regarding the principle-nature (*tattva*), its phenomenal function (*vṛtti*) pervades all things; this means that both principle and phenomena are universally pervasive.
If it were not so, how could it be called the "Dharmatā-body beyond the realms" (*dharmadhātu-bāhya-dharmatā-kāya*), whose radiance and physical form are immeasurable and boundless?
By this, it is clarified that the segmented birth-body (*pratisaṃdhi-kāya*) possesses a marvelous and majestic dignity identical to space, precisely because it is the principle itself.
Yet, there is no functional application [of these marks], for the *lakṣaṇas* and *vyañjanas* are boundless.

If one were to say that the marks of the sixteen-foot, delimited, birth-body (*janma-deha*) are all-pervasive, how could this clarify the pervasiveness of the majestic, distinctive body of the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) beyond the realms?

Therefore, one must not indiscriminately conflate them by claiming their identity because their essence is the same, nor divide them permanently because their forms are different. The *Wenju ji* (Commentary on the Text) states: "Only when one grasps the true meaning..."

"Knowing that the four Buddhas are identical in essence yet distinct in function" is the second inconceivable phrase. The commentary explains this by taking the Tathāgata’s robe as an admonition, stating:
"When the teacher has already employed skillful means, the disciple likewise conceals his reality. The Record says:

"If both the Buddha and his disciples have inferior bodies, they both conceal their tranquil patience and endure their own clumsiness. Examining the meaning of the text now, it clearly elucidates the relationship between teacher and disciple.

The *saṃbhogakāya* conceals its marks of excellence—the subtle, soft, and superior robes of *śānti-kṣānti* (the patience of quiescence)—and manifests the inferior form of the sixteen-foot [body] characterized by the coarse and worn garments of *utpatti-kṣānti* (the patience of birth) and *dharma-kṣānti* (the patience of the Dharma). One must understand that this inferiority exists in two senses:

first, in comparison to the superior response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) in the Pure Land of Co-residence, whose physical dimensions are vast and tall; second, in comparison to the [bodies] within the realm beyond [the triple world].
The distinctive features of the Svabhāva-Sāmbhogakāya Buddha are infinite; therefore, although they reside within the same realm, those measuring one *zhang* and six *chi* are termed "inferior.
While there are two interpretations, both are distinguished as superior or inferior based on the size of their physical forms.

Thus, the *Fahua wenju* (Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra) quotes the *Xiangfa jueyi jing* (Sutra Resolving Doubts During the Semblance Dharma Age), which says: "Some see a small body, some see a large body."
The realization of the Buddha’s pervasive power manifests as both the sixteen-foot body and the special, exalted body (vairocana-kāya) accompanied by the image of a bhikṣu;

for the inferior must be contrasted with the superior, and the great must be contrasted with the small. Thus we know that the small is the sixteen-foot body, while the base and inferior is the great, exalted, and supreme response-body.
Therefore, one must not simply equate the base and inferior with the exalted and supreme.
Question: If the *Lotus Sūtra* reveals the provisional to manifest the real (*kai-en ken-jitsu*), why is it said that it conceals the real to manifest the provisional (*on-ji shi-en*)?

Answer: The three metaphors of the lotus all metaphorize the Sublime Dharma (*myōhō*). Therefore, within the Sublime Dharma, there are the acts of manifesting (*shi*), revealing (*kai*), and abolishing (*hai*).

Thus, while "concealing the real to manifest the provisional" involves manifesting the inferior from the superior, the appearance of the sixteen-foot [Buddha-body] remains distinct; one should know that "revealing the real by opening the provisional" is precisely manifesting the superior from the inferior.

The light of the body shines universally; as explained in the preceding "Introductory Chapter," the manifestation of a sublime and victorious radiance from an inferior state signifies the opening of the provisional and the revealing of the true aspect of the Dharma.
Therefore, the reabsorption of the light here refers only to the *zhànglù* (sixteen-foot) form. This must be understood in terms of concealing the real and manifesting the provisional. Why?
Because the inferior radiance of the *zhànglù* form of today derives from the provisional teachings manifested in the past. Thus, it is obtained.
The present manifestation of the sixteen-foot body in its humble form is rooted in the past practice of concealing the ultimate and manifesting expedient means.
Although that past humble form was directed toward those of limited capacity, now that the humble and the sublime are revealed to be of the same essence, what hindrance could there be?

Even the sixteen-foot body in the *Lotus Sūtra*, clad in soiled garments yet possessing the thirty-two marks, remains ultimately radiant. Moreover, the mention of "soiled garments" is merely a description of the past; even in that former state, [the true nature] still remained.
How could the expression "stainless garment" possibly be identical to the phrase "necklace"?

Now that it is called a "soiled garment," it further reveals that the provisional [teaching] of one's own practice is itself the internal, secret, and wondrous skillful means. Previously, the application of the provisional was termed "transforming others";

now, clarifying the revelation is shown to be "one's own practice. Therefore, both the application and the revelation are directed toward those to be transformed; their underlying principle is non-dual.
Therefore, from beginning to end, these are merely the sixteen-foot inferior response-body (*pratibhāsa-kāya*).
If one claims this is not so, how can it be said that the Buddha and his disciples are identical in their response-bodies, yet both their bodies are equally lowly and inferior?

Since the meaning of the text is thus, how can you claim that the wondrous One Vehicle is instead reduced back to the Tripiṭaka? If you claim that during the eighty years [of the Lotus Sūtra], the Buddha was lowly and inferior...

If it were always impossible to speak of the Dharma of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa), then why did the Buddha—despite having been afflicted by illness for eighty years and entering nirvāṇa between the twin trees—suddenly discuss the eternal and discern the nature [of reality]? (This objection appears in the *Miaoxuan*).

Therefore, one should know that although the present and the past are both the same in being the six-foot, inferior form, there is a distinction between the "body outside" and the "body inside," which people fail to perceive.
Their sincerity is truly pitiable. The third section of the *Wenju* (Exegesis of Phrases), explaining the matter in terms of the Tathāgata’s Sanctuary as a warning, states:
"The Tathāgata’s compassion overlooks the great trichiliocosm; one ought to be lofty and yet record [the truth] below. The sub-commentary (*Ji*) states:

"One should dwell in the unconditioned and settle within this defiled land. It further concludes: "All manifestations of deportment and places where the Dharma is preached possess these three warnings as the standard for propagating the Sūtra."

Therefore, one should know that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* can clearly state that the teaching master was originally a transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) with a segmented birth-body; there is no need for doubt.
Thus, the *Commentary on the Sixteen Contemplations Sutra* states: "The Dharma-body has no form and truly does not depend on a place to dwell.

However, for the sake of benefiting others, it follows the transformation body to clarify the dwelling place of the teaching master. The *Contemplation Sutra* is a teaching of the Pure and Perfect [Teachings].

Since the Lord is a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), how could it be otherwise that the present sutra now possesses all four [bodies]? Moreover, since it is revealed that they are identical in essence, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is likewise so.
Thus, the characteristics of the beginning and end of the preaching of the Dharma across the five periods are all instances of the segmented, manifested, and transformation bodies.
As the *Wenju ji* states: "In the stage of reality, the future successor assists the transformation Buddha to manifest the passing through the five flavors"—this is precisely that meaning.
The Hīnayāna describes this as the construction of karma and afflictions, wherein there is fixed arising and fixed cessation, and where all remains are extinguished without remainder.
The Mahāyāna describes it as the merging of wisdom with the essence, capable of initiating great function; it is not born by being born, yet he manifested his substance in the royal palace;

it is not extinguished by being extinguished, yet his spirit became serene at the Śāla trees. Thus, he manifests extinction here in this land while appearing in transformations throughout the ten directions, creating further emanations—this is what is meant.
People do not see this [form], but hearing only the words of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, they all uniformly refer to it as the "exalted" (*viśeṣa*).

Therefore, I have distinguished it as above, though I am conscious that the text has become prolix. It is like throwing things into rock honey; the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "It is like boiling rock honey;
when it is about to be finished, if one puts various other things into it, they all become rock honey, because its wondrous flavor is so abundant. The Bodhisattva is also like this.
Thus, because the power of this prajñā is so preeminent, all various dharmas are united with prajñā to become a single flavor.

Next, the explanation of the passage on the "True Praise" (bhūtapraśaṃsā) is divided into two parts: first, the analysis of the text through four categories—*ji* (entrustment), *jue* (transcendence), *wei* (comparison), and *kuang* (analogy)—to praise and extol its virtues. "Entrustment" means to rely upon; "transcendence" means that it is beyond the reach of words;
"comparison" means to match or contrast; and "analogy" means to praise by means of metaphorical likening.

Next, the explanation of the meaning of the text is divided into two parts. First, the explanation of the praise expressed through metaphorical language is further divided into two. First, the explanation of the brief praise and brief comparison. Regarding "Jambūnada gold":
this Jambūnada gold appears as golden light floating upon the sea off the northern shore of this continent (Jambudvīpa).
Beside it stands a Jambū tree, half of which borders the land and half of which borders the sea. If a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) appears in the world...
The yakṣa deities then took this gold and brought it to the human realm; they briefly praised and compared it, saying that its golden brilliance was like Mount Sumeru.
Extensively praising it further, they said its merit was towering and its radiant net was manifest and shining—surely a sign of supreme and extraordinary honor.
The scripture further states that it is adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics.
Adorning the body—is this not precisely the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics with which the Dharma-body is adorned in the *Lotus Sūtra*?

Is this not identical to what follows below, where the primary praise concerns the *vairocana-kāya* (the body of supreme marks) while also encompassing the *nirmāṇa-kāya* (the body for saving beings) above and below the *dharmatā-kāya* (the body of dharma-nature)?
Thus we know that although the two individuals, the Dragon King and Śraddhālakṣaṇa, differ in their past and present lives, the Buddha-body they praise is wondrously the same.
The meaning is no different.
Next, the explanation of the extensive praise and the extensive analogy is further divided into two parts. First, the analysis of the text to explain the meaning; this section is divided into two.

First, the explanation of the extensive praise; this is divided into four parts: first, explaining the extensive praise of the unsurpassed golden color; second, explaining the extensive praise of the Buddha’s color being stainless.
The third explanation extensively praises the Buddha’s physical form as abiding in *sphāṭika*—which here is translated as "water-jade" (*shuiyu*).

Since the preceding passage already mentioned the thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics, and this passage further states that his merit is sublime and his wondrous color is vast, how could this not be a praise of the *paricchinna-utpanna-kāya* (the body born of karmic retribution) with its fourfold sets of eight marks?
Furthermore, it manifests the *dharmatā-vigraha* (the majestic body of the dharma-nature) beyond the realms. How much more so!

The "Comprehensive" (Tong) Buddha refers to the sixteen-foot *zuntè* (exalted special) body appearing in the form of a bhikṣu; the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) in its classification of teachings assigns this sutra to the Comprehensive category.

Since the *zuntè* body encompasses both the Separate (Bie) and Perfect (Yuan) vehicles, and the Comprehensive teaching further includes these while clarifying the Perfect, and since there is nothing in the Separate or Perfect that is not the merging of wisdom with the essence (*tǐ*) capable of giving rise to great function (*yòng*), it is therefore praised as "Great."

Regarding the application of superiority and inferiority, what contradiction could there be? Therefore it is said: "neither permanent nor impermanent. The eight arts are fully possessed, and the two functions are perfectly manifest (*et cetera*).
Fourth, the extensive explanation praising the Buddha’s physical form removes the deluge of suffering. The *Yùpiān* states that "lǎo" (潦) refers to the overflowing of rainwater;
"kūhé" (枯涸) means to be parched and dried up. "Jiěshǒu" (稽首), according to the *Shuōwén*, means to lower the head; it refers to the head touching the ground. Next...

The commentary on the passage of extensive illustration is divided into two parts: first, the analysis of the text; second, the explanation of the meaning. The text itself is divided into two sections:

first, the explanation of the extensive illustration of mental activity (xíng, level tone); second, the explanation of the application of the analogy. The commentary on the expression of the ineffable praise is further divided into two parts:

first, the analysis of the text; second, the explanation of the meaning. The text itself is divided into two sections: first, the explanation of the actual expression of the ineffable praise; second, the explanation of the restatement of the analogy and its application. Third, the commentary on the concluding praise.

The fourth section, the commentary on the text for making vows and practicing repentance, is divided into two parts. First, the introductory explanation of the intent and the division of the text from the beginning up to "the fruit fulfills the vow" consists of four further sections;

this is the introductory explanation of the intent, and subsequent sections should be understood accordingly. Regarding the phrase "like an ox without a driver," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"For example, although an ox has the strength to pull a cart, it requires a driver to reach its destination. [This refers to] purifying the Buddha[-field].
The aspiration for the world is likewise: its merit is like an ox, the aspiration itself is like a driver;
it is like a painting without glue that cannot remain firm for long, or like unbaked clay (a *piṇḍa*) that cannot be used until fired by fire, or like the moon in water which lacks reality.
One formulates such an aspiration precisely for the sake of repenting the offenses of regression.

Next, the explanation of the meaning according to the text is divided into two parts. First, the explanation of the text of the vow-making is divided into two. First, the explanation of the self-vow is further divided into two.
First, the explanation of the fulfillment of the fruit of the vow is divided into four parts. First, the explanation of the intention to attain Buddhahood:
because the Bodhisattva’s resolve to seek the Buddha-way is fulfilled when the wheel of the mind is perfected through attaining Buddhahood. Next, the explanation of the vow to preach the Dharma.

First, the fulfillment of the Wheel of Speech through the three [aspects] destroys Māra; second, the fulfillment of the Wheel of Body through the manifestation of supernatural powers enables the destruction of Māra.

Fourth, the fulfillment of the vow to abide for a long life through compassion: if it were not for compassion, how could one remain for inconceivable eons to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings?

Next, the explanation of the fulfillment of the causes of the vow is divided into two parts: first, the presentation of the outline, and second, the detailed explanation of the text, which consists of four sections.

First, the explanation of the fulfillment of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and the aspiration for the perfection of conditioned merit (*saṃskṛta-guṇa*). Regarding *zhiguan* (cessation and contemplation), it says:

"The six perfections are all adornments of merit. Since both the *Fahua wenju* (Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra) and its commentary take the six *pāramitās* to be the adornment of merit, we know that this refers to the perfection of conditioned merit; this is because the cultivation of the six perfections involves purposeful activity. Next...
3. Explaining the perfection of the merit of the vow to sever afflictions and attain the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*): Since afflictions have been severed, there is nothing further to be done;

therefore, this is the perfection of the merit of the unconditioned. 4. Explaining the perfection of mindfulness of the Buddha through recollecting past lives. 5. Explaining the perfection of encountering the Buddhas.

Next, the explanation of the text for making vows for others is divided into two parts. First, regarding the division of the text, the *Miaoxuan* (The Profound Meaning) clarifies that the Wheel of Body manifests as the body of the King of Medicine Trees and the body of the King of Wish-fulfilling Jewels;
what is now called the "precious jewel" is precisely the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*). The *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the Profound Meaning) states:
"The body of the King of Medicine Trees manifests a form that is formidable for destroying evil. Thus, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says, "For example..."
The medicinal tree is called the "King of Trees" because it is the most excellent among all medicines, capable of extinguishing all diseases. Yet the tree does not form the thought:
"Whether one takes its branches, leaves, bark, or trunk," for although it does not form such thoughts, it can cure all ailments. Nirvāṇa is likewise [as described at length].
As for the body of the King of Wish-fulfilling Jewels (*cintāmaṇi-rāja*), it manifests in a form that is lovely and inspires wholesome states; thus it is said in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
It is said to be like a *maṇi* jewel (here, *maṇi* refers to the wish-fulfilling jewel; if one follows the two jewels of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, they are distinct).
In whatever place it resides, no non-human beings can find an opportunity against it. When this jewel is worn on the body, it provides light in the dark, coolness in the heat, and warmth in the cold.
If placed in water, it manifests colors according to the objects [nearby]. In the *Fuxingzhuan* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning), quoting the *Jīvaka-sūtra*, it says: "Jīvaka, the youth..."
The son saw among the large bundles of firewood at the place where the goods were being stacked a piece of wood that emitted a brilliant light; it was named "King of Medicine" (Bhaiṣajyarāja).
When leaned against the body of a sick person, it illuminated all the various diseases within the body.

Next, following the explanation of the text, there are two parts. First, the explanation of the passage on Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) which uproots suffering, which is divided into four sections:

first, explaining the general uprooting of all sufferings; second, explaining the uprooting of the suffering of impaired faculties; third, explaining the uprooting of the suffering of illness; and fourth, explaining the uprooting of the suffering of royal calamities.

Next, the explanation of the passage on Great Loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) which bestows happiness, which is divided into two parts: first, the analysis of the text; second, the explanation of the meaning, which consists of three sections. First, the explanation of "bestowing" [happiness].

Regarding the *Shìjiān guǒlè jīng* (Sutra on Worldly Fruits and Happiness), it states that the *kōng hóu* (harp-lute) is also called *kǎnhóu* according to the *Fēngsù tōng* (Comprehensive Account of Customs).
During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Han, when he was sacrificing to Taiyi and Houtu, he ordered the musician of the Hou clan to create the *kǎnhóu* based on the *qín* (zither);

"kǎn" refers to its rhythmic, thumping response to the musical beat, while "Hou" is used as a surname to head the title. The *Xù Hànshū* (Continued History of the Han) records that Emperor Ling was fond of foreign attire and had it fashioned.
Regarding the *hú kōnghóu* (the hollow lute), the *Shìmíng* (Explanations of Names) states: "The *kōnghóu* was created by Shíyán as the 'Mímí' music; it was favored by the lords of empty states.
Alternatively, it is said that it is called *kōnghóu* because its interior is hollow. The *Dàlùn* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra) states: "The *kōnghóu* has a soundbox, a neck, leather, and strings;
when struck with the hand, these various conditions combine to produce sound. [This applies to] the *zhēng* (zither).

(From the *Cèjìng* rhyme group): The *dí* (flute) is a musical instrument created by Meng Tian of the Qin dynasty. The *Fēngsú Tōng* states that it was also a musical instrument created by Qiu Zhong during the reign of Emperor Wu.
As for the *qín* (zither), "qín" means "to restrain"; the gentleman maintains it to restrain himself.
According to one account, Shennong carved paulownia wood to make the zither; others say it was created by Fuxi. The large versions have fourteen strings or twenty strings. In the present day...
This does not exist [in the original texts]. Shun made the five-stringed *qín*; King Wen of Zhou added one string, and King Wu added another;
what people today call the "two strings of Wen and Wu" refers to these. The *sè* is also a musical instrument; the *Shiben* states that Pao Xi created the *sè*.
