Because these six dharmas are coarse, they belong to the sphere of external consciousness; thus they are called *āyatana* (entrances) and also called *viṣaya* (objects).
"Object" (*viṣaya*) takes the sense of defilement, for they are able to defile the sensory consciousnesses; hence they are collectively termed "objects.

The old translation calls them *āyatana*, while the new translation calls them *āyatana*. To say "opening the mind into two" should rather be expressed as "opening form into ten *āyatanas* and one *āyatana*."

A small portion of the mind-base (*manāyatana*) and a small portion of the phenomena-base (*dharmāyatana*) constitute the single mind-base; thus, the phenomena-base contains both matter and mind, forming two small portions.
The mind-base is exclusively mind, while the remaining ten are exclusively matter. One should know that within the phenomena-base there are four categories of phenomena:

unmanifest form (*avijñaptirūpa*), mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*), and the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). Among these, one should understand the unmanifest form.

These are: matter (rūpa), mental factors (caitta), formations dissociated from mind (cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra), and unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma) which do not arise from the mind; these are not subsumed within the three aggregates (triskandha).

If categorized by way of the elements (dhātu), the dharma-element (dharmadhātu) likewise contains both matter and mind. Within the dharma-element, four [elements] are subsumed under matter, while the ten bases (āyatana) are likewise [subsumed]:
seven bases are matter and three are mind.
Next, regarding the explanation of the eighteen *dhātus*: the mind is divided into eight and form is divided into ten, following the previous exposition.
Within this, there are two parts: first, stating the intent and outlining the sections; second, explaining the meaning according to the text. The text has three parts.

First, explaining that consciousness pervades all sense organs and is like an illusion (*māyā*): an illusion is something that does not exist yet suddenly appears; likewise, the roaming of the mind is also...
"Rú (如)" means to gallop, and it also means to run. It is like a person who "gallops while sitting" throughout the world;
their body sits here, but their mind gallops through the world. However, when one "sits and perishes" the mind, it becomes pure and still.

This should not be confused with the "sitting-perishing" of Zhuang Zhou, for Zhuang Zhou’s sitting-perishing was characterized by having words but lacking practice. The commentary states that "yún yún" (云云) refers to the *Wénjùjì* (Record of Textual Phrases).

The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states: "Suppose there were a king who placed four venomous snakes in a single basket and ordered a man to feed, nurture, and watch over them, attending to their every movement.
He commanded that if even one snake were to become enraged, he should be executed according to the law in the marketplace.
Upon hearing this, the man abandoned the basket and fled; at that moment, the king further dispatched five *caṇḍālas* following him with drawn swords."
He secretly dispatched one person, feigning to be a close friend, and said to him, "You may come back.
That man did not believe him and entered a village, where he could not find him at all. Unable to obtain anything, he sat down on the ground;
then he heard a voice from the air saying, "Tonight there shall be six great thieves coming. The man became terrified and abandoned his search, leaving until he encountered [the others] on the road.

A river cuts across the current and flows away; it is said that if a snake harms a person, they do not fall into the evil realms, yet without the power of the Three Studies, one will surely be harmed by the *caṇḍāla* of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
If one does not recognize craving as a deceptive kinsman, one is deluded; contemplate the six sense bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*) as if they were an empty village inhabited by a band of thieves.
Within the six objects and the six sense bases, one desires to abandon them, yet again encounters the swift current of afflictions (*kleśa*).

One should use the raft of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) to cross the river by moving hands and feet with great effort; even those in the ten stages (daśabhūmi) have not yet escaped it, for only the Buddha reaches the ultimate end.
The original sutra text uses this as a metaphor for the beginning and end of the Three Vehicles. In the present text, however, it is used as a metaphor for delusion:

because one does not know that the faculties (indriya), objects (viṣaya), and emptiness (śūnyatā) are perilous, one is harmed by the thieves. Next, [the text] explains that consciousness (vijñāna) constantly resides within the faculties and objects, citing the *Śāstra* (Treatise) as proof, exactly as previously detailed.
In the phrase "I have heard," the three explanations are resolved. Regarding consciousness (vijñāna) in relation to the sense organs (indriya), its entry and exit are not fixed;
the term "intermediate" (*jiānguān*)—where *jiān* is also written as *jiàn*—refers to an obstruction or limitation. Its entry and exit are characterized by ruggedness and hardship.
The commentary states "and so forth" (*yúnyún*) to indicate that the mind constantly relies upon the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*).

The third section, "Explaining the Conclusion: The Text on the Two Emptinesses of the Object of Higher Birth," is divided into two parts: first, the presentation; second, the explanation, beginning with "The body is empty. This explanation is further divided into two parts.

First, the explanation of the conclusion regarding the emptiness of the object of higher birth: as for "nurturing" (*puṣṭi*), it refers to the false conceptualization within the phenomena of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the aggregates (*skandha*), the sense-bases (*āyatana*), and the elements (*dhātu*) that "I am able to nurture others," and thus it is called nurturing. Furthermore, it involves the conceptualization that "I [arise] from..."

Since birth, one has been nurtured by one's parents. Next, there is also the section "There is no subordinate" (*mūla-nāsti*), which explains the aforementioned state of the emptiness of dharmas (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
This is further divided into two parts. First is the introductory explanation. Regarding "there is no primary master": the earth element possesses the four subtle particles (*catur-aṇu*).

These are dull because they consist of the four subtle forms—namely, color, odor, taste, and tangibility; thus they are called the "four subtle particles. That which is heavy is termed "dull. Water possesses three subtle particles; among these four, odor is absent.
Fire possesses only two atoms; in the triad [of earth], there is no taste; wind possesses only one [atom], yet its power of touch is greatest.
Since the mind is not material, it has no atoms; thus, in the subsequent explanation, there is no dispute.
Next, the explanation of the passage concerning the objects of the cause of origination (*samudaya-hetu*) is divided into three parts: first, the analysis of the text;

second, the clarification that the preceding three [sections] are the objects for those who practice through wisdom (*prajñā-carita*), specifically the objects for the correct contemplation of the cause of origination, namely the three categories (*triskandha*);

and third, the clarification that the final one is for those who practice through conduct (*caryā-carita*), wherein the latter two practices—water, fire, and wind—are the provisional conceptualizations (*parikalpa*) that assist the path.
This is the objective realm (*viṣaya*). Furthermore, the meanings of the provisional and the real, the primary and the auxiliary, and so forth, have already been indicated in the preceding text;

they are merely restated here. Regarding "the former one arises from ignorance": the first two lines clarify the characteristic of the arising of the accumulation (*samudaya-lakṣaṇa*). Regarding "the latter one ceases from ignorance":

this refers to the objective realm of the auxiliary path of contemplation (*anuloma-mārga-bhāvanā*), as in the passage beginning with "when it is dispersed, extinguished, and destroyed. The phrase "ignorance is fundamentally unarisen" clarifies [the nature of cessation].
The Mahāyāna is neither arising nor ceasing, yet it arises and ceases.

Third, the explanation of the text from "From all [the lower realms]" onwards is divided into three parts. First, the explanation of the passage on the characteristic of origination (*samudaya-lakṣaṇa*) is divided into two.

First, the general demonstration that suffering and its origination universally arise from causes and conditions: as when Śāriputra, upon hearing the teaching of the Three Truths from Aśvajit, said, "All phenomena arise from..."

The Truth of Suffering arising from conditions is also the teaching of the Dharma regarding the Truth of Origination. Next, the text providing a detailed explanation for the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) is divided into two parts.

First is the explanation of the causes and conditions for the arising of provisional names; this section is further divided into two. First is the refutation of the Lesser Vehicle, which is itself divided into two.

First, the statement of the Lesser Vehicle's position: "The Lesser Vehicle refutes the four great elements down to the subtle dust of the *paramāṇu* (neighboring atom). Regarding the term *paramāṇu*: it refers to the neighboring atom.
This refers to the *paramāṇu* (the subtle atom), for this particle is the most minute. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* explains that the smallest unit of matter (*rūpa*) is the *paramāṇu*.

The treatise states: "The *paramāṇu*, the *aṇu*, the gold-dust, water-dust, rabbit-hair-dust, sheep-hair-dust, ox-hair-dust, window-dust, ant-dust, louse, barley-corn, and finger-joint—each subsequent [unit] increases sevenfold.
Twenty-four finger-joints make one *hasta*; four *hasta* make one *dhanus* (bow-length); five hundred *krośas* make one *yojana*. This is the measure.
Eight *yojanas*. The *Miaoxuan* states that the number [of atoms] exists as *paramāṇus*. The *Lunpo linxu* (Refutation of the *Paramāṇu*) discusses the four great elements.
The Abhidharma masters cited in the *Sijiao* state: "One analyzes form down to the subtle dust of the *paramāṇu*; when one sees that this subtle dust possesses a real principle, one attains the Way.
The masters of the *Shi cheng lun* (Tattvasiddhi-śāstra) state: "To see that the subtle form of the *paramāṇu* exists is a skillful means for disciplining the mind."
If one cannot attain the Way because the analysis of matter down to the subtle dust of the *paramāṇu* results in emptiness, then one attains the vision of the Way.
This refers to the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) position that, upon breaking down the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) to the subtle dust of the *paramāṇu*, there is both exhaustion and non-exhaustion.

Next, the following section clarifies the refutation of these errors: "Now it is clarified that the coarse can be analyzed to exhaustion" refutes the Sāṃkhya school; "the subtle dust is also exhausted" refutes the Vaiśeṣika school.

Regarding the term "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*), the following section provides the formal explanation of the text, which can be understood accordingly. Regarding the "deluded discrimination" (*vikalpa*) mentioned next, the subsequent five phrases explain the causes and conditions for the arising of substantial phenomena (*dharma*).
As for the term "mechanism" (*yantra*): the *Wenju ji* (Record of Textual Explanations) states that "mechanism" (*ji*) refers to the sense of something subtle that can be activated;
"joint" (*guan*) refers to the joints that move by means of a person [as the operator]. Thus, all formations of body and speech arise from the movement of the mind.
Since it is said that the formation of karmic actions is an "empty village," it is fundamentally empty.

Next, the explanation of the characteristics of the accumulation [of suffering] where they devour one another is divided into two parts. First, the explanation of the initial four lines is divided into three sections.

First, the explanation of how they increase and decrease according to time and mutually harm one another: as for the statement that there are ten distinct periods, such as those found in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, these refer to internal and external forms.
There are ten distinct internal stages of physical form: first, the stage of the kalala; second, the stage of the arbuda;
third, the stage of the peśī; fourth, the stage of the ghana; fifth, the stage of initial birth; sixth, the stage of infancy; seventh, the stage of childhood;
eighth, the stage of youth; ninth, the stage of maturity; and tenth, the stage of old age and death.
External forms are likewise so. Regarding the differences in time—sprout, stem, branch, leaf, flower, and fruit—Gushan (Mount Solitary) says:

"New" refers to the arising of the various sense-faculties (*indriya*), while "old" refers to the cessation of the various sense-faculties. Furthermore, that which is nourished by food and drink is termed "new," whereas tears, earwax, and the like are termed "old.

For the detailed explanation of the phrase "and so forth" (*yǒuyún*), see the extensive commentary in the "Chapter on Eliminating Disease" (*Chúbìng pǐn*) below. Next, regarding the analogy "just as...": this is explained as being like the four [elements].

Regarding the statement that "the four snake-like [defilements] and so forth are like the elements," the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* states: "To distinguish them briefly, the three poisons correspond to the three great illnesses;
because they arise equally in the three locations, they are called 'equal-parts' (*sabhāga*). The earth-element illness arises from greed. The *Sūtra* says:
'The river of craving swirls and submerges sentient beings; blinded by ignorance, they cannot escape. Craving can moisten karma, just as water does.'"
Moisture gives rise to anger; when the mind of anger arises, it burns away roots of goodness. Ignorance corresponds to wind;
because of ignorance, there are the four inversions, which are like violent winds capable of toppling mountains and leveling peaks. The earth possesses the three qualities [of fire, water, and wind].
When water, fire, and wind all gather within a single body, the sūtras and śāstras employ metaphors according to circumstances: sometimes fire represents desire, and water represents anger.
Wind is likewise not fixed; furthermore, it is through the four elements that the *saṃbhogakāya* (recompense body) is manifested, which possesses birth, old age, sickness, and death.

As stated in the *Śrī-garbha-sūtra* (or *Śrī-garbha-vyākaraṇa*), "it is as in the present text. Regarding the phrase "with additions and subtractions," the note says "and so forth," which refers to the section on "Eliminating Sickness" (*Vyādhi-parivarta*) in the following text.

Although the "additions and subtractions" of the four great elements primarily clarify the characteristics of accumulated karma devouring one another, the three explanations [of this] reside together in a single casket.

"Stinging insects (*śīzhì* [shǐ zhǐ]) spread poison. The commentary states "and so forth," which should be interpreted through analogy as follows: the body sustains the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) like a cage holding a bird;
when the body perishes and the elements vanish, it is like the cage breaking and the bird escaping. Yet, though it has escaped this cage, it enters another cage.

Thus, the *Zhi guan* (Stopping and Contemplation) says: "Entering one cage after another; the seal is destroyed and the text is formed" (and so forth). Next, from "its nature" (*qí xìng*) downward, the latter ten [categories] are explained.
The term "clause" (*jù*) is synonymous with "category" (*xìng*). The character "like" (*biàn*) is likely an error and should be "by" (*yóu*).
In the east, there are two intermediate directions: one is the yang direction above, which is southeast; the other is the yin direction below, which is northeast.
The commentary states "and so forth" to indicate that the sutra says earth and water sink downward, while wind and fire rise upward. This [character *pí* (pronounced *zhì*)] means "near. Since...

Because they cannot be pushed and cannot be examined, one knows that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are not substantial. As for the great differences in the rising and sinking of the fruits of suffering:
"great" refers to fire; that is, earth and water sink downward, while wind and fire rise upward.

The commentary states "and so forth" to prompt a discernment of the differences between accumulated karma—whether good or evil—namely, the vast disparity between the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*) and the ten unwholesome actions on one hand, and the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions on the other.
It is said that "Heaven is perverse.

Regarding the passage "the three consciousnesses," the subsequent explanation states that they are called "mind" (*citta*) because they correspond to the number of the three [aggregates]—feeling, perception, and formations—and thus the mind is the sovereign.
That which is produced is called "intellect" (*manas*); one should rather say it is "that which produces" [the mental factors].

Regarding the *Yì* (mind) in the *Fǎjiè Cìdì Shì* (Explanation of the Sequence of the Dharma Realm), it states: "When the mind (*xīn*) encounters all phenomena (*dharmas*), there is the function of being able to cognize those phenomena;

this is termed 'mind' (*yì*). The mind is the sovereign of the mind (*cittarāja*). Furthermore, regarding what is produced [by the mind], the *Fǎjiè Cìdì Jiě* (Explanation of the Sequence of the Dharma Realm) explains the *manovijñānadhātu* (mental consciousness element):
"If the five consciousnesses can produce mental consciousness, then the preceding five consciousnesses serve as its faculty (*indriya*)."
Subsequently, the mental consciousness acts as the mental consciousness; when this mental consciousness ceases, the succeeding consciousness arises in continuity.

Thus, the preceding mental consciousness gives rise to the subsequent mental consciousness. In this way, it is also possible to be liberated. The names "root" (indriya) and "consciousness" (vijñāna) are transmitted and received such that that which can produce is designated the root, and that which is produced is designated consciousness.
What is now described as the consciousness that is produced is the sphere of mental consciousness (*manovijñānadhātu*). This is the consciousness that has arisen.

The consciousness element (*vijñānadhātu*) is not the faculty of mind (*manendriya*) that is capable of producing [consciousness], because we are currently clarifying that it is precisely the faculty of mind that is capable of producing it.

The consciousness produced by it is as stated in the following passage: "The faculty of mind and the mental consciousness cannot be considered one," because the faculty of mind is the sovereign mind (*cittarāja*), which is the mind-base (*manāyatana*) among the twelve bases, whereas the mental consciousness is the consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*) among the eighteen elements.

For this reason, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states: "That which arises collectively is called 'mind' (*citta*); that which deliberates is called 'intellect' (*manas*); that which cognizes is called 'consciousness' (*vijñāna*)," and so forth.
Regarding the two natures of good and evil, these refer to the nature of the constituent elements (*dharmatā*), not the nature of ultimate truth (*tattva*).

As for the statement that "the mind arises prior" and so on: that which arises prior to the mind is the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*); that which arises subsequent to the mental consciousness is the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*). This is the position of the Sarvāstivāda school.

Several people say that the King arises simultaneously with the various [beings]. The commentary states that "various" refers to the discernment of good and evil karma according to the retribution of the twenty-five realms of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).
Furthermore, because one is pulled by both the forceful and the habitual, one falls into karma and follows it.

Moreover, in the sutras, it is explained that one falls into the various realms of existence according to the karma one has performed; this explains the aforementioned person who undergoes retribution in accordance with their karma.
If one were to say that the ears of the various heavenly realms are not so, how could the Buddha have laboriously repeated such meanings? Therefore, the commentary states "and so forth.

Next, the explanation of the objects of conceptualization (*parikalpita-viṣaya*) is divided into two parts. First, the direct explanation of the sutra text, which is further divided into two. First, the general explanation of the various phrases:
regarding the statement "the karma abandons the vessel of suffering," this refers to what was previously called "the cessation of ignorance. Second, the specific explanation of the Great [Vehicle].
Regarding the "Minor Impurity," following this is the section on the "Summary and Indication of the Auxiliary Path Text," which is divided into three parts: first, the formal summary and indication;

second, the citation of evidence from the *Śrāvakabhūmi* (the "Exposition of the Path") below; and third, the explanation that the "Dharma of Opening the Gates" refers to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*), for by practicing these thirty-seven factors, one is able to open the three gates of liberation (*trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni*), and by opening the three gates of liberation, one enters the city of *nirvāṇa*. Not so.

Regarding the purification through the nine notions (*navasaṃjñā*) and so forth, the *Zhiguan* states: "Next, to clarify the arousal of the meditation on impurity: first, we speak in terms of the nine notions. The nine notions are:
(1) the notion of bloating, (2) the notion of decay, (3) the notion of being smeared with blood, and so on, up to the ninth, the notion of burning.

If one is a person who destroys [the body], they cultivate the nine notions; if one is a person who does not destroy [the body], they proceed from the initial notion of bloating until they abide in the notion of bones."
Next, one visualizes burning until light rays are obtained (and so forth).

Third, if one cultivates the lower levels of *ābhāsvara* (luminosity) and the *vibhūta-śūnyatā* (liberation through mastery), these serve as aids to bring forth the main text, which consists of four parts. First, the main explanation has three sections:
(1) possessing internal forms while perceiving external forms; (2) lacking internal forms while perceiving external forms; and (3) the pure liberation (*śubha-vimokṣa*) of the body.

The realization of the four emptinesses, the five consciousnesses, the six [stages] of nothingness, the seventh [stage of] neither-perception-nor-non-perception, and the eighth liberation through the cessation of feeling and perception—these constitute the "Great Impurity.
To verify the preceding "Small Impurity" as the primary gateway for destroying desire:
the term "destroying desire" refers to the destruction of the six desires: first, desire for form; second, desire for physical appearance; third, desire for deportment and graceful bearing.
Fourth is the desire for speech and sound; fifth is the desire for fine textures; sixth is the desire for human forms. Furthermore, there are miscellaneous desires:

some people are attached to all five matters, but by skillfully cultivating the nine meditations on repulsiveness (*navasaṃjñā*), one can destroy them. How so? By first using the meditation on the corpse as recently deceased, one destroys the two desires for deportment and speech;
next, by using the meditations on the bloated, the decomposed, and the devoured, one destroys the desire for physical appearance; and next, by using the meditation on the blood-smeared...

The contemplation of the livid corpse (*vinīlaka-saṃjñā*), the contemplation of the festering corpse (*vipūyaka-saṃjñā*), and the contemplation of the dismembered corpse (*vikhāditaka-saṃjñā*) primarily eliminate desire for physical beauty; the contemplation of the skeleton (*asthi-saṃjñā*) and the contemplation of the burning corpse (*vidagdhaka-saṃjñā*) primarily eliminate desire for smoothness and softness.

The nine contemplations (*navasaṃjñā*) eliminate miscellaneous desires as well as the desire for the personal characteristics of those one is attached to. The contemplation of being devoured (*vilohitaka-saṃjñā*), the contemplation of the scattered corpse (*vikṣiptaka-saṃjñā*), and the contemplation of the skeleton (*asthi-saṃjñā*) specifically eliminate the desire for the human form.

This is as explained in the *Zhiguan Chanyumen* (The Gate of Meditation on the Cessation and Contemplation) of the *Miaofa Lianhua Jing Xuanzan* (Profound Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), and so forth. Regarding the "Great Impurity" (*mahā-aśubha*), the sequence is indicated in the *Zhiguan*.
The contemplation of great impurity (*mahā-aśubha-bhāvanā*) is also called the "great liberation" (*mahā-vimokṣa*).

While the previously mentioned contemplations—which involve observing and removing the skin and flesh to focus intently on a skeleton or a corpse’s impurity, whether it be one corpse, two corpses, or the overflowing impurities of cities, towns, and villages—are termed "small impurity" because they concern only the primary retribution (*vipāka*) of oneself and others, how could this be so for the contemplation of great impurity? It is not merely... [as before].

The primary retribution overflows with impurity, and the secondary retribution of the dwelling, wealth, grain, clothing, food and drink, mountains, rivers, gardens, groves, and ponds—all such material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*)—are entirely impure. Worms and pus flow forth from these foul-smelling, putrid places;
the house is like a burial mound, the money like dead snakes, the soup like excrement broth, the rice like white worms, and the clothing like...
The stinking mountains are like heaps of flesh, the ponds are like rivers of pus, the groves are like dry bones, and the oceans and rivers are like pools of filth.
Seeing that there is not a single good place upon this great earth, one realizes that neither the primary body nor its environment can be craved; this is called "Great Impurity.

Next, according to the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, it is explained that this is both real and illusory; because one perceives what is unreal and impure as being impure, it is called [the contemplation of] impurity.
Because emptiness can destroy greed and desire, it is called "reality. This third section on impurity also possesses the two kinds of emptiness.
Regarding the eight-colored flowing light, a detailed explanation is found in the *Cānabōluómì* (Dhyānapāramitā). The *Fǔxíng* (Subcommentary) also states:
"One sees the color of earth as a ground that is yellowish-white and pure; one sees the color of water as water that is clear and limpid like a deep abyss; one sees the color of fire as..."
The smokeless, pure fire appears like the color of wind; the wind, as utterly clear and stainless as being free of dust, appears like the color blue;
it appears like the color yellow, like a mountain of refined gold; it appears like the color red, like the morning glow of spring;

it appears like the color white, like mother-of-pearl, shells, or snow. The *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* says: "Its form is like flowing water, and its light envelops the skeleton" (and so forth). These four great elements are precisely [this].

Since the real dharmas of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) are now no longer perceived, the dharmas are empty. This is concluded by way of the [remaining] four lower aggregates to assist in manifesting the primary point;
thus it says, "ultimately established.

Next, the explanation of the contemplation on the two emptinesses of arising and dharmas consists of three parts: first, the division of the text; second, the concise demonstration of the text, which itself has two parts. First:

The question is followed by the answer, which is further divided into two parts. The first part provides the direct response based on both the general and specific meanings, which is itself divided into two sections.

The first section provides the direct response and is further divided into two subsections. The first subsection clarifies the general intent; it contains two parts, the first of which is the direct clarification. Regarding the phrase "note:

etc.," since it states, "In the past, I and you did not see the Four Noble Truths," we know that both the Two Vehicles and Bodhisattvas all contemplate the Four Truths through the principle of dependent origination. Thus, by means of the Four Truths...

This is because the twelve links of dependent origination are merely differences in the expansion and contraction [of the four truths]. Furthermore, regarding the statement that "ordinary beings have suffering but no truth" and so forth, the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) states:
"The fourfold four-truths are the text from the 'Chapter on the Noble Practices' (*Ārya-caryā*) in the eleventh fascicle of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.

First, the eight sufferings are used to explain suffering, which refers to the suffering of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-duḥkha*). At the end of the section on the Truth of Suffering, it is distinguished by means of the four truths."

Ordinary beings possess suffering but lack the realization of the Truth; Śrāvakas possess both suffering and the Truth of Suffering (duḥkha-satya); Bodhisattvas understand suffering as being without suffering, and the same applies to the remaining three truths.
This constitutes the Bodhisattva of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) as distinguished from the Tripiṭaka Teaching (Sanzang).

First, regarding the first point, the truth of origination (samudaya-satya) is explained through the categories of wholesome and unwholesome craving, as well as the nine similes, which refers to the origination of arising and ceasing (shengmie-jí). This concludes the section on the truth of origination.
Briefly summarized according to the Four Noble Truths: ordinary beings have suffering but no Truth; those of the Two Vehicles have both suffering and the Truth of Suffering;
Bodhisattvas understand suffering as being without [inherent] suffering and possess the True Truth (satya). The same applies to the remaining three truths. The Commentary states:

"Since it was not stated that there is a 'True' [Truth] at the end of the previous section on the Truth of Suffering, we know this refers to the general [category]. Now, because it says 'the True,' and 'True' means ultimate reality (tattva), we know this refers specifically to the next [section]."
Furthermore, regarding the first kind of truth that is not sequential: this refers to the distinction between the Separate and Perfect [teachings] in contrast to the Tripitaka.
At the end of the section on the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), it simply states: "Because afflictions are severed upon seeing cessation, and because there is no affliction, it is eternal;

because it is the causal condition for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, it is called pure; because it is free from the twenty-five existences, it is called self. At the end of the section on the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), it simply states: "It is eternal, yet eternally non-existent."
In the passage concerning the unconditioned, conditioned, and so forth, at the conclusion of the discussion on cessation and the path, it simply states "the four virtues.

Since this is no longer being compared or contrasted with the Two Vehicles, we know that this is explained solely in terms of the Separate and Perfect [Teachings]. Were it not for this school’s perfect integration of the sūtra’s intent, how could the Buddha’s skillful and concise expressions be understood?
Even the subsequent passage regarding "inferior wisdom" and "middling wisdom" refers to these as the four types of the Four Noble Truths.

This is the explicit meaning (*vyañjana*). Later, based on Mañjuśrī’s questioning of the Buddha, there is a broad response concerning the seven kinds of two truths, followed by a detailed explanation of the one reality (*eka-tattva*), as found in the *Miaoxuan* (in extenso).
Next, regarding the reason for this, it says: "The two vehicles contemplate the finite Four Truths. "Finite" (*pramāṇa*) is also called "conditioned finitude" (*kṛta-pramāṇa*);
"finitude" refers to numerical measure, and "conditioned" refers to fabrication. When the two vehicles contemplate these truths, they do not attain the Dharma.
Because all further activities have been exhausted, it is called "attainment through action" (*kṛtābhisamaya*); because the Dharma has not been exhausted, it is limited.

The Bodhisattva is the opposite of this, and is therefore called "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) and also "without action" (*akṛta*). Although a Bodhisattva of sharp faculties differs from those of the Two Vehicles who possess dull faculties, they are nonetheless the same in their status as Bodhisattvas;
for this reason, it is said in general that the Bodhisattva contemplates both the measurable and the immeasurable. This is...
Based on the distinction between the "small" and the "great," one may differentiate between the finite and the infinite;

however, the infinite should be further opened up to clarify the distinct meanings of the Separate (Vyavasthāna) and Perfect (Samantabhadra) teachings, as explained in detail in the *Miaoxuan* and other texts. Furthermore, as previously explained regarding the meaning of the "infinite void":

for the Two Vehicles, the True Truth (*satyadharma*) is the finite void, whereas for Bodhisattvas, the Middle Way is the infinite void. Regarding the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), there are four types of sequential order.

The meaning can be understood by correlating it with the four teachings. Furthermore, regarding the subsequent section which clarifies the distinct intent: if one follows various texts, the teaching that this is a dharma exclusive to Bodhisattvas constitutes the Distinct Teaching (*bye-kye*, *pratyekabuddha*);
however, seeing Dīpaṃkara Buddha, attaining patience (*kṣānti*), and receiving a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) therein constitutes the Shared Teaching (*tong-kye*, *śrāvaka*).

According to the following passage, which clarifies the meaning of the sharp-facultied Bodhisattva’s realization of the emptiness of essence, this refers to the Perfect and Subtle [Teaching], wherein the three wisdoms are unified within a single mind; therefore, one must now...
Following the intent of the subsequent text, one should know that the next section is a concluding critique.

The passage beginning with "Although the followers of the two vehicles... clarifies the differences in the contemplative methods (*dhyāna-dharma*) of the three vehicles. This section is divided into two parts: first, the formal clarification; second, [the concluding critique]. The first part, the formal clarification, is further divided into two:

first, clarifying the differences in the contemplative methods of the two vehicles, which is itself divided into two: first, the general summary; second, the specific explanation. The first [of these] is the general heading. Next, the sound... [text continues].

Regarding the subsequent detailed explanation following the introductory section, the passage beginning with "Furthermore" clarifies the differences between the two vehicles and the bodhisattvas; this text is divided into two parts.
The first part, which clarifies the two vehicles as well as the bodhisattvas in general, is further divided into three sections.

First, a brief indication: the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) cultivate their own morality, concentration, and wisdom; they purify themselves through morality, discipline themselves through concentration, and deliver themselves through wisdom.
Furthermore, "disciplining oneself" is named according to the cause, whereas "delivering oneself" is spoken of from the perspective of the result.

Since Bodhisattvas act for the sake of sentient beings, this distinguishes them from the self-deliverance and other practices of the two vehicles. As for the "four equalities," these are the four immeasurables (brahmavihāra).

The immeasurables of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) are so called because they are immeasurable with respect to their objects; since these four objects are immeasurable, the mind is likewise without distinction or limit.
Because the mind is directed toward these four, they are called the "four immeasurables. As for the statement that they are all alike in "breaking down" phenomena (*dharmas*):

if one follows various texts and distinguishes between the Hīnayāna and Mahāyāna, then according to the Tripiṭaka teaching, it is merely the breaking down of phenomena, whereas the Mahāyāna gate is [the realization of] the essence (*tattva*).
In the following passage, Hōnen states that since the analysis of dharmas (*dharmapratibheda*) for Bodhisattvas is treated as being identical to that of the Two Vehicles, he further concludes:
"This is the Bodhisattva’s analytical realization of the two emptinesses of birth and dharmas. Is this not because the distinction is made in reference to the *satyagarbha* (the True Middle)?

Thus, the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*) are treated as being identical to the Two Vehicles in their analytical deconstruction of dharmas; furthermore, he summarizes this by concluding: "This is the Bodhisattva..."
Does the analysis of the two aspects of emptiness regarding produced phenomena not involve a distinction based on the "True" (the ultimate) and the "Middle"?

Therefore, using the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching as an analogy for the Two Vehicles' analytical dharma-emptiness (*prajñapti-śūnyatā*), assigning "substantial emptiness" (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) to the Bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching is because the three wisdoms of the Middle Way are unified within a single mind.

Thus, the subsequent passage rebukes various Mahayana masters, stating that although they speak of substantial emptiness, they still remain identical to the Lesser Vehicle; this refers precisely to this point.

It is because those Bodhisattvas of dull faculties in the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) employ only the wisdom of essence (*tihuì*) and are unable to realize emptiness, provisionality, and the middle within a single mind;
thus, the principle they realize is no different from that attained by the Small Vehicle through the analytical negation of dharmas (*zhèfǎ*).

Therefore, since the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching contemplate dharmas in the same manner as the two vehicles of the Tripitaka who analyze dharmas, one must know that the various passages concerning the "lesser Mahayana" cannot be conflated [with the higher teachings].
This is brought here to harmonize with the meaning of analyzing the substance.

Next, the following passage on the characteristics of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is presented in two parts. First, the passage clarifying the characteristics of contemplation by the Two Vehicles is divided into two sections.

First, the direct clarification, which is further divided into two. First, the clarification of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), which is further divided into two. First, the presentation of an analogy for the formation of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Sentient beings are like five fingers clenched into a fist. If there were a sentient being within a single aggregate (*skandha*), there would have to be five sentient beings;

just as one finger makes one fist, so too one aggregate would make five fists. If there is no sentient being within a single aggregate, then even though there are five, there is still none—just as if there is no fist in one finger, how could there be five?

Since their existence cannot be established, is this not the emptiness of living beings (*sattva-śūnyatā*)? Next, from "self" (*ātman*) and "person" (*pudgala*) downwards, [the text] applies this analogy.
Fearing that one might conceive of the *dharma* as existing apart from the aggregates (*skandha*), he further refutes this by stating that even seeking its origin, it cannot be found.

Although one seeks for a fist and so forth below, the text next clarifies the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). This section has two parts: first, clarifying the objective realm of the emptiness of phenomena; this, in turn, has two parts. First, he presents a simile.
Although, as stated above, the self and the person cannot be found when sought, the substantial reality of the five aggregates has not yet been forgotten; therefore, he provides the following simile:
Although one may seek a fist and fail to find it, this does not preclude the existence of the fingers, skin, and bone;

next, although one may seek a person, [the text] proceeds to the section on the "conformity with the Dharma" (合法), and next, the section on the two vehicles (二乘) explains the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (法空觀). This text is divided into two parts: first, distinguishing between attainment and failure.

Although one has attained the emptiness of persons (生空), one has not yet attained the emptiness of phenomena; therefore, it is said that there is still "failure. Thus, the *Miaoxuan* (妙玄) states: "The Three Piṭaka [teachings] contemplate persons..."

Having attained the Way through emptiness, one further contemplates the two objects of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of birth (*jāti-śūnyatā*), which are not yet fused. The *Śīkṣānanda Commentary* states:

"If the delusions of seeing (*darśana-heya-kleśa*) are destroyed, one receives the name of Srotāpanna; after attaining the emptiness of birth, one subsequently proceeds to sever the delusions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) and only then attains the emptiness of phenomena.

Next, the text below correctly clarifies the emptiness of phenomena, which is divided into two parts. The first part correctly clarifies it, and this is further divided into two: first, citing a metaphor to analyze [the point].
Regarding the five aggregates and the four great elements, they are without reality, just as when one strips away the skin, flesh, bone, and marrow of a finger, nothing can be found.

Next, the application of the analogy to the dharma is that mindfulness is precisely the mind; the mention of "feeling and perception" is abbreviated because the text is concise, omitting only "volitional formations.

Next, seeking [the essence] beneath the finger, the conclusion and demonstration is divided into two parts: first, concluding the analogy; second, from "seeking the dharma" onwards, concluding the dharma.
Since the subsequent [realization] cannot be attained, one then establishes the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*).

If one merely forgets the objects of arising phenomena but cannot forget the wisdom of the two kinds of emptiness, then although the clinging to essence (*svabhāva-grāha*) has been removed, the clinging to characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-grāha*) remains; therefore, both subject and object must be discarded together in order to realize the two kinds of emptiness.

Next, to clarify that the contemplation of the Shared Bodhisattva is likewise: this clarifies that the dull-facultied Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching employ only the emptiness of essence (*tǐkōng*) and do not perceive the Middle Way because they lack the three wisdoms in a single mind.
Thus, even at the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), they are criticized as being identical to the Two Vehicles' analytical method (*pīchàfǎ*).
However, if one distinguishes between the Small and Great Vehicles, it cannot be treated with such generality.
This constitutes the concluding summary of the three lower [vehicles]. Regarding the note "and so forth": although self and other differ, the analysis of dharmas is the same;

though they are the same in one respect, they differ in another. Therefore, the *zang* (Āgama) and *tong* (Vaipulya) [teachings] do not confuse their respective methods of analyzing and realizing the essence.

Next, regarding the discussion below that clarifies the distinct Bodhisattvas as being fundamentally different from those mentioned previously: the term "distinct" is used because they manifest a distinct principle by destroying distinct delusions.

However, this meaning of "destroying and manifesting" encompasses both the Separate (Pratyekabuddha) and Complete (Bodhisattva) teachings; although their paths differ, their realization of the Way is the same.

Furthermore, since it was previously established that those of dull faculties in the Shared Teaching are identical to the Two Vehicles through analytical contemplation, one must now [discuss] those of sharp faculties who perceive the Middle Way.

The three wisdoms within a single mind are termed "distinct" (bie), just as the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) classifies the teachings: the Shared Teaching (tongjiao) already implies the distinct, and the teaching that reveals the Perfect (yuan) while carrying the distinct is precisely this meaning.

This section is divided into three parts: first, a general explanation; second, a specific explanation following the phrase "as seen below"; and third, the text itself, which is further divided into three.
First, the text on the contemplation of emptiness (kongguan) consists of two parts. First, it presents a metaphor; here, the fist and fingers are used as a metaphor for birth.
"Phenomena are suspended" means they are hung or bound; forms arise in opposition to images as if merely hanging there. "Substance" refers to the physical entity.

A fist or finger within a mirror is empty space that is easy to understand; a fist or finger outside a mirror is empty space that is difficult to understand. By borrowing phenomena to match principles, one clarifies deluded sentiments;
thus, the easily understood emptiness of the image within a worldly mirror is used as a metaphor for the delusion outside the mirror.

The mind takes hold of emptiness—which is difficult to understand—and causes it to be as easy to understand; therefore it is said that since the fist and finger within the mirror are empty, the fist and finger outside the mirror are likewise not real.
Next, regarding the section on "the assembly," the text for harmonizing the dharma is divided into three parts. First, the formal harmonization:

"Originally empty by nature, not something made empty through investigation. This is spoken in terms of contemplating the principle of *tathatā* (suchness), employing the principle as the contemplation.

This contemplation on the non-duality of phenomena and emptiness is precisely the entry into emptiness through analytical investigation; the details of both the phenomenal and principled contemplations are fully explained in the *Yuan-tong-ji* (Record of Perfect Penetration) on the *Fen-pu-erh-men* (Gate of Non-duality), etc.
Next, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (*Dapin*) cites scriptural evidence: "The nature of the self is itself the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*);

the nature of form is itself the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Since both are stated to be "as such" (*tathatā*), how could they not be mutually identical? If the nature of form is thus, the same applies to the other four aggregates (*skandha*).

If one follows most texts, they frequently cite this as evidence that the essence of the Shared Teaching (Sādhāraṇa-yāna) is emptiness; however, the present text judges it to belong to the distinct Bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching (Pratyeka-bodhisattva).
Regarding the passage "In this life... and so forth, it uses the fruit to illustrate the cause. The five fruits refer to the present consciousness, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), and so on.

The two causes refer to past ignorance (*avidyā*) and formations (*saṃskāra*). "Arising from ignorance" refers to the production of the five fruits, which are the phenomena (*dharma*) that arise. If...

Following the preceding text, this should also state: "Since one cannot attain the objects of the two emptinesses—of persons and of phenomena—one likewise cannot attain the wisdom of the two emptinesses of persons and phenomena.
If it were not so, why would the subsequent text say: "Although one does not attain the two objects," and so forth?

Following the phrase "although one does not attain the two objects of persons and phenomena," the text clarifies the provisional contemplation (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*), stating that although one does not attain the two objects of persons and phenomena, one is nonetheless able to understand them clearly.
Regarding "thoroughly penetrating the two objects," this is the meaning of what the *Fuxing* (Subcommentary) describes as "though extinguished, yet existing.

Since the objects are thus, the wisdom is likewise so; because there is no error regarding the object or the wisdom, nor between the subjective and objective, it is called "clearly realized" (*liǎoliǎo*).

If it is already called "clearly realized," is it not the provisional contemplation (*jiaguān*) that distinguishes without error? Since one has clearly realized the object, one is not defiled by it; furthermore, one thoroughly penetrates the wisdom.

Thus, it is neither that which is purified, nor is it subsequent defilement or purification; below, the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*) is clarified as illuminating both simultaneously to manifest perfect fusion.
Therefore, its intent accords with the immeasurable and profoundly deep *dharmatā* of this sutra. Once the three virtues (*triguṇa*) are perfected, it is as the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"The adamantine treasure-store is obtained in its fullness. These three points constitute the concluding summary and demonstration.
Next, the refutation by the various Hīnayāna masters is divided into two parts. First, the refutation based on principle, which is further divided into two.

First, the refutation that the Great Vehicle is similar to externalists; this is found in the Four Teachings and the *Miaoxuan*, where such a refutation is made in full detail as cited previously by several scholars (and so forth).
Second, the refutation that the Great Vehicle is similar to the Small Vehicle, because a single essence of emptiness cannot, within a single mind, simultaneously be empty and provisional.

Because the Middle is thus identical to the Small, what is the reason? It is precisely because one cannot realize the provisional through emptiness; consequently, one lacks supernatural powers and cannot purify Buddha-lands.

Being unable to realize the Middle through the simultaneous identity of emptiness and the provisional, and failing to apply both negation and illumination, one is therefore unable to fully explain the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
If this were the case, how could the three wisdoms be attained within a single moment of mind, and how could the five eyes penetrate all things?

The *Ming juzu wumie* (Clarifying the Endowment of the Non-extinguishing) states that since one lacks these virtues, they are like those of the Lesser Vehicle who destroy dharmas, for they do not possess the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*) and so forth.
The *Zhiguan* says: "The nine contemplations have two types: first, those who destroy dharmas; second, those who do not destroy dharmas.

If one who destroys dharmas fully cultivates the nine contemplations, they seek only to sever suffering and burn away the skeleton, urgently seeking to attain the wisdom of the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*)."

In the liberation that does not delight in objective observation, since there is no skeleton to be observed, there is then no meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), transformations, or the knowledge of vows (*praṇidhijñāna*).

Regarding the "Crown of Meditation" (*mūrdha-dhyāna*), although it is said that [the body] is incinerated, in reality there is still a physical body present. If one is not a person of indestructible nature (*akṣayadharmin*), from the initial perception of bloating (*ādhmātaka-saṃjñā*) until the perception of bones (*asthi-saṃjñā*), one does not proceed to the perception of burning (*vidagdhaka-saṃjñā*).
Thus, one attains the flow of light, the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), and the cultivation of the refinements (*parikarma*) of meditation.
Regarding the phrase "cultivating the supernormal powers and transformations, all merits are perfected, and one attains both types of liberation":

the *Fuxing* (Commentary on Practice) explains that this refers to the "Culmination of Vow-Knowledge" (*praṇidhijñāna-śīrṣa-dhyāna*). This refers to those who destroy the Dharma and do not cultivate the liberations (*vimokṣa*) up to the "transcendental meditations" (*abhibhvāyatana*).

Because this transcendental meditation is the most supreme and lofty, it is called the "Culmination. Furthermore, because this meditation can transform longevity into merit and transform merit into longevity, it is called a "Vow."
Regarding "wisdom," the *Mahā-śāstra* states: "If one wishes to know the events of the three periods of time, one knows them immediately according to one's vow.

It is also called "non-contention" (*araṇā*) because it can prevent contention from arising in the minds of others. This transcendent dhyāna also possesses the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).

Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* says: "Taking a vow as the precursor, one brings forth sublime wisdom; because one understands things according to that vow, it is called 'vow-knowledge' (*praṇidhi-jñāna*). For details, see the *Dhyāna-mukha* [section] (etc.). (3)

The clear knowledge of past lives brings clear understanding of the suffering of the past, giving rise to great wearying detachment; the divine eye brings clear understanding of the suffering of the future, giving rise to great wearying detachment;
the clear knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows enables one to practice correct contemplation and sever all afflictions. The supernormal power of the body is merely a form of craftsmanship;
the divine ear is merely the hearing of sounds; the knowledge of others' minds merely takes the distinct thoughts of others as its object. This is so.

Therefore, these three can only be considered *abhijñā* (supernormal knowledges) and cannot be considered *vidyā* (clear insights); the other three are both *vidyā* and *abhijñā*. If that is so, what is the distinction between *abhijñā* and *vidyā*?
Answer: Directly knowing the past is called *abhijñā*; knowing the causes, conditions, karmic actions, and deeds of the past is called *vidyā*.

Directly seeing death here and birth there is called *abhijñā*; knowing the convergence of causes, conditions, and circumstances is called *vidyā*. Directly stating the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*) is [the third *vidyā*].
The name "Knowledge" (*vidyā*) refers to the thorough understanding of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), such that one is no longer subject to rebirth;
this is termed "clarity. Next, according to the text below in this sutra, among the words used to exclude [other meanings], the term "head and axis" (*shouxu*) refers to the beginning and the end.

The "Introductory Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*) constitutes the beginning, and the "Praise of the Buddha" constitutes the end. Since this work consists of four fascicles bound together by a wooden axis, the axis is thus used to represent the very conclusion.
Nor is there any need for revision; how could one possibly employ the substance of a Mahāyāna master?

If we follow the previous refutation of the various Hīnayāna masters—wherein their teaching of "emptiness through analysis" is shown to be identical to that of the non-Buddhists—and the various Mahāyāna masters—wherein their teaching of "emptiness as substance" is shown to be identical to the Lesser Vehicle—it is evident that this sentence is merely a redundant interpolation.

Next, following the sequential explanation of the text, there are two parts. First, the explanation of the passage on the cultivation of the two emptinesses regarding phenomena and persons (*dharma-pudgala-śūnyatā*) has two sections.

First, the explanation of the passage clarifying the two emptinesses regarding phenomena and persons in relation to suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*) has two sections. First, the explanation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). This, in turn, has two parts: first, the division of the text;
second, the explanation of the text beginning with "O virtuous daughter," which has three parts. First, the explanation of the passage exhorting [the listener] in response to suffering.
Second, the initial explanation of "good daughter" (kuladuhitṛ) is further divided into two parts. First, the direct explanation of the text is divided into four sections:

first, regarding the world (*loka*), which refers to both the speaker and the addressed, as well as the inclusion of others, thus belonging to the world; second, regarding persons (*pudgala*), specifically the assembly of men below;
third, regarding the remedy (*pratipakṣa*), specifically the Buddha below; and fourth, regarding the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*), where the Bodhi tree is itself enlightenment (*bodhi*).
This is the section on the sequential indication following the title; next is the explanation of what should be contemplated.

Next is the explanation of the passage pointing back to the aforementioned object, which is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of "all dharmas," and second, the explanation of the phrase "thus. This second part is further divided into two:

first, a general explanation, and second, the specific clarification that "thus" refers to the general contemplation. That is to say, the two characters "thus" (evam) collectively encompass the three contemplations.
The object of contemplation consists of phenomena (*dharma*), which is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), and principle (*tattva*), which is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

That which is neither phenomenon nor principle is the Middle Way, the Truth of the Supreme Meaning (*paramārtha-satya*). [In the phrase] "neither phenomenon nor principle," the word "principle" (*li*) is omitted below;

next, the section beginning with "as with phenomena" provides a detailed explanation, which is further divided into two parts. First, the direct explanation: it states that the "non-existence of both phenomena and dharmas" refers to what was previously called "contemplation."

The sixteenth [view] is the contemplation of non-self, wherein the five aggregates are seen as non-existent dharmas; the dual negation of both phenomenon and principle is precisely the *dharmatā* and the *dharmakāya*.

Next, furthermore, regarding the integration of phenomena and so forth: since these are taken collectively, they are neither identical nor different; yet because individual phenomena are distinct, they are likewise both identical and different.

Third, the correct explanation of the contemplation: although these four phrases do not transcend the three contemplations—since the first two phrases constitute the contemplation of emptiness—they are now divided into four according to the method of the respective phrases. The preceding passage states: "If this body before one's eyes is false and illusory, and the body is already false and illusory, where is the person?

The following sections all employ the term "pointing out" (*diǎnchū*), which refers specifically to pointing out the characteristics of the three contemplations (*sānguān*). explains that sentient beings (*zhòngshēng*) are likewise [non-existent], asking: "Where could there be sentient beings? Third, the explanation of the fundamental [nature].

Next, "if one knows" and below, this explains the arising of the disease and the emergence of the medicine by means of the dissolution of the object and the disappearance of the contemplation. For the time being, one may distinguish them as follows:

the essence is fundamentally tranquil; so how could the medicine be applied? It is like speaking of emptiness in response to flowers; even the "empty flowers" cannot be found, let alone the emptiness itself.
How could there be a name such as this that so clearly manifests ultimate purity? It is like space: one does not call it "great space" merely because of a small space.

Because it does not arise from inference and is thus dull and sluggish—since this is true for all sentient beings without exception—as detailed in the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* cited in the supplementary notes to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (etcetera).

Regarding those who give rise to notions of "self" and so forth within suchness, these are the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*), beginning with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

Next, in the passage beginning with "Even if," the superior is used to illustrate the inferior; as the *Zhiguan* (Cessation and Contemplation) says: "It is like the Long-nailed One (*Dīrghanakha*) and others, who were profoundly attached to the heterodox paths."
It has not yet escaped being called a fallacy; how so? The *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states:

How much less so for others who are dull-witted and merely respond to questions as they arise? As for the term "long-nailed one": [it refers to the aforementioned individual].

Therefore, it is said that by performing twenty kinds of contemplation, one eliminates substantial delusions; this means eliminating delusions regarding substantial phenomena.

This refers to the arising of attachment; "subduing craving" means subduing discursive thought (*vitarka*). While the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) have not yet been eliminated, one is able to subdue discursive thought regarding the attachment to provisional names (*prajñapti*).
Furthermore, one proceeds to enter into the conceptualization of a self within real dharmas (*dharmatā*).

[The following applies to] the five aggregates (*skandha*). (And so forth. As for the "inchworm," it refers to the silkworm. The *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it is an insect that contracts and extends.

The *Xici* of the *I Ching* says: "The inchworm contracts itself in order to seek extension. Therefore, the Great Scripture says: "It is like the inchworm, which must rely on its front legs to move forward."
Because the hind foot is moved, it is a metaphor for abandoning one thing and taking up another. Regarding the necessity of further performing twenty kinds of contemplations upon the real dharmas:

since one has already reckoned "self" within the five aggregates as real dharmas, and further gives rise to the four attachments—existence and so forth—based on these, the "self" arises in relation to the five aggregates;

Next, the explanation of the passage on the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) is divided into two parts: first, the introduction of the intent and the division of the text; second, the word-by-word commentary on the meaning of the text. Regarding the first part, the introduction of the intent and the division of the text:

the statement that one who attains realization through the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) simultaneously realizes the emptiness of phenomena is as stated in the preceding text: "In the Mahāyāna, it is clarified that the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) inherently includes [the view of phenomena]," and so forth.

For example, the three meanings of the emptiness of persons refer to what was previously called "pointing out the contemplation of principle" (*li-guan*), and so forth. Next is the word-by-word commentary on the meaning of the text.

Regarding the first of the three [sections], the correct explanation of the text, there are two parts: first, the correct explanation itself; second, the exhortation to believe. Regarding the first of these, there are three parts.

First, the explanation of the contemplation that phenomena are empty while they are functioning (*pratītyasamutpāda*). This section has four parts. First, the general explanation: among the five aggregates (*skandha*), one first contemplates the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*);

therefore, it says "the various great elements," which refers to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). By analogy, the four mental factors such as sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth are likewise found to be unobtainable. If, next, regarding the four great elements... [text continues].

In the *Pṛthakvyākhyāna* (Separate Explanation), it says: "Regarding 'the earth element maintains solidity,' etc.: Earth is the cause of the substantiality [of solidity] among all things that are produced.

Although what is established has no inherent existence (*abhāva*), sentient beings conceptually grasp it as existent; this very existence is solidity. Therefore, one gives rise to emotional attachment (*saṃjñā-abhiniveśa*) toward the earth element as being solid.
Now, by relying on the substantiality of the object to refute the solidity of the emotion, the refutation states: 'It should not move or be warm; for movement is wind, and warmth is fire.'"

Where does this nature of great solidity reside? Once the solidity of earth has been thus deconstructed, the other three elements may be understood by analogy. Solid ice is earth; the movement of waves is wind; charcoal fire is indeed true [solidity], for it is also solid, and its flickering flames are also movement. That which can support things belongs to earth; that which stops upon hitting a wall is water. Third, citing the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra* as proof: The Buddha told Ānanda: "If you wish to see Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, you must first purify your mind. If you do not purify your mind, you will not see him. If you purify your mind, you will see him. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva’s body is made of pure light. If your mind is impure, you cannot see him. If your mind is pure, you will see him. Furthermore, Ānanda, if you wish to see Avalokiteśvara, you should contemplate the nature of all phenomena. What is the nature of all phenomena? It is the nature of emptiness. What is the nature of emptiness? It is the nature of non-arising. What is the nature of non-arising? It is the nature of non-extinction. What is the nature of non-extinction? It is the nature of the Middle Way. What is the nature of the Middle Way? It is the nature of the Dharma-realm. What is the nature of the Dharma-realm? It is the nature of the Tathāgata. What is the nature of the Tathāgata? It is the nature of liberation. What is the nature of liberation? It is the nature of ultimate reality. What is the nature of ultimate reality? It is the nature of the unconditioned. What is the nature of the unconditioned? It is the nature of the ungraspable. What is the nature of the ungraspable? It is the nature of the ineffable. What is the nature of the ineffable? It is the nature of the inconceivable. What is the nature of the inconceivable? It is the nature of the unobtainable. What is the nature of the unobtainable? It is the nature of the Tathāgata. Therefore, Ānanda, if you wish to see Avalokiteśvara, you must contemplate the nature of the Tathāgata. This passage demonstrates that the essence of all phenomena is ultimately the nature of the Tathāgata, which is beyond conceptualization and grasping.

Thus, the solidity of earth, the movement of wind, and the nature of fire are all manifestations of this single, fundamental reality. When one realizes this, the deluded attachments to the solidity of the four elements are naturally dismantled. This is the profound meaning of the *Avalokiteśvara-sūtra*.
Regarding the phrase "the limit of reality" (*tathatā*) mentioned therein, the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) is precisely ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).

In the *Fuxingzhuan* (Commentary on the *Mohe zhiguan*), under the section "Following One’s Own Intent," it also cites the *Pumenpin* (Universal Gate Chapter) and the refutation of the solidity of the earth, etc., to explain that both nature and characteristics are empty.

Thus, it says: "There are four phrases for not abiding: [not abiding] in mere emptiness; nor abiding in the absence of the four phrases; nor abiding in the ineffable [which refers to the emptiness of characteristics]."

Furthermore, if one summarizes [the truth] according to the Four Noble Truths and the Five Aggregates: the nature of suffering is grasped as the origin (*samudaya*), the observation of phenomena is the path (*mārga*), and the limit is cessation (*nirodha*).

Therefore, the preceding section clarifies the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths as common to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Since it has already been explained that within the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) there are both the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), one should know by analogy that the same two types of emptiness—of nature and of characteristics—are likewise taught regarding the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Thus, the "Pervasive Destruction of Phenomena" in the *Zhiguan* [is established].
The middle [section] states: "Seeking for a self or a person within the nature and characteristics [of phenomena] such that they cannot be found is called the emptiness of persons;

seeking for the aggregates (skandhas) and sense bases (āyatanas) within the nature and characteristics [of phenomena] such that they cannot be found is called the emptiness of dharmas. However, in the present text, according to the principle of "following one's own intention," one seeks the nature and characteristics within the aggregates and sense bases and finds them unobtainable;

whereas in the "Pervasive Destruction of Dharmas" (Pó fǎ biàn), one seeks the aggregates and sense bases within the nature and characteristics and finds them unobtainable. Therefore, we know [this distinction].

When neither nature (*svabhāva*) nor characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) can be apprehended, one then establishes the two emptinesses of arising phenomena (*dharma*) and persons (*pudgala*). That arising phenomena cannot be apprehended is precisely because both nature and characteristics are empty.

If people do not perceive this, they will claim that the emptiness of persons and phenomena and the emptiness of nature and characteristics are entirely distinct and separate; this is profoundly incorrect.
Above, one examines the emptiness of persons; below, there are four examples; finally, one concludes and demonstrates.

Next, the explanation of "the contemplation that phenomena are neither empty nor provisional" begins with the first [point]: "principle is identical to phenomena. Regarding the second point, "the two extremes are principle":

Next, the explanation of the passage clarifying the two types of emptiness—of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*)—through the twelve links of dependent origination is divided into three parts. First, the text analyzes the divisions and indicates the intent;

Furthermore, conventional designations exist by virtue of deluded thought; since deluded thought is itself ignorance (*avidyā*), conventional designations are thus ignorance, which is the sphere of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
Again, citing the *Śāstra* (Vyākhyā), it says: "Who is it that ages and dies? It is 'I'.

If there were no "who" who ages and dies, then the self, the person, and sentient beings would be empty—this is the sphere of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). To provide scriptural proof for this, it quotes: "Aging and death, sorrow..."

Regarding "affliction" (*daurmanasya*): because it is expressed by a single term as "old age and death, sorrow, and affliction," and does not refer to the provisional designations of self, person, or sentient being, we know that this is the sphere of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

Furthermore, the meaning of the *Śāstra* (the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*) can be understood through its citation: if there were no such thing as old age and death, that would be the emptiness of phenomena.
Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* cites the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, stating that the twelve links of dependent origination proceed from ignorance (*avidyā*) up to old age and death.
Regarding death, if someone says "this is old age and death," or asks "who is it that grows old and dies," both give rise to false views; this applies equally to everything down to ignorance.
If one says there is no one who grows old and dies, know that this is false; this is called the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
If one says there is no such thing as old age and death, know that this is false; this is called the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*); this applies equally to everything down to ignorance.

In that sutra, while the Buddha was staying in the village of Govinda, he addressed the bhikṣus on what is good in the beginning, middle, and end, even unto the purity of the holy life—namely, the Mahāsuññata Sutta. If someone were to ask: "To whom does this aging-and-death belong?
To whom does it pertain? one would say: "I am aging-and-death; now aging-and-death pertains to me; aging-and-death is mine. If, however, ignorance is abandoned...
That which gives rise to ignorance—whom does that aging and death belong to? When aging and death are severed, their root is cut; thus ignorance ceases.
When ignorance ceases, the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) cease. Because it possesses both kinds of emptiness, it is called "Great Emptiness" (*mahāśūnyatā*).

Therefore, one should know that the emptiness of the Lesser Vehicle regarding "mine" is called the "emptiness of phenomena" (*dharma-śūnyatā*), while its emptiness regarding the person is called the "emptiness of sentient beings" (*sattva-śūnyatā*). As for the Bodhisattvas...

To claim that emptiness, nirvana, and the Buddha-dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges constitute "emptiness of phenomena" (dharmashūnyatā) is a view held by some who say that the Hinayana does not clarify the emptiness of phenomena and has not understood the intent of the sutras;

even if there were sincere teachings stating that śrāvakas attain only the emptiness of persons (pudgalashūnyatā), such words of granting and withholding are merely concessions made to the Bodhisattvas.
Now, following the twelve [links], the next section clarifies the differences in the causal conditions (*nidāna*). This text is divided into two parts:

afflictions are the cause and condition for karma; karma is the cause and condition for suffering; and suffering is the cause and condition for further suffering.

Because they thus revolve and act as mutual causes and conditions, this is called the twelve links of dependent origination across the three periods of time. As for the twelve links of dependent origination regarding retribution, it is based on—
Regarding the two periods of the present and future, as explained in detail in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra*, ignorance (*avidyā*) is distinguished from the stage of the embryo (*kalala*).
Thus, it is said that the first ten links of dependent origination belong to the present, while the final two links belong to the future;

Third (and so forth): Regarding the twelve links of dependent origination within a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), this refers to the fact that within a single lifetime, as soon as a single thought arises, it is already complete with the twelve links.

these points follow the same structure as the three contemplations in the preceding text.
