Thus, through the clear observation of the twelve links of dependent origination, the three [contemplations] are established.

The Buddha-nature has both universal and specific aspects. Universally, it refers to the true principle of *tathatā* within the twelve links of dependent origination, which is the nature of the direct cause (*hetu-hetu*);
wisdom is the nature of the revealing cause (*parijñā-hetu*). The full possession of all practices is the nature of the contributing cause (*pratyaya-hetu*).

If viewed specifically, ignorance, craving, and grasping are the nature of the revealing cause; volitional formations and existence are the nature of the contributing cause; and consciousness and the other links are likewise [the nature of the direct cause].
The seven limbs are the primary causes; while specific contemplation involves taking up the meaning of opposition, universal contemplation is based on the principle of pervasiveness.

Since it is thus that the twelve links of dependent origination are manifested as the three Buddha-natures, how could it not be so when these very twelve links of dependent origination serve as the contemplating subject?
Following this general sense, one therefore employs the various sufferings [to contemplate].
To practice the Middle Way as something inconceivable is to be neither empty nor existent. That "birth and death have no limit" means they have no boundaries;
because birth and death are themselves the Dharma-realm of the Middle Way, they have no boundaries.
Furthermore, it is not only that there is no prior limit to birth and death, but also that there is no subsequent limit to nirvana; therefore, it is called "limitless. Thus, it is...
The severance of the prior and subsequent limits while the cycle of rebirth continues without rest refers to the twelve links of dependent origination, which are like a wheel.

Because a wheel must necessarily revolve, and because this revolving never ceases, there is no passing away or transformation. Thus, the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "The characteristics of the world are eternally abiding.

The *Wenju ji* (Commentary on the Words and Phrases) explains: "The state of sentient beings’ awakening and their deluded positions are non-dual; to manifest delusion is itself the principle, and that principle is eternally abiding. This is the Buddha.
Based on worldly cultivation, one realizes through ultimate reasoning that this principle has existed in the world from the beginning; therefore, it is said to be "eternally abiding" (*nitya*).

Furthermore, the designation "world" (*loka*) applies to both the defiled and the pure causes and effects. For now, following the perspective of awakening to reveal delusion, and using the pure to reveal the defiled:

while the awakening to the pure constitutes the actualization of the eternal reality, deluded attachment to the defiled merely bears the name of the "eternal principle. Thus, it is called the "characteristic of the world" (*loka-lakṣaṇa*).

"Permanently abiding" (*nitya*). Next, the two lines clarify the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*): since both are said to be "non-existent," they belong to the contemplation of emptiness.

"Arising" refers to sentient beings as mere provisional designations (*prajñapti*), and thus there is fundamentally no arising; this is the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). "Combination" refers to the combination of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and thus there is also no combination;
this is the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). The former refers to the past, while the present refers to the latter.

Furthermore, regarding "unwholesome reflection" (*ayoniśomanasikāra*), it exists separately within the category of "formative action" (*saṃskāra*) and is also pervasive across both afflictions and karma—as noted in the commentary.

Since this is the case for unwholesome reflection, the same principle applies by analogy to all mental formations (*citta-saṃskāra*). Moreover, the detailed meaning of the three contemplations has already been explained above;
here, I shall briefly indicate their names merely to enable the student to synthesize the preceding intent in order to clarify the present text. Next, although they are named...

Thus, the preceding text states: "The clear exposition of the three contemplations exists within the sutras; how could one not believe them?"

Next, for the sake of the lower capacity, the text is presented again in two parts. First, a brief indication of the characteristics of the contemplation of emptiness, which consists of three sections.

First, the heading; second, "If one calls it a 'provisional name'"; third, the detailed explanation. This last section consists of two parts. First, a horizontal examination of the four natures in relation to one another—hence it is called "horizontal.

This also refutes the attachment to the other-arising of conventional designations. Whether through combination or separation, these points can be understood according to the text.

Since one examines the four modes of being (*catuskoṭi*) and finds that conventional designations cannot be established, it is said: "Present conventional designations possess only names; these names do not exist within."

since this is accomplished by the single phrase "because it is unobtainable," the two emptinesses of nature and characteristics constitute the non-abiding in the four propositions.
There is no abiding in the four propositions. Next, in observing real dharmas, the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā) is clarified.

Among the five factors of the present fruit, "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa) belongs to the second member. This consists of the four aggregates; when contrasted with the aggregate of form, these constitute the five aggregates.

Therefore, by examining name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) in relation to karma, one sees that in reality name-and-form arises spontaneously and should not depend upon karmic action;

this refutes the attachment to the self-arising of substantial dharmas. because of the emptiness of living beings, phenomena (*dharma*) are also empty. Therefore, the preceding text states: "Since names are merely provisional designations, phenomena are also not substantial entities.

This is because, within the contemplation of breaking through merit, the three contemplations—both horizontal and vertical—break through the three delusions;
that is, the three contemplations sweep away attachment to the reality of phenomena (*dharmas*).

Next, the explanation of the passage on the accomplishment of the fruit and the arising of its function is divided into two parts: first, the analysis of the text; second, from "All those who hold views" onwards, the explanation of the meaning, which is further divided into two.

First, the explanation of the accomplishment of one's own practice, which is again divided into two. First, the explanation of the fulfillment of the virtue of wisdom, which is again divided into two.

First, the explanation of the accomplishment of the contemplation of the two emptinesses of birth and phenomena, which is again divided into two. First, the formal explanation, which is again divided into two. First, the explanation of birth...

Since the accomplishment of the contemplation of emptiness regarding sentient beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) involves the destruction of the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), one knows that the severing of the fetters of various views and so forth constitutes the accomplishment of the contemplation of emptiness regarding sentient beings.
Next, the section beginning with "by means of wisdom" explains the accomplishment of the contemplation of emptiness regarding phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*). Regarding the upper and lower metaphors:

because the metaphor of the sword lies between the severing of views and the tearing of the net, one knows that the upper metaphor represents the severing of views and the lower metaphor represents [the subsequent stage].

Regarding the separate clarification of the ten *paryavasthānas* (entanglements) in the context of abandoning the afflictions (*kleśa*), they are explained separately from the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).

Therefore, in various treatises, eighty-eight delusions of view, plus the ten entanglements and the ten types of discursive thought (*vitarka*), constitute the one hundred and eight afflictions. Thus, the *Abhidharmakośa* states:

"The eight entanglements are shamelessness (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), envy (*īrṣyā*), avarice (*mātsarya*), along with regret (*kaukṛtya*), sleep (*middha*), and restlessness (*auddhatya*)."

Torpor (*styāna*) consists of ten [afflictions], while anger (*krodha*) and concealment (*mrakṣa*) are common to all ten secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). These ten secondary afflictions pervade the three realms;
this is because the ten modes of thought (*daśa-cintā*) of the three realms are also termed the "ten proclivities" (*daśānuśaya*).

Since it is stated above that the former is an analogy for severing wrong views and the latter is an analogy for severing afflictions (*kleśa*), we know that afflictions pervade the ten proclivities and the delusions of thought. *Lājñā* (or *lāguḍa*) refers to a bird-net.
What is called "lao-jian" (羅罥) means to hang or to bind and capture; it refers to a net spread to catch wild beasts.

Regarding the text that distinguishes and indicates what is severed by the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), there are two parts: first, the distinction between what is severed by the two vehicles and the bodhisattvas.

"Common delusions" (*tong-huo*) refer to the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and afflictions (*kleśa*). "Specific delusions" (*bie-huo*) refer to specific views and specific entanglements (*paryavasthāna*). "Specific views and entanglements" refer to specific delusions.

"Separate delusions" refers to ignorance, specifically associated ignorance; this is explained from the perspective of one's own practice (*sva-caryā*), for such practice consists solely of abiding in emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

If one includes the transformation of others (*parārtha*), separate delusions then encompass both internal and external "dust-sands" (*reṇu-vāluka*), because these dust-sands obstruct the path of transformation.
Regarding the statement that one is "attached to flowers" due to not having severed separate views, Zhiyi of the Four Clarities said:

When Kāśyapa heard the sound, he was unsettled; this refers to the afflictions of thought (*cintā-kleśa*) within the same substance. Śāriputra’s removal of the flower refers to the *dhūli-rajas* (dust-like) habitual tendencies outside the realms.
Xiachuan refutes this, saying: "Śāriputra was precisely defiled by the objects of form (*rūpa-viṣaya*) outside the realms;
how could these not be afflictions of thought? Now I say: Xiachuan merely adheres to one side and labels them afflictions of thought. This is what Siming established as the *dhūli-rajas* fetters.
Regarding the practice of having no teaching to rely upon: the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-ṭīkā* states that the followers of the Two Vehicles loathe the five desires of the world and seek nirvana;

thus, their minds harbor notions of acceptance and rejection. Now, seeing that the Bodhisattvas' retribution also involves the five aggregates and five desires, they likewise deem them improper and attempt to abandon and reject them, yet they cannot do so.
The celestial maiden, using a mind free from discrimination, confounds them by returning [their own logic].
The non-discriminating mind scatters the flowers of the non-discriminating minds of all bodhisattvas, so that they do not adhere.
Yet Śāriputra and others discriminate between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa as being different; this discrimination is precisely a biased view (*bhinna-dṛṣṭi*). Furthermore, it is said:
"If one discriminates within the Buddha-dharma, that is not in accordance with the Dharma. Since there is discrimination, it is a delusion of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). Moreover—
It is said that because habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have not yet been exhausted, flowers adhere to the body; thus, there are still afflictions of thought (*kleśa*). Furthermore, it was asked:

"In this sutra, it is stated that because habitual tendencies have not been exhausted, flowers adhere to the body. How does this relate to the 'separate afflictions' (*pṛthag-kleśa*)? The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"What is called 'habitual tendencies' (*vāsanā*) in the Śrāvaka sūtras is called 'fundamental proclivities' (*anuśaya*) in the Mahāyāna; these are precisely the separate afflictions. It was further asked: "Are these definitely the separate fetters (*pṛthag-saṃyojana*)?"

Question: Is that which has not yet been severed the habit-energy (*vāsanā*) of the universal fetters? Answer: If one refers to the Shared Teaching (*paryāya-yāna*), it is like Kāśyapa, for whom this is habit-energy.

If one refers to the Distinct Teaching (*bheda-yāna*), it is because the distinct fetters have not yet been severed, and thus habit-energy remains. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains, there are two kinds of fetters and proclivities (*saṃyojana-anuśaya*):
first, those severed by the Śrāvakas; second, those not shared with the Śrāvakas. Regarding these, Kāśyapa has already severed the shared ones, but as for the unshared ones—
Kāśyapa had not yet severed [the afflictions]; since this sutra clarifies the inconceivable liberation, it specifically employs the Separate and Complete [teachings] for severance.
However, the absence of explicit textual statements in the sutra is because the Vaipulya teachings still retain elements of expedient means, unlike the Lotus Sutra.

Next, regarding the following passage which demonstrates what is severed at the stage of Buddhahood, the text is divided into three parts. First, it correctly clarifies that both the general and specific ultimate exhaustions reside in the Buddha:

because the internal and external *censa* (sands-of-the-Ganges) obstructions to the *tathāgatagarbha*, the general and specific obstructions of *darśana-heya* and *bhāvanā-heya* to the *paramārtha-śūnyatā*, and the fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*) obstructing the *paramārtha-tattva*—since the fruit of Buddhahood is the perfect illumination of the three truths, these are all exhausted.

Having understood that the three delusions have been fundamentally severed, although this current text mentions only the exhaustion of the general and specific *dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana* (view-afflictions), its actual meaning encompasses the simultaneous disappearance of all three delusions;

this is because the two types of emptiness—of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*)—pervade the three contemplations. Next, regarding the intent of the commentary’s citation of scriptural evidence below:
the ten dharma-realms are collectively termed "persons and phenomena," and the supreme, provisional, and real stages of Buddhahood are the ground of the Buddhas.
If one is not deluded, is this not the birth of dharmas within the Buddha-realm? Yet these dharmas are unobtainable; if it were otherwise, how could they be called the "two emptinesses"?

Since even the dharmas born within the Buddha-realm cannot be obtained, how much less so those of the nine realms? Thus, when all ten realms are empty, both birth and dharmas are extinguished—this is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

If one points to emptiness to discuss the provisional (*prajñapti*), then the three thousand [realms] are perfectly manifest. If emptiness and the provisional are identical with the Middle Way (*madhyamā pratipad*), then...

If the two extremes are not established and the Middle Way illuminates both simultaneously, then emptiness and the provisional coexist; this is what is meant by the "fusion and subtlety" of the three contemplations.
Regarding the convergence of differing interpretations in the sutras and śāstras below, the text is divided into two parts: first, an account of the differences between the sutras and śāstras.

[It states that] wisdom is termed "uppermost" because it is ultimate, while delusion is termed "lowest of the low" because it is severed first; furthermore, the power of ignorance is great, and so forth.
This explains that the Buddha’s supreme wisdom (*anuttara-jñāna*) eliminates the lowest grade of delusions. In the *Daben* (Great Root) section of the *Four Teachings*, it is asked:
"The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states that the power of the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*) is the greatest; what is it that can eliminate it? Is it the Buddha's bodhi-wisdom? The answer is:

"If one distinguishes between the separate and the combined teachings, then the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*) constitute the Buddha's bodhi-wisdom. Why is this so? As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "The ninth stage is called... [and so forth].

Hearing and seeing the names of the Ten Abodes is called "seeing with the eyes"; although one sees the Buddha-nature therein, it is not clear or distinct because the path of non-obstruction coexists with delusions, and thus it is not clear or distinct.
The Buddhas and Tathāgatas see it clearly; this is true liberation, transcendent and beyond all burdens.
If one abides in the stages of the Separate and Perfect [Teachings], one can then employ the wisdom of the Buddha’s Bodhi to sever the first grade of afflictions.

From the stage of *vidyā* (clear understanding) up until the final thought-moment before equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), [afflictions] are finally severed and exhausted. Yet, this present text states that "both the active afflictions (*vāsana*) and the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are completely exhausted, leaving nothing remaining.

If this is understood according to the Separate and Shared [Teachings], it may be known as explained above. If understood according to the Separate and Perfect [Teachings], from the first ground (*bhūmi*) and the first dwelling (*vihāra*), it is as cited in the *Zhi guan* from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
"At the very moment of first generating the mind of awakening, both the active afflictions and the latent tendencies are simultaneously and entirely exhausted."
There are those outside the realm whose correct habits (*vāsanā*) are not yet exhausted; these are simply those within the realm for whom the correct habits are exhausted.

Because one cuts off the views (*dṛṣṭi*) through the first faith, cuts off the thoughts (*saṃskāra*) from the second to the seventh faith, and cuts off the habits from the eighth to the tenth faith—exhausting them all—one looks back from the initial realization of the First Abode (*prathamabhūmi*) toward the ten faiths, and thus it is said that "correct [afflictions] and habits are both exhausted.
If this is discussed in relation to Equal Enlightenment (*samāpatti*), it is as stated in the preceding text:
If one enters the ninth stage of the pure and purified dhyāna, all afflictions—both general and specific, as well as their residual habits—are completely exhausted.
Regarding the statement that there are "those with something above them" (*sopadhiśeṣa*) and so forth, the *Great Text on the Four Teachings* asks:

"Is it by employing the diamond-like wisdom (*vajra-jñāna*) that one severs ignorance, or is it by employing wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*) that one severs ignorance? The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* replies: "That which has something to be severed is called 'having something above it.'"
A person who has nothing further to sever is called the Unsurpassed Person (and so forth). Next, this refers to the lower [level], which integrates [the teachings] according to the *siddhānta*.
Regarding the note "and so forth": one should take the four *siddhāntas* and correlate them with the person, the time, the country, and the awakening;
by interpreting the meaning according to these four perspectives, it should likewise be understood that they accord with the four intentions.

The text "Realizing there is neither superior nor inferior" next explains the fulfillment of the qualities of birth (*jāti-dharma*); the full passage regarding the primary and auxiliary paths can likewise be seen therein.
The section beginning with "Opening the gate of the nectar of immortality" next explains the fulfillment of the qualities of cessation (*nirodha-guṇa*). This is divided into two parts:

first, the direct explanation of long life, physical security, great strength, and the radiance of the body, which are presented in sequence as metaphors for permanence (*nitya*), bliss (*sukha*), self (*ātman*), and purity (*śubha*); these can be understood by reflecting upon them. However, following this, [the text] proceeds to correlate...

The *Fahua wenju* (Textual Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) states that there are four [interpretations], the first corresponding to the various stages in the *Avataṃsaka*, and the second corresponding to the four wisdoms in the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Regarding the note "and so forth," the *Fahua wenju* says: "Second, regarding the four wisdoms: we now wish to correlate the four wisdoms of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) with the four stages;

this is not like the explanation of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*) within the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Furthermore, the *Zhi guan* (Stopping and Contemplation) says: "The four wisdoms are as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*."

Regarding the explanations of *mārgajñatā* (path-knowledge), *mārgākārajñatā* (knowledge of the aspects of the path), *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), and *sarvākārajñatā* (knowledge of all aspects), there are several interpretations.

Some say that within the causal stage (*hetu*), there exists only the essential nature of principle, which is termed *mārgajñatā* and *mārgākārajñatā*; whereas at the resultant stage (*phala*), when both phenomena and principle are fully perfected, it is termed *sarvajñatā* and *sarvākārajñatā*.
Others say that within the causal stage, the provisional and the real are termed *mārgajñatā* and *mārgākārajñatā*, while upon entering [the resultant stage]...

Emptiness is the wisdom of reality (*bhūtajñāna*), while entering into the conventional is the wisdom of skillful means (*upāyajñāna*). Some say that the names "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*) and "knowledge of all modes" (*sarvākārajñatā*) refer to the provisional and the real on the level of the fruit:
directly taking the Middle Way as its object is called all-knowledge, while simultaneously illuminating both truths is called knowledge of all modes.

Others say that these refer to the general and the specific within the cause, or the general and the specific within the fruit. Still others say that the wisdom of the path (*mārgajñatā*) and the wisdom of the aspects (*ākārajñatā*) are the single exposition of the provisional.

In truth, the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*) and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) are further clarifications of the provisional and the real; such are the various explanations of the four wisdoms.

Although there are these various differing interpretations, for the time being, they are annotated as "and so forth" (*yathā-vistara*) in relation to the opening of the ambrosia (*amṛta*) and other such matters.

Third, in relation to the sequence of "opening, showing, awakening, and entering" (*vivaraṇa-darśana-avabodha-praveśa*) from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it may be seen according to the text. Fourth, in relation to... [text ends].

Regarding the explanation of the four virtues of *nirvāṇa* as previously interpreted, the phrase "referring to the direct explanation of the text" indicates that the main commentary provides the primary exposition.

As for the note stating "and so forth," it means that the sequence of opening [the gates] and so on is merely presented as such because they are both non-different and yet different when applied to the permanence, bliss, self, and purity;
in reality, the state of the four virtues is perfect and wondrous, and is not characterized by temporal succession.

Next, the explanation of the passage concerning the fulfillment of benefiting others is divided into two parts: first, the analysis of the text; second, from "In other sutras... onwards, clarifying the underlying reason.
As for why supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and the preaching of the Dharma appear either before or after one another, it is simply because they are adapted to the capacities of sentient beings.

Regarding the cultivation of the primary and auxiliary practices during the causal stage and the possession of the Dharma-preaching and supernatural powers in the resultant stage—take, for example, the person of "liberation through both parts" (*ubhayatobhāgavimukta*) in the Hīnayāna; even in their causal stage, they must still cultivate these practices.

Only upon reaching the fruit through the shared foundations of mindfulness can one realize the principle and manifest supernormal powers; how much more so for the Buddha-fruit, where wisdom and the abandonment of afflictions are perfected?
This is because one does not cultivate the primary and auxiliary paths within the causal stage.

As previously explained, by cultivating the two emptinesses of persons and phenomena—the primary path and the auxiliary path—during the causal stage, one is now able, upon reaching the fruit, to preach the Dharma and manifest supernormal powers.

Next, the teaching of the "Lifting of the Dharma" (dharmodgraha) is presented through four analogies; the following section explains the meaning according to the text, which is divided into two parts.

First, the explanation of turning the wheel of Dharma to transform others is further divided into two parts. First, the explanation of transforming others by preaching the Dharma is further divided into two parts. First, the direct explanation is further divided into two parts: first, a general indication;

second, the specific explanation beginning with the phrase "blowing the conch," which is divided into two parts. First, the direct explanation of the text is divided into four parts. First, the explanation of "blowing."

The *Dafalüzhōng* (Great Dharma Conch) states: "Blowing the conch signifies changing one's designation and transforming the ordinary nature of the suffering-acceptance (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) of a worldling into the true nature of a sage.

The *Miaoxuan* (Sublime Mystery) explains the seven sages, stating: "Sage" means correctness; through the manifestation of the clarity of suffering-acceptance, one abandons the state of a worldling to enter the state of a sage and attains the vision of true reality.
The *Shiqian* (Explanatory Notes) states: "Abandoning the worldling to enter the sage" refers to having reached the stage of suffering-acceptance.

In the sequential and uninterrupted path, one necessarily enters the first fruit (*srotāpatti-phala*). Now, speaking from the subsequent perspective, it is generally said that these are "noble ones" (*ārya*).

Thus, the first two stages among the seven noble persons—namely, (1) the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*) and (2) the follower by dharma (*dharmānusārin*)—both consist of fifteen moments of mind; it is upon reaching the sixteenth moment of mind upon entering the first fruit that they are collectively designated as "noble.
If one considers only the fifteen moments themselves, they are not yet called "noble," as they still remain within the stage of the cause (*hetu*).
Therefore, although all sixteen moments of mind are untainted (*anāsrava*), they are designated merely as "heading toward" (*pratipannaka*) up until the fifteenth moment.

This marks the transformation from the partial nature of ordinary beings and sages into the perfect nature of the Middle Way. Regarding those who attain the seventh stage of the Shared Teaching (*pāṭha-sādhāraṇa-yāna*), the first stage of the Distinct Teaching (*pratyeka-bhūmi*), and the first dwelling of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*):
the seventh stage of the Shared Teaching is termed "sage" (*ārya*). This is explained according to the reception of the lower capacity, based on the lower capacity.

Because one arrives at and dwells in the first stage (*bhūmi*) of the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*), it is called the "first dwelling" (*prathama-vihāra*) of the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-śāsana*);
therefore, the text below states that one enters the Middle Way from the partial. Thus, prior to reaching the stages and dwellings, one is termed an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

Furthermore, if one speaks solely in terms of the Separate and Perfect Teachings, both the stages and dwellings of these teachings involve transforming the biased nature of the two extremes and entering the Middle Way.

Because its nature is round, it is said that one enters the Middle Way from the partial; since the changing of titles is clarified by traversing the three teachings, we know that the Mahāyāna is not found exclusively in the Round Teaching alone.
Next, the explanation of "beating the great Dharma drum" refers to the method of military arrays: hearing the drum, one advances; hearing the gong, one stops.
The drum solemnizes the military host and causes the vanguard to move forward; "solemnizing" (肅) also implies the restraint of advancing.

"Yedu" (也督) means "to lead," "to encourage," and "to correct. Regarding the stage of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) situated in the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* clarifies that the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) consists of sixteen moments of mind, which is the First Fruit (*srotāpanna*). The Second Fruit is indeed the Path of Cultivation.

All *Abhidharma* treatises clarify that the Path of Seeing occurs within fifteen moments of mind, while the Path of Cultivation comprises the sixteenth moment. This is consistent with the eighth stage of the Shared Teaching (*pāṭha-sādhāraṇa-yāna*).
Reflecting upon this, the Separate Teaching (biejiao) is situated at the stage of the Ten Practices (shixing);
since this is explained in terms of horizontal progression, when contrasted with the Ten Practices, it cannot be hindered by a vertical discussion of the stages of Seeing and Cultivation (jianxiu).

Therefore, these Ten Practices and those mentioned below in contrast to the Ten Transferences (shihuixiang) are all horizontal contrasts between different stages; they are not textual errors. As for the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao), it is situated at the First Dwelling (dizhu).
This is also a horizontal correspondence [to the stages]. The *Fahua wenju* states that the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) is called "True Cultivation" (*bhūtayoga*);

this refers to the same meaning. The subsequent mention of "kindling a torch" also occurs at the first stage; both are horizontal correspondences. Regarding the third explanation, "kindling the great torch of the Dharma":

"Way" (*mārga*) refers to the path of transformation (*pariṇāmanā-mārga*), and "Contemplation" (*dhyāna*) refers to the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*). (And so forth. Regarding the fourth explanation, "raining down *sarvajñā*": this is translated as "all-knowledge" (*sarvajña*), and it is called "great."

Regarding "Constant" (恒): because among all rivers the Ganges is the greatest, it is called "Great. Next, if one obtains the following examples, the text is interpreted as having two parts: first, the direct application of the example to this single dharma; second, the summary of the horizontal and vertical [dimensions], where the vertical refers to the depth of cause and effect within this specific teaching, and the horizontal refers to the differences between the various stages of the four teachings. The note states: The term "constant" (*nitya*) is used because the Ganges is the greatest among all rivers; thus, it is called "great. Next, if one obtains the following lower examples, the text is divided into two sections:

first, the direct application of the example to this single dharma; next, the summary based on the horizontal and vertical [perspectives]. The vertical refers to the shallow and deep levels of cause and effect within this specific teaching; the horizontal refers to the differences among the various positions of the four teachings. The commentary notes:

The term "it is said" (yun zhe) means that because this present sutra is subsumed within the Vaipulya (fangdeng) class, it may manifest horizontally or vertically according to the various types of beings without obstruction.

Hereafter, the text proceeds to distinguish and indicate [the meaning], stating that all four analogies are called "great" (da). The fourth is termed "superior-to-the-superior" (sheng-sheng), which is also "great," following the pattern of "great," "much," and "superior.
Regarding the general explanation that "great" does not refer to a small stage: however, in the preceding explanation...
The blowing of conchs and beating of drums also clarify the positions of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*); this is because the Mahāyāna incidentally encompasses the stages of the Lesser Vehicle.

Next, regarding the explanation of supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) for transforming others, as for "the non-Dharma king being indestructible," if it were not by the power of the Dharma King, [it could not be so].
"Destroying the hosts of Māra. *Hui* (pronounced as in *xǔwéi*) means "to signal with a banner. The *Shuowén* states that a banner is used for signaling and commanding.

Next, the text explaining the four great vows (*caturmahāpraṇidhāna*) regarding the transformation of others is divided into two parts: first, a general indication; second, the specific explanation beginning with "Delivering all...

This latter section is further divided into four parts: first, the explanation of the first vow; second, the explanation of the second vow; third, the explanation of the fourth vow; and fourth, the explanation of the [third] vow.
Regarding the phrase "the three vows, with notes, etc.," it is intended to provide a detailed exposition; thus, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra Śāstra* states in verse:
"The meaning of *dāna* encompasses the six [perfections]: material gifts, fearlessness, and the Dharma. Among these, the first, second, and third are called the "abodes of cultivation.
In the Sanskrit language, *dāna*; in the Chinese language, "generosity" (*bùshī*). There are three types of generosity: first, the gift of material goods, which is the *dānapāramitā*.

The two kinds of fearlessness-giving consist of the three dharmas of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and patience (*kṣānti*); the dharma-giving consists of diligence (*vīrya*), meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Giving for the sake of livelihood is of only one kind—generosity (*dāna*)—whereas fearlessness-giving is of two kinds, namely ethical discipline and patience, because one is not afraid of evil;

dharma-giving is of three kinds, namely diligence and so forth, because one does not grow weary and knows the mind as it truly is and speaks accordingly. This includes the relinquishing of body, life, and wealth.

Regarding the attainment of the indestructible and eternally abiding at the limit of the future, which is called a *pāramitā*, the *Zhiguan* states: "In the Perfect Teaching, one relinquishes the factors of enlightenment;

one relinquishes the physical bodies of the ten dharma-realms; one relinquishes the life-force that sustains the ten dharma-realms; and one relinquishes the dependent retribution of the ten dharma-realms.
Such body, life, and wealth do not enter into the two extremes. Why is this? 'Wealth' refers to the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). If one calculates..."

If one can abandon the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), give them to another person, and possess the capacity for selfless giving, such a giver enters the limit of existence within the six sense objects.
If all three factors [the giver, the recipient, and the gift] are empty, one falls into the limit of non-existence. Now, observing that wealth is empty, one does not enter existence;
observing that wealth is provisional, one does not enter emptiness. This non-dual relinquishment is equal to the future limit of birth and death, and is free from old age and sickness.

Death is imperishable and eternally abiding; having a limit refers to birth-and-death (saṃsāra), which belongs to the prior limit, while emptiness refers to nirvāṇa, which belongs to the subsequent limit.

Since both of these are empty and entirely unobtainable, they are called "equal. Being free from old age, sickness, and death means that because the prior limit is empty, one is free from the old age and death of segmented existence (pariccheda-jarāmaraṇa);
because the subsequent limit is empty, one is free from the old age and death of transformation (pariṇāma-jarāmaraṇa). These two deaths are forever [extinguished].
Because it is exempt [from destruction], it is called "detachment" (*li*). To attain that which is indestructible and eternally abiding is precisely the Middle Way and the *dharmatā*.
Since the Dharma is eternal, the Buddhas are also eternal. This wealth of eternal abiding cannot be damaged;
this body of eternal abiding cannot be bound; this life of eternal abiding cannot be severed. Thus, one accomplishes the ultimate *dānapāramitā*.

Adorning oneself with honey means being lofty vertically and broad horizontally; this refers precisely to what is called "accumulating merit to a great height" and "encompassing the Dharma extensively.
These matters are explained in detail within the section on the "Aids for Counteracting and Opening up" in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*.
Furthermore, some versions of the sutra contain an additional verse beginning with "joyful giving" and so forth below this point; this was merely added later by others.

The third major section: Explaining the Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings. The text of the section on the dissemination of the teaching is divided into two parts: first, an individual explanation of the title of the "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings";
second, from this point downward, a general explanation of the thirteen chapters. The first part is further divided into two.

Regarding the initial explanation of "ascending" and so forth in terms of causes and conditions: sinking downward constitutes the earth, while ascending upward constitutes heaven. Heaven is further divided into the three realms, which differ from one another.
Since the Four Heavenly Kings (*Cāturmahārājika*) are the first of the ascending [realms] and the beginning of the lower worlds, they are called the "primordial head" and the "first heaven.
As for "dwelling on half of Mount Sumeru": *Sumeru* is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "Peaceful Brilliance" (*Anming*), and is also called...
The four precious substances that constitute Mount Sumeru give it its name "Wondrous" (Miao), while its emergence above the seven golden mountains gives it its name "High" (Gao).
Mount Sumeru is eighty-four thousand *yojanas* high, which is three million three hundred and thirty-six thousand *li*.
The Heaven of the Four Great Kings resides halfway up this mountain, at a height of forty-two thousand *yojanas*; according to the *Loutan jing* (Kāṣāyaprabhāsa-sūtra), this is half of Mount Sumeru.
It is twenty-four thousand *li* wide; one who reads the *Fahua Wenju* (Treatise on the Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra) must understand this explanation (*etc.*).

The *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "The *Sumeru* has four terraces, each separated by ten thousand [yojanas]. Extending outward, they measure sixteen, eight, four, and two thousand [yojanas] respectively.
The hosts of the Great Kings—Vajrapāṇi, Mālādharī, Sadāmada, and Mahārāja— Dwell in succession upon these four levels, as do those on the remaining seven."
The Four Heavenly Kings of the Mountains are the external ministers of Śakra, like military generals.

The term *dà* (pronounced *dingguǒ*) used for the east, west, south, and north refers to earthen mounds (*tǔdà*). Gandharvas are translated as "Fragrance-Sniffers" (*xiùxiāng*), as they take fragrance as their food;

they are also called "Fragrance-Heaps" (*xiāngyīn*) because fragrance issues from their bodies. They are the deities of secular music belonging to the Heavenly Emperor. Pūtanas are translated as "Masters" (*zhǔ*).
The *uṣṇa-roga-graha* (fever-demon) is a *kumbhāṇḍa*, which means "jar-shaped" and resembles a winter melon (*alābu*).

The *pīlīta* (or *vetāla*), which means "grandfather," is the lowest among the hungry ghosts (*preta*). The *piśāca*, which means "demon that devours vital essence," consumes the vital essence of humans and the five grains.
The *yakṣa*, which means "swift demon," and the *rākṣasa*, which means "man-eating demon."

Next, regarding the interpretation based on contemplating the mind (*guanxin*), this is the "contemplation based on phenomena" (*tuoshi guan*). The *Fahua wenju* also states that the wisdom contemplating the Four Truths is itself the Four Kings;
under each Truth, the removal of the two delusions of craving and views constitutes the protection against the eight [types of] craving and views.
In the present text, the directions—east, west, south, and north—are first correlated with the Four Truths, which represents the sequential order of cause and effect.
Birth is why the East is called Accumulation, the South Suffering, the West the Path, and the North Cessation.

If one summarizes this according to the correspondence of cause and effect, then it should be said that the East is Accumulation, the West Suffering, the South the Path, and the North Cessation. The principle of the Four Truths constitutes the four Heavenly Kings;
this is the natural principle of the First Noble Truth (Paramārtha-dhātu), which serves as the basis, while the Heavenly Kings are those who dwell therein. Therefore, [it is so designated].

The wisdom that contemplates the Four Noble Truths constitutes the Four Heavenly Kings. Within the Truth of Suffering, there are those with sharp and dull faculties of both *dṛṣṭi* (view) and *kleśa* (affliction):

the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth are the sharp, termed "view," while greed, anger, and so forth are the dull, termed "affliction. This can be applied by analogy to the Truths up to Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
When the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* refers to these as "ghosts and spirits," it is based on the verses in the "Fire House" chapter of the Parable Chapter (*Upamā-parivarta*). From—

Regarding the six lines of verse below [the passage on] "owls, crows, eagles, and vultures," they clarify that the burning of birds and beasts serves as an analogy for the five dull afflictions (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*).

Next, from the ten lines of verse beginning with "In every place there are... onwards, they clarify that the burning of ghosts and spirits serves as an analogy for the five sharp afflictions (*pañca-kleśa*).

Now, ghosts and spirits possess supernatural powers and intelligence, whereas birds and beasts do not; therefore, the sharp afflictions are used to illustrate ghosts and spirits, while the dull afflictions are used to illustrate birds and beasts.
It is like birds and beasts; since the current text explains this from the perspective of the five benefits, it merely refers to these as "ghosts and spirits.
Furthermore, among the eighty-eight afflictions (*kleśa*) within the Four Noble Truths, there are fifty-two volitions (*cetanā*) that take views (*dṛṣṭi*) as their basis;
for this reason, they too may be likened to ghosts and spirits, whereas the volitions that are deluded regarding phenomena (*vastu*) are not so. "Scattered" (*bèng*) also means dispersed.
"Controlling" means leading; "governing" means managing.
Next follows the general explanation of the thirteen chapters, which is divided into two parts: first, the exposition of the intent and the division of the text;
the latter part is the conclusion. "Obscuring" means hiding or obstructing. "True Reality" refers to the profoundly deep *dharmatā*. "Encouraging" also means exhorting, as well as assisting.
"Also accomplished," "also praised," and "also strenuous. "Square tracks" (fāng guǐ) means that the tracks are the law (*dharma*). Regarding "the celestial deities and so forth":

the celestial deities are called *shén*, and the terrestrial deities are called *qí*. That the benefits are profound and weighty means that the ordering of the sutra’s teachings will be widely practiced.

As for the repeated notes "as follows" (*yún yún*) at the end of each section, there are two intentions: first, to cause the meaning of the categorized phrases to be explained; second, to point toward the subsequent text.
The "gao" (pronounced *gōng láo*) explained in this chapter is the essence of the spirit; it means fatness. "Sǒu" (pronounced *yǔ zhū*) also means fatness.
Below the character "yú," there is an extra character "wèi" (taste), which was added arbitrarily by later generations. "Rǎng" means to ward off with the hands;
it means to remove, to drive away, or to stop.
Next, regarding the section from the "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings," there are six sections; following the text, the explanation of the meaning is divided into seven parts.

First, the explanation of the five chapters from the "Chapter on the Four Kings" to the "Chapter on Vaiśravaṇa" clarifies how the Heavenly Kings made vows to exhort and encourage human kings to widely proclaim this sutra; these constitute five parts.
The initial explanation of the "Chapter on the Four Kings" clarifies how the power of the celestial deities protects the petitioner; this text is divided into two parts.
First, the essential words of the section are marked with level tones (ping sheng). Second, following the expression of reverence, the meaning is explained in six sections.
The initial commentary on the first instance of the Four Kings’ address to the Buddha regarding their capacity to protect the nation is divided into two parts.

The first part explains the Four Kings’ address to the Buddha, which is further divided into two sections. Regarding the phrase "as in the text" (*ru wen*), it means it can be seen according to the scriptural text;
subsequent passages should be understood accordingly. Furthermore, in the Western Regions, rulers, fathers, and teachers all face east, and thus they regard the north as the superior direction.

The author of the sutra first lists Vaiśravaṇa; furthermore, when a disciple approaches a teacher, he must manifest reverence, and thus he bares his right shoulder and places his right knee on the ground, which differs from the practice in this land of exposing one's torso to apologize for a transgression (the details of "exposing the torso to apologize" are as cited in the supplementary notes of the *Dabù*).
This is merely a difference in custom between the two lands of the East and West. As for the term "hu-kuei" (hukuei), it has been used since ancient times...

When translating vernacular dialects, those who had not yet mastered the conventions would claim that the language of the Western Regions was "Hu" (barbarian) speech, and that kneeling there was "Hu-kneeling.

It was only from the Sui to the Tang dynasties that various masters finally distinguished between the Hu and the Vedic (Brahmanical) traditions, as fully demonstrated in the supplementary notes to the *Mahāvaipulya* [Sūtra] (etc.).

Therefore, one must understand that the ritual of the Western Vedic tradition consists of kneeling with both knees on the ground, raising the three points [the two knees and the crown of the head], bowing the body, and joining the palms before the eyes.
The commentary on "venerating the honored countenance" does not refer to the prostration style of the Hu (foreign) countries.

Next, the explanation of the text "Correctly Whiting the Buddha" is divided into two parts. First, the intention is set forth and the text is analyzed; regarding the praise of the three [jewels], that which briefly subsumes the extensive is as follows:
although the text of the preceding formal exposition is voluminous, the current praise of the three jewels during the dissemination of the teaching is precisely what briefly subsumes the extensive.

If these three are taken collectively, they constitute the "explanation of the title" (*shiming*); if they are analyzed individually, they constitute the "characteristics of the teaching" (*jiaoxiang*).

Therefore, the five meanings of the title’s commentary may be understood through their corresponding textual passages. Next, regarding the passage on "the principle of the nature of phenomena" (*faxing zhi li*) and below, the meaning is explained according to the text.

This section is divided into three parts. First, the explanation of the praise of the essence: "The principle of the nature of phenomena is that which the Buddha protects and keeps in mind. This means that awakened wisdom is in profound accord with the principle, thereby guarding against and preventing delusions.

That which gives rise to and maintains the principle without losing its phrasing is the *sūtra*. "Principle" (*li*) is the king; "phrasing" (*wen*) is that which can express, and "principle" is that which is expressed.

To "express" means to reveal and to summon. By citing that which expresses to reveal that which is expressed, it is therefore called "phrasing-expressing. Because it expresses this principle, it is called the "king of sūtras.
If, as the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) says, "The title 'Sūtra' is the King, and the teaching encompasses all scriptures," this is taking the expressed [the principle] as [the subject].

Because it manifests the capacity [of the teaching], it is subsumed within the category of the "explanatory" (vācaka) scriptures; there are many such examples throughout the various texts of our own school.
Since Siming did not understand this, he falsely leveled his criticisms. Now, when it says "King of Sutras," one knows this is praising the essence (tattva);
that is, the passage in the introduction stating "the king of all sutras" describes the essence. Yet, in the current text, the preceding phrase refers to it as "this *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*."

Although this passage includes the title, it is actually praising the essence itself. Furthermore, that which is called "subtle and wondrous" refers to the immeasurable and profoundly deep *dharmatā*, which is neither vertical nor horizontal.
Nevertheless, even though the three virtues (*triguṇa*) are neither vertical nor horizontal, one must specifically point to *dharmatā* as the essence;
for fear that the essence might be confused [with the other two], the two virtues are distinguished from the three virtues to specifically identify the *dharmakāya*.

"It is the essence itself" (and so forth). Next, regarding the section on "praising the fundamental tenet" (*zhongzong*) based on the essence, the phrase "cultivating practice based on the essence" (*yue ti xiuxing deng*) refers to what the *Wenju ji* states:
"The essence is neither cause nor effect; it is that upon which one relies to distinguish cause and effect.
Thus, the beginning of practice is the cause, for it enables the bodhisattva to possess the two adornments; the end of practice is the fruit, for it enables one to reach the ultimate stage."

However, this present sutra takes the eternal fruit as its primary tenet; since the fruit is realized through causes, it is stated thus. "Possessing the two adornments" refers to the two causes of cultivated virtue:
the *pariniṣpanna* (perfect) cause and the *pratyaya* (conditional) cause. *Pariniṣpanna* is the adornment of wisdom (*prajñā*), which is manifest clarity;

*pratyaya* is the adornment of merit (*puṇya*), which acts as an auxiliary support. By taking these two as causes, one achieves the ultimate fruit—the dual virtues of wisdom and the severance of afflictions.
Therefore, the Sūtra speaks of "profound and wondrous merit. Thus, the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) states: "Adorning the profound and wondrous merit of the Bodhisattva is taken as the central theme.

Regarding the third of the world's three expositions on praising the function: from the passage in the Sūtra text beginning with "Constantly revered by all the devas" downwards, this constitutes the praise of the function.
Therefore, the *Xuanyi* states: "It illuminates the hearts of all the devas, causing them to give rise to joy."
To take "Joy" (*xi*) as the "function" (*yòng*) seems inconvenient, given that in the *Sijiming* (Record of the Four Clarities), the "World-Heaven" (*shìtiān*) is taken as the "essence" (*jīngzōng*).
Furthermore, since the text concludes by stating, "Knowing this praises the essence; knowing this praises the essence;

knowing this praises the function," how can one not consider the "World-Heaven" and so forth? The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*, in the "Chapter on King of Virtue" (*Dewangpin*), states that there are four kinds [of Dharma].
The four types of heavens are as follows: first, the worldly heavens, such as various kings;

second, the heavens of birth, ranging from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception; third, the heavens of purity, ranging from the Srotāpanna up to the Pratyekabuddha;

and fourth, the heavens of meaning, which refers to the Bodhisattvas of the ten stages who perceive that all phenomena have the meaning of emptiness. As a sutra says: "All heavens are not outside of these."

Regarding the fourth point: the fact that this current text lists only three types of devas is likely due to an omission, rather than implying that the Heavenly Kings were originally *upapattideva* (beings born as gods) while the commentary failed to mention it.

Since the threefold offering constitutes the cultivation of wholesome roots (*kuśalamūla*), we know that the portion of the sutra to be employed must be that starting from "for the sake of all devas" and below.
If it were otherwise, [the passage concerning] the Honored King Golden Dragon (*Suvarṇanāgarāja*)...
Regarding how to interpret the phrase "using this sūtra to generate goodness" in the *Gandavyūha-sūtra* (The Sūtra of Reverent Salutation and Praise):

the previous section, from the hells below up to the bodhisattvas above, clarified that the three types of karmic offerings are used to generate goodness; therefore, this section now clarifies that the sūtra is used to extinguish evil.
It is precisely for this reason that the word "also" (*yòu*) is employed. Since the sūtra text states that "this sūtra can cause [the hells]... [the connection is established].

The rivers of the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals are parched and dried up; yet it is said that [this teaching] can eliminate all sorrow and affliction and extinguish all hundreds of thousands of sufferings and distresses.

Thus we know that from the hells below to the bodhisattvas above, as long as ignorance is not yet exhausted, there is universally the presence of feverish affliction (*tāpa*). Otherwise, how could the term "all" be explained? This is what the praise intends.
The phrase "as stated in the notes below the text" indicates that one should speak in such a manner.

Next, from the passage beginning with "Then, from the World-Honored One," the explanation of the text on "Protecting the Nation" is divided into two parts. First, the analysis of the text, which refers to wisdom and strategic planning.

Second, the explanation of the meaning of the text, which is further divided into two parts. First, the explanation of the internal section on protecting the nation through the Dharma, which is divided into four parts. First...
The reasons why Śāriputra protects the nation through his body and so forth, as well as the four benefits, can be understood by consulting the sūtra.

However, these four benefits arise not only from the phenomenal level (shi), but necessarily also from the principle level (li). Therefore, it is further stated that "one obtains two benefits through principle.

Thus, we know that when the sūtra speaks of "bodily strength and mental virtue," it encompasses both the phenomenal and the principled. Next, the following section explains how protecting the Dharma protects the nation; this is precisely to describe that [method].
The reason why the Dharma protects the nation is precisely because we are able to expound the True Dharma and practice it accordingly.
This meaning corresponds exactly with the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*), for the intent of being able to speak and practice accords with the purpose of contemplating the mind.
Therefore, the preceding explanation of the title of the "Chapter on the Four Kings" was based upon the contemplation of the mind.

It is precisely because these mental factors (*caitasika*) do not function that Prajñā functions; this meaning is illustrated by the fact that while all phenomena (*dharma*) are non-arising, Prajñā arises.
Because it is guided by wisdom (*jñāna*), it is said that that which is able to expound the True Dharma and which observes the mind with discerning wisdom is called "internal.
Therefore, it is referred to as "internal. Such is the reason for protecting the state; such is the reason for protecting the state.

Since it is named "Internal," one should know that "Protecting the Nation" (*Huguo*) refers to the external; therefore, the sutra says: "He acts as a Dharma King of the world, governing the world with the Dharma.

As for the statement by the Fourth Master (Sima Chengzhen) that "the reason *Huguo* has both internal and external aspects is that the internal is the mental dharmas and the external is the worldly dharmas," this is likely not correct.
The three masters below explain [the title] by taking "Tian" as the clan name and "Huguo Shuai" as the official title.

"Guide" (dào) means to lead; "faction" (dǎng) refers to those who are elders or those who are honored, namely the various devas; it also refers to a group or a cohort, namely the nāgas, ghosts, and so forth. This also corresponds to the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*); as explained previously regarding the contemplation of the mind, the "eight classes" refer to the suffering, accumulation, cessation, and path [of the Four Noble Truths], and below these are the sharp and dull faculties, the views and afflictions (*jiansi*), and so on. As it says: The eight classes of beings, from the beginning, Are all subject to the four truths. Whether sharp or dull, They are all encompassed by views and afflictions. Furthermore, the *Shiqian* (Ten Thousand Questions) states: Question: What are the eight classes of beings? Answer: They are the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas. These eight classes are the retinue of the Four Heavenly Kings. Furthermore, there are the eight classes of beings within the desire realm: first, the six heavens of the desire realm; second, the four great kings; third, the eight great nāga kings; fourth, the yakṣas; fifth, the gandharvas; sixth, the asuras; seventh, the garuḍas; eighth, the kiṃnaras and mahoragas. These are called the eight classes of beings. Furthermore, there are the eight classes of beings within the form realm: first, the Brahmā-pāriṣadya heaven; second, the Brahmā-purohita heaven; third, the Mahābrahmā heaven; fourth, the Parīttābha heaven; fifth, the Apramāṇābha heaven; sixth, the Ābhāsvara heaven; seventh, the Parīttaśubha heaven; eighth, the Śubhakṛtsna heaven. These are called the eight classes of beings. Furthermore, there are the eight classes of beings within the formless realm: first, the Ākāśānantyāyatana; second, the Vijñānānantyāyatana; third, the Ākiṃcanyāyatana; fourth, the Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana; fifth, the Avṛha heaven; sixth, the Atapa heaven; seventh, the Sudṛśa heaven; eighth, the Sudarśana heaven. These are called the eight classes of beings. Furthermore, there are the eight classes of beings within the world of humans: first, the four continents; second, the eight great mountains; third, the eight great oceans; fourth, the eight great rivers; fifth, the eight great forests; sixth, the eight great treasures; seventh, the eight great medicinal herbs; eighth, the eight great precious stones. These are called the eight classes of beings. Furthermore, there are the eight classes of beings within the realm of hungry ghosts: first, those who eat filth; second, those who eat vomit; third, those who eat pus and blood; fourth, those who eat excrement; fifth, those who eat fire; sixth, those who eat wind; seventh, those who eat water; eighth, those who eat food. These are called the eight classes of beings. These are called the eight classes of beings.
