and the Ten Dedications (*shihuixiang*) cultivate the Middle Way (*zhongdao*) to destroy ignorance (*wuming*) and ascend to the First Ground (*chudi*) to realize the Middle Way’s Knowledge of All Aspects (*zhongdao-yiqiezhong-zhi*). These three knowledges, in their varying depths and sequential order, are not [simply] called... [the same].
Because it is subtle and secret, it is distinguished [from the preceding]. Next, the first section clarifies the Perfect [Teaching], which is further divided into two parts.

First, the main body clarifies the Wisdom of the Secret: "The wisdom of all wisdoms," etc. Regarding this, the *Sijiao yi* (Meaning of the Four Teachings) states: "The first phrase is the wisdom of emptiness;

the second phrase is the wisdom of the provisional. I say this is not so. Why? Because within the *Zhiguan* (Stopping and Contemplation), the inconceivable three wisdoms are explained as follows: first...
The "knowledge of all" (*sarvajñatā*) refers to phenomena produced by causes and conditions, which are also termed "provisional names";

this is the "knowledge of the paths" (*mārgajñatā*), which is expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). The "single knowledge of all" is what I describe as emptiness; this is the "knowledge of all aspects" (*sarvākārajñatā*), which is ultimate wisdom (*paramārtha-jñāna*).
Being neither one nor all, yet being both one and all—this is also called the meaning of the Middle Way; this is [the essence of] the One.

The wisdom of all modes (sarvākārajñatā) simultaneously negates both the provisional and the real, while simultaneously illuminating both the provisional and the real. Therefore, these three wisdoms are unified within a single mind;
the more they are analyzed, the more they harmonize. For this reason, it is called "inconceivable," and that which is inconceivable is called "secret.
Thus, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* clarifies the "Secret Treasury" (and so forth). Next, the passage beginning with "If one attains... serves as an illustration to explain the sūtras in general.

"Text" (or "words") refers to the following: if one grasps the purport of the three types of knowledge mentioned above and applies that principle to the five phrases of the sūtra text, they can be understood.
As for the "five phrases": knowing all phenomena and all conditioned phenomena constitutes the first phrase;

comprehending all phenomena is the second phrase; knowing the specific limits of phenomena is the third phrase; and abiding in accordance with the Dharma [is the fourth phrase]. [The fifth phrase is] as follows: abiding in accordance with the Dharma.
The four propositions regarding the nature of all phenomena as suchness constitute the first phrase; the inclusion of all phenomena within all phenomena constitutes the five phrases.
That one phrase contains the five phrases is the single wisdom of omniscience; that one wisdom contains the five phrases is the omniscience of single wisdom.
That which is neither one nor five, yet both one and five, is the Middle Way of simultaneous negation and simultaneous illumination.
Therefore, following the passage on the "inconceivable threefold wisdom" in the *Zhiguan*, it states:

"One provisional [wisdom] is all provisional; one real [wisdom] is all real; neither one nor all, neither provisional nor real," and so forth. Following the pattern of the preceding text: "One emptiness is all emptiness;

the provisional and the middle are both empty"—this is the general contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). "One provisional [nature] is all provisional; the empty and the middle are both provisional"—this is the general [contemplation of] the provisional.

"Pseudo-contemplation" (jiaguān) means that within one, all are "middle" (zhōng); "pseudo-emptiness" (jìkōng) means all are "middle. This is the contemplation of the collective middle (zǒngzhōngguān).

The *Fǔxíng* (Subcommentary) explains that by means of the preceding three contemplations, the collective characteristic is established. Since the three contemplations are thus, the three wisdoms (sānzhì) are likewise so.

Therefore, one knows that in the present text, among the five phrases, one phrase is "cessation and contemplation" (zhǐguān): "one emptiness, all are empty; pseudo and middle are all empty"—this is the collective emptiness contemplation (zǒngkōngguān).

The phrase "one sentence, five sentences" refers to what the *Zhiguan* calls "the one is all false; within emptiness and conventionality, all are false"—this is the comprehensive contemplation of the false (*zong-jia-guan*).
"Neither one nor five, yet one and five" refers to what the *Zhiguan* calls "within one, there are all;

within emptiness and conventionality, all are middle"—this is the comprehensive contemplation of the middle (*zong-zhong-guan*). One must simply understand that the initial passage concerning "one wisdom, all wisdoms," and so forth, is...

This section on *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* explicitly clarifies the three wisdoms; according to the interpretation in the current text, this is an explanation by analogy that shows how *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* complete the general characteristics of the aforementioned three contemplations.
Only when these two intentions mutually support one another can they manifest both the exoteric and the esoteric. Zhiyi (Siyi) criticized [other views], saying:

"If one points to all phenomena as 'all,' it may not necessarily be exhaustive; however, if one takes emptiness, provisional existence, and the Middle Way as 'all,' there is nothing left unaccounted for."
I fear this may not be possible.
Question: Since the Great Master Yongjia, who was awakened in his former lives, employed the fundamental tenets of Tiantai—why did he say, "All numerical phrases are non-numerical phrases;
what connection have they with my numinous awakening? Answer: He was referring to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.

The Sūtra states that "countable phrases" and "innumerable phrases" are teachings accompanied by expedient means; therefore, they are vastly different from the perfect, sudden, and numinous awakening.
How, then, could they be mutually related? Furthermore, one should know that "countable" and "innumerable" are both partial attachments to the two extremes.
If one clings to these two extremes, it is not the numinous awakening, the true mark of reality, the profound source and foundation of the Dharmakāya. Moreover, if...
If one rigidly adheres to the four positions (*catuskoṭi*) and the non-positions, one is identical to the Māras and externalists.

However, if one is free from the attachment to the nature [of things] and clearly understands the four positions and the non-positions, only then does one realize the perfect, sudden, and inconceivable Dharma. This is just as the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:

"Dependent origination is itself emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. To fixate on the four positions as having a determinate nature constitutes frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*); whereas the four positions as mere designations (*prajñapti*)... [are the true teaching].

Only when phrases serve as gateways can one attain the vision of the Way; thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* speaks of "counted phrases" and "non-counted phrases," and the present text states that "only counting" and "only esotericism" are all merely provisional names and signs spoken within the realm of namelessness and signlessness. How could these be identical to fixed attachments?

It is simply that those who do not yet understand have not yet abandoned their clinging to inherent nature (svabhāva-grāha); therefore, [the text] rebukes them, asking: "What [do these have] to do with our numinous awareness?"
Because they do not intersect, the self-awakening of one's own practice is different from what is provisionally established;

thus it is said that self-practice exists only within the void (*ākāśa*), while transforming others through the three thousand [realms] accords with things. This shall be further demonstrated when discussing the "objective realm" (*ālambana*). (And so forth.

If it is argued that the present text concerns only the Numerical [School] and the Esoteric [School], and thus has no intersection with the principle of "spiritual awakening" mentioned by Yongjia, why did Yongjia say...?

In the *Sujue ji* (Collection of Innate Enlightenment), regarding the Perfect and Sudden Teaching of Tiantai, it is stated: "The principle of the Dharmakāya within the single realm of the Three Truths is eternally pure;

the illumination of Prajñā within the single mind of the Three Wisdoms is constantly radiant. Realm and wisdom are in profound union, and the response of liberation accords with the capacities of beings.
It further states: "The three responses within the Perfect must be fully possessed; the three responses within the Partial must be distinguished; there is one and not two."
Therefore, because it is not perfect and because it is not perfect, it is not of the same nature [as the Perfect Teaching].

Is this not identical in its intent to the "perfection" and "wonderfulness" of the present text, as well as to the principles of "only the Numerical" and "only the Esoteric," and the exclusion of the partial?

Furthermore, since the present text states "only the Numerical" and "only the Esoteric," it does not merely serve to explain the name of Saṃjñeya, but also reveals the secret principle of the three virtues (*triguṇa*) of the Great Sūtra; thus, the present...
The reason the Central Commission established the three bodies and the three Buddha-natures is precisely because of this; those of high virtue who study Chan should consider it.

Next, regarding the text on the "object" (*viṣaya*), there are two parts: first, the exclusion of partiality, and second, the exclusion of biased wisdom. Since the former has already excluded partiality, we now proceed with the sequence of shallow and deep levels.

The exclusion of "partial objects" refers to the exclusion of those things that are knowable and expressible; one should understand that the sequence of shallow and deep is precisely this state of being knowable and expressible.

This is merely a variation in phrasing used to demonstrate their characteristics. Therefore, whether it concerns the objects or the wisdom of the partial teachings, their sequences of shallow and deep—being merely knowable and expressible—are neither perfect nor sublime, and thus do not constitute the secret [teaching]. For this reason, they must be excluded.
Therefore, one must know that wisdom illuminates the object and the object gives rise to wisdom. These four propositions used for estimation all follow from the attachments of individual natures;
they are all products of discursive thought and belong to the realm of expedient means. Why is this? Because the perfect object and wisdom are inconceivable.

That which truly illuminates is the illumination itself, not the teaching of expedient means; while the oral explanation of the teaching may be exhausted, the illumination itself should be understood as not being the teaching of expedient means. Wisdom is [the illumination].

That which can be understood through illumination is what one speaks of when referring to the non-expedient teachings; the wisdom that can exhaustively illuminate is what should be understood as the non-expedient teachings of oral discourse.
Therefore, it is not the same as what the world calls "stubborn objects" (insentient matter) being taken as the object of illumination.
Nor is it the same as taking the deluded mind of the partial and limited vehicles as the object of illumination. Nor is it the same as taking the conventionally established *tathatā* (suchness).

Since that which is illuminated and the illuminator are thus, the illuminator likewise cannot be taken for granted; this is fully explained as in the *Zhi Guan* (Calming and Contemplation), so readers should constantly keep this in mind while practicing.
Next, regarding the passage "cannot be known by wisdom" (*bù kě zhì zhī*) and below, which reveals the text on the Perfect [Teaching], it is divided into two parts.

First, the explicit clarification of the inconceivable nature of the object: as for the phrase "cannot be known by wisdom," one must not interpret it as "wisdom illuminates the object through wisdom," nor as...

One knows that it cannot be produced by cognition, for cognition illuminates objects through wisdom; one knows that it cannot be produced by consciousness, for consciousness illuminates objects through wisdom;
one knows that it cannot be produced by naming, for naming expresses objects through wisdom.
Because it is free from the fault of clinging to intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it cannot be known by wisdom, it cannot be cognized by consciousness, and it cannot be named by names.

That which can be expressed through speech, known through wisdom (*jñāna*), and cognized through consciousness (*vijñāna*)—all such things are conceivable because they are merely skillful means (*upāya*).
Therefore, to be free from these attachments is called the "inconceivable" (*acintya*); this alone is the reality. Why?
Because within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), not even a single dharma can be apprehended; how then could one apprehend it through wisdom, knowledge, or consciousness? For this reason:
One should know that if there is anything attained, one will be confused with the various heterodoxies, all of which follow from the fault of attachment to nature;
if one can transcend and penetrate through identity and difference, whether vertically or horizontally, then all hundred deliberations will vanish and ten thousand ends will be discarded.

Only then is it called the Perfect and Sudden, inconceivable, absolute, secret, and subtle realm, as described in detail in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Mohe Zhiguan). Next, following this sequence, we shall apply this principle by analogy to the scriptural texts.
The preceding passage briefly distinguished the partial [teachings] by means of the separation between the wisdom that illuminates and the objects it perceives;

now, this current sutra text discusses the esoteric [teaching] in terms of the number five. By taking the present objects as an analogy for the previous wisdom, it can be understood. As for "it can be understood":

since the objects and wisdom have already been described as "one wisdom and all [objects]," etc., the objects may likewise be inferred; and since wisdom has already been established, [the same applies].

It is said that the five phrases and the single phrase, as well as their respective objects, follow this same principle. Since it is stated that "wisdom is merely number" and "merely subtle," the objects likewise follow this principle;
thus, they are called "analogous to the preceding," which can be understood from this.

However, one must understand that the statements "one wisdom is all wisdom" and "one object is all objects" are merely provisional designations established based on the causes and conditions of the *siddhānta*. Therefore...
Objects and wisdom possess only names; they do not exist internally, externally, or in between, for they are eternally self-existent and so forth.
Thus, one knows that these are merely established by others for the sake of others. Therefore, it is called "one wisdom" and "all-wisdom," "one object" and "all-objects," and so on.
For this reason, the Sūtra says: "I know all dharmas; I thoroughly understand all conditioned dharmas... and so forth, even saying 'I'..."
Observing that the light of inconceivable wisdom and the torch of inconceivable wisdom are merely enumerations and merely conventional designations,
one knows that these are indeed taught through provisional names and signs within the inconceivable realm that is devoid of names and signs.

It may also be said that wisdom can illuminate objects and objects can illuminate wisdom, such that they mutually illuminate one another without any obstruction, for the mind is likewise capable of illumination.
Subject and object are both mind; the essence of mind is all-pervasive; and mind and mind illuminate one another.
This principle is extremely clear, and thus the inconceivable realm is initially described as "the realm is itself contemplation. Based on this, a fourfold analysis is established:

the realm illuminates the realm, the realm illuminates wisdom, wisdom illuminates the realm, and wisdom illuminates wisdom. Therefore, if one does not first sweep away the attachment to the nature [of things], [one cannot realize this].

Thereafter, if one is clear regarding the provisional establishment of *siddhānta*, then [the distinction from] Māra and non-Buddhists would be blurred; by what means, then, could one clarify such phrases as "the light of inconceivable wisdom"?
The *Wenju ji* (Record of Literary Phrases) states: "If there were no causes and conditions, it would not differ from externalist calculations;
this is precisely because people do not see this—how can they understand and resolve it? Regarding *rasmi*, this is translated as "mystery" (*mi*). How is this transmitted?
Because he bestowed the methods of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, Nāgārjuna composed this treatise to expound the Buddha’s intent.

First, he cleansed all attachments through the emptiness of non-apprehensibility (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*) and purified all phenomena; thereafter, he pointed to emptiness and extensively explained all phenomena by means of the fourfold formulation (*catuṣkoṭi*).
These words were established as mere designations, free from any dwelling or attachment—just as one may only proceed to eat after an illness has been cured, and only once the food has been digested.
Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "One who is well able to discern the characteristics of all phenomena does not waver from the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
The nature of words is itself free [from conceptualization], which is liberation. How can one be attached to the idea that liberation exists apart from words?
To claim that wisdom illuminates the object and the object gives rise to wisdom is to fail to eliminate even the fundamental delusions while still engaging in such conceptual proliferation. Now...
Furthermore, regarding the new attachments one encounters, it is like adding water to a long block of ice; how could the freezing not increase? How can it ever be melted away?
This is explained in detail in the *Zhi guan yi li zuan yao* (Essentials of the Compendium on the Meaning of Calm and Insight), and so forth.
Next, regarding the correct exposition in response to the preceding [objections], one should understand that the above text first discussed cognition and then its object.

Fearing that this might lead to the misconception that object and cognition are separated in time and space, this section provides the correct exposition to harmonize the previously mentioned object and cognition, bringing them back to a single principle.
Thus, there is no object outside of cognition, and no cognition outside of the object; when object and cognition are as one, being neither before nor after, they are truly called the *dharmadhātu*.
Through right understanding and right contemplation, one attains right discernment; one correctly understands the conditions and is truly able to awaken to them. Within this, there are two parts:

first, distinguishing the partial from the biased to clarify the "right" in contrast to the "false. This clarifies the "right" of the emptiness of *nirvāṇa* in contrast to the "false" of *saṃsāra*, Māra, and externalists;
furthermore, it speaks of the Middle Way in contrast to these two extremes of existence and non-existence. Thus, it is called "right."
This Nirvana is correct, yet it is not [merely] correct; this is free from extremes and the middle, yet it is not [merely] the middle, because of the sequence of shallow and deep stages.
Therefore, that which is not fused, wondrous, inconceivable, and secret is sequential and thus deviant. Below, the Perfect is revealed, which is further divided into two parts.
