Vairocana Buddha further notes: "In foreign editions, the beginning of all sutras contains this phrase, and the introductory sections of all treatises likewise first offer homage and respect.
For example, the beginning of Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa’s *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith* says:

'I take refuge in the Most Victorious One throughout the ten directions, the Omniscient One, etc. This text is the conclusion of the exposition. As for the phrase "etcetera," this was spoken by Vajrapāṇi himself.
The subsequent expression of this homage does not mean that these are the words of the compiler; rather, the taking of refuge in the Triple Gem can be sought within the text itself.
"Precious Flower" refers to Śākyamuni Buddha, the Buddha-Gem; the "Subtle and Wondrous Dharma Torch" refers to the Dharma-Gem; and "Merit and Great Eloquence" refers to the Sangha-Gem.
There are two kinds of Sangha: namely, the Bodhisattva Sangha and the Bhikṣu Sangha; these two interpretations are now presented here.
The Sangha of Bodhisattvas consists of two types of harmony; this present case refers to harmony through principle (*dharmasāmagrī*). "Taking refuge" means to take life in [the Triple Gem].
For a detailed explanation of the Sanskrit term *namo*, the student should consult the *Fahua Wenju* (Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra).
New Commentary on the Words and Phrases of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, Fascicle Six;
New Commentary on the Words and Phrases of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, Fascicle Seven.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Congyi of Yongjia.

The commentary on the "Chapter on Establishing the True Doctrine" (*Saddharmavyavasthāpana-varga*) follows. Next, the commentaries on the two chapters "Skillful Collection" (*Kuśalasaṃgraha*) and "The Heavenly King’s Assistance" (*Devendraparigraha*) clarify how human kings propagate the sutras and how heavenly kings provide protection and aid; the text is divided into two parts.

First, the commentary on the "Chapter on Establishing the True Doctrine," which is further divided into two parts. First, the commentary on the title of the chapter, which is further divided into two parts. First, the explanation of the name: "Worldly Sages."
This refers to King Baladhararāja; this king is a Cakravartin (Wheel-Turning Sage King). "Sage" (*ārya*) here refers to the sages of the Three Vehicles.

The term "nucleus" (*hu-gé* [cut]) means to examine and verify actual facts. The correct Dharma of the world is called "factual reality" (*vastu-satya*), while the supramundane correct Dharma is called "principle-reality" (*tattva-satya*).
Therefore, the subsequent explanation of the meaning clarifies that, prior to the four *siddhāntas*, the three [types of] factual reality are its intended meaning.

It can be seen that since it is stated that the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is entirely the fundamental *suvarṇaprabhāsa* (Golden Light) of worldly goodness, how could this not be the actual reality?

Furthermore, this is explained from the perspective of the present chapter alone; however, if one were to discuss it by comparing the present chapter with the subsequent "Chapter on the Collection of Goodness" (*Kuśalasamuccaya*), one might say that the present chapter concerns the factual reality of the world (*loka-satya*), whereas the "Chapter on the Collection of Goodness" concerns the transcendent rational reality (*lokottara-yukti-satya*). Therefore, [it is said] below:
The preceding passage explained how mundane right view moves heaven and earth;

this current section explains how supramundane right view moves the worthy and holy ones—how much more so, then, when the text of this very chapter itself asks, "What is called the Right Discourse for Governing the World?

Is this not indeed the case? Furthermore, since this chapter on the "Accumulation of Goodness" clarifies that hearing this sutra brings about the fulfillment of Bodhi, is it not [the case that this is so]?
The principle of the supramundane is indeed real.

Following this chapter, the explanation of the text is divided into four parts. First, regarding the world-siddhānta (*loka-siddhānta*): since it speaks of "world" after "world," is this not the world-siddhānta?
Second, from "the king’s conduct" onwards, it concerns the person-siddhānta (*pudgala-siddhānta*); because the people are harmonious and concordant, it belongs to the cultivation of wholesome roots.
Regarding the term "hundred grains" (*bai gu*): the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) states that "grain" (*gu*) refers to the fruit; those of five kinds that produce fruit are called grains. These five are:

*shu* (millet), *ji* (panicled millet), *mai* (wheat/barley), *dao* (rice), and *ma* (hemp). Yang Qian’s *Wuli Lun* (Treatise on the Nature of Things) says: "Liang" is the collective name for *shu* and *ji*;
"dao" is the collective name for non-glutinous and glutinous rice; "shu" is the collective name for various beans. These three groups of grains, with twenty varieties each, constitute sixty.

The fruits of ten types of vegetables and ten types of grains assist the [cultivated] grains; together they constitute the "hundred grains. Regarding the Altars of the Soil and Grain (*sheji*), the *Baihutong* states:
"Why does the King possess the Altars of the Soil and Grain? It is because he seeks blessings for the world and repays the merit [of the land].

Man cannot stand without soil, nor can he eat without grain. Since the land is vast and extensive, it is impossible to pay reverence to it all at once; and since the five grains are numerous, [it is impossible to honor them all individually].
They may be sacrificed to one by one; therefore, earth is mounded and the *she* altar is established to manifest the reverence for those who possess land.
*Ji* is the chief of the five grains; therefore, an altar is mounded for *Ji* and sacrifices are offered to him. Regarding the equality of the people's conduct, the *Xiaojing* says:

"The former kings possessed the ultimate virtue and essential way to bring harmony to the world, so that the people’s conduct was concordant and harmonious, and there were no resentments between superiors and subordinates. The commentary notes: "This refers to the ultimate path of filial virtue."

This is the essential point: that the sagely and virtuous kings of former generations were able to accord with the hearts of the people throughout the world and practice this most essential transformation;

thus, those above and below, ministers and subjects, were harmonious and peaceful, free from resentment. The Three Kings employed the *adhobhūmi-saṃgraha* (lower-level comprehensive treatment) to remedy *vyāja* (deceit and fraud).
The *Shangshu* states: "Robbers, thieves, and *jiaojou*" (the latter pronounced *gui*), with the commentary explaining that these are groups who engage in collective plundering and robbery.
It is said that "a robber" refers to one who kills a person; "a thief" refers to one outside the state, while "a rebel" refers to one within.
This speaks to the consequence of a lack of moral instruction. In the current text, because it addresses external enemies, it uses the term "internal rebels.

If a ruler employs this method, then external enemies and internal rebels will not dare to plot or cause alarm against the Sage Ruler. As for the character *yāo* (妖), it means "seductive" or "strange"; the character should properly be written as *xiāo* (祅).
This concludes the fourth section on "Scattered Fragments. Below this, regarding the first principle of *siddhānta*, the foundation of worldly goodness is the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*.
As explained previously, within the "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings," all state affairs performed and all worldly treatises composed—whether mundane or supramundane—are based upon this sutra;
such is the meaning here. Furthermore, in the subsequent text, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* will be analyzed and examined once more.
This is the foundation of the correct treatise (and so forth).
Next, from this point downward, the explanation of the text of the chapter is divided into two parts. First, the introduction of the intent:
"The words 'the sage who is in darkness'—the sage who is in darkness refers to the sages of emptiness, namely the various devas of the upper realms."

Next, within the prose section, the following is an explanation of the text according to its meaning. This section is divided into two parts. First, the explanation of the prose concerning the fundamental matter of the event:

The *Abhiṣeka-parivarta* states that regarding the station of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says that the mother of the crown prince born of a Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*) is the principal queen, her physical marks being fully perfected;
that Universal Monarch causes this crown prince to sit upon the "Elephant-Jewel" made of exquisite gold.
A great net-curtain was spread upon the throne, a great Dharma-banner was erected, incense was burned, flowers were scattered, and various musical instruments were played.
The waters of the four great oceans were taken and placed within a golden vase; the King held this vase and poured the water over the crown of the Prince’s head.
At that moment, he was named as having received the royal position and entered the ranks of the consecrated Kṣatriyas. He was then able to fully practice the ten paths of wholesome action.
He is named a *cakravartin* (Wheel-Turning Sage-King).
Next, the commentary on the verse explains the prose of the treatise in two parts: first, from "What is it? (*katama*) onwards, the Tathāgata raises the inquiry;

second, from "The verse says" (*śloka āha*) onwards, there is the formal explanation of the verse. This section is further divided into two: first, the division of the text; second, from "The first line" onwards, the explanation of the text.
It consists of four parts.

First, the explanation of the passage on assembling the assembly is divided into three sections: first, explaining the Buddha’s description of his own venerable marks as he intends to preach the original dharma of former kings to his son;
second, explaining the Buddha’s description of his own venerable marks as he exhorts the listeners to attend; third, explaining the location where the discourse was delivered.

Next, the explanation of the text concerning the formulation of the question is divided into two parts: first, the presentation of the outline; second, from "First, the question" onwards, the word-by-word commentary, which consists of four sections.
First, the explanation of the question: "Why is a person called a 'deva' (heavenly being)? Regarding the term "four guardians" (*zhèn*): "guardian" (*zhèn*) means to suppress and protect;

it refers to the Four Heavenly Kings who suppress and protect the four continents. As for the phrase "to raise a question": according to the rules of propriety, whenever there is something to be asked, one must...
First, it is explained that one must rise from one's seat to manifest respect; second, it is explained why those not born of the gods (asuras) are called "sons of heaven" (*devaputra*);
third, it is explained why those who dwell in royal palaces are called "gods"; fourth, it is explained how those who govern the world through human laws can be called "gods."

Regarding the third explanation, which comments on the transition from the preceding to the subsequent section, the phrase "the note 'and so forth' beneath the character 'ke' (可)" indicates the intention of establishing the former and initiating the latter.
This means that although [the meaning] may be seen [implicitly], it must still be explicitly pointed out; therefore, it says: "Question: Since there are four [questions], the answers are also four.
The first answer concerns Devapāla and others. To speak of the fruit within the cause refers to performing good causes and thereby producing the fruit of rebirth in heaven.
Furthermore, this passage explains and establishes what precedes and follows; the masters of Gushan and Siming consider it to be an answer to the *Zhenglun* (Treatise on the Correct).
However, I fear that their initial interpretation of the meaning of the text may not be correct; let scholars examine this carefully.

From "Now, from you... onwards, the fourth section explains the response to the *Abhidharma-kośa* (the treatise on correct doctrine). This is divided into two parts: first, the analysis of the text; second, the explanation of its meaning. The text itself is further divided into two parts.
First, the explanation of the brief response, which has four sections. The first is the acceptance of the response, the scriptural text of which is evident.

Next is the brief citation of past causes and present results as a response to the King's question. Regarding the meaning of the King's inquiry: although he previously posed four questions, though he asked about those named "gods," he was actually asking about...

Since the text refers to a "human king" (*nrpati*), it is said that this answers the question regarding the meaning of "king. Regarding "because of the gathering of leaves," this refers to the past cause;

"born among humans" and so forth refers to the present fruit. As for the term "ruler" (*wang ling*), the character *wang* is pronounced with a departing tone (*qùshēng*), signifying a sovereign ruler.
Following the response concerning the devas, three meanings are presented; this is the third section, which explains by citing these three meanings to answer the question regarding the devas.
Regarding "Meaning" (*artha*), he answers the four questions posed by the Devaputra by means of three meanings; thus, he answers the third and fourth of the previous questions with the third meaning.
This is divided into three parts: first, a general presentation of the three meanings—namely, the single meaning of not entering the womb and entering the womb;
second, the two meanings of the distribution of virtues (*guṇa*); and third, the three meanings of power (*bala*). Alternatively, it may be that he first provides protection...
"Even before entering the womb," [it is said] because he protects the fetus. Next, the following passage explains by answering the four questions with three meanings.

Regarding the term "dividing merit" (*fēndé*): "dividing" (*fēn*) means to apportion, to bestow, and to distribute. It refers to how the various devas, using their own majestic virtue, apportion and bestow hidden sustenance as gifts upon this person;
therefore, he is called a "Son of Heaven" (*Tiānzǐ*). The phrase "the power of his spiritual faculties is added to him," etc., answers the first [question].

Regarding the third and fourth questions: one who, through the mastery of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-vaśitā*), distances themselves from evil and cultivates goodness so as to be reborn in the heavens and the like—such a person is called a "heavenly being" (*deva*) because they dwell in celestial palaces and govern the world with the True Dharma. The answer is that "half [of them] are named heavenly beings.
This concludes the three meanings. As for the phrase "this concludes the three meanings of 'half are named heavenly beings,'" it refers to the subsequent scriptural passage which states "half."
The "Famous Man" (Renmin) King verified that the preceding text refers to half [the category] as being "Heaven.

From the section "From the Famous Man King" downward, the fourth explanation provides a triple-meaning response to the question regarding the meaning of "King" (*rājan*). This text is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of why he is called a "Man-King" (*renwang*) due to three reasons;
it says: "one who 'clings to joy' (*zhile*). Here, "cling" (*zhi*) means to hold, to preside over, or to guard. This is from the *Liji* (Book of Rites), "Music" (*Yue*).
The *Records* state: "Rituals regulate the minds of the people; music harmonizes the voices of the people. Great Music is in harmony with Heaven and Earth;
Great Ritual is in accord with the rhythms of Heaven and Earth. Because of harmony, all things do not lose their place; because of rhythm, one sacrifices to Heaven and worships Earth.

The *Yijing Hou* (Divination of the Book of Changes) states that in times of Great Peace, it rains once every ten days. Regarding the *Ji-rang* (the wooden clapper), the *Fengtu Ji* (Record of Local Customs) states that it is made of wood and held in front.
At its broad end it is wide, tapering to a point at the back for three or four *chi* (inches) in length; its shape is like that of a sandal. During the winter solstice festival, youths play with it.
The *Yishi zhuan* (Biographies of Recluse Eminent Men) states that during the time of Yao, there was a man named Rangfu who played with it on the Kang Road.

The *Yijing* (Classic of Arts) states that "striking the *xiang*" was an ancient game, and "bamboo horses" are the toys of young children. Furthermore, regarding the "blocking of evil," this should also be understood through the scriptures.
The two characters "Luo-che" (Rākṣasa) and "Kui-kui" (Butcher) are used to encompass those above; thus, even kings are also called Rākṣasas, Kui-kuis, and so forth.
That heaven does not suffer from excessive drought and earth does not suffer from torrential floods indicates that the Yin and Yang are clear and do not deviate.
"Excessive" (*kang*) means high or drought; when Yang is excessive, there is drought, and drought means no rain. "Torrential floods" refers to great waters.
*Ye-li* (the *li* is pronounced with the *lì-zhì* initial) means pestilence. The Sūtra says "Kui-kuai" (魁膾), which is explained below;
furthermore, *kui* means leader or head, while *kuai* means finely minced meat. When the King possesses such power, he is like a rākṣasa leader;
by being the chief who minces human flesh, he causes all people not to dare commit transgressions. If it were not so, how else could he subdue those who lack restraint?
Measuring all evils, they are able to act as a lower [standard]; next, it is clarified that for three reasons they are also called "Heaven" (*deva*).
The *Baihutong* states: "The Son of Heaven (*Tianzi*) is a title of rank. Why is the title 'Son of Heaven' used? Because the King takes Heaven as father and Earth as mother, he is the Son of Heaven.
The Son of Heaven acts as the parent of the people and serves as the King of the world; because his words encompass [all things] like Heaven."
The Earth supports all those who rule over the world; therefore, the Preface to the Book of Documents says: "In ancient times, when Fuxi ruled the world...

[From here, the text proceeds to explain the subsequent passage in detail, dividing the commentary into two parts: first, the formal explanation, which is further divided into two sections. First... [The remainder of the original text follows this structural outline.]

Regarding the phrase "the six meanings of 'not the Dharma' are all lost," the commentary states "and so forth" because the intended meaning can be understood by applying this principle to explain the text.

The commentary says "and so forth. The Sūtra speaks of the "three anomalies": these are the three kinds of calamities—fire, water, and wind—and the three kinds of transformations of the sun, moon, and stars.
As for the "three realms of existence" (*trai-dhātuka*), they refer to the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm.

Third, regarding these three points, the fact that cause and effect do not perish is termed "existence" (*bhava*). Following the section on "proper governance," the following explains the six meanings of the True Dharma (*saddharma*), which are all established.
This is further divided into two parts. First, the formal explanation: "The one who presides over the army"—here, "presiding" means being the master;
the one who masters the army is the commander-in-chief, the leader. The commentary notes "and so forth," which may be understood by analogy with what preceded. Next, within this [section]...

Regarding the instruction to "contemplate the meaning" (思觀義) with the note "and so forth" (*yún yún*), this is intended to clarify the meaning of contemplating the mind, objects, and wisdom through the sixfold interpretation.
Since the subsequent section analyzes these by correlating the six meanings with the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, the contemplation of the mind, objects, and wisdom can thus be understood;
for this reason, the text merely provides the note "and so forth. Gusuan states that the object is able to give rise to wisdom, which is precisely what is meant by "Heavenly Protection" (*Tianhu*).
When wisdom and its object merge, this is the quality of the divine nature (*devabhāga*), for through the union of object and wisdom, one transforms from an ordinary being into a sage;
this is the empowerment of supernatural power (*ṛddhi-bala*), and thus this king is "half-divine" (*ardha-deva*). Furthermore, that the object can give rise to wisdom is the meaning of "parents";

that wisdom can destroy delusion is the meaning of "preventing evil"; and that through the union of object and wisdom, delusion is transformed into awakening, is the meaning of "attaining bliss. This...

The third [character] is half of a "king" (rāja), thus it is named "King. Furthermore, since the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* is entirely composed of metaphors for the Dharma, we know that these three do not go beyond the contemplation of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*):

the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) is "Gold," the contemplation of the radiant light (*prabhā-vipaśyanā*) is "Light," and the contemplation of the conventional (*parikalpita-vipaśyanā*) is "Radiance.
One may understand the six pairs, such as "Heavenly Protection" (*Devagupta*) and so forth, by applying them to the three contemplations. (And so on.)

Next, the analysis of the text is divided into two parts. First is the question: one should know that this question arises from the preceding explanation of the title, where it was stated that "this worldly goodness is fundamentally the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, for this treatise emerges from the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*. Now the question is asked:
"The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* is the basis of this treatise; what is its significance? Next, the answer beginning with "Furthermore, 'Heavenly One'" is divided into two parts.

The first section, which correctly elucidates the root of the treatise, is further divided into two parts. First, it explains the three meanings of "Heaven" (*deva*) by means of the term "half" (*ardha*).
The note stating "and so forth" (*ādi*) intends to point out that the phenomena themselves serve as metaphors;

because all phenomena are established from the groundless root (*amūla-pratiṣṭhita*), this world’s correct treatise proceeds from the fact that the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*—the profound, immeasurable, and inherently complete reality-body (*dharmatā*)—is fundamentally present.

This is merely the fundamental basis; therefore, one knows that the "correct discourse of the world" (*lokayātra*) is precisely the dharma that is established. It is said that only through the inherent presence of principle (*li*) can there be the functioning of phenomena (*shi*); this is what is meant.

Furthermore, regarding the sequence of "parents" and so forth, next, by means of the half-verse concerning the three meanings of a "human king," the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is shown as the parents.
One must know that the nature of phenomena possesses both the provisional (*upāya*) and the real (*bhūta-tathatā*); it is the provisional nature of phenomena that serves as...
The Father is the true *dharmatā* (the nature of reality), and the Mother is the provisional; the real wisdom is likewise to be understood accordingly.
Furthermore, one should understand that the *dharmatā* of provisional wisdom is the myriad distinctions of phenomena, which is precisely the "wondrous provisional" of the three thousand realms.

The *dharmatā* of real wisdom is quiescent and undifferentiated, which is precisely the "emptiness" where all things are extinguished and vanish. (And so forth. Following this, the next section provides a concluding indication: taking this as the foundation...
Because this *dharmatā* is the root of non-abiding, it is able to correctly establish discourse;

that is to say, both mundane correct discourse and supramundane correct discourse are simply the wholesome dharmas that are established. Now, regarding this correct discourse, its secondary matters must necessarily relate to the fundamental principle of *dharmatā*.
If they were not related, from what would this present correct discourse be established? Having been established, [it functions as such].

How could Dao-sheng’s view not be so? Since Gu-shan takes the orthodox discourse on transcending the world as his foundation, how can he reconcile this with what is said in the "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings":
"All worldly affairs performed and all worldly treatises composed, both mundane and supramundane, all derive from this sutra"?
Thus we know that those who do not understand matters mundane and supramundane fail to realize that they all proceed from the principle of this sutra.
[The text] stands upright.

Regarding the initial explanation of the title of the "Chapter on Good Accumulation" (Śubhasaṃcaya-parivarta), it is divided into two parts. First, the direct explanation, which is further divided into two. First, the direct explanation based on the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), which is further divided into...

The second part, the primary correct explanation, is further divided into two sections. First, a specific explanation of the two pāramitās of giving (*dāna*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), where "yá" (pronounced as either *yà* or *yú jī*) means the limit of water or the edge of a river.
Next, from "giving and wisdom" onwards, this serves as an illustration that the remaining pāramitās are likewise so. Following "from practice," the next section concludes the names of these six.
Subsequently, there is a conclusion based on the four *siddhāntas*, which is further divided into two parts; first, the conclusion that the six pāramitās are established.
Fourth, from here below, the four *siddhāntas* are successively established; following this chapter, the distinctions from the preceding section are analyzed. Regarding the note "and so forth":
it has already been clarified above that mundane right view moves heaven and earth; below, it will be explained in detail that supramundane right view moves the worthies and sages.
While the preceding formal discussion was not without reference to the supramundane, this current "Good Collection" [is specifically focused upon it].

It is not that the mundane does not exist; therefore, the preceding text states: "That which is correctly termed 'noble' (ārya) is of two kinds: first, the mundane noble; second, the supramundane noble.
Regarding the examination of names and realities, there are two types of examination: first, the examination of factual reality; second, the examination of logical reality.

The text is divided into two parts; next, the commentary on the chapter's text is explained in two sections: first, the division of the text, and second, the explanation of its meaning. This is further divided into two:

first, the prose section, and second, from the verse section downward, the explanation of the verses. The explanation of the textual passage is divided into two: first, the formal interpretation, which is further divided into two:

first, the division of the text, and second, the explanation of its meaning. The text is divided into two: first, a general clarification of the practice of giving as practiced on the causal stage, wherein one gives away precious jewels.

Regarding the phrase "giving away external wealth," giving up one's wife, children, and so forth constitutes giving away the "external body"; giving up one's own internal body constitutes giving away the "internal body.

Only when both the internal and external are given up can it be called "giving away body and life. Next, the explanation of the specific passage on the accumulation of merit through the giving of material wealth and the giving of the Dharma is divided into two parts:
first, the presentation of the outline; second, from the sixth line of the first section downward, the detailed explanation of the text, which consists of six parts. First:
Explanation of the Main Text: This section explains the Holy King’s Request for the Dharma in three parts. Regarding the Venerable One’s proclamation of the Sūtra:
"Cè" (廁) means "mixed," and "tián" (填) means "to fill or block. "Zéng" (繒)—pronounced *jílíng*—is a general term for silk fabrics. "Sāluó" (娑羅) is translated here as "firm and solid.
As for "joining palms and bowing to the seat," according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, whenever one intends to preach the Dharma, it is necessary to bow to the seat and sprinkle water upon it.
Scattering flowers is a way for those with future virtue to look up to and follow the sacred model; if one were to ascend directly [to the seat], it would surely contravene the ritual laws.
Therefore, one cannot cite the incident of the Śrāvakas prostrating at the seat in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* as a precedent for such censure.
*Mandārava* is translated here as "that which accords with the mind"; *Mañjūṣaka* is translated as "soft and supple," or alternatively as "small white," "small red," or "large white" and "large red."

The *Caturvidha-cakravarti-dāna-sūtra* states: "Xi-yi" (熈怡) means joy and delight. "Gui" (璝)—pronounced with the initial *gōng* and rhyme *huí*—is correctly written as "guī" (瑰) and is also written as "xiàng" (瓖);
it refers to a stone that ranks below jade. "Qi" (琦) refers to the color of jade; furthermore, "qi-wei" (琦瑋) means rare and precious.

"Wei" (瑋)—pronounced with the initials *yǔ*, *guǐ*, *yǐ*, or *guì* and rhymes with *èr*—refers to an ear-ring (*ērdāng* [耳璫]). "Ēr" (耳) should be written as "ěr" (珥); it refers to a pearl worn in the ear.
Fifth, the explanation that reconciles ancient and modern [teachings]. Sixth, the explanation that cites cause and effect to provide proof and exhortation.

Next, herein below, the basis for the accumulation of goodness is clarified; since the preceding text has already shown the basis of the primary treatise, it now clarifies the basis for the accumulation of goodness.
This section is divided into three parts; first, regarding the six perfections, it concerns the accumulation of the *pāramitās* and the "gold."
This is as previously explained: the pāramitās are the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), and that which is realized through the ultimate truth is the *dharmatā*, which is taken here as "gold.
Prajñā is wisdom (*jñāna*), while the other five perfections belong to merit (*puṇya*);
therefore, they are likened to "light. Next, regarding Ratnākara: the cave represents the basis of reliance, which is the *dharmatā*, taken here as "gold"; [and] the full moon.

Because Zhiyuan’s recitation is an external application, it corresponds to the "Light" (Guangming) and "Ears" (Er). Regarding the two persons, because one wishes to know that wisdom resides in speaking, speaking is taken as the light.
This concludes the explanation of the "Chapter on Ghosts and Spirits" (Shiguishenpin).

The initial explanation of the title of the chapter is divided into two parts. First, the direct explanation of the title: the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) cites the *Erya*, which states, "Ghost (*gui*) means 'return' (*gui*).
It further quotes the *Shizi*: "In antiquity, the dead were called 'those who have returned' (*guiren*). It also says, "The spirit of humans is called a ghost (*gui*);

the spirit of the earth is called *qi*; the spirit of heaven is called *ling*. Some say that "hunger" refers to the thought of being famished. In secular tradition, there was the elder brother of Ruan Ji.
Sun Dan, whose courtesy name was Qianli, consistently maintained the doctrine that there are no ghosts. Once, a guest arrived and the conversation turned to the matter of ghosts and spirits;
the guest, who was Li Ku, flushed with indignation and said, "Ghosts and spirits are acknowledged by the sages and worthies of all ages;
why do you claim they do not exist? I am a ghost myself! He then transformed his appearance and vanished. Sun’s father, Ruan Xian, had a nephew named Xiu, who likewise maintained this view.
The proponents of the theory that there are no ghosts said: "When a person dies, they become a ghost; why do you alone claim there are none? [The Master] replied:
"Suppose there is someone who claims to see a ghost wearing the clothes it wore while alive. If a person has ghosts, would their clothes also have ghosts? The proponents were thus confounded.
This was because the proponents did not understand that the ghost transforms into clothing to resemble what that person wore while alive. Although this is commonly said in the world...
Because they do not possess exhaustive knowledge, secular teachings perceive only a small portion of humans and animals and fail to see the other four realms of existence;
thus Confucius said, "If one has not yet understood life, how can one understand death? If one has not yet served humans, how can one serve ghosts?

This was not intended to deny the existence of ghosts. The *Liji* (Book of Rites), in its *Yueli* (Record of Music), states: "In the realm of clarity there are rites and music; in the realm of obscurity there are ghosts and spirits."
The *Shangshu* says: "The High Lord does not bestow his favor permanently; he sends down a hundred blessings upon those who do good, and a hundred calamities upon those who do evil.

The *Zhouyi* says: "The Great Man unites his virtue with Heaven and Earth, his brilliance with the sun and moon, his order with the four seasons, and his fortune and misfortune with the ghosts and spirits.
It further says: "Essential qi forms things; wandering souls undergo transformation."

Thus, one knows the nature and conditions of ghosts and spirits; since these are all textual passages from the masters of the Confucian tradition concerning ghosts and spirits, it cannot be said that ghosts and spirits do not exist.
Regarding the phrase "Asura" with the subsequent commentary, there are two meanings:
first, to distinguish that Asuras are subsumed within the realm of ghosts (*preta*); second, to cite the scriptural text to demonstrate the characteristics of what is to be feared.
Why is this? Because the asuras—here translated as "those who are not gods"—constantly engage in battle with the various devas and are frequently filled with fear.
Therefore, the *Buddhadhyānasamādhi-sūtra* states: "When the asuras fought with the Lord of Devas, a wheel of blades descended from the sky;
as the bodies and limbs of the asura hosts fell away, they were immediately struck with terror and fled into hiding."

As for the lotus fiber, this asura is categorized among the hungry ghosts (preta) and thus resides on the seashore; if categorized among the animals (tiryagyoni), he resides at the bottom of the ocean.

Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* speaks of four types of asuras: first, those who belong to the realm of hungry ghosts and, through the power of protecting the Dharma, attain supernatural powers to enter the air—this asura is born from an egg and is subsumed under the category of hungry ghosts; second, those who have declined in virtue within the heavenly realms.
First, those who dwell in places adjacent to the sun and moon where they are cast down and degraded; these asuras are born from a womb and are categorized within the human realm.
Second, those who possess the power to sustain the world, penetrate all things with fearlessness, and can contend for victory in battle against Brahmā and the various devas;
these asuras are born through transformation and are categorized within the celestial realms. Third, there are others who are inferior and distinct.
The asuras are born from the heart of the great ocean; these asuras are born from moisture and are categorized within the realm of animals.
The reason their abodes and palaces are so magnificently adorned is precisely because, in their past causes, they practiced the five constant virtues and the ten wholesome actions.
That they constantly delight in fighting and their fear is boundless is precisely because, in their past causes, they practiced suspicion, jealousy, and malice toward the virtuous and good.

In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is asked: "Why are there six realms of existence, yet elsewhere five are mentioned? The answer is that five hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, various schools emerged with differing divisions;
each took Buddhist sūtras and interpreted them according to their own tenets, thereby causing uncertainty as to whether the realm of asuras exists or not (and so forth).
As for "spirit" (*shen*), it means numinous power. The *Xici* commentary on the *Book of Changes* states: "That which cannot be measured in terms of yin and yang is called spirit."
This chapter generally adjudicates the following sections; as for the title "The Heaven Already Attained" (*yītiān*), the character "already" (*yǐ*) is an error and should be "already having" (*jì*).
"Already having" (*jì*) means "having already" (*yǐ*); this refers to the chapters on the Four Heavenly Kings and so forth.
This chapter is the third; next, the explanation of the text of this chapter is divided into two parts. First, the section on stating the intent and dividing the text;

second, from "Distinguishing by way of phenomena" onwards, the section on explaining the meaning according to the text. This [second] part is divided into two: first, the explanation of the long prose introduction, which is further divided into two.

First, the formal explanation, which is again divided into two: first, the explanation of the specific scriptural passages citing examples, from the beginning where the Buddha says "The Buddha told... up to "...the profound practice."
Since it is stated that the "three periods of time" constitute the objects of offering, these are distinct;

and since the offerings themselves are also diverse, the entities of the subject (the offerer) and the object (the offering) are fundamentally different, which is why they are said to be "distinct in terms of their phenomena. However, this distinction between phenomena is merely provisional.
Why? Because the sutra text states: "One desires to use inconceivable and wondrous articles of offering to make offerings to the Buddhas of the three periods of time."
World-Honored One, is it not the case that listening to the sutras is itself the sublime offering?
Therefore, the subsequent passage further clarifies the meaning of the "time of prediction" by re-explaining it; thus we know that this re-explanation is perfectly consistent with the sutra text.

That the sublime requisites for offering accord so well with the teaching on "listening to the sutras" shows there is indeed a profound reason for this re-explanation. Regarding the three Buddhas taken individually, they represent the three periods of time.
This refers to the profound sphere of practice of the two Buddhas, Retribution and Response; it is the Dharma-Buddha.

Since the scriptural text states, "and if one wishes to know this," it follows that the Dharma-Buddha exists separately from the three periods of time and the Buddhas of Retribution and Response, and thus they are established as distinct.

Therefore, the preceding passage explaining the "Chapter on Praise" says: "Vertically encompassing the three periods of time and horizontally encompassing the ten directions—the world and its directions are [the realms of] Retribution and Response."
The subtle and quiescent nature of these matters is, in fact, the general principle of the Dharmakāya.
If these three were to be viewed as either sequential or simultaneous, identical or distinct, they would merely constitute the separate [teachings] of the three Buddhas in this current text.

However, if they are neither sequential nor simultaneous, they constitute the perfect and wondrous [teaching], being essentially one and no different from the meaning of "perfect offering" in the subsequent text. Thus, what is here called "separate" is merely a provisional description for the time being. If...

The practice of ritual offerings is also distinct: one must offer material wealth to the *saṃbhogakāya* (the Responsive Buddha), offer the wisdom that can contemplate to the *dharmakāya* (the Dharma Buddha), and offer the object contemplated to the *nirmāṇakāya* (the Manifestation Buddha); thus, their accomplishment is likewise distinct.

Next, regarding the explanation of perfect offering (*pariṇāmanā-pūjā*), the scriptural passage from "At this time, that person... down to the end of the prose section constitutes it; this refers to listening to the sutra.

Regarding that which is the Dharma-offering: in the "Chapter on the Dharma-offering" of the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, Prince Candracchattra addressed the World-Honored One, saying, "Among all offerings, what is the Dharma-offering? The Buddha told Candracchattra:
"The Dharma-offering refers to the profound and subtle sūtras taught by the Buddhas; upon hearing such sūtras, one believes, understands, accepts, and upholds them. As for this method...
To diligently explain to sentient beings how to protect these teachings is called the "Dharma-offering.

Furthermore, to practice all dharmas according to the teaching, to abandon all false views, and to attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*)—this is called the supreme Dharma-offering.
Because this Dharma-offering is the highest among all offerings, the most excellent, the foremost, and peerless, for this reason...
One should honor the Buddha with the offering of the Dharma by listening to this sutra. As for this offering of the Dharma, how does one offer it?

One offers it to the Dharmakāya and the Nirmāṇakāya Buddhas. Therefore, one must know that the scriptures are the words that can explain; these words, in turn, contain both the expressive and the expressed.
Since the three [bodies] are not separate from words, one should know that it is simply by being able to listen to this scripture [that one makes the offering].

This means that making offerings to the three bodies in one essence (*trikāya-ekakāya*) is what is meant by "being able to revere," for it is also the reverence shown toward the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Regarding the statement that the three Buddhas who hear the sutra are explained solely in terms of this single essence:

since the *dharmakāya* Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods—who have attained fruition through cultivation—originally arise from hearing the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras, one knows that [the merit of] hearing [the Dharma is supreme].

The meaning of the note "and so forth" (*yún yún*) in the passage concerning the veneration of the single essence of the letters as the three Buddhas—which is also an offering to the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods who have attained fruition through cultivation—is as follows.
Furthermore, this section concerns the distinct and perfect offerings regarding phenomena;
it is merely a provisional treatment, which is why the note says "and so forth."
Furthermore, the subsequent section, "at another time," is a second explanation of the underlying intent.

This serves as a general explanation of the prose passage, wherein all four vows are unified as a single exhortation to listen to this sutra; it differs from the initial explanation which divided them into two sections.
Thus, one should know that this interpretation exhaustively reaches the profound purport of the scripture, as can be understood from the text itself without the need for further elaboration.

Next, the explanation of the verse text is divided into two parts: first, the introduction by the narrator of the sutra; second, the formal explanation of the verses. This latter section is further divided into two: first, the presentation of the outline;

second, the detailed explanation of the text following the phrase "If one desires... and so forth. This second part is further divided into two: first, the formal explanation; second, the translation of the names.
The first of these [the formal explanation] consists of six sections.
In the initial commentary on the long prose preceding the verse, the text cites "perfect subtlety" (*pariniṣpanna-sūkṣmatā*) to encourage practice, stating:
"If one enters this sutra, one enters the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*)," and so forth, up to: "Within this scripture, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, one shall behold me, Śākyamuni, and others.

As the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) states: "The Buddha has reached the ultimate realization of this dharma-nature; as such, the dharma-gate itself is the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*. Therefore, it possesses golden radiance."
If the Tathāgata Prabhāsa and others are thus [identical], why is he specifically named Śākya? It is because, from a particular perspective, he is Śākya;

yet from a universal perspective, he is named *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* (Golden Light), which is identical to all Buddhas. Therefore, the "Chapter on Praising the Buddha" states: "The body of the Tathāgata is golden and subtle.
If one were to say this is not so, how could the Sūtra state: "If one enters this sūtra, one immediately enters..."?
Is Śākyamuni seen within the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* of the Dharma-nature?

Next, the commentary explains that listening to this sūtra can dispel calamities and encourages its cultivation, stating: "Wherever one goes, even if there were a hundred *yojanas* filled with raging fires, one should pass through them.
The *Suvikrāntavikrāmī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* (or *Ratnarāśi-sūtra*) says: "Even if a great mass of fire were to fill..."
To traverse a hundred *yojanas* for the sake of hearing this King of Sūtras, enduring hardship without complaint, is precisely the meaning of sacrificing one’s body for the Dharma.
Third, the commentary cites the miraculous omens resulting from hearing the sūtra to encourage its practice, stating: "If this expounder of the Dharma... [if he descends to the lower realms].
That those in the assembly still see the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is because this sutra is constantly protected by the four Buddhas of the four directions,
the Buddhas of the ten directions always keep this sutra in mind, and all Bodhisattvas universally revere it; therefore,
those who listen to the sutra experience such spiritual portents.
The fourth explanation cites the power of listening to the sutra to encourage its practice. The text says "què" (却), which means "to retreat.
The *Hanyu Pian* states that it means "to guard. If written as the character "hàn" (悍), it is glossed as "fierce."

Regarding the fifth explanation concerning the passage on "raising [the voice] and listening" which states that it can attract devas, nāgas, spirits, and deities to encourage practice, Gushan (Gushan Zhiyuan) remarked:

"The phrase 'the scripture protects the four quarters' is followed by two lines—'there is a fundamental abundance' and 'may there be no calamities and one forever leave all suffering'—which were falsely added by later generations.
He further noted: "The scripture says: *sattva-kilidha-he-ba-he-āgaba-ra-maga*."
The four lines concerning Aṅgulimāla were also added later by someone else. Now, it is said that if one takes the three phrases—
“Caṇḍa Caṇḍālī” (the Great Ghost Woman), “Kūṣmāṇḍī Kūṣmāṇḍī,” and “Dantī”— as a single line, then the four lines beginning with “Tahī Pahī” must be removed,
and only the two lines beginning with “Mā bhavatu vyasanam” (May there be no calamity) should remain for this to be correct.
The forty-nine and a half verses of the sutra state: "Let these sentient beings..."—the two characters "let these" (*liè shì*) are merely terms used for reference.
*Yama-ra* is also called *Yama-rāja*; this is translated as "Twin Kings" (*shuāng wáng*). This is because both the elder brother and the younger sister serve as lords of the hells;
the brother governs the affairs of men, while the sister governs the affairs of women, hence they are called the Twin Kings. Furthermore, [it refers to] suffering and pleasure...
The pair together is also called "the twins. Nārāyaṇa is translated here as "the Wrestler with the Hook and Chain.
Nanda is translated as "Joy," and Upananda as "Worthy Joy"; these two brothers are dragons who bring rain and wind according to the proper seasons, thereby causing people to rejoice.
"Worthy" (*xian*) refers to their nature being both virtuous and excellent. Vemacitra is translated as "Pure Mind. (From the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*).

Translated [into Chinese], he is called *Hǎnggāo* (Echo-Lofty); he is also said to dwell in caves (*xuéjū*). The correct transcription is *Vemacitra*, which means "Exhausting the Variegated" (*qǐjìn*), or alternatively "Jeweled Ornament" (*bǎoshì*).
He is the father of Śacī, the consort of Śakra; his name is *Kharaskandha*, meaning "Broad Shoulders" (*guǎngjiānjiǎ*).

Among the six classes of non-humans, he is renowned for listening to the sutras and being able to bring peace and happiness to the land, thereby encouraging practitioners to cultivate the path. He acts for the sake of all sentient beings.
From the end of the preceding section, there are twenty-seven [verses] that attain increase;

however, fearing that there may be a surplus, if one includes the two lines "the immeasurable merits as described above," there would be twenty-seven and a half lines. Please examine this further. Regarding the note "and so forth" (云云):
because all six sections of this verse-text take listening to the sutra as their foundation, they are able to ward off calamities and even bring peace and happiness to the state.
Furthermore, these verses merely elaborate upon the merit of listening to the sūtra as set forth in the prose.

The sūtra says "fēnfù" (馇馥), which may also be written as "pójì fēnfù" (馝馚); both refer to fragrance. "Yùn" (馩) [pronounced fēn] and "yún" (馧) [pronounced yúnyún] describe the intensity of such fragrance.
"Xié" (斜) means not upright; "lì" (戾) means crooked. "Utpala" and so forth refer to the various colors, such as blue, red, yellow, and white.
The four are the colored lotuses.
Regarding the subsequent section on the translation of names for *gūdō* (sorcery), Guishan suspects that this passage concerning the translated names was added by later generations (*unspecified*).
As for the phrase "due to omissions and so forth," this explains the first section of eleven lines of verse; the preceding prose commentary can only serve as a basis for listening to the sutra.

This passage cites the perfect and wondrous [nature of reality] to encourage practice; it is able to cause all sentient beings to attain liberation and cross over the great ocean of suffering and existence.
Why is this? It is because the phrase "liberation from suffering" necessarily implies crossing over and being delivered from the three obstacles.

The first part of the "Explanation of the Chapter on Bestowing Prophecies" (Shi Shouji Pin) explains the title of the chapter in two sections. First, regarding the brief indication: there are four kinds of prophecies in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, and the present [text] is subsumed under two of these.
The note "and so forth" (yun yun) is intended to cite the four kinds of prophecies from the *Śūraṅgama* to provide a clear illustration.

The present sutra is intended to be subsumed under these two categories; however, regarding the four types of prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) cited in the *Fahua wenju* and the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra-ṭīkā*, there are not a few differences and similarities.
Why is this? The *Fahua wenju* states: first, prediction for those who have not yet resolved their minds;

second, prediction for those who have resolved their minds; third, prediction in the presence [of the Buddha]; and fourth, prediction of non-arising (*anutpāda*). If one refers to the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra-ṭīkā*:

The second is called the "Secret Prediction" (guhyavyākaraṇa); the rest is the same as in the *Wenju* (Explanations of the Words) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. However, if one follows that sūtra, where the Buddha tells Dṛḍhamati:
"There are four kinds of those who receive predictions. What are the four? There are those who have not yet aroused the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) and yet are granted a prediction;
because there are sentient beings wandering through the six realms who are born among humans and take delight in the Buddha-dharma for more than a hundred thousand [eons]."

Some must first resolve their minds [on enlightenment], pass through incalculable *kalpas* (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) practicing the bodhisattva path, making offerings to Buddhas and benefiting sentient beings throughout those kalpas, before they shall attain *bodhi*.

(And so forth. There are those who, upon first resolving their minds, are immediately granted a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). These individuals have planted various roots of goodness over long kalpas and have taken delight in the Great Dharma;

thus, as soon as they resolve their minds, they abide in the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*). For this reason, their resolution of mind is accompanied by a prediction. (And so forth. There are...
Regarding "secret prediction" (*guhyavyākaraṇa*): there may be a bodhisattva who, though never having received a prediction, has practiced the six perfections until their merit is fully perfected.
The devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings all think to themselves, "When will this bodhisattva attain enlightenment? The Buddha cuts through this doubt and grants him a prediction;

the entire assembly knows it, yet this single bodhisattva alone does not know it (and so forth). There are also those who have attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*) and manifest it.
The "prior prediction" refers to that which is bestowed in the presence of the great assembly upon one who has attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti),

and so forth. Thus, while the *Fahua wenju* omits the third "secret prediction," and the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-śūtra-ṭīkā* omits the second "prediction upon the initial arousal of the mind," both the *Fahua wenju* and the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-śūtra-ṭīkā* include the fourth [category], the "prediction of non-arising."
The single category of "manifest" (pratyakṣa) prediction is divided into the third and fourth types; this is likely an error.

Nevertheless, the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary on the *Mohe Zhiguan*) also cites the four types of prediction from the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, where the names of the first three predictions are identical to those in the sutra, though it omits the two characters "manifest" (xianqian) for the fourth. From this, we know that this text refers to the "present."

If these two types are compared with the *Fahua wenju* (Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra), they correspond to the third, "manifest" (*xiànqián*), and the fourth, "non-arising" (*wúshēng*) of the four kinds of prediction (*jì*).
This is likely an error; it should rather be stated that this present bestowal of prediction, among the four kinds of prediction in the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, is precisely the fourth:
obtaining the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and receiving the prediction in the presence of the great assembly. Thus, [it is] sixteen.

The *Contemplation Sūtra* states: "Having attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), they receive a prediction [of enlightenment] before their eyes; this is fully explained within the discourse on rebirth" (and so forth).

Both Gusuan and Siming both maintain that the two types of prediction mentioned in the present text refer to the prediction for those who have merely resolved their minds (*cittotpāda*) and the prediction for those who have attained the patience of non-arising.
This is because they had not thoroughly investigated the various texts; the citations from the sūtras they provide differ slightly from the actual sūtras. (And so forth.)

Regarding the next section, which explains the definition of "bestowing" (*śāsana*): The *Fahua Wenju* (Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra) further states that "bestowing a prediction" (*jueji*) is also called "receiving a prediction" (*shouji*), "receiving a decision" (*shoujue*), or "receiving a prophecy" (*shoubie*).

"Bestowing" (*shou*) has the meaning of giving; "receiving" (*shou*) has the meaning of obtaining; "prediction" (*ji*) means recording an event; "decision" (*jue*) means determination; and "prophecy" (*bie*) means a clear revelation.
One should know that herein it refers specifically to bestowing a prediction upon the eightfold body of marks (*aṣṭalakṣaṇakāya*). This is conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
Therefore, because it records the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it does not discuss the bestowal of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*) [and so forth].

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* refers to a bodhisattva as a "Great Being" (*mahāsattva*) and also calls them an "Opening Being" (*kaishi*) [and so forth]. *Bie* (莂) should be written as *bie* (別), meaning "to distinguish.

This is for the purpose of circulation. Next, the text of the chapter is explained, which is divided into two parts; first, the intention is stated, followed by the division of the text and the citation of the headings.

Regarding the "practice of the sūtras" and so forth: in the preceding Praise Chapter (*Stutiparivarta*), the causes for practicing the sūtras were presented through the example of the Golden Dragon King (*Suvarṇanāgarāja*) praising the Buddha and making vows in the past;

subsequently, in the Flowing Water Chapter (*Jalavāhana-parivarta*), the causes for practicing the sūtras were presented through the example of ten thousand devaputras who, having previously been fish, heard the most profound and wondrous Dharma.
These acts will soon lead to the attainment of the ultimate fruit (*phala*). As for this "ultimate fruit," it refers to that which is imminent.

Since the initial stage of abiding in the fruits [of the path] is far removed from the ultimate fruit of wondrous enlightenment, this is cited to prove that the merit of expounding and upholding the sutra does not go to waste, thereby encouraging people of today to emulate the Great Being and circulate the Mahayana *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*.

First, regarding the "conditions" (*pratyaya*), the following section explains the meaning according to the text, which is divided into two parts. First, the explanation of the "bestowal of records" (*vyākaraṇa-dāna*), which is further divided into two parts. First...

The commentary on the bestowal of predictions upon the three great bodhisattvas is further divided into two parts. First, regarding the assembly of those with common conditions (*samanvāgata-pratyaya*):
this refers specifically to the ten thousand devaputras who came from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to constitute that assembly of those with common conditions.

Siming (Siyi) states: "The past common conditions are not mentioned in this sutra; they may be found in another sutra" (and so forth). However, the textual passage in the "Chapter on Praise" asks: "All vows..."
Why did [the Buddha] not grant a prediction? He answered by referring to his future dharma-companions;

it will not be long before they arrive, specifically referring here to the ten thousand devaputras from the Trāyastriṃśa heaven who have come as dharma-companions and gathered together with those of similar affinity. Because the fourth [master] did not understand this, he fell into error.
Next, following the section "Second, the actual granting," the commentary on the actual bestowal of the prediction states that one should discuss four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Among these, the first is that which changes its designation while its substance does not change; this is like the world described in the present sutra, which at that time changed its name to "Pure Banner" (*Vimaladhvaja*), yet it was merely a change of the land's name, with no alteration to the substance of the land itself. The second is that which does not change the substance of the land, but changes [its designation];
this is like the ancient Śākyamuni taking the name "Sahā" for his land, and the present Buddha does likewise—this refers to the current designation of the land.
Without changing [the essence], the substance of the land undergoes transformation through formation and decay. In the third case, both name and substance transform together;
for example, when Avalokiteśvara observes Amitābha’s land, its name is transformed into "that which is accomplished by all precious jewels"—this is the transformation of the name.
All its adornments are superior to the realm of Sukhāvatī—this is the transformation of the substance. If the substance did not transform, why would it be ten times [superior]?

Is it superior to the Land of Ultimate Bliss? In four cases, both the substance and the name do not change, as in this present sutra where the second son’s world, Silver Light, has names identical to their original forms.
If one looks back at the world of Gold Illumination belonging to Faith-Aspect, then the name has changed;

yet if one looks back at the world of Silver Aspect, both are named Pure Banner—how could this not be a case where both the name and the land do not change? For now, we shall follow the perspective of Gold Illumination.

Because the world-system is renamed "Pure Banner" (*Vimaladhvaja*), it is said that this is the first among them. If one follows the world-system of the second son, "Silver Light," its name remains unchanged from the original;

including the former, it should be stated that this is the second. According to the *Fahua wenju* (Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra), regarding the passage on Śāriputra attaining the eight marks and preaching the sutra, there are ten points; here, they are briefly correlated one by one.
1. Regarding the *kalpa*: it is now said that in a future age, after immeasurable [eons]. 2. Regarding the two types of causal practices:

the text here is deficient because they were already explained in the previous "Chapter on Praise. 3. Regarding the attainment of the fruit: it is now said that one shall attain *samyak-saṃbodhi*. 4. Regarding the land:
