From the words "O virtuous daughter" downward, the sixth section explains the passage on "knowing and universally treating," which is divided into two parts: first, the heading that outlines the categories;

second, the detailed explanation of the text, which is further divided into two parts. First, the formal explanation, which is again divided into two: first, explaining the lightness of the illness, [whereby] upon hearing the teaching, immediately...

Regarding the passage beginning with "The sequence for treating serious illnesses through heavy medication and prescriptions to eliminate demonic afflictions (*nōju*), etc.," there are two intentions:

first, as explained below, it is an interpretation based on the contemplation of the mind; second, it is intended to lead into the texts of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight). Why is this?

Within that *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*, regarding the objective realm of illness, it quotes the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*: "Upon merely hearing these words, the illness is immediately cured. This is precisely the meaning of the initial contemplation. Furthermore—

There are those with deep-seated and difficult-to-cure illnesses who go to a physician to have various medicines compounded; once the illness is cured, this corresponds to the latter nine contemplations.
Regarding the meaning of the *Fuxing* (Explanatory Notes): the first meaning is a metaphor for hearing the inconceivable realm and attaining entry into the First Stage (*prathama-bhūmi*);

the subsequent meaning is a metaphor for everything from the arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) up to the departure from craving, which likewise constitutes entry into the First Stage—even if one has not yet entered that rank, one attains entry into the fifth [stage].
The title of this chapter is "Minor Elimination of Differences.
Next, regarding the text on contemplating the mind, it is divided into six sections: first, clarifying the medicine and the disease; second, clarifying the faith in the Dharma;

third, clarifying the timing; fourth, clarifying increase and decrease; fifth, clarifying transgressions and contacts; sixth, clarifying the treatment and the cultivation of *vitarka* and *vicāra*. The phrase "details as noted below" refers to this.

There are also two meanings: first, that the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) remedies anger and so forth, as explained in detail in the *Zhiguan Duiji Zhukai* (The Counteractive Aids for Opening the Practice of Calming and Contemplation);
second, that this mind of loving-kindness remedies anger and so forth, as Zhanran stated: "The five grades are the skillful means (*upāya*) of the Perfect [Teaching].

Judging from the Small [Vehicle] in relation to the Great, they correspond to the five cessations (*pañca-nivāraṇa-pratipakṣa*) of the Tripitaka; specifically, the first grade, 'Rejoicing,' corresponds to the Perfect Teaching’s cessation through the mind of loving-kindness."

The method for treating the third grade of envy within the Dharma-realm is the practice of *ānāpāna-smṛti* (counting the breath) and the stabilization of the mind according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjia*), which universally treats the three grades of applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*) within the Dharma-realm.

The method for treating the fourth grade of delusion regarding self and others within the Dharma-realm is the practice of preaching the Dharma according to the Perfect Teaching, which stabilizes the mind through the principle of *pratītyasamutpāda* (dependent origination) and universally treats the four grades of delusion regarding self and others within the Dharma-realm.

Furthermore, the simultaneous practice of the six *pāramitās* according to the Perfect Teaching is the practice of *aśubha-bhāvanā* (contemplation of impurity), which serves as the first name for the stabilization of the mind against the six hindrances (*ṣat-kleśāvaraṇa*).
If one abandons greed, then both the cause of desire and the fruit of desire are abandoned. Because they are abandoned, there is no longer a retributive body; it is neither pure nor impure.
The five grades of correct practice and the six perfections are the nianfo (Buddha-recollection) of the Perfect Teaching.

When the mind is stilled during the practice of the six perfections, phenomena and principle do not obstruct one another, and thus no hindrance can be discussed. The general meaning is as follows... (etc.). Discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*) are distraction.

Furthermore, coarse mind is called *vitarka* (applied thought) and subtle mind is called *vicāra* (sustained thought); because there are these coarse and subtle states of mind, they constitute distraction.

In the initial commentary on the title of the "Flowing Water" chapter, the text is divided into two parts; first, the commentary on the title of the chapter is divided into four sections, the first of which is the "double indication," meaning the pointing to the text.
"Yunye and Shui" refers to the next section, which provides a dual explanation of the text in two parts: first, the explanation of "bestowing water," and second, the explanation of "flowing water.

Regarding the term "three refuges" (*triśaraṇa*), although there is no explicit textual mention of the three refuges in the sutra, they must logically be present according to the underlying meaning; this is why it is so stated.
This is because one must first take refuge in the sequence before the Dharma can be preached. Siming states that although the version by Baoshan Chanshi lacks the word "most" (*zui*).

The *Jingwang jing* (Sūtra on the Victorious King) contains the most excellent king; as for the *Weijian wen* (Text on What Has Not Yet Been Seen), I fear it is a mistaken reference by the Four Ming Masters.

Furthermore, "bestowing the Three Refuges" is a general enumeration, while "explaining the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination" is a specific enumeration of the Dharma Jewel, and "invoking the Ten Epithets" is a specific enumeration of the Buddha Jewel.
Since the Buddha and the Dharma already exist, how could there not be the Sangha Jewel? Moreover, the three jewels of one essence are themselves one.
Thus, the three [aspects] are themselves the true Three Refuges. Please, Father, descend. The section on resolving doubts regarding the four pairs of knots has two parts:

first, the doubt; second, the resolution within the text. As for the resolution: since the scriptural passage clearly establishes the meaning of "bestowing water" by naming you "Flowing Water" (*Liushui*), it further states that there are two conditions for being named "Flowing Water": first, the ability to flow; second, the ability to...
Since the two conditions of "with water" (*sajala*) and "mountain" (*parvata*) are both designated as *jalaprabha*, the title of the chapter need only employ the term *jalaprabha*.
This naturally encompasses the meaning of "with water," so there is no need for further elaboration; thus, the two meanings of "water" and "with water" are simultaneously revealed.
Were it not for the skillful arrangement of the one who produced the scripture, how could a title have been established that so comprehensively includes [the meaning]?
Next, regarding the explanation of the ten meanings of the "Elder’s Son" (*śreṣṭhiputra*) in the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra), the *Wenju* (Textual Exegesis) states:
"An elder of the world is endowed with ten virtues: first, noble lineage; second, high status; third, great wealth;

fourth, majesty and power; fifth, profound wisdom; sixth, advanced age; seventh, pure conduct; eighth, complete etiquette; ninth, praised by those above; and tenth, sought after by those below. These are explained in detail as follows.

He says (and so forth). This passage is for the purpose of severing doubts; next, the text of the chapter is explained in three parts. First, the explanation of the third section, "The Proximity," is divided into two:

first, the division of the text into one line of verse on the grace [of the teacher], and next, the word-by-word commentary on the text, which is itself divided into two: first, the explanation of the introductory phrase (*praṇāma*).
This section has two parts: first, an explanation of practicing kindness and spreading virtue; second, an explanation of the people’s praise as recorded in the scripture.
From the passage beginning with "Respected" (*satkṛta*) onwards, this is the praise offered by the people of the country for the son of the elder.

Specifically, it refers to how the people of the country respect and revere this son of the elder, and further utter words of admiration such as "Excellent! (*sādhu*). Next, [the following] is explained.
The immediate proximity [of the text] is divided into two parts: first, the headings of the sections; second, the detailed explanation of the text below. This section has three parts:

first, the explanation of the retinue, which refers to his wife, children, and so forth; second, the explanation of the circumstances of seeing the fish—"circumstances" (yuan) here meaning "causes" (you);

third, the explanation of leading his two sons to travel sequentially through cities and towns, which concludes with the scriptural passage stating that there were many fish before the matter was completed.
Regarding the cause of the fish’s condition: it is parched because the water has run dry; it is like wood that has withered and decayed, and for this reason it is called "parched.
Third, the correct interpretation and resolution of the *Sūtra on Saving the Fish* follows the passage beginning:

"At that time, the son of the elder, having seen these fish, gave rise to a heart of great compassion... As for "determining the reality according to the name," it means one should follow the name "flowing water."
This is to ascertain whether the fish is truly in the water; if it were not so, would it not be a mere empty name for "flowing water"?
The term "jǐ suǒ" (幾所) means "how much" or "to what extent. *Pù* (曝)—pronounced *bào*—is correctly written as *bào* (暴), meaning to dry or wither.

*Wǎn zhuǎn* (宛轉)—*wǎn* is correctly written as *wàn* (踠) or *yǎn* (㣿)—refers to the body being bent and twisted. Therefore, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* (The Most Victorious King Sutra) states: [text follows].
This character "bi" (夕*匕) refers to the turning of the body in a circular motion. Regarding "shady and cool": the character for "yin" (陰) should be explained as derived from "grass";
the *Shuowen Jiezi* states that it means "the shade cast by grass upon the ground. "Pu" (薄故切) means to seize; "jue" (古穴切) means to flow forth. The *Beishi* states:

"In times of drought, [water] is released from the dikes to become rain; in times of flood, it enters the channels and ditches. Thus, above there is no worry regarding the lack of clouds or stars, and below there is no suffering from darkness or inundation."

The character 墊 (dù niàn; also pronounced xué, qū jué) means "to bore through. The character 廐 (jiù; jū yòu) means "a collection," specifically the place where elephants and horses are gathered, that is, the stables for elephants and horses.

The character 盛 (shèng; pinyin: chéng) [is used here]. The characters 彷徉 (fáng yáng; upper radical: fú fāng; lower radical: yǐ zhāng) mean "to loiter" or "to wander about. They refer to pacing back and forth.

Next, the explanation of the fourth section, the text on the formal conclusion of the connection, is divided into two parts: first, the analysis of the text; second, the word-by-word commentary, which consists of four sections.
First is the making of the vow, which is the vow to bestow the food of the Dharma in future ages.
Second is the contemplation regarding the preaching of the Dharma, beginning from the phrase "once again he contemplated" and ending with the passage "he preached the profound and wondrous Dharma."
The third is the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (or *Saṃyukta-āgama*); its textual passage beginning from "Having reflected thus, he immediately entered the water," and so forth, is this very sūtra.

Since this sūtra is subsumed within the Vaipulya (Vaipulya-piṭaka), the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination must encompass the meanings of the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, Bodhisattva, and Perfect (Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, Bodhisattva, and Perfect) teachings.
Furthermore, since the *Xuan-yi* (Profound Meaning) judges this sūtra to belong to the Shared Teaching (Pratyekabuddha), it necessarily carries [the implications of] the other three.

Because the section on "Clarifying Perfection" separately explains it, the twelve links of dependent origination can be understood by applying this principle to the classification of teachings (*jiaopan*). Only in this way is the profound and wondrous Dharma revealed.
Furthermore, as the preceding text states, "When reading and reciting Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras, one should reflect upon them thoroughly.

Regarding the passage on the Fish Repaying its Kindness, it is divided into four parts; the fourth part explains the fish’s transformation of its rebirth into heaven to repay its debt of gratitude through offerings. This section is further divided into two.
The first section consists of the textual analysis, followed by the word-by-word commentary, which is divided into four parts.

First, the *Sūtra on the Fish Changing Its Rebirth and Being Born in Heaven* begins from the passage "Good Woman, descend" and concludes with "Having ended its life, it was born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Regarding the repayment of kindness (*pratīkāra*), there are two meanings.
Next, the commentary on the passage where the deity repays its kindness and descends to the earth begins from "Having been born in heaven... and continues as follows:
The passage following "having reflected" refers to this. It is understandable that water belongs to the category of material things (*vastu*) for consumption;

likewise, the ten titles based on causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-daśa-nāmadheya*) also belong to the category of material things, because these ten titles and so forth all pertain to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).

Since water and the other three [elements] already belong to the category of material things, it is therefore appropriate to repay their kindness with forty thousand pearls, let alone for the previous vow one made.
Since it is said that one shall bestow the food of Dharma in the future, if this were not based on principle, what would constitute the "food of Dharma"?

Therefore, it is by recourse to principle that the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* cites the bestowing of food to enable others to obtain life, thereby manifesting permanence; for without food, life does not persist.
Thus, obtaining life manifests the quality of permanence. Since *nirvāṇa* is a state of peace and bliss, one thereby obtains bliss.
This is because although one has attained *nirvāṇa*, if one has not yet realized it or attained mastery over it, the realization itself is designated as the virtue of "self.
Since seeking wealth in accordance with the Dharma is free from defilement, it is called "pure"; thus, the matter of receiving food represents these four virtues.

For this reason, the devas offered forty thousand pearls to repay for the virtues of permanence (*nitya*), bliss (*sukha*), self (*ātman*), and purity (*śubha*). Since the offering of food is likewise so, [the same principle applies].
The remaining three cases are to be understood by analogy. Thus, these four types all pertain to both phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*tattva*).
For the sake of convenience in this text, the four virtues are illustrated through the act of giving food. The Sūtra states that a "pavilion" (*lǒu*) refers to a multi-storied building.
When the Three Kings saw the light and inquired about the omen, the Four Enlightened Elders provided a definitive answer. "Inquiry" (*zhēng*) means to summon or to verify.
This means that he dispatched his son to investigate the matter and report back with the facts.

Fifth, the final three sections resolve the connection between the past and the present by addressing those who doubt the number of fish; they do so by identifying the Buddha of the present as the Elder Son of the Flowing Water (Śrotas-udgata) of the past.
Thus, there are distinct doubts and resolutions for both the present and the past. As for the question, "Which Buddha was the Elder in the past? [the answer follows].
The son had already doubted the number of fish, yet the tree deity examined and determined it for him;

now the tree deity doubts that the shallow was recorded as deep, so the Buddha explains that there is a wondrous causal connection. Since the past and present are interrelated, they must be brought together [in conclusion].
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* (The Most Victorious King Sūtra) brings together the ancient and the modern slightly differently; thus, that sūtra says: "The Elder Stream-Water..."
The son was none other than my own self; the Elder Jālinīprabha was the Wondrous Banner (Miaochuang), who is now the one known as Xinsiang in this sutra.
Those two sons were the present-day Silver Banner (Yindang) and Silver Light (Yinguang), who are now the ones known as Yinxiang and Yinguang in this sutra.
That King Divaukasaprabha was the present-day Bodhi-tree deity, and those ten thousand fish were the ten thousand devaputras.

The first section, "Explaining the Title of the Chapter on Relinquishing the Body," is divided into two parts. First, regarding the questioner’s inquiry: the meaning of "relinquishment" (*tyāga*) is manifold;

it refers to the wealth of the six sense-objects, as well as high-ranking positions and even one's life-span. Why, then, does the title of this specific chapter refer exclusively to "relinquishing the body"?
That which is appropriate to the name is its primary subject. Here, from the following, the meaning of the title is explained:

this chapter is titled "Relinquishing the Body" (*sheshen*) precisely because it takes the principal and essential point as its designation. This is because for the recipient—the tigress pressed by hunger—only the flesh of the body was required;
other wealth, status, and so forth were not what was essential. Moreover, for the donor, the very act of relinquishing the body was the primary means to save the starving tigress.
Since other assets, status, and so forth are likewise relinquished incidentally, the title of this chapter refers only to the primary act, speaking simply of "relinquishing the body.

The subsequent text serves as an explanation for the following; it is divided into two parts: first, the division of the text, and second, the word-by-word commentary, which consists of four sections.
The initial explanation of the tree spirit questioning the "small person" refers to the people within the kingdom; the "small insects" refer to the fish within the pond.

The "two generations" refer to the present and the future. As for the calamity befalling the people and the hunger of the fish, they all obtain present peace and happiness and satiety, and in the future, they are born in heaven, freed from suffering, and receive a prediction [of enlightenment];
therefore, it is called "benefit. *Yun* (pronounced *yu min*) means to perish. If one is merely deluded...

How can the subsequent text—wherein contemplation, understanding, vows, and practice support one another—clarify the matter of how profound resonance and ultimate accord arise from practicing suffering to achieve a joyful fruit?
The *Wenju ji* (Record of the Textual Phrases) states: "By means of non-dual contemplation, one contemplates the non-dual object, accomplishes non-dual practice, and realizes non-dual emptiness.
When contemplating in this way, suffering becomes the Dharma-realm; if it were otherwise, it would merely constitute [a limited attainment]."

Regarding fruitless ascetic practices, the Buddha offered earnest admonitions that one should truly first consider why one would throw oneself from a cliff—only to invite the censure of outsiders—or enter fire—only to incur the ridicule of the inner assembly.
This is surely because internally there is rational contemplation and externally there is a clear understanding of one's aspirations.
Thus, it was through this that Jvalamukha dispelled Sudhana’s doubts and Nirgrantha gave rise to the realization of Ugra. This is most profound.

Discussing his practice of the Way: only when one’s mind is focused on what is correct can right conduct and right wisdom be realized; erroneous matters and wrong practices must not be abandoned, nor should wisdom be lost.

Thus, those of later generations shall not forfeit the benefits of the Dharma (and so forth). As for the phrase "speaking briefly" in the Sūtra, it is, for example, like the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* saying, "I pray that you will explain it briefly."

Next, the explanation of the Tathāgata’s response is divided into two parts. First, the analysis of the text; second, the word-by-word commentary. Regarding the first, the analysis of the text, it is divided into ten sections.
First, the explanation of the emergence of the earth and the stūpas. The *Sūtra on the Emergence of the Earth and Stūpas* speaks of "supernormal power" (*ṛddhi*).

The *Abhidharmadharmaskandhapāda-śāstra* states that its wondrous function is difficult to fathom, hence it is called "supernormal" (*ṛddhi*); because it can serve as a basis for that [function], it is called "power" (*pāda*). The Buddha possesses [this].

The four bases of supernatural power (*ṛddhipāda*) are: first, the base of supernatural power consisting in the practice of concentration on the meditative absorption of mastery; second, the base of supernatural power consisting in the practice of concentration on the mind;

third, the base of supernatural power consisting in the practice of concentration on diligence; and fourth, the base of supernatural power consisting in the practice of concentration on ethical discipline.

A detailed explanation is provided in full in the *Daibu Buzhu* (Supplementary Notes to the Great Section), etc. Regarding the "sixfold earthquake," the term "sixfold" refers collectively to the various forms and sounds [of the trembling].
Third, as for "shaking" (*kaṃpana*), this is one of the three categories—form and sound—listed separately.
Regarding the six types: first, shaking; second, roaring; third, awakening—these three are sounds. Fourth, moving; fifth, rising; sixth, surging—these three are forms.

Within the first [category of shaking], there are again three: namely, shaking, pervasive shaking, and so forth. Shaking, universal shaking, and direct shaking constitute "shaking"; shaking the four continents constitutes "pervasive shaking."

The "movement" [of the earth] refers to the Great Trichiliocosm shaking; "equal movement" and "universal movement" are likewise applied to the other five [directions], totaling eighteen types, which manifest the purity of the eighteen dhātus.
As for *stūpa*, it is fully called *stūpa* or *thūpa*; this translates as "square mound," "spiritual temple," or "caitya. Regarding the "bodiless one":
since this stūpa contains śarīra (relics), it is not a caitya, because a caitya is... [without relics].

The term *śarīra* is translated as "bone-body" (*asthi-śarīra*). In the *Ekottarika Āgama*, after the Buddha had personally held up a *śarīra* in his hand and praised it extensively, he commanded that a *stūpa* be erected at a crossroads.
The Buddha said: "Four types of persons should have towers erected for them: namely, a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), an Arhat, a Pratyekabuddha, and a Tathāgata.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The height of a Tathāgata’s stūpa shall be thirteen stories; that of a Pratyekabuddha, ten."

The Arhat is the first stage; the Wheel-Turning King is the fourth stage; the Tathāgata is beyond all stages. Why is this? Because [the others] have not yet emerged from the suffering of the three realms of existence.

When a Tathāgata appears in the world, out of compassion for sentient beings, he awakens to the Dharma through its causes and conditions and penetrates deeply into the nature of phenomena, thereby serving as a field of merit for humans and devas.
An Arhat has exhausted the conditions for rebirth and can serve as a field of merit for the world. A Wheel-Turning King... [is likewise a field of merit].

The King transformed sentient beings through the ten wholesome paths; for this reason, one ought to erect stupas and make offerings. Regarding the *Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination*, there are eight types of stupas, all of which possess a *āmalaka* (exposed canopy).
A Buddha-stupa has eight tiers; a Bodhisattva-stupa has seven; a Pratyekabuddha-stupa has six; the fruit of Arhatship has five;
the fruit of Non-returning has four; the fruit of Once-returning has three; and the fruit of Stream-entry has two. A Wheel-turning King [has one]; an ordinary monk likewise [has one]. However...

The world has not yet reached the level of the "fire-jewel" atop the plantain leaf; how could those who have not attained even the first fruit (srotāpanna) dare to equal the Universal Monarch (cakravartin)?
After his passing, they build stupas without knowing whether they have made progress or not; whatever they do, they invariably reach three, five, seven, or nine tiers.

Even if the modern structures are called "square mounds," the fact that they are carried on shoulders still results in a single tier. Though the ignorant may be dim-sighted, is this not a dark perversion of the first fruit?
There are those who, beside square mounds, claim they are constructing merit-dedication stupas; their understanding of the meaning is lost.

This causes the ignorant to worship only our own teachers, or even to bow to the lowly while facing the high. Furthermore, when the honorable and the humble are placed side by side, it creates an improper and inconvenient situation that cannot be fully discussed.
If one makes offerings to the relics of the Buddha, the merit belongs to humans and devas; if one offers to ordinary material objects, it is difficult for such an act to produce merit.

1. Regarding the statement that "the virtuous follow it and should not conform to worldly customs": this sutra is now the manifestation of a precious stupa containing the relics of a Great Being (Mahāsattva).

2. Regarding the second explanation concerning the great assembly of Śākyas giving rise to doubt: since the sutra text states they "gave rise to a rare mind," we know this refers precisely to the arising of doubting thoughts.

3. Regarding the third explanation of the Buddha rising to pay homage: since the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that when a Śrāvaka enters meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there is [no movement].
It has been taught that when a Buddha is in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he is able both to preach the Dharma and to travel;

therefore, in this present sutra, in the "Introductory Chapter" (*Nidāna-parivarta*), the Buddha dwells in the wondrous concentration of the immeasurably profound *dharmatā* and is likewise able to preach the Dharma.

Thus, within this introductory chapter, it is stated that [the Buddha] is able to walk and stand; for this reason, within this very chapter, he rises from his seat and pays homage to this stūpa with reverence.

Having respectfully circumambulated [the Buddha], they returned to their original seats; from this it is known that while the Wheel of Speech preaches the Dharma and the Body-Wheel manifests supernatural powers—arising, sitting, departing, and returning—there is no obstruction to the profound nature of reality (*dharmatā*) or wondrous meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Up until the "Chapter Praising the Buddha," the tree deity requests, saying:

"I only pray that the World-Honored One will manifest his body for me. It is only then that the Tathāgata arises from *samādhi*; thus we know that prior to this, [he remained in meditative absorption].

The seven chapters of this sutra are all situated within meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Regarding the fourth explanation, concerning the tree deity’s inquiry on the manner of salutation, the term "World Hero" (*lokanātha*) refers to the Great Master;

this has already been explained previously (etc.). Regarding the fifth explanation, the Tathāgata’s response to the salutation. Regarding the sixth explanation, the command to Ānanda to take [the bowl], it says:
"This is indeed the immeasurable six *pāramitās*," because from the initial generation of the mind of awakening, one practices the six perfections to gather in the assembly.
At the time of birth, there are five distinctions, namely: humans, devas, and those of the four teachings;

since all practices are none other than the conduct cultivated by Bodhisattvas, there are four lands that horizontally and vertically encompass sentient beings, and thus they are called "immeasurable.
Furthermore, because each of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) possesses all six, they are called "immeasurable"; this is precisely what is meant by adorning with the five.
From *dāna* (generosity) up to the fifth [perfection], when these are adorned by wisdom (*prajñā*), they are collectively described as being "endowed with the six.

This is the case for all the Mahāyāna sūtras, such as the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*; the six perfections are all thus explained. Seventh, the explanation of Ānanda describing the physical form of the bones.

Eighth, the explanation of the life-span and the showing to the great assembly. Since the scriptural text already states that [the bones] were "brought forth," is this not intended to show them to the great assembly? Ninth.
Śāriputra Ānanda, having received the command, took it up to show it; "taking up" means to lift. He held the casket before the Buddha, which was to present it to the great assembly.

(10) The tenth [section] explains how the Tathāgata exhorted them to pay homage to the field: the meaning of "field" is that of a source of birth. One pays homage to these śarīras because they can preside over pure merit;
therefore, they are called the "Field of Merit."

Next, the explanation of the passage on the "correct relinquishment of the body" is divided into two parts: first, the analysis of the textual structure; second, from "First, clarifying the basis" onwards, the word-by-word commentary, which is further divided into two sections.
First, the explanation of the main prose section is divided into four parts.
The initial explanation of the text on the primary retinue is divided into five parts.

Regarding the first part, regarding the two characters "not detailed" (未詳) in the commentary following "Dàdù" (大度), Mount Gushan states that they were added arbitrarily by later generations. I, however, say this is not so;

for how could it be that whenever there is a note stating "not detailed" in various texts, it is all an arbitrary addition by later people? One should know that the notes stating "not detailed" in the present text are merely...
One should not doubt the meaning of the translation, for it was not arbitrarily added by later generations. The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* (The King of Sutras) states: "The king was named Mahāratha;
his son was named Śūra, whose mind was always intent on giving without stinginess. The prince had two elder brothers named Mahānagna and Puruṣa.

Therefore, while one Buddha acts as the praiser, he simultaneously becomes the praised object for the three successive assemblies of bodhisattvas; this is precisely how it should be understood.

the meaning of the passage is self-evident, so why do you fail to see it and instead fabricate false explanations? As for "the one who can entreat," this refers to what the sutra says:

therefore the Buddha praised them, saying, "Excellent is this speech! "Excellent" (*kaṣṭa*) refers to that which accords with the mind—that which is delightful and acceptable.

thus the commentary says "and so forth.
Next, the analysis of the text is divided into two parts. In the initial question, it says "entering meditative absorption and samādhi"; the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary) cites the *Mahā-*.

In Sanskrit, *samādhi* is translated here as "concentration" (*ding*). Therefore, in the present text, entering [the state] is termed "concentration," while arising from it is termed "*samādhi*";
these are merely variations in phrasing appearing alternately. Next, regarding the meaning of the response: in the initial *Parivarta*, he dwelt in...

The immeasurable and profoundly deep *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) is precisely what constitutes entry into meditative concentration (*samādhi*), for it is because the *dharmatā* is quiescent that it is termed "concentration.

"The Pratyekabuddhas are not of a measure that can be gauged, and even the Great Sages and Bodhisattvas cannot fathom them. I only pray that the Tathāgata will take pity on me, constantly allowing me to behold the body of Great Compassion.

thus it says, "if one enters the dharma-nature. Regarding "sovereignty over the dharma-nature": the dharma-nature is quiescent and unchanging, and the King of Sutras exercises sovereign control over it.
Since the dharma-nature is itself the King of Sutras, it is called "sovereign. Therefore, the preceding text speaks of "the principle of the dharma-nature."

Because this text elucidates the principle protected by the Buddha’s mindfulness, it is called the "King of Sutras. As for the statement that it is the "King of Sutras," the wisdom praises its essence as being the five Buddhas:
the four Buddhas of the East, such as Akṣobhya, together with Śākyamuni Tathāgata, constitute these five Buddhas.

Regarding their "dwelling in the same place," because their essence is identical and their characteristics are mutually inclusive, the four Buddhas occupy a single location, which all sentient beings perceive together.
Furthermore, because they differ and because their locations are distinct, sentient beings perceive four Buddhas or five Buddhas each in their respective places.
Moreover, the preceding text states: "If one sees the four Buddhas as having the same *viśeṣa-ātmabhāva* (exalted body), being a single body and a single wisdom, this is the eternal body.
Since the assembly of disciples is one, how could it not be that in the present text, the four Buddhas and five Buddhas occupy the same location and assembly?
That they are born together and see one another is primarily because they all rely upon the Dharma-nature body (dharmatā-kāya) outside the realms;

therefore, it is called "dwelling in the same place and seeing together. Furthermore, it is said that if one sees four Buddhas, their Buddha-bodies are not identical, as there are many disciples who are responsive transformations (nirmāṇa).
Is this not precisely what is meant in the present text by the various places and different visions of sentient beings regarding the four or five Buddhas?
This is because they all pertain to the *paricchinna-śarīra* (segmental body) within the realm; therefore, it is called "distinct views in various locations.
As the *Vimalakīrti-sūtra-vyākhyā* states: "different substances and different views," and so forth. Regarding "four comings and four goings":
this refers to the coming of the four Buddhas of the four directions due to the arising of conditions, while the single Buddha Śākyamuni dwells in the four directions of Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa at Rājagṛha.

Because the Buddha’s karmic momentum has ceased, he has departed; yet because the conditions for Śākyamuni Buddha have not yet ceased, he still remains within the city of Rājagṛha and inside Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.

Therefore, it is said that according to what each person perceives, there are no obstacles whatsoever. This is because the essence of *dharmatā* is sovereign.
This is because they are identical in their common characteristics.
Third, the explanation of the text by way of contemplating the mind is divided into three parts. First, the direct clarification states: "The three karmas of the bodhisattvas are as follows:

prostrating with the five limbs is the karma of the body; speaking with one voice is the karma of speech; and when both body and speech together accord with the intention, that is the karma of the mind. Thus, there are three.

This merely clarifies the matters of the three karmas. Regarding "next, the contemplation of the mind through the three karmas":

"The six dharmas of phenomena and principle. Here, "dharma" refers to the dharma of contemplation. Regarding the "six dharmas of phenomena and principle," there are six for both phenomena (*shi*) and principle (*li*).
Regarding the six dharmas of phenomena (*dharma*), those who practice them possess three types of action (*karman*) for both the one who praises and the object praised.

Regarding the six dharmas of principle (*li*), since observing one's own three actions is itself the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*), how could it not be the same when observing the three actions of the Buddha? Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says:
"Observe the true mark of the body; observe the Buddha in the same way. Since this is so for the body, one may infer that it applies likewise to speech and mind. Furthermore:
